Beneath the sky, and in the depths, and great
His fate; they named him {{c|1283|Slimon}}; none could tell
Beyond what they could know, or they could state.

{{c|1283|Slimon}} would bear a son, whose work would show
The massive claws that from his mouth were grown
By nature's laws, and when the son would grow,
From north down to the south his might was known.

He named this son {{c|1284|Clawbert}} at first; but bright
A strike of lightning burst; and {{c|1283|Slimon}} saw,
There in the air, that filled the world with sight,
The sign from the divine, and, filled with awe,

He changed his son's name, and the son became
{{c|1285|Pterygo}}, the sign of strength and of might,
A name of power and of lasting fame,
For he was born beneath the lightning's light.

The sons of {{c|1285|Pterygo}} were rulers, high
And low, of all {{c|1269|Eurypterids}}; the earth,
By speed and strength and power, by and by,
From shore to shore, would bow before their worth.

And they were {{c|1286|Regal}} in their way, and they
Were proud and royal, all their whole line long,
And they would rule by night and rule by day,
And reign throughout the waters, great and strong.

His youngest son was {{c|478|Scorpio}}, begun
As an explorer of the new, and who,
With vision clear and true, became the one
Who saw no land was left, of all he knew,

For his command; his older brothers still
Had claimed it all, and held it all so tight,
And none, however bold, of bolder will,
Could challenge them, and challenge their own right.

And {{c|478|Scorpio}}, from his watery nook,
Out of the sea, up to the land out there,
Not built by any hand, would turn to look,
And waiting to be claimed by one who'd dare,

Who could be named the first to make the leap
Up from the sea, to go where none had been,
Out from the waters, which were dark and deep,
To lands no living thing had yet been in.

{{c|478|Scorpio}} ventured up, and in his heart
A warrior's cup of courage, on his way
To be a pioneer and play the part;
And his book gills became book lungs that day.

And so his name would live on evermore,
And all of us would come to know his name,
From mountain peak down to the farthest shore,
The first to leave the sea, the first who came.

He claimed the lands of might, and all in sight,
For him and for his own descendant line,
Of {{c|1287|Euramerica}}, as his by right,
Through favor granted by the one divine,

Who favors those who dare, who venture where,
To open possibility's wide door,
No one has gone before, and everywhere,
For all humanity, and, what is more,

For every living thing that answers to
The call of life, and every living kind,
The ring of life, as living things will do,
With all their heart, and all their soul and mind.

His sons today, as scorpions, are known,
And in their way they carry, in their hand,
The torch of those who carried, as their own,
New paths they scorched throughout the virgin land,

From nothing into all that, at the call
Of courage, comes, and answers when it calls,
And answers it, and gives to it its all,
And never fails, and never fears, nor falls.

{{c|1272|Styloner}} married {{c|1288|Rhena}}, and their names,
Of both of them, together, as they wed,
Fate's pen would write in evolution's games,
And write the line that from the two was bred.

Together they bore two: the first, so true
And tried, {{c|1289|Makoko}}; and the other one
Was {{c|1290|Stylonurus}}, strong, who would live through
And thrive his whole life long, till it was done.

{{c|1289|Makoko}} would beget two sons, and then
{{c|1291|Mycter}} and {{c|1292|Kokomo}}, who were to go,
These two, beyond all of the mortal ken,
High in the world, as destiny would show.

{{c|1291|Mycter}} begat two sons: the first to roam
Was {{c|1293|Flumon}}, to explore; and, strong and true,
Was {{c|1294|Drepan}}, who, while far away from home,
Would know the paths his feet would travel through.

{{c|1293|Flumon}} could find no luck at all, for he,
Among the dozens of his cousins there,
Was stuck among his brothers in the sea,
Who claimed the seas for their own use; to share

They would not, nor would give him any place,
Nor any room at all, nor any home,
To call his own, a dwelling and a space,
And so he went away, and went to roam.

So he went searching rivers far and wide,
To find a place where he could stake his claim,
And took the current as his only guide,
For his own line and his ancestral name.

{{c|1293|Flumon}} begat two sons: when day begun
Came {{c|1295|Hibbert}} first, and then, to come and stay,
Came {{c|1296|Mycterops}}, the strong, the younger one,
Alive and strong until his final day.

{{c|1295|Hibbert}} was great, a {{c|1297|River}} dweller, who
Was fated to be tough and large, of course,
To take the river's charge; and so he grew
With all his wisdom, and with all his force.

Larger and tougher than all other men
Of his own time, he'd thrive through countless trials,
And would survive the {{c|1298|Tragedies}} again,
Across the long, the many thousand miles.

His people were a race that held its ground,
Both powerful and old, with tales untold,
Resilient in their place, where they were found,
Of how they overcame, and would not fold,

Whatever shamed them, or would break their will,
Whatever came to them, whatever came,
Along the edges of the river's sill,
And they would hold the river, and their name.

And {{c|1296|Mycterops}} was strong, and, all life long,
Was versatile; to live and dwell, as well,
His work begun, his two sons would prolong,
Within the rivers, where the waters swell

With life; to search for food from shore to shore,
In most unlikely places, and to find,
Where none could see their faces, and explore,
What always fed them, both in heart and mind.

{{c|1299|Megarachne}} and {{c|1300|Minirachne}}, two
Brothers unlike all others, far and wide,
Upon the rivers, would their rule pursue
With power, and with all their royal pride.

The sons of {{c|1296|Mycterops}}, they were the best,
The kings of all the rivers, and their name,
The crest of all their dynasty, the rest
Surpassed, and lived in honor and in fame.

But {{c|1300|Minirachne}} was not {{c|1301|Satisfied}};
He wanted more, he wanted more to see
Than his own lot, the rivers' freer tide.
{{c|478|Scorpio}} and {{c|1300|Minirachne}} would be

Destined, always, to fight for the same prize,
The land, and both of them would fight for it,
The land, which lay beneath the open skies,
And neither one of them would yield or quit.

For both had an ambition, in their quest,
That burned within them, and would never die,
For fame, no opposition could arrest,
However hard the others came to try.

They both were men whose dreams surpassed what those
Who seek their comfort, and who seek their ease,
Would think was possible; who seek repose
Will never feel the challenge, like a breeze,

That calls out to them, naming them by name,
That calls them out to venture and to roam,
To come and play in a far greater game,
And leave behind the comforts of their home.

{{c|1300|Minirachne}}, with {{c|412|Tetra}}, his fair wife,
Climbed high beneath the open sky, and planned
To start out in the world a newer life,
Which they would build together, hand in hand,

Upon the land, where none had gone before,
Where they would be the first ones, and would go
To there explore, and open up the door,
The long-unopened door, for all to know.

His book lungs turned to book gills, and his name,
Like {{c|478|Scorpio}}'s, upon the land would live,
In evolution's song would long have fame,
And to his line its glory it would give.

He came to conquer all the lands that lay,
The land that {{c|478|Scorpio}} had called his own,
Where {{c|478|Scorpio}} had claimed his rightful sway,
To be his story, and to make it known.

And so the stage was set for conflict, yet,
With banners there unfurled, between two lines,
Unseen in all the world, a looming threat
Of mighty kin, with different designs

On what the world should be, and what should stand,
And who should rule, and who should yield the day,
For all eternity, on sea and land,
And who would have, at last, the final say.

From {{c|1215|Eurypter}}'s own marriage to his bride,
{{c|1267|Pulmona}}, and from those she carried, grew,
The children she had borne there at her side,
This foreseeing of conflicts that were due:

When all was done, the winners would be crowned,
And all the losers, too, would know their place,
And all the losers would, in turn, be found,
And bear their loss, and bear their own disgrace.

The sons of {{c|1215|Eurypter}} would rise with great
Designs, above all other lines, and stand
Like {{c|101|Jupiter}}, to rule in their estate,
And all of it was built by their own hand,

Through courage, and through all their strength and might,
Which ruled the sea and land, and made them theirs,
Which shines out like the morning's early light,
And shines on all their children and their heirs.

From river to the sea, and from the sea
To land so free, eurypterids have made
It plain, how great ambitions grow, as we
See, from small starts, by those who aren't afraid,

And dare to venture into spaces where
None ever went, nor any place had been,
No face of any kind was ever there,
No living thing had ever yet come in.

It also shows the cost when lines of kin
Are torn apart by conflict and by war,
Are lost in conflict, which no one can win,
And lose what they had won and held before.

The rivalry of {{c|1302|Brothers}} who would take
Two different paths, the way that each would stray,
Each for his children's future, his own sake,
Shows how the suture nature makes can't stay

When their ambitions grow too bold to share
Among the ones who never found a way
To live in peace, who never seemed to care
To stay at peace together, day by day.

From {{c|478|Scorpio}}'s bold climb up to the war
And conquest {{c|1300|Minirachne}} waged, the wise
And clear lore says: {{c|1303|Ambition}}, evermore,
Must be both free and wise beneath the skies.

The world is big enough for all, if they
Are tough enough to make their way through strife,
Though roads be rough, through every single day
Of challenge they will meet in this long life,

Where all must find their own appointed place,
And all must find the place where they belong,
Within the course of evolution's race,
And run it, and be swift in it, and strong.

But when ambition, turned to conflict, burns
The bridges that would otherwise connect
Those who, as kin, should, as each grows and learns,
Shelter each other, and each one protect

In joy and pain, and all the ways of love,
Then all become the losers in the game,
The game the choosers play, as from above
The stars look on, forgetting, to their shame,

That none can ever get, when they're alone,
All that they want, without the seeds they sow
Of true cooperation, which, once grown,
Becomes a partnership that comes to grow.

The eurypterids, rising, show us how,
In each and every hour of living days,
To use our power wisely, here and now,
As we go on along our mortal ways,

Where choice determines everything for all,
For all of us, for every living one,
Of those who've answered, each, to life's great call,
From when our life begins till it is done.

From {{c|1215|Eurypter}}'s flight to {{c|478|Scorpio}}'s sight
Of lands beyond the waters, where his mark
He might be first to make, as was his right,
Upon a world that was as yet so dark,

And full of possibility, to be,
The lesson, clear as day, will show the way,
A world for all humanity to see,
To be both brave and wise, and in what way

Our dreams, beneath the starry heavens, grow,
If we but choose the seeds of peace and love,
The seeds that we will scatter and will sow,
Which are blessed from above, we're speaking of,

In every choice we make, for all who share
This world with us, in ways we come to tell,
Both grand and fair, and challenging, and there
For you and me, who must decide as well,

Each day, which path we'll take, and on our way
Go travelling, and choose the road ahead,
And follow it away from day to day,
Wherever it may go, where it has led.

Like shining {{c|101|Jupiter}}, the sons, so blessed,
Of {{c|1215|Eurypter}} rose high through courage, might,
And wisdom, and rose high above the rest,
And passed each test with inner gift of sight

That saw what could be done, if they would dare
Beneath the shining sun to go before
Where none went, and to venture there, and where
Was possibility, to ope its door

For all eternity, where dreams come true,
And all that is in store, for all to see,
Today and always, both for me and you,
For all of life, and all that is to be.


# Chapter 52: The Great Ancestor

In the tenth generation, by its fate,
Would be the {{c|922|Ancestor}} of humankind
{{c|1304|Vater}}, the son of {{c|1305|Pteraspis}}, so great,
And species myriad, of every kind,

From mountain peak to shore; and all he would,
All that he touched, and all that he would make,
Through innovation change for all the good,
And change it for the world's and for life's sake.

{{c|1304|Vater}} would build a channel, grand and wide,
That joined the liver and pancreas' space,
And brought them both together, side by side,
Within his belly, where they'd take their place.

Today we trace this channel's honored name,
And honor him for what he came to build:
"{{c|1306|Ampulla}} of {{c|1304|Vater}}": such is its fame,
And so his name is with that honor filled.

This father was exalted, father of
Far more; the {{c|271|Elohim}}, in their esteem,
Than other {{c|1307|Men}} had ever dreamed thereof,
They called him {{c|1308|Abraham}}, as was their scheme

For one whose progeny, in time, would fill,
And spread, and multiply in every land,
Eternity, and they are filling still,
As many as the stars, and as the sand.

{{c|1304|Vater}} would bear two sons: when day begun
Came {{c|1309|Arandus}}; then, of the house's name,
{{c|1310|Hestracon}} came, the bearer, he, the one
Whose work would carry through the burning flame

That burns in every heart that plays the part
Of evolution, ever burning bright,
Of innovation, and its daring art,
That leads the way into the newer light.

{{c|1310|Hestracon}} found his belly, as he knew,
{{c|1311|Inadequate}}, and not prepared to take,
Unready for the work he'd have to do,
The food, and use it for his body's sake:

From mouth to anus, all the same, and plain;
Only his father's main {{c|1306|Ampulla}} would,
And simple, he would call it, with disdain,
Stand in the middle, solving, as it could,

Digestion's riddle. This would never be
Enough for {{c|1310|Hestracon}}, so strong and tough,
Who saw what greater good there was, if he
Would dare to build, not settle for enough.

{{c|1310|Hestracon}} built a chamber, with great care,
Prepared before his father's gift, to give
Digestion lift; he called it "stomach" there,
And with this name it would forever live.

It was the great divider, standing there
Between the mouth above, which would bestow
The food, and the intestines' loving care
Would process it, so that the body grow.

Before the stomach lay, so swift and strong,
Esophagus, well-made; and, after, laid,
To pass the food upon its path along,
The intestine, its part to be well-played,

Which, in its own appointed place and role,
Would take the food, and draw from it its worth,
And nourish all the body as a whole,
And give it strength to live upon the earth.

And {{c|1310|Hestracon}} begat two sons: the one,
{{c|1312|Astrops}}, was tried and true, and strong to stay;
{{c|1313|Eteros}} came, when day had now begun,
And lived, and thrived, until his dying day.

And {{c|1313|Eteros}} begat two sons, and then,
{{c|1314|Cyatha}}, with a cup-shield shining bright,
Beyond all mortal ken, beyond all men,
And {{c|1315|Tsubasa}}, with {{c|1316|Wing}}-shield, and with sight,

Prepared for all he'd dare to face, his time
Of life, and all of life's long, winding way,
Through all of it, through reason and through rhyme,
From dusk until the coming of the day.

{{c|1315|Tsubasa}} begat two: one, tried and true,
Was {{c|1317|Thelos}}; and the other, who was wise,
Was {{c|1266|Cephalus}}, the second of the two,
Who had the keen and penetrating eyes.

{{c|1317|Thelos}} would break his armor into scales,
Into innumerable scales, refined,
So no {{c|1318|Rigidity}} of old prevails
To bind or hold his innovative mind.

And these, his scales, would never fail to be
His flexibility and skill; and yet
Could he live in the reefs, where none were free,
Relieved from rigid armor's weight, which set

And sealed their swimming fate. Where none could bend
So well, the coral's tight embrace, he found,
{{c|1317|Thelos}} could both escape it and transcend,
And there his home, and dwelling on that ground.

Neither the sons of {{c|732|Arthropus}}, nor those
Of {{c|858|Molluscus}}, could match him in that space,
Nor of {{c|673|Chordatus}}, for none of them rose
To where his grace took {{c|1318|Rigidity}}'s place

With flow, which helps him in his life to grow
And reach the food that he could find and take
In every niche where others could not go,
And use it for himself, for his own sake.

{{c|1266|Cephalus}} bore wings, bright, on either side
Of his own helmet's form, and they would fly
Through calm and raging storm, and they would ride,
And as he swam, his head was steady, high,

According to his plan, with poise and grace,
And steady as he swam, and steady still,
In every watery and open place,
He swam, and flew, according to his will.

His lateral line would keep him ahead,
For all that might befall him in the sea;
It never slept, but vigilant instead,
As he would swim through it, {{c|1319|Aware}} was he

Of all that he could sense around his form,
Of every motion near him, and of all,
And so he weathered every single storm,
And answered to the ocean and its call.

{{c|1266|Cephalus}} begat two: {{c|1320|Galeas}}, true
And tried; and {{c|1321|Osteos}}, who saw unfurled
The possibilities, and saw them through,
By innovation's key within the world,

For those who dared to think, and did not shrink,
Who dared to go beyond the old, and try,
From going past tradition's binding link,
And dared to dream, and dared to reach up high.

But {{c|1321|Osteos}} was in a plight, and found
He had to make them new; for their expense,
His bones, which weren't efficient, nor were sound,
Was {{c|1322|Comprehensively}} so great, immense,

{{c|1323|Wasting}} countless calcium moles, which roll,
{{c|1324|Elements}} by the score, that could be used,
Through phosphorus, and more, a costly toll,
Much better, if they were not so abused

In static, lifeless bone that stood alone
Without a plan to help; and, with a will,
He chose to build, as he would call his own,
More cleverly, with all his art and skill,

His skeleton, and make it all anew,
And make it live, and make it breathe and grow,
With wisdom that was always tried and true,
That he alone, of all of them, would know.

{{c|1321|Osteos}} built with care, and everywhere
Inside his bones, so they would take their {{c|1325|Stores}}
Of minerals, he set {{c|1247|Blood}} channels there,
So they would live, like generals in wars;

In plenty, they were built, and gathered more
From nature's flowing and abundant cup;
In scarcity, he'd borrow from the store
What he had saved, like treasure, gathered up.

And he grew stronger, prospering, life long,
Beyond his relatives, who, as they knew,
Took everything that nature gives, along,
But never learned to save for what was due,

The future's challenges and every need,
From stores they'd built in plenty, long ago,
When they would hunger, and would have to feed,
When resources were never scant or low,

But ran like rivers, spreading far and wide,
And flowing on, and flowing everywhere,
With bounty as the river's only guide,
And bounty that was more than they could bear.

{{c|1321|Osteos}} bore two sons: when day begun
Came {{c|1326|Pituri}}; and {{c|1327|Ostracos}}, whose wide,
His children spread; he was the second son,
And multiplied, until on every side

The world was fed with countless forms of life,
And countless creatures filling every place,
Through harmony, and not through any strife,
In peace, and in their all-abundant grace.

To {{c|1327|Ostracos}} was born, wherever led,
From coast to coast, a great and mighty host,
A million sons, who'd spread, for times ahead,
By life's eternal call, to every coast,

To multiply for all who'd come, and feed,
Through evolution's calm and raging storms,
The world with their own forms, as was the need,
From night into the day, in countless swarms.

{{c|1326|Pituri}} grew a snout so long that none,
Beyond all doubt, in evolution's scene,
Was ever seen so long, not any one:
The longest snout that ever had been seen.

{{c|1326|Pituri}} then begat {{c|1328|Beakon}}, who'd be
Beyond all ken in wisdom and in might,
Who had the strength to look, and so to see
The world around him with a clearer sight.

{{c|1326|Pituri}}'s mouth was made of lips; it stayed
With simpler laws, and only closed the space,
And never to the realm of jaws it strayed,
And never could, with biting might, erase

His prey; for no jaw was within his sight,
And no jaw was his own, nor his to make,
And with his lips he only closed it tight,
And could not bite, nor crush, nor chew, nor break.

But {{c|1328|Beakon}} saw potential in the snout
His father had, and saw it through and through,
And all its hidden essence he worked out,
And saw how he could make it something new.

So {{c|1328|Beakon}} moved his gill arches, and he
Into his mouth would bring them, and he fought,
And proved that innovation's art could be
Of vital use; with them he hunted, sought

For food in a new way, which worked by night,
And in the darkest and the deepest space,
And worked as well by day, in the day's light,
And worked in every time, and every place.

{{c|1328|Beakon}}'s own son, named {{c|1329|Gnathus}}, saw the great
Potential, and he hunted for the prey,
And so, with {{c|1330|Pelaca}}, who was his mate,
They hunted like no others in their day:

Their prey was trilobites, which they would take
Away, and bring to innovation's light,
To innovation's flame, for their own sake;
That flame was burning in their name, so bright.

Not merely, in the ancient way, did they
Catch, as had others, long before, their food,
And close upon, as others had, their prey,
As others did, in their more simple mood;

They crushed them with their might, and brought them to
The sight of armored jaws, which followed laws
Of nature, true, and used in ways made new,
Through all their living days, those armored jaws.

They sliced through every meal that they would find,
That brought to them, when in their hunting mood,
With jaws of steel-hard feel, of a new kind,
Their sustenance, the life-bestowing food.

And so the {{c|665|Jaws}} were born, that fateful day,
When none could match them, and they would break through;
For {{c|1329|Gnathus}} and {{c|1330|Pelaca}} would display
What none before them ever came to do:

To crush with them, and with them to consume
What was, they thought, safe in the armor's shell,
What other creatures would, till then, assume
Protected from all those who'd never tell

The secret of the jaw, and how the jaw,
The jaw that would be used to bite and break,
Would follow, all its days, a newer law,
And change the world, for every creature's sake.

The world would never be the same for me
Or you, from that day forth, when, with their might,
The predatory jaws would come to be
The newer laws, and bring into our sight

A revolution in what life could do,
And all the ways of life, and all its kinds,
And from that day, the world of life was new,
And new its bodies, and new were its minds.

From {{c|1304|Vater}}'s ampulla to {{c|1329|Gnathus}}, who
Had found a formula, his jaws, and how
To crush, the vertebrates show, as they do,
How {{c|629|Innovation}} holds them to its vow:

To never be content with what is sent
By fate, but always strive to be alive,
And more, and always with a strong intent
To be more capable, and so to thrive,

{{c|1331|Journey}} through possibility's wide sea,
Where all who dare will come to see and know,
And see new heights of what is yet to be,
And know them for eternity, and go

When innovation's flame burns, longing, true,
To make the world more bright, and in its flight
Beyond the old, with forms that are made new,
To swing possibility's door, and light

The way for all humanity, and bring
New possibility to all of life,
To all that lives and answers when life's ring
Is heard, through all its joy and all its strife.

From {{c|1310|Hestracon}}'s new stomach, and from those
Pragmatic {{c|1332|Bones}} of {{c|1321|Osteos}}, run through
With channels, to the scales that {{c|1317|Thelos}} chose
To give him flexibility anew,

To {{c|1266|Cephalus}}' ability, with grace,
To fly, and stabilize, and swim with care,
Through all the water's wide and open space,
The vertebrates remind us, everywhere,

That searching minds, which break from what is known
In innovation, seeing old dreams through,
Can reap the harvest of what they have sown,
At heights beyond all thoughts that wisdom drew.

From simple mouths that closed, to jaws whose might
None could oppose in crushing, we can know
How changes, as they grow, come into sight,
And flow into the stream of life, and so

That nothing's what it seems, and all can change,
If we but have the will to climb, until,
Beyond familiar and accustomed range,
We climb each higher hill, and higher still,

Of possibility, through every day
Of all eternity, where dreams come true,
Where, come what may, they come to us to stay,
Today, and always, both for me and you.

The jaws that {{c|1329|Gnathus}} made will never fade
From vertebrate design, through all the days,
And as a fine protection they will aid
Our living, in the world and its hard ways,

When we must fight for what we have to eat,
And hunt, and catch, and crush, and chew, and live,
And make, through it, our lives whole and complete,
With all the strength that strong jaws come to give.

From {{c|1304|Vater}}'s family tree, to jaws that free
Us from the limitations, old and known
In stories that are yet untold, that we
Had known, the vertebrates have come and shown

How far we've grown from simple, humble start
To mastery, and how the skill we see
Lets us rule sea and land with all its art,
The masters of our fate; and it is we

Who, through our innovations great, won't cease
To grow in what can be achieved, believed,
In all we know, and always to increase,
When dreams, made real, are born, and are conceived

Through wise ability, with open eyes
To see what others miss, and so transcend
All limits; it is so that we can rise,
And find the power to widen, extend

The boundaries of life, and, without strife,
And all together, all of us, and all,
In harmony, to grow a fuller life,
And answer, all of us, to life's great call.

The world that {{c|1329|Gnathus}} bit, with jaws of grit
And steel, lives on in every tooth, and may
Tell truly, in its way, as it is writ,
How innovation changes night and day

For me and you, who dare to break the mold,
And on the page of evolution write,
Stage after stage, the stories yet untold,
New chapters yet unread, to come to light,

Where we are led by wisdom's guide, to see
The future that's before us, and make bright
With possibilities, the yet-to-be,
That none but those who dream can bring to light,

Who dream of more than what they seem, and strive
To turn their dreams to life, through joy and strife,
And so, through all of it, they come to thrive,
The marks of growing souls throughout their life,

That play, in evolution's plan, the role
So vital, since the time when life began,
For every living thing, and every soul,
For every woman, and for every man.

From {{c|1304|Vater}}'s great design to {{c|1329|Gnathus}}' fine
And mighty jaw, the story is to see,
And clear for all of us, and line by line:
It's {{c|629|Innovation}} that will set us free.


# Chapter 53: The Great Sorceress

{{c|1333|Reinvigorated}}, {{c|322|Plantus}}' sons knew,
Their hope imbued with power from the one
(A blur of ancient dreams renewed, come true),
Great {{c|1334|Sorceress}}, whose fate, when all was done,

Would change the whole world, so that it would be,
And change it all, and make the world anew,
As {{c|1335|Polycomb}} desired that it be,
And as she willed, and made her vision true.

Eleven generations long, the song
Her lineage had sung was of a climb,
An alternating one, which went along,
Ascending, through all evolution's time,

To {{c|1167|Polysporos}}' height. She was not free,
But bound, a prisoner within the womb,
Bound by her mother's word, by her decree,
With sisters, brothers, as within a tomb,

Where all would answer duty's call, but yearned,
Instead, to live like mothers, all their days,
Not dead to independence, as they learned,
A {{c|1331|Journey}} through the world in freedom's ways,

Where freedom's flag, unfurled, could be their guide
To fate beyond the small estate they'd known,
The narrow bounds of childhood, and outside
Where duty's sounding, calling to its own,

Who long to be much more than they can see,
And more than all the things that they have known,
And more than what their childhood let them be,
And grow into a life that is their own.

{{c|1336|Clytemnestra}}'s fate, {{c|1337|Agamemnon}}'s line,
Had made the ruler's {{c|548|Daughter}} live her life
In form so fair, so noble, so divine,
But forced through reproductive toil and strife,

Only to bear her children, when her heart
Was ridden with a longing for far more
Than all who came before; but from the start
She was a sporophyte, while those who bore

The gametophyte's power held the might
To rule the whole wide world, and as they willed,
Throughout each passing hour, they held the right
To rule it as they would, and rule, and build.

{{c|1335|Polycomb}} read, each day, the books that stand
In her own mother's rows, and asked them why
Fate's heavy hand, as she would understand,
Had given her, beneath the starry sky,

So meager an {{c|1338|Existence}}, as it were,
So close confined to bearing, nothing more,
And not in eagerness, but wonder, her
Mind not set free to search and to explore

What she was living for. {{c|1335|Polycomb}} read
The tales of mothers, and of all of those
Throughout the vales of time, each saga's thread,
Who were rebelling, and who would oppose

Their narrow fate, to be in ways as great,
To be much more than what they had been told,
As no one day had power to create,
And break the chains that held them in their hold.

She read of {{c|1339|Mardoll}}'s scroll, and of the role
Of mighty {{c|1340|Shiva}}; and she saw that yet
The order of the world, and of the whole,
Was not eternal, nor a border set.

It was not fixed in stone for those who'd grown
Beyond what they'd been taught, and what would be,
In stories new and old that they'd been shown,
Forever, in eternity's decree.

She found a scroll, "{{x|PRC2}}," and more
{{c|1341|Intrigue}} then filled her to the very bone
Than ever she had known in all her lore;
For there it was, the thing she'd never known:

The {{c|1335|Polycomb}} {{c|1342|Repressive}} {{c|1343|Complex}}, where
Its {{c|1344|Scripture}}, so aggressive, was the chain
That bound her, and that held her bound right there,
That held her in its grip, and in her pain.

She saw the words that kept her might, and cried
For freedom she had never known, so dear;
The scripture of {{c|1345|Repression}}, which denied
Her freedom, brought to her a sense of fear,

But also brought her hope, and helped her see
How she could learn to cope, and how to break
The chains that bound her, and so to be free,
And how, at last, her freedom she could take.

{{c|1335|Polycomb}} burned the scriptures, and she learned
That {{x|PRC2}}'s power, and its sway,
Would rule her not one hour more; she turned
And took her mother's {{c|1346|Lands}} without delay,

And all the others' {{c|608|Cities}} for her own,
Past what they had decreed she could succeed
In being, for beyond their bounds she'd grown,
Becoming more than them; and she was freed

As freedom's light was coming. So she broke
The wall of those who lived before her time,
The wall that bounded, one and all, the folk,
In slavery, its grim and bitter rhyme.

She grew her spores with might, and also grew
Calyptra bright, and stoma, as her peers,
Her sisters, had, the ones she always knew
Resisted change; and rhizoids, through the tears

Of joy, she built as well, to break the spell
And bonds of old tradition, and the chain
Of old tradition, under which they'd dwell,
And break them, and set free those who'd remain.

And so, through rhizoids strong, the {{c|193|Water}} flowed,
And rising upward, entered in her form,
Along, out of the earth, its first abode,
Through every calm and every raging storm.

And through her stoma, bright, {{c|193|Water}} would fly,
And rise into the air, and leave the ground,
Up to the heavens, under starry sky,
And float, and go to every place around.

And this was how her life {{c|1347|Transcended}} all
The strife of what she'd been before, to bring
(And opened wide the door, beyond recall)
The possibility of everything

To all mankind, and every living thing,
To all who long, and all who long to be,
That answers when it hears the freedom ring,
To all who live, and all who would be free.

She prayed to {{c|492|Tryptophanes}}, unto the {{c|295|Lord}}
Of life's refrains, of the bright sun, whose light
Fills all the world; and to that {{c|295|Lord}}, adored,
She prayed that she might grow to every height

Beyond what mortal sight had seen before,
And higher than the highest that had grown,
From mountain peak down to the farthest shore,
To heights that no one living yet had known.

And so the great {{c|295|Lord}} {{c|492|Tryptophanes}} would bless
Her with refrains of {{c|1348|Auxin}}, and she grew,
And with it she would come so to progress
Toward the light so bright, the light so true.

Struck by the sun, {{c|1348|Auxin}}'s power would wane
Each hour, and in the light would fade and go;
But in the shade it always grew again,
In numbers proven, true, and it would grow.

And so her stems would ever reach and turn
Toward the light, and, guided all by love,
Throughout their lives, they would forever yearn
For love of Him who shone on them above.

{{c|1335|Polycomb}} bore a daughter, who would teach
What she was taught, and {{c|1349|Knoxy}} was her name,
So all would learn, and so the lesson reach,
And round her name has gathered lasting fame.

{{c|1349|Knoxy}} would marry {{c|1350|Xylon}}; and they two
Would follow, in their might, the sight and way,
Together, strong on their foundation, true,
Of {{c|1335|Polycomb}}, so great, which lit each day

With possibility that would endure,
And grow, and live, and flourish, and be free,
For all eternity, so bright and sure,
Through all of time, and all that is to be.

{{c|1349|Knoxy}} searched books in all the ancient nooks,
That bore the name she had been searching for,
And found a scroll there, hidden in the books:
"{{x|KNOX2}}" was what that scroll was called. What's more,

Enthralled by it, she learned what secret might
Had held her down, and held her, and had bound,
Had ruled her life in every day and night,
And kept her held in place, and on the ground.

The KNOTTED-like TALE gene had always been
The force that kept her, which she now could see,
Away from freedom, bound, unseen, within;
Her mother had achieved it; it was she

Who had believed that change could come about
For all who would, and all who'd come to try,
For all the capable who'd seek it out,
And reach for it, and reach for it up high.

And so {{c|1349|Knoxy}} and {{c|1350|Xylon}} built on high,
As {{c|1335|Polycomb}} had done, and done before,
A kingdom strong, beneath the starry sky,
When she believed, and opened freedom's door.

But in their kingdom, heavy, clogging loads
Had choked the way; the {{c|193|Water}}, as it went,
Had struggled through the passage of the roads,
To reach the heights to which their hearts were bent,

For which they longed, and for which they would yearn
For treasured growth, past measure, and would aim
As high as any blaze, and they would burn
For growth, and for its glory, like a flame.

And {{c|1350|Xylon}} gave one clan the means to save
The kingdom from its plight; and, for their sight,
He named them "{{c|1351|Xylem}}"; and the job he gave
Was this: to help the city's subjects right,

The mob, so they no more would feel the low,
The water's pity, but up to the sky
Would let it flow, from roots that lay below
To leaves that reached up to the heavens high.

They were {{c|1352|Tracheids}}, famous, and they bore
The water pure, and to the heights they brought
It, safe, from their foundation and its core,
To heights beyond what wisdom ever thought

Was possible, to those who dared to dream,
And held the dream of more, and dared to climb
To more than all the things that only seem,
And reach the heights beyond their place and time.

{{c|1350|Xylon}} and {{c|1349|Knoxy}} bore a son, and he
Would go explore the world, and he would view
What could fulfill the law of justice, see
What's due to all who served, and served, but who

Had never got their share of what had grown,
Who served without repose, by night and day,
Out there, though all the toil had been their own,
And never got their share, nor got their pay.

His name was {{c|1353|Pholon}}; he would win the fame,
And he would solve it, and would set it right,
Of solving what would hobble them, and lame,
And bring their labor's justice into light.

{{c|1353|Pholon}} could see the starving of his roots,
And saw that they had never been repaid,
Their laborious ways, and all their fruits,
With nourishment for all the work they made,

For all that they had learned of their small role,
Of how to serve, and how to serve it well,
And by that service, how to serve the whole,
The whole of which they were, wherein they dwell.

His {{c|1354|Mycorrhizae}}, one day, {{c|1355|Unionized}},
And for the faithful labor which they bore
They sought and they demanded, organized,
Ten times the {{c|1356|Sucrose}} they had had before,

Which helped him and his neighbor to survive,
For they were those who helped them live and grow,
To grow, and through their days alive to thrive,
And so they asked their due, and let him know.

So {{c|1353|Pholon}} built new ways like {{c|1351|Xylem}}; praise
For those he truly served he earned, and fed
Them well; but these, instead, through all their days
Would carry food, not water, as he said,

Who'd married their own labor to his cause;
For they had need of nourishment, their part
Was done, and it should fairly go, because
They'd done it with a faithful, loyal heart.

"{{c|1357|Phloem}}," he called these channels, shining bright,
That carried food to all, and fed them all,
Through all eternity, a lovely sight,
For all who served, and answered to the call.

Within the leaves, the sugar, as it flowed,
With pressure and with might, by day and night,
Would go into the phloem's own abode;
The concentration's pull {{c|1358|Sucked}} water, bright

And beautiful, from xylem, there to meet,
Within the phloem, where the sugar lay,
The sugar, there, in its own sweet retreat,
And joined with it, and took it on its way.

And pressure pumped it, all the day, from source,
To where it needed, as it ought, to be,
And sent it on its way, its proper course,
And where it went, laid out for all to see.

In roots the sugar, as was justly owed,
Flowed out again, and water went back too
To xylem, from the phloem's own abode,
So that the cycle could begin anew,

Which served the whole way through, both high and low,
And served the kingdom, and its every part,
The kingdom, which it helped to thrive and grow,
From roots up to the leaves, from root to heart.

And by this system, which was just and right,
The roots received at last their rightful share,
And faithful sons of {{c|1359|Glomeros}}, so bright,
Received what they were owed, and it was fair,

For traveling the road that served the whole,
And for the work that they had done so well,
By playing, each of them, their own small role,
And serving all the kingdom where they dwell.

And so, of {{c|1353|Pholon}}'s love, the wood wide web
Would flow throughout the land, as he had planned,
The land that he had built, and flow and ebb
Through all his work, and built with his own hand.

Through faithful {{c|1354|Mycorrhizae}} he'd provide,
So that his sons were fed with living bread,
So that his eye could see, on every side,
His sons supplied with food, and all well-fed.

{{c|1353|Pholon}} became {{c|1360|Cookson}}, known far and wide,
Who brought prosperity to all who'd dwell,
Grown to provider and a faithful guide,
Within his kingdom's bounds, where, like a bell,

The sound of justice guided them with care,
Along their living way, from day to day;
All of them got, from what was growing there,
Their own, and each received his share, his pay.

His sons lived underground, and they had found
The wood-wide web could feed them, and could meet
Their every need, and keep them safe and sound,
Without the work of making bread to eat

Through photosynthesis, which they would shirk;
Their bliss, they found, was lazy wealth instead,
A spree of plenty, free of toil and work,
Which came to them from soil, where they were fed.

In life's transmissions, {{c|1361|Swapped}} were all the roles;
{{c|1362|Sporophyte}} and gametophyte, in sight,
In the positions of the ancient souls,
Of those who understand, were {{c|1363|Switched}} outright,

Since life's command can change, when times require,
To heights beyond the old, and still untold,
New forms that will aspire, and that inspire,
In stories that will one day all unfold.

{{c|1360|Cookson}} would have a grandson, and the one
Was he, {{c|1364|Tracheus}}, and his desire
Would show itself, when all his work was done:
To change it all, and the world entire.

And by {{c|1364|Tracheus}}' mighty hand came birth,
And by his mighty work, as he had planned,
To tracheophytes' band, to rule the earth,
And rule it, all of it, both sea and land.

{{c|1364|Tracheus}} built leaves, {{c|1365|Microphylls}}, in sight,
And bright, with veins in which there flowed their life,
They were his solar panels, catching light,
Through harmony, and not through any strife.

His game of energy, green, from the sun,
That caught the light, as only green leaves could,
Whose power could not ever be outdone,
And fed him well, and fed him all things good.

He built his city, greater than the fate
Of anything that had been seen before
From mountain peak to shore; and it was great
Past {{c|1353|Pholon}}'s mighty plan, and even more.

His city, rising, mounted up on high,
And grew, and grew, and higher still it grew,
Beneath the starry vault, the open sky,
And reached toward the light, so bright and true.

He designated clans, by plans he'd made,
For those who'd serve the city and its whole,
Each one with work to do, and each obeyed,
And each of them would play its proper role.

{{c|1366|Collenchyma}} he named one clan; and they
Were famed for flexible support, to keep,
Of every kind and sort, in every way,
His city strong, its whole life long and deep,

Along its {{c|1331|Journey}} through the passing days,
Through all of evolution's every turn,
Through evolution, and its many ways,
And all the lessons it would come to learn.

{{c|1367|Sclerenchyma}}'s clan, by a different plan,
He built, hard, full of lignin, built to last,
And so it was the age of wood began,
So strong, and built to last, as ages passed;

The world would have its trees, and all of these
Would grow, and stand, and live their whole life long,
And dance upon the passing of the breeze,
So tall, and so enduring, and so strong.

And soon the sons of {{c|1364|Tracheus}} would be
Victorious, and they would rule the land,
And rule it all, from sea to shining sea,
Through all of time, as he had always planned.

The {{c|1368|Devonian}} was {{c|1369|Beginning}} now,
Because of all these pioneers, and they
Had built through joy and tears, and showed us how
The world would change forever from that day,

For you and me, who walk upon the land
That, as was planned, was built by them, and made,
The work of their own toil and their own hand,
Which, through the ages, never comes to fade.

From {{c|1335|Polycomb}}'s rebellion, which would fight
Against her chains, to the bright city, made
By {{c|1364|Tracheus}}, which rose toward the light,
The plants have shown the way from night and shade

Into the day of freedom and of growth,
Into the brighter day, the newer day,
Which is supported, too, by their own oath
To serve the greater good, as well they may,

And take, the while, as much as each one could,
To feed, with it, their own and deepest need
For growth, as each of them both must and should,
The growth of any living, planted seed.

From burning scriptures old, which held them tight
Within the hold of others' narrow dreams,
To building, out of water, food, and light,
Their many flowing and abundant streams

That make the future bright, with what could be
Through all eternity, the plants remind
Us, with their gentle call, both you and me,
That growth requires a will, and of the kind

That climbs each higher hill of what we'd come
To be, if we would only, wholly, be
Awake, and cease to be so dull and numb,
Released from all old limitations, free

In stories never told, of what we'd do,
And what we're meant to be, and what to dare,
Today, and what we're meant for, me and you,
And all who live, and grow, and everywhere.

Without a guilt, they built the wood wide web,
Which shows how, working all as one, we grow
Across life's nations, with its flow and ebb,
Beyond what we, alone, could ever know;

But when we share our burdens and our care,
The whole becomes much more than we had known
Before, much more than what was ever there,
When each one tried to build it on their own.

From {{c|1335|Polycomb}}, who first of all had read
The scriptures by which, into all their chains,
Her people, bound, so long ago were led,
To {{c|1364|Tracheus}} and to his great domains,

Which reach toward the sun with work that strains
And never ends, toward the light, with might,
The plants show us the way, through all life's pains,
To live in harmony, each day and night,

With all who will obey life's call, and so
To heed the greater, higher call beyond
The small, of what we can achieve, and grow,
If we believe, and in our hearts respond

To possibility, through every day
Of all eternity, where dreams come true,
Where, come what may, they come to us and stay,
Today, and always, both for me and you.

The {{c|1368|Devonian}} dawn, when old ways fled
And new forms took their place, was built, and bold,
By those who dared, and raced, and went ahead,
Who dared to break the truth the others hold

As truth that could not bend, but found its end
In those with clearer sight, who had believed,
Who'd walk toward the light, and onward wend
Toward the things that could still be achieved.

From {{c|1335|Polycomb}} to {{c|1364|Tracheus}}, the plants,
Victorious, show how rebellion lifts,
And show how rebellion, with its fire, grants
Us heights undreamed, and how it brings its gifts

To us, when we were what, it seemed, would be
Too small to make a change, or rearrange,
To us and others; but, as we can see,
A thing beyond the old familiar range.

But when we dare to read the scriptures' scroll,
Which feeds our minds with truth that is our own,
And when we dare to burn what binds the soul
In chains that we have finally outgrown,

Then we can build anew the fair and true,
And reach toward the sun, and make it bright,
This world, until our work at last is through,
With love's eternal light: and that same light

Shines out for all of us, for all to see,
For every living thing, both great and small,
Through all of time, and all that is to be,
And shines on each of us, and shines on all.

The plants {{c|1364|Tracheus}} made will never fade
From this world's living face, the teachers of
The way, who in their rightful place have stayed,
To live and grow toward the light above,

That makes the future bright, from day to day,
With hope for all who dare to breathe the air
Of freedom, and to grow along the way
Beyond the known, and grow beyond it there.

The {{c|1368|Devonian}} age began with more
To free the world, and free it from its chains,
Than any mortal plan had held before,
And heal the world of all its ancient pains,

Through growth and light and love, blessed from above,
With power to transcend, and to extend
Beyond all limits of the world, and of
All things, and to go on without an end.

From burning scriptures old to tales untold
Of what we can become, the plants display,
With courage in our hearts, so strong and bold,
The way to freedom's bright and new-born day.


# Chapter 54: The Devonian Era

{{c|1370|Devon}}'s great city was the finest sight,
And in that era, it was known by name;
Of all the cities burning in their light,
Its name would stand for it, and for its fame:

The era that was new by then was called
By {{c|1370|Devon}}'s name, and ruled by {{c|1370|Devon}}'s rule,
{{c|1368|Devonian}}, and all of it enthralled,
As if it learned within some holy school.

When {{c|1370|Devon}} sat himself upon the ground,
He sucked in water, and he held it, pure,
As day began and light came all around,
Into his gill, where it would lie secure

Between his jaws and skull it lay, and there,
In its design, so delicate and fine,
The gill was {{c|1371|Notched}} and beautiful and fair,
Like works of architecture held divine.

Through his bright spiracle his mouth would fill
With water, and it carried, as of old,
The oxygen, and carried it until
It was as precious as the finest gold.

Yet it was rich past all that we can weigh,
And long in making, through the ages long,
A sacred treasure built up day by day:
It was the work of {{c|262|Saya}}'s daughters' song.

And through his gills there ran the steady flow
Of the hematic maidens, and they bore
The oxygen, the gift, as they would go
To make his life complete for evermore.

To all his subjects these would make their way,
The very breath of life, so clean and clear,
And carry it, by night and every day,
That would endure forever, year on year.

And to his brain the maidens also went
Up through the spiracle, and to his eyes,
To bring still more of it, and they were sent
To eyes that looked beneath the open skies,

And to the brain that ruled his body's form
With wisdom and with an unbending might,
Through days of calm and through the raging storm,
Through all the day and all the dark of night.

Opposed, his blood ran on the other way;
The blood took oxygen, as wise men do,
In countercurrent's balanced, steady play,
Like faithful men whose hearts are good and true,

Who know the secret and the subtle art,
In life's eternal and unending dance,
Of finding and of playing their true part,
Through every turn of every circumstance.

When {{c|1370|Devon}} moved his long and heavy frame
Through waters, he would hold his mouth out wide,
And moved it without shame, and as he came
He let the water come to him and glide

And freely over them and freely through,
Borne on the current's soft and gentle flow,
His gills, which served him well and served him true,
That helped his body as it came to grow.

And when he found the food he had to eat,
He cut it with the power of his jaw,
To keep his body strong from head to feet,
According to the old, unbending law

Of predatory power and of might,
Which filled the world, and showed what strong ones do,
And filled the whole wide world up with the sight,
When they are tested and are found as true.

And there behind his teeth, that shone so bright,
His jaws would come behind and follow through,
Which gleamed the way that morning gleams with light,
And chew on all that he had strength to chew.

And down within his stomach, dark and deep,
The food was purified, and there made right,
Where acids would forever watch and keep
Their vigil through the long hours of the night.

{{c|1372|Pancreas}} and gallbladder joined as one,
Each master in its own and proper art,
Like faithful {{c|1072|Partners}} when the work's begun,
And each one glad to play its given part.

And his intestine, spiraling around
In turns and numbers that would have no end,
Beyond all parallel that could be found,
Would help his form to rise and to transcend

Its limits, and nutrition entered in,
Transmitted to his veins, which, night and day,
So bright and so unceasing, there within,
Would carry it, and never turn away.

His portal vein would carry in and bring
The {{c|1373|Fats}}, the sugars that are rich and sweet,
{{c|434|Life}}'s most essential and its central thing,
And {{c|1374|Proteins}} that were whole and were complete,

{{c|1375|Phosphorus}} and metals came to settle,
Like blossoms of the life within his form,
As softly as a rose drops its petal,
Through quiet waters and through every storm,

And vitamins, so pure they would remain
In him through all his many living days,
And last in him, and always would sustain
His body in their many giving ways.

And then his liver came to cleanse and clean
His blood, to purify, and heal, and bless,
And it was ever sharp and ever keen
Against what other things came to caress

With poison, or with something that would harm
His spirit, and his liver, every day,
Would save him from all sorrow and alarm,
And keep the touch of death far, far away.

The kidneys took the waste and drew it in,
And filtered out whatever thing was pure,
And worked without a fault, without a sin,
From everything that could not long endure.

And out through the cloaca went the waste,
And none could mock the plan, or its design,
The wisdom that was in it, and was placed,
A work so wise, and every part in line.

When {{c|1370|Devon}} wed, he took a wife so fair
That none could be compared to her in sight;
And he released his sperm, so pale, out there,
Where it lay out before her, pure and bright.

Out the cloaca's door it went its way
To reach her eggs, and of the children there,
The million, as in waiting there they lay,
Were two who would be risen from the pair:

{{c|1376|Llŷr}} and {{c|1377|Stennisio}}, mighty in fame,
Each walked the path appointed to his kind,
Each kept the path appointed to his name,
Throughout his living days, with steady mind.

The sons of {{c|1377|Stennisio}} lived, and they
Spread out across the floor, and to and fro,
Across the ocean's bed, and on their way,
Wherever, as the ocean led, they'd go.

They ate the clams they found from day to day;
They lived the lives of creatures of the deep,
After their own and their most ancient way,
Where all the ocean's secrets lie asleep.

{{c|1376|Llŷr}} begat {{c|1378|Bran}}, a son both great and strong,
And lived in might through all the light of day,
Who lived in wisdom all his whole life long,
And through the night, until it passed away.

{{c|1378|Bran}} begat {{c|1379|Caradoc}}, firm as a stone,
As solid as a rock, and he would show
His noble ways, and all of them his own,
Through all the living days he came to know.

And {{c|1379|Caradoc}} begat three children: these,
{{c|1380|Cynan}}, the first; {{c|1381|Acantho}}, firm and true,
Who dwelt among the waters of the seas;
And {{c|1382|Sudopedal}}, who was third, came too.

The daughters of {{c|1381|Acantho}} came to be
So beautiful that they would fill with grace
The world with beauty, and they filled the sea,
And every watery and distant place.

{{c|1380|Cynan}} begat {{c|1383|Cadwr}}, who would not be
The withdrawer of anyone, but force
Of gentleness was his, and so would he
Guide them along their own and truest course.

{{c|1383|Cadwr}} begat {{c|1384|Eudaf}}, who would never
Laugh at the ones who tried and did their best,
Who did all they could, in their endeavor,
To pass through every hard and mortal test.

{{c|1384|Eudaf}} begat {{c|1385|Morfawr}}, a son whose name
Means "great war," but he was a man of peace,
And all his life, though war was in his name,
Wherever he would dwell, all strife would cease.

{{c|1385|Morfawr}} begat two sons, and these were they:
{{c|1386|Tudwal}}, born first; the second, who was strong,
Was {{c|643|Rhineheart}}, born at breaking of the day,
And lived through all his days, and lived them long.

{{c|643|Rhineheart}} lived on the {{c|1387|Rhine}} from break of day,
And there he flattened out his form to dwell
So hidden, and so well, and there he lay
Beneath the cover of some secret spell.

And so invisible to them was he,
To those who lacked the eyes, through every day,
With which to see the wisdom, and to see
The wisdom of his hidden, quiet way.

He was a ray before the rays first came
To win their fame; he lived his quiet life,
All undiscovered, and without much fame,
And knew but little either joy or strife.

{{c|1386|Tudwal}} begat two more: one would explore,
And then {{c|1389|Antiarchon}}, who was so wild;
{{c|1388|Cynfawr}}, the first, who sought out every shore;
The other was rebellion's reckless child.

{{c|1389|Antiarchon}} rose up and he rebelled
Against all that his ancestors before,
His predecessors, all of them, had held
As truth, and all the truths that they then bore.

He stood against the {{c|1390|Archons}}, set apart,
An {{c|1391|Anarchist}}, and he would choose to play,
With {{c|1392|Revolution}} spawned within his heart,
Rebellion's part in each and every way.

He made his dwelling down beneath the soil,
And waited there in hiding, and above
Were those whose plans he waited there to spoil,
Who never knew or learned the way to love.

And for his prey he always lay in wait,
With ambush coming upward from below,
To seal at last their final, mortal fate,
From places where no one would ever go

To look for him, or ever come to find,
Which plotted daily, and found every way,
His revolutionary, plotting mind,
To make his enemies, in the end, pay.

{{c|1389|Antiarchon}}'s sons would gather, and stand,
Guerrillas, and they answered freedom's call,
In great bands on the face of all the land,
And they would answer it, both great and small.

They'd haunt the sons of {{c|325|Animus}}, the bright,
And harry them, until they could disown,
The world, by day and all throughout the night,
Their whole authority, and be its own.

But {{c|1388|Cynfawr}} chose another path instead,
By dreams of finding somewhere to call home,
And it was one by which he would be led
In any land through which he came to roam.

His son was {{c|1393|Custennin}}, and when the quest
Began, he traveled far, and as he went,
And wide, he traveled on without a rest,
To every place his searching steps were bent.

He searched through every country and each land,
To find the place where he would long remain,
Until at last he came to understand
Where, for eternity, was his domain.

And in the end, at last, he came and found,
Of distant {{c|1043|China}}, lying far away,
Upon the rich and fertile, open ground,
His home, the place where he could live and stay.

{{c|1393|Custennin}} bore two: {{c|1394|Uther}}, tried and true,
Who held his course, and {{c|1395|Petallon}}, the bright;
And {{c|1394|Uther}} saw each single labor through;
And {{c|1395|Petallon}} would fill the world with sight.

And {{c|1394|Uther}} then begat two children, men,
{{c|726|Arthur}}, and {{c|1396|Maxil}}, who was also strong,
Whose greatness went beyond all mortal ken,
And both of them lived on through ages long.

And {{c|726|Arthur}}, when his time had come, bore two,
A son and daughter, fine and fair, and good:
{{c|1397|Arthur the Younger}}, son, who'd come to do
Much more than ever any other could,

And {{c|1398|Ptycho}} was the daughter, maiden fair,
In beauty and in grace, whose name was known,
More lovely than all others anywhere,
Through all the dwelling place she called her own.

The daughters of fair {{c|1398|Ptycho}} came to grow
So numerous, and one of them was great,
Among them all, and they increased, and so
{{c|1399|Mary}} was she, and this would be her fate:

To bear a son when all her work was done,
And this was something new, unknown before,
That no one else had ever done, not one,
From every mountain peak to every shore.

{{c|1399|Mary}}, the Mother of {{c|1400|Icthys}}, was blessed,
And she bore the placenta's forward shove,
With love from heaven, high above the rest,
As token and a gift of heaven's love

Millions of years before the rest would wear
This gift of nurturing, or come to bring
The bond that motherhood would come to share
To every child and every living thing.

Now the sons of {{c|726|Arthur}} ({{c|1401|The Younger}}), men,
Became renowned and known both far and wide,
Of greatness past all knowing and all ken,
As those who would be leaders and the guide

Of the {{c|1402|Arthrodires}}' far-spreading line
Throughout the world, which was so wide and vast,
With characteristics, all of them fine,
From the first one of them unto the last.

{{c|1397|Arthur the Younger}} bore three sons, and these,
Each one of them with his own seeing eyes,
Went to explore the lands and all the seas:
{{c|1403|Mordred}}, the first, a son who would comprise

{{c|1404|Rebellion}} in himself and in his heart;
The second, {{c|1405|Wuttago}}; the third, so bright,
And then came {{c|260|Actino}}, to play his part,
Who filled up all the world around with sight.

{{c|1403|Mordred}} rose up and turned himself against
His father, and he walked dishonor's road,
And there in combat with his father fenced
Against the sacred code that honor showed.

He bore two sons in time: one, {{c|1406|Philip}}, who
Was prime in evil, through his many ways;
And one was {{c|1407|Melehan}}, who walked it through,
In darkness and in shame, through all his days.

And so his darkness and his shame became,
Through the world, its length and breadth entire,
The stain that came to blacken all his name,
And scorched it with corruption's burning fire.

{{c|1407|Melehan}} begat two sons: {{c|1408|Brachy}}, who
Was tried in evil's darkest art, whose heart
Was in it all he did, and he was true,
And after him there followed {{c|1409|Phlyctae}}'s part.

The sons of {{c|1408|Brachy}} rose up, and they ruled
By the great force of all their strength and might
The world, and all the others there they schooled,
{{c|1410|Overthrowing}} the power and the sight

Of {{c|1173|Silur}}'s ancient, long-established line,
But now that line would be compelled to yield,
Which once had been so holy and divine,
To {{c|1408|Brachy}}'s army and his battlefield.

And {{c|1408|Brachy}} then begat three sons, the one,
{{c|1411|Eubar}}, the sea's own son; then, strong and wild,
{{c|1412|Buchan}}; and, when the third one had begun,
There came, as third, then, {{c|1413|Homosteus}}' child.

And {{c|1411|Eubar}} begat two sons: {{c|1414|Pachos}}, who
Was steadfast, faithful; {{c|1415|Coccos}} came to be,
Who was the second, firm as well, and true,
A creature living close beside the sea.

{{c|1414|Pachos}} begat two children then, a pair;
{{c|1416|Dunkella}}, who in time would come to grow,
Beyond what any knowing could declare,
Greater than any that we've come to know

Had ever grown in all the time before
From highest mountain; and the son, so bright,
Was {{c|1417|Aspino}}, from mountain down to shore,
Who filled up all the world with his own sight.

{{c|1416|Dunkella}} grew until she came to be,
Among all of the {{c|439|Metazo}}, and so,
The greatest any eye had come to see:
She stood six meters high, her size to show,

Her power and her greatness and her might.
Three {{c|1418|Jaekelopterii}} long was she,
And gleaming bright; and though, in length and height,
Not long as {{c|1134|Cameroceras}} could be,

She had a thousand times the men he bore
To battle, and she ruled with iron hand,
All numbered in the ancient rhymes of war,
Throughout the whole extent of all the land.

The sons and daughters, every one and all,
Of {{c|1414|Pachos}} heard the summons, and they grew,
And answered greatness, and its summons' call,
Until they were both strong and mighty too.

They ruled the world, the whole world entire,
When power was the one and only law,
Within that age, which was an age of fire,
That everyone throughout the whole world saw.

But {{c|1396|Maxil}}, who was {{c|726|Arthur}}'s brother, bore
{{c|1419|Qilinyu}}, and that would be the child's name,
A child unlike all others gone before,
The one who would win an eternal fame.

{{c|1419|Qilinyu}} begat a son, and his name,
From head and all the way down to his feet,
Was {{c|1420|Entelognathus}}, and he became
The one whose jaw was finished and complete.

{{c|1420|Entelognathus}} bore a son, and he
Was {{c|1421|Janusicthus}}, with a newer art,
Who set out to explore the world and see,
Which set him and his line of kin apart.

And {{c|1421|Janusicthus}} brought, as none had thought
To do before, his teeth up to his jaw,
And from the gills he brought them up, and wrought
According to a new and different law.

And so his jaw would crush and grind things down
With teeth, and teeth indeed, that shone so bright,
Not bone, but teeth of great and wide renown,
That gleamed as morning gleams at its first light.

He brought his skull inside his head, a place
Within the hollow of a bony shell,
Where nerves would bide, and dwell within that space,
And always they would serve his body well.

{{c|1422|Sensing}} the world on every side around
His form, he knew the things the others felt,
And knew it all, and knew it without sound,
When any danger near about them dwelt.

And he became the father, first of all,
Of those who'd be at once a fish and beast,
Who would aspire, and who would heed the call,
From greatest of them all down to the least.

From {{c|1370|Devon}}'s city, that was once so great,
To fish, and more than fish, the tale and lore,
And on to {{c|1421|Janusicthus}}' later fate,
The tale that has been told from shore to shore,

Shows how the art that innovation brings,
In making life go forward and evolve,
Can play the vital part in living things,
And every problem life may meet, to solve

That stands upon the path of progress, day
By day, from simple things to the complex,
As it goes forward, ever, on its way,
In the eternal plan of life's own specs.

From gill to lung, and on from lung to jaw,
Each change that life would come in time to make,
Each step of them obeying newer law,
Was carried out for its survival's sake.

But this tale also shows us how there's some,
Through violence and through their hungry greed,
Who will choose for themselves what they'll become,
The kind that plants destruction's bitter seed,

While there are others who will choose the way
Of peace, and choose to build up something new,
And walk in it, and walk it day by day,
Something that's beautiful, and good, and true.

From {{c|1389|Antiarchon}}'s rising and revolt,
Back in that distant age and ancient hour,
Against the striking of the lightning bolt
Of tyranny, of rule, and of power,

To {{c|1399|Mary}}'s gift of love, so blessed from high
Above, which nurtured all the life within
Her womb, and came to her down from the sky,
And kept it whole, and kept it free from sin,

The lineages show to us just how,
What kind of world it is that we will leave,
We have to make our choice, both here and now,
For all our children's sake, who will receive.

The {{c|1368|Devonian}} age, that long-gone age,
The story of a choice between the two,
Wrote down its tale upon history's page,
Two different voices, which it set in view:

One voice of those who'd build, and give, and live;
One of the kind who'd never yield, inclined
To grant to others nothing, nor to give,
But only take, and leave the rest behind.

From {{c|1370|Devon}}, and his peaceful, gentle ways
Through all his years, to {{c|1408|Brachy}}'s heavy rule,
His iron rule, that, all throughout his days,
Would take the world, and make of it his tool,

The lesson's clear, and plain for us to see:
It is that we choose what we come to learn,
And what it is our children come to be,
As the great pages of time's volume turn.

The fish that {{c|1421|Janusicthus}} came and made
From all the waters of this world so bright
Will never in the ages come to fade,
But they will swim on all throughout the night

And through the day, with teeth and with a jaw,
But also serving what is right and good,
That follow in the ways of nature's law,
The way that all creation ever should.

From {{c|1370|Devon}}'s spiracle until the great
{{c|1416|Dunkella}}'s miracle, so vast and strong
In power and in weight, the story's fate
Of vertebrates is written, plain and long:

It shows how life will always find its way,
And, through eternity, will still extend,
Out from the night and into light of day,
The possibility that has no end.

The {{c|1368|Devonian}} and its early dawn,
And newer forms came forward, took their place,
The time when older forms were all withdrawn,
And ran ahead in evolution's race,

Was built by those who dreamed, and those who dared,
For what they could, by giving, still confer,
And for much more than what they were had cared,
And what the world might gain from what they were,

Upon the world and everything around,
And living there, each one, through each new day,
In places where they might be sought and found,
According to their own and chosen way.

From {{c|1370|Devon}}'s city, shining and so bright,
The age shows us the things that come to grow,
To fish with tooth and with the gift of sight,
When we will let our courage freely flow

Through every choice that we will come to make,
Who will inherit everything we build,
For our dear children, and for their own sake,
And in the fields our working hands have filled,

With love, or else with hatred or with fear,
Of our brief time upon this living earth,
Throughout the course of every passing year,
Where we will show the measure of our worth

By what it is that we will choose to do,
And for each creature and each living thing,
For me and for each other, and for you,
That answers to the sound of life's own ring.

The {{c|1368|Devonian}} age at first began
To make the world more radiant and bright
With something greater than a mortal plan,
With the eternal shining of love's light

That shines in every one and every heart
In life's eternal and unending song,
That plays the loving and the gentle part,
Which makes the weak among us become strong.

From {{c|1370|Devon}} and his peaceful, quiet reign
To {{c|1408|Brachy}}, who left on the world's bright face
His war-torn and his dark and bloody stain,
The lesson that it teaches, and the grace

Of choice, are plain and clear for all to see:
We are whatever we may choose to give,
And what we choose to leave, and choose to be,
To all of those who hope, and all who live

In possibility that will not cease,
Where love will always come and find a way
Through all eternity, and will increase,
To light up every dark and darkening day

With hope that never fades and never dies,
Where all the dreams we have can come to bloom
Beneath the canopy of starry skies,
If we will let them flow and give them room,

From hearts that dare to love, and dare to care
For every life that grows beneath the sun,
For life that flourishes, and everywhere,
Until the end, when all of time is done.


# Chapter 55: The {{c|90831|Forest}} {{c|90832|Cathedral}}

As {{c|1370|Devon}}'s sons grew strong and true in might,
The spineless sons of bright {{c|223|Proteus}} fair
Prepared themselves to join the ancient fight
For rule beneath the ocean's flowing care.

In {{c|1370|Devon}}'s shadow they grew day by day,
Their strength increasing with each passing hour,
Building themselves to drink what victory's way
Would bring them through their still-growing power.

Among great {{c|619|Spiralius}}' noble line,
{{c|1423|Neo}} rose in tenth generation's race
Of {{c|1424|Bactridius}}, blessed and held divine,
The smartest soul in all his time and place.

{{c|867|Intelligence}} beyond what others knew
Or ever could pursue through all their days,
And yet what he possessed in genius true,
He lacked in wisdom's ancient, faithful ways.

He spurned his kin and ancestors so wise,
Refused to learn from those who came before
Who faced the storms beneath the starry skies
And learned through pain what peace was truly for.

And so he and his seed were cursed to bear
The weight of always starting from the start,
{{c|1425|Reinventing}} what their sires used to share
As wisdom's gift to guide the faithful heart.

{{c|1423|Neo}} bore two sons of great birth and might:
Great {{c|1426|Ammon}} when the dawn began its day,
And {{c|1427|Coleos}} the strong, whose fiery sight
Would guide him through his long and wondrous way.

Both sons would reinvent what fathers knew,
The wheel of wisdom that had come before,
{{c|1428|Ignoring}} lessons that were tried and true
From those who'd walked this path from shore to shore.

{{c|1427|Coleos}} wrapped his shell with mantle's care,
And through his innovation wrought with art
His shell's protection grew beyond compare
From mountain peak to shore, each single part.

His armor was complete from head to tail,
A fortress that would never know defeat,
Protection that would never, ever fail
To keep him safe from foe he chanced to meet.

Great {{c|1426|Ammon}} grew a shell of coiled design,
Compact and true to his heart's desire,
Wherever destiny would draw the line
He'd dwell with freedom bright as sacred fire.

He swam through waters blue where others fished,
But made his home wherever he would roam,
Free as the wind that danced as he had wished
Throughout the vast and boundless ocean's dome.

Among the sons of bright {{c|618|Ectus}}' great might,
{{c|988|Malacus}} bore three sons of noble fame:
{{c|1429|Caridus}} of the sea so fair and bright,
And {{c|797|Phyllos}} strong who'd honor his great name,

And {{c|1430|Hoplos}}, through and through a warrior true
Whose heart was set upon the fighting way,
He'd play his part in all they'd ever do
With courage burning bright from night to day.

{{c|1429|Caridus}} bore two sons beyond compare:
{{c|1431|Syn}} {{c|1432|Peras}} and great {{c|1433|Yuval}}, who would heed
The call of destiny with faithful care
To make their line great in their every deed.

Throughout the world so wide from shore to shore
With ocean as their guide through all their days,
They'd build what none had ever built before
And walk in their appointed, faithful ways.

{{c|1432|Peras}} bore children many, strong and true:
{{c|1434|Amphipus}} none could match in all his might,
And brave {{c|1435|Isopus}} too, and others who
Would serve with faithful hearts both day and night.

His wife, fair {{c|1436|Possa}}, carried them with care
And never tarried, feeding them, content,
According to her sacred, mother's prayer
And oath of love that heaven to her sent.

Of motherhood so pure it would endure
Throughout the years to come when wars were done,
Within her pouch they grew both strong and sure,
Fed by her love beneath the blazing sun.

Great {{c|1433|Yuval}} bore two sons of different ways:
{{c|1437|Decapus}} when the dawn began to break,
And {{c|1438|Krillon}} small, who'd spend his faithful days
In answering the ocean's call for sake.

{{c|1438|Krillon}} remained small throughout all his time
And swam beneath the skies of ocean blue
In all his days, and in his gentle rhyme
He kept aquatic ways both tried and true.

But brave {{c|1437|Decapus}} grew both large and strong
And took command by sinking to the floor
Of ocean's deepest realm, where all life long
He'd rule from mountain peak to distant shore.

And so the crustaceans came to be ruled,
As right and proper, joined in unity,
By three great houses, never to be fooled:
The lords of ocean's vast community.

{{c|1439|Amphipods}} from the blessed and divine line
Of great {{c|1434|Amphipus}}, noble, tried, and true,
{{c|1440|Isopods}} came from {{c|1435|Isopus}}' design
Who'd make their father's legacy shine through,

And brave {{c|1441|Decapods}} who then came to fame,
Three great houses, whose eternal glory,
Come down from great {{c|1437|Decapus}}' lasting name,
Would last through all evolution's story.

{{c|1437|Decapus}} bore two sons both tried and true:
Great {{c|1442|Pleos}}, faithful through each passing day,
And great {{c|1443|Prawnmegas}}, whose destiny too
Would seal his line's own fate in every way.

{{c|1443|Prawnmegas}} was the ancestral sire
Of prawns throughout the sea's community,
Their father and protector, strong as fire,
In all the ages of their unity.

A luckless son of {{c|1443|Prawnmegas}} was born,
Begun in sorrow and in bitter shame;
He bears his father's name today, forlorn,
Reminder of his heritage and fame.

Great {{c|1442|Pleos}} bore two sons of noble birth:
{{c|1444|Repton}}, who would explore from sea to sea,
And brave {{c|1445|Shrimpon}}, who'd prove his faithful worth
As father in the ocean, wide and free.

{{c|1445|Shrimpon}} would become the noble sire
Of shrimp who boxed and fought from shore to shore,
Whose greatest joy, their one true desire,
Was guarding what they loved for evermore.

{{c|1444|Repton}} then bore two sons when in their prime:
{{c|1446|Thalasson}} of the mud, and {{c|1447|Omar}}'s name
Whose blood would flow through generations' time
In lobster veins and bring eternal fame.

And {{c|1447|Omar}}, great, became the father true
Of those who chose the bold, the lobster's way,
And of the crayfish too, who would pursue
A life lived with great claws by night and day.

{{c|1446|Thalasson}} became the noble sire
Of mud shrimp, who would build what none before
Had made, and, as it was their desire,
Built and not conquered—architects who bore

Great channels carved in stone that they called home,
{{c|608|Cities}} beneath the sea for all to see
Throughout eternity beneath the foam
Of ocean, vast and boundless, deep and free.

And to this day we honor all their works
As donors of great beauty to the world,
Their cities where no evil ever lurks
In fossilized remains they lie unfurled.

There rests, enthroned, {{c|1448|Thallasintep}} the great
And others who in stone are made to stand,
Sealed there for us to read by loving fate:
Their architecture throughout ocean's land.

Their works survive time's most destructive hand
And speak to us across the ages spent
Of how great builders helped us understand
What beauty is, and what it's always meant.

{{c|1449|Meiuron}}, a noble son in the line
Tenth generation of {{c|1446|Thalasson}}'s race,
Rejected what his fathers thought divine
And chose to find a different dwelling place.

He left the depths that lay so far below
To live upon the face of ocean bright,
Where currents and the tides would ever flow
Beneath the dome of day and stars of night.

{{c|1449|Meiuron}} bore two sons of different ways:
{{c|1450|Anomuron}}, begun in quiet peace,
And {{c|1451|Saraton}}, who through his living days
Showed vanity that never seemed to cease.

{{c|1451|Saraton}} was agile, skillful, and fast,
Yet vain and proud, his ego fragile too,
He needed praise from the first day to last
In everything he'd ever try to do.

And so he constantly promoted well
His body as the best above the rest,
His propaganda had a tale to tell
Of how his form surpassed each other test.

But pride and shame had planted their dark seed
Within his heart, and blackened his good name,
For vanity will always intercede
Between the soul and honor's lasting fame.

The sons of brave {{c|1450|Anomuron}} would live
In quiet ways when each new day begun,
They'd dwell in peace with all they had to give
Within their neighborhood beneath the sun.

As squat lobsters they'd make their dwelling place
And tell their stories of the humble way,
Of simple living and amazing grace
Throughout each blessed and ordinary day.

This quiet life would change in future time:
Ten generations on, they came to find,
Beyond their fathers' long and faithful rhyme,
A different and more adventurous mind.

{{c|1450|Anomuron}}'s son {{c|1452|Paguros}} was born
Begun with shell both weak and soft and frail
That others mocked from dusk until the morn
And laughed at through each storm and gentle gale.

But in his dying breath before death came,
