One ancient father's signature they share,

Whose patient children parted, some to ride
North, some to walk south; and the mark would creep,
Intact for fifty thousand years, and bide
Into two cultures that would never keep

Within two of the most distinctive ways
Of living earth has known; and they have grown,
Yet neither marked the other, all their days,
Nor knew the other was: unmet, unknown.

The disconnected branches of our kind
Share deep ancestry: silent, deep-down things,
That no one living member calls to mind,
More quiet than a language are its strings.

The {{p|Arnhem Land}} man, singing out his range,
Knows no {{p|Mongolia}}, no grass, no snow;
The {{p|Mongolian}} shepherd, in exchange,
The {{p|Dreaming}} does not know. One, long ago,

Belongs to both of them: deep in the past,
A father, and his children, who would go
In opposite directions; now is cast
His {{p|Y}}'s long shadow on them both, below,

Upon {{p|Australia}}'s continent, the same
As on the central {{p|Asian}} grasslands; on
Two continents, and no divergence came
To split the line, one man, and he long gone.

{{c|1849|C}} is the unsplit. {{c|1849|C}} is what can claim,
In name though not in story, the one case,
Two of the most distinctive roads, the same,
Where splitting rules did not hold to their place.

No catastrophe here; no {{p|Toba}}; no
Fracture, no refuge; just the flow, unplanned,
Of a migration going two ways, so,
A marker that would not divide its strand,

Or not as much as others did. They stand,
Together by a shared and unseen sign,
The steppe and desert continent, one band,
Of fathers, one patrilineal line.

And then the steppe goes on its way: the horse
Is tamed; empires of the grass arise;
The mounted nomad finds his gait and course,
And fall and rise again before all eyes,

And all the tension of the grassland, set
Against the settled towns, is born; its ground,
{{p|Eurasia}}'s, it will shape so much; and yet
The horsemen of {{c|1892|Genghis Khan}} are still found

To carry, mostly, {{c|1849|C}}. That line runs through
From the first migrants, through the hordes as well,
That followed them, and down to those who, too,
In {{p|Mongolia}}, {{p|Kazakhstan}}, now dwell.

And so {{p|Australia}}'s story goes its way:
The most complex, sophisticated plan
{{c|1888|Aboriginal}} peoples build, and stay,
Of non-farming society of man

On earth. They were the stewards of a land
Whole. No writing came, and they never chose
The walled-in city, nor the city grand,
As {{p|Mesopotamia}}, {{p|China}}, rose,

Or {{p|Mesoamerica}}, a fortified
Civilization rose, a thing wherein
(They never tried to "civilize," nor tried)
No shallow colonizer, who had been

Born in the eighteenth and nineteenth, could see
At all: a way of being human, grown
With its own deep achievement, and so free,
Peculiar register of time and tone.

In song were fifty thousand years; and so
In painting fifty thousand; and as long
The patient reading of the land, the slow;
{{x|Gaiad}} will not rank them below the throng

Of city-builders. {{x|Gaiad}} honors them
As them. And all the while, through every mile,
The same {{c|1893|Y}} mark is carried, stem to stem,
By {{p|Mongol}} horsemen, in their nomad style:

Vast, varied; and the horseman never came
To know that, south, a cousin also shows,

The chromosomal gift, the name, which flows.

These two will never meet, nor ever know;
Their steeples and their songs will each, within,

Here only. So it ends, and so it leaves
The strange unsettled fact: one blood, the {{c|1849|C}},

In silence, bound together through the frame

The house of {{c|1849|C}}, one house in two designs;

One house, which on the steppe and in the sand

And if they met, in one or other land,

And still they are one house, the house of {{c|1849|C}},

It is just what it is, and so it stays;

To last the farming change, and, though displaced,
The steppe invasion too, it had survived,
From dominance by then, and much erased.

But it is here: the {{p|Nordic}} basin; still,
{{p|Croatian}} villages, where, one by one,
{{p|Sardinian}} highlanders on the hill
Still bear the hunters' sun, and every son,

Descended from the hunters of that land.
{{p|Magdalenian}} heritage, the made,
The {{p|Gravettian}} culture, near at hand,
{{x|Aurignacian}} paintings in {{p|Chauvet}}'s deep shade

Of stone; and {{c|1901|Gravettian}} figurines:
All these are carried still, and, as of old,
In certain {{p|European}} folk, in genes;
The old lives yet; old {{p|Europe}} has not tolled

Its final hour. Fulfilment in the chase
Was turned, by pressure, to the plow, the herd,
The city, and at last, another place,
Modernity; but still, though long deferred,

The {{c|1893|Y}}-chromosomal mark of the first
Settled the continent, and lives on now,
Whole in the many millions, not dispersed;
The patient continuity, somehow,

Of {{c|1875|I}} across some forty thousand years,
The longest tie of any folk and land
On one continent, oldest of its peers,
In all the {{p|European}} tale. They stand

New, all of them: the {{p|French}}, the {{p|Germans}}, there,
The {{p|Romans}} new; the deepest, oldest view
Belongs to {{c|1875|I}}, deep in the house of prayer,
The body's house, the oldest presence, too.

This chapter honors them: the first to hunt
In all old {{p|Europe}}; they who did not break,
Of glacial maximum who bore the brunt;
The painters of the {{p|Lascaux}} cave; and make

Of them the makers of the {{x|Venus}} forms,
Defiant; patient, who re-held the land
Post-ice, and who outlived the glacial storms,
The substrate under all that later spanned

The long ages. {{c|1896|Haplogroup I}}: the card
Of old {{p|Europe}}'s ID; and on the ground,
The hunter's patient look and long regard
Upon the land he lived on, and he found

The deep kinship with river and with cave,
With forest; and when chapters hence reach sleep,
Of animism, which the deep past gave,
The carrying-on of old ways, we keep

Pre-{{p|Neolithic}} hunting ways again
In half-settled form, where {{c|1875|I}} shows, and so
There came {{c|1902|Cucuteni-Trypillia}}, then,
The old reply that {{p|Europe}} gave, we know,

In wood and clay: its towns, its painted walls,
Its female iconography; and free
Of hierarchy, in its open halls,
Its peaceful order, as it used to be:

These were old {{p|Europe}}'s working out of all
The farmers offered; it was, there and then,
From its own magic register, its call;
{{p|Yamnaya}} came upon that flower, when

Their time arrived. But we are not there yet.
For now, it's the old {{p|Europe}}, and the one,
The mother-goddess carver; hunter's net;
Who painted caves; who saw the ice begun

And gone again; the patient background line;
The brother, sister, uncle, and the heirs
Of the old {{c|1893|Y}}, the ancient mark and sign
In every {{p|European}} who still bears

The old land's mark; the one who came before;
The hold of will to last; the hand that kept;
{{c|1896|Haplogroup I}}, {{p|Old Europe}}. All the more,
The continent's whole tale is layered, stepped

On top; but {{c|1875|I}} is still the bottom, where
The tops descend, when they have finished, high
And visible, to stand; and layers there
That come and go, will come and go, and die.

The bottom does not stop. The cave remains
Within the limestone, and the paint, as still,
Its place upon the wall of stone retains;
The ochre's goddess; and the {{p|Y}} will fill

The men of {{p|Balkans}} and the men of north,
And of {{p|Sardinia}}, whose blood has shown
And calls from {{p|Europe}}'s deepest past, set forth;
Great-great-grandfathers of their mothers, grown

In ice-age light, went to the cave to trace
The horse, the bison; and remembers it,
The continent, the bull's own painted face;
The haplogroup is memory, and writ

In patient continuity, the {{c|1875|I}},
In all the long, long years that it has known:
The body's longest word, and does not die,
And lives, and lives, and lives, and is its own.


# Chapter 136: G Builds the Neolithic

While {{c|1875|I}} still hunted reindeer on the plain
Of {{p|Europe}}, {{c|1862|F}}'s proliferating name
Had set another branch, and chain on chain,
In {{p|Fertile Crescent}}, changing all the game:

Not the old running, following the sign
Of any herd; but planting; and in pits
The storing of the grain; and row and line,
And harvest; grinding wheat on stones. It fits

A whole remaking of the human mode:
The old script of the nomad, set aside,
The loping forager, who long had strode,
For something scarce conceivable: to bide.

The choice to stay. The choice to not be chased
By food in season; and the choice, to feed
Myself, to say to the land, firmly placed:
I plant, and wait, and then I reap the seed;

I will not leave. I stay in this one place;
And that is vastest of all plans, for it,
Until I die, my son stays in my space,
Makes of one ground a future. Thus was writ

{{p|Neolithic}} Revolution. The {{p|Y}}
Was found, consistently, to be the one,
That walked beside the farmers, by and by:
{{c|1903|Haplogroup G}}, the farmer's line, begun

In that first crescent. {{c|1873|G}} is he whose sons
Left {{p|Fertile Crescent}}, and with grain they went,
With sheep and goat, as the first farming runs,
To {{p|Anatolia}} and {{p|Europe}}, sent

With all the pattern of the new life. {{c|1873|G}},
The first farm wave to come to {{p|Europe}}'s shore,
Marks {{p|Linear Pottery Culture}}; he,
The founder of it, at its very core,

Of farming villages whose layers lie
In {{p|Greece}}'s valleys, {{p|Italy}}'s own ground,
And in {{p|Balkan}} stratigraphy, so high;
And {{c|1873|G}} is in the bones that have been found

Of {{p|Ötzi}}, {{c|1904|Iceman}} of the {{p|Alps}}, who lay,
A frozen body; and his {{p|Y}} makes plain,
Five thousand and three hundred years away,
That {{p|Alpine}} farmers of that age and grain

Of time, the late stone and the copper days,
Were {{c|1873|G}}, securely. Now, before the grain
Was sown, before the fields, the story stays,
Before a seed was planted, and is plain:

It starts, and it is here it starts, at one
Great hill in {{p|Turkey}}: of the many sites
That digging ever found, the work there done
Is most astonishing: those stony heights

Of {{p|Göbekli Tepe}}: built in days of old,
Six millennia ere {{c|1898|Stonehenge}}, and more;
Eleven thousand five hundred years old,
It stood; and by a thousand years before

The settled towns of {{p|Jericho}}. And they
Who built it were not settled, nor the mild,
Grain-storing villagers of later day,
Not farmers: they were hunters, and the wild

Wandering hunter-gatherers, whose hands
Had no precedent for such work, and stone:
A ring of great T-pillars, where it stands,
Some over five meters, of tons, full-grown

And carved with animals: with fox and snake,
With scorpion, wild boar, and vulture's wings,
Arranged in rings, for holy meeting's sake,
Like temple pillars, though of no such things

As settled peoples build. A temple, raised
By hunters, by the laws that they had known,
For gathering, for which they came, amazed,
In a place no one dwelt, where grass had grown

An ample, undramatic edge; and they
Would pledge whole generations, far and near,
To come, with visits, and the place repay,
Elaborating what they built, each year:

Two thousand years of it. It was no town,
No dwelling-place; it had a different worth:
A ritual site, a site of renown,
A center like no other on the earth,

Where all the scattered bands would come and meet
From all the region, there, to meet and be
As one, and make the gathering complete;
And since they had to gather, and to see

The building through, they had to eat; to feed
The crew, they grew the grain; and so began
The farming, and the sowing of the seed,
The first time ever, by the hand of man:

Farming was seeded by the temple, not
By need, nor hunger; and the first things sown,
Einkorn and emmer, not by climate's lot,
Were for the feast-days at the pillared stone

At {{p|Göbekli Tepe}}'s gatherings. The grain
Was born to serve the temple, and the thing
The temple needed settled it again;
And staying grain, the grain made people cling

To one place; settlement then made the field
And furrow; and the fields, then, later on,
Made not grain only, all that they would yield:
The immanence of cities. First was drawn

The temple; then the city; then the crown
And kingdom: so it went, in order laid:
The temple first, then farming, then the town,
Then kings; and so the world of men was made.

The people gathered round the stone, and so,
To build what they adored, they came, and found,
In service of that worship, how to grow
The bread to keep them, gathered on that ground;

Their gatherings, which grew, would come to keep
And build our whole civilization, too:
The scripted ritual life, which runs deep,
And, of the proto-priests, the priestly crew,

Who made there and set going what would be
All that came after; and that priestly clan,
The builders, and their {{p|Y}}: it all was {{c|1873|G}}:
{{c|1873|G}} built {{p|Göbekli Tepe}}; and {{c|1873|G}} began

The farming; it was {{c|1873|G}} who bore the plan
And wheat to {{p|Europe}}, generations, who,
From {{p|Anatolia}}, as they began,
Brought grain and sheep and pots, the package, too.

Long-walking farmers from the crescent, they
Took {{c|1873|G}} across the continent; its rates
In {{p|Sardinian}} men are high today,
Extraordinary: there the early gates

Of island settlement were opened wide
To {{p|Neolithic}} farmers; and apart
{{p|Sardinia}} was kept by sea and tide,
Preserving {{c|1873|G}}; and on the mainland chart

Of {{p|Europe}}, they are later shown as thinned,
When {{p|Yamnaya}} arrived; but there it stays,
{{p|Sardinia}}, untouched by the steppe wind:
The {{p|Neolithic}} dominant; these days,

{{p|Sardinian}} men on the hills are heirs,
That {{p|Göbekli Tepe}} line, the builders' own,
In many cases, of those ancient prayers:
First priesthood of the greatest work in stone

And faith the {{p|Near East}} knew, is carried still,
As by an ancient and unbroken thread,
In shepherds' bodies, walking the same hill,
Where, in the ancient days, their fathers led.

{{c|1873|G}} is alive. {{c|1873|G}} built what {{x|Gaiad}} calls
The founding monument, and with its seed
Began civilization, with its walls;
The island shepherds keep the herds they feed

On {{p|Mediterranean}} hills, the ways
Their grandfathers once walked, and walk them still,
And keep the herds through all their living days,
As they have kept them, and as they still will.

{{c|1873|G}} built the temple, and invented, too,
The farming; the foundation, and the whole
Decree, the package, which would come to view
And shape all later life, and play its role,

Was made by him. The {{c|1873|G}}-borne farmer, west
And north to {{p|Europe}} walking, is the lore
Of how in farming {{p|Europe}} would be pressed;
The {{c|1875|I}}-borne hunters met, upon that shore,

The coming farmers: sometimes there was fight
And sometimes blending; and the farmers' hand
Did not erase the hunters by its might,
But it reshaped the ledgers of the land;

{{p|Europe}} was draped in layers: {{c|1875|I}} below,
The base; and {{c|1873|G}} the second, as it came;
Of {{c|1884|R}} above, the third, the later flow,
When the steppe riders came. The texture, frame,

And weave of modern {{p|European}} blood:
From hunter, to the farmer, to the man
Who rode the steppe: three waves, and one great flood,
Mixed in the {{p|Y}}, as in a written plan.

{{c|1873|G}} is the second wave; the builder, priest,
And farmer of that first revolt, who raised
The first stone pillars up, and raised the feast,
Religious-agricultural, and praised

The first great gathering for its own sake.
And {{c|1873|G}} walked west with grain; and then the whole,
In settling, settling, settling in its wake,
Economy of {{p|Europe}} changed its role

Forever, by the farmers' coming. And
This fact, that temples first, and not the field,
Were built, is how it was; and so was planned
Theology made quiet: fields would yield

As servants to the temple: first the god;
The grain came after, at the hands of men.
The harvest, that would feed a town, the sod
Gave first as offering, and laid down then

At the stone pillar's foot, and there to feed
The gathered hunters, come to worship; so
They sang their words, and spoke their ancient creed,
And worshipped there, as all the ages know.

They gathered, and they worked; and we know, too,
The crop went home with them; and in their toil,
Their common practice, all their ranges through,
Made first civilization from that soil

Of gathering, and building, and the grain
Grown all together; it was so, and so
The flame began; its carrier was plain,
Its carrier was {{c|1873|G}}. And is it so

That {{c|1873|G}} is still alive? It is: still found
In {{p|Sardinia}}; frequencies are high
In {{p|Georgia}}, the country, on {{p|Georgian}} ground;
In pockets of the {{p|Caucasus}}, and nigh

The {{p|Alps}} as well. Small consolation, weighed
Beside the grandeur, which was great and long,
The grandeur of the thing that they had made:
The {{p|Göbekli Tepe}} chorus sang a song

Among the first of all. The singers, gone
Long since, left children who today still tend
Sheep on {{p|Sardinian}} hills; on and on,
The story has not come yet to its end;

The pillars still are there, and they are borne,
Reburied, and re-dug, in open air;
The dawn they set in motion is the morn
In which we live; and cities everywhere

Since then were built as they built, in a ring
Of gathered hands; and from their choice, the stay,
The choice of every later age, would spring;
The fanfare of the modern world today

Is downstream of one voice, which sang before,
Of stone, a carved fox on it, long ago,
At {{p|Göbekli Tepe}}, at the pillar's floor,
Eleven thousand years. {{c|1873|G}} made it so:

{{c|1873|G}}, farmer; {{c|1873|G}}, the builder and the root
Of all the {{p|Neolithic}}; {{c|1873|G}}, whose slow
And patient settled dwelling, as its fruit,
And priesthood too, would come at last to show

The model for all dwellings that would stand.
Honor him; honor those who raised the stone,
The pillars; honor all that building band:
They built the first fane, and it was their own;

And the first thing we swallowed was the grain
They grew to feed the hands that built it. So
The grain fed up the builders; and again,
The builders fed the god, as we now know,

Who now is gone. The grain remains; and on
The world that dawned, their choice still lights the way;
And every town and city since has gone
Along their path, and trod it to our day.

And it was {{c|1873|G}} who first broke through the sod,
And every stay of ours, in every land,
{{c|1873|G}}, the {{p|Neolithic}}: so have we trod,
Descends from that first settled choice to stand.


# Chapter 137: J — The Semitic World

When {{c|1895|IJ}} split in two, the sister pair
Went each its way: {{c|1875|I}} walked into the north,
To {{p|Europe}}, hunting; {{c|1876|J}} stayed on, back there,
Near where the two of them had issued forth,

Where {{p|Anatolia}} and {{p|Zagros}} meet,
And the {{p|Levant}}, and {{p|Arabian}} sand:
The grinding meeting-place, the crossing street;
And there it spread, through all that central land.

{{c|1876|J}} is the {{p|Middle Eastern}} house, and sent
The fountain of its ancient seal, the men
Of the first cities, where the first laws went,
Who made the writing, and began the pen.

{{c|1876|J}} has two houses, {{c|1907|J1}} and {{c|1908|J2}},
That parted, and went off to other lands:
{{c|1907|J1}}, the house of {{p|Arabia}}, grew
The {{p|Bedouin}} and the {{p|Yemeni}} bands,

The {{p|Saudi}}'s house, the father-line, the name
Of all the {{p|Bedouin}}; the Desert {{c|1876|J}},
On camel-paths where {{p|Rub' al Khali}} came
And blew its sands across the trackless way,

And spoke {{c|1909|Afroasiatic}}, of kin,
The proto-{{c|1863|Semitic}}; and in its way
It made the {{c|1910|Arabs}}, and the tribes within
{{p|Arabia}}, the tribal sound and sway.

{{c|1908|J2}}, northern and {{p|Levantine}} and wet,
The fertile-crescent {{c|1876|J}}; and there we find
The tillers of the vale, the early set
Of valley farmers, of the settling kind:

{{p|Natufian}}; {{p|Levant}}'s first farms; and those
Of {{p|Anatolia}}, and {{p|Jordan}}'s, too;
With {{c|1873|G}} beside them, in the fields and rows,
They mingled, and the first of cities grew:

{{p|Mesopotamia}} began, the dawn
Of {{p|Sumer}} and of {{p|Akkad}}, from the blend
Of {{c|1908|J2}}, {{c|1873|G}}, and others, they were drawn,
And set up cities that would never end:

{{p|Uruk}} and {{p|Eridu}}, and {{p|Lagash}}, too,
{{p|Ur}} and {{p|Nippur}}: and all the founders' sign,
The fathers' {{p|Y}}, it came out of {{c|1908|J2}};
The building of the cities, by design,

Which moulded all the nations yet to come,
Six thousand years of them, sprang from the hand
Of {{c|1876|J}} and {{c|1873|G}} together, and the sum
Of all the labor of that ancient land.

And it is {{c|1863|Semitic}}, the tongue it bore,
The family of speech the {{p|Arabs}} speak,
And {{p|Hebrews}}, and {{p|Assyrians}} of yore,
{{p|Akkadian}}, {{p|Aramaic}}, at peak;

{{p|Amharic}} and {{p|Tigrinya}} and the speech
Of {{p|Maltese}}, grown from {{p|Arabic}}, and known
On one sea-island; all, within the reach
Of early {{c|1876|J}}, are children of its own.

Above them is the broader family,
{{p|Afroasiatic}}: {{p|Egyptian}}, and
{{p|Berber}}, {{p|Cushitic}}, by the {{p|Horn}}'s own sea,
{{p|Chadic}} in the central {{p|African}} land:

A tree whose branches span two lands, immense,
And {{c|1876|J}} the house that speaks its speech, the yeast
Of all {{p|Semitic}} tongues, and all its sense,
From {{p|Africa}} unto the far {{p|Near East}}.

{{p|Mesopotamia}}: the land that lies
Between the {{p|Tigris}} and {{p|Euphrates}}; there
The city first began, beneath old skies,
And there {{p|Ur}}'s floodplain ran, its fields and air;

The ziggurat of {{p|Eridu}} was reared;
{{p|Uruk}} dug its canals; and, rise and fall,
{{x|Sargonid}} kingdoms, with their walls, appeared,
Three thousand years of the old world in all.

{{p|Akkadians}} and {{p|Babylon}}, the proud
{{p|Assyrians}}, each nation in its place
Along {{p|Tigris-Euphrates}}, and allowed
Their wars, their kingdoms, and their laws' long race;

And {{c|1876|J}} is the sign of the first {{p|Near East}},
Where the first city stood, where, quick on clay,
The first arithmetic was scratched; the feast
Of cuneiform, of writing, that day;

Where first of epic poems, and the best,
Was {{c|1913|Gilgamesh}}, who wrestled with his grief,
Who crossed the waters of the dead, his quest,
And lost {{c|1914|Enkidu}}, and found no relief:

And {{c|1914|Enkidu}}, the friend of his own heart,
Who met the bull of heaven. All of it,
The ancient writing, and the {{p|Sumer}} art,
By {{c|1876|J}}-born scribes, who left no name, was writ:

Invention of the written word; the first
Accounting tablet; contracts; and the hand
That penned the marriage; and the law's own thirst;
First dynastic history of the land.

That literate civilization, laid
Along {{p|Tigris-Euphrates}}, is the debt
The human project owes to {{c|1876|J}}, and made
Its contribution, which it pays us yet.

On the dry peninsula, {{c|1907|J1}} bore
A parallel and separate way: the tent,
The caravan, the dice, the desert lore,
The poems of the {{c|1915|Bedouin}}, and bent

Their genealogies, they kept in rhyme;
The desert poetry; and, long and slow,
{{c|1907|J1}}'s descent through all the length of time,
The bliss and hardship that the sand would show,

The tribe, the camel's rhythms, and the guide
Of stars that lead across the trackless bars
Of dune: {{c|1907|J1}} inherited it, wide
Across the sand, beneath the desert stars.

Meanwhile the {{c|1908|J2}} {{p|Near East}} world would grow
Through rack and ruin, and rebuild, and rise;
And {{c|1876|J}} would build the cities, and would know
The written word, beneath the crescent's skies,

The heir of the old hunting folk, who learned,
By meeting with the {{c|1873|G}}-farmers, to dwell
In cities; for the {{c|1876|J}}-born men had turned
To {{p|Uruk}}, {{p|Ur}}, and {{p|Eridu}} as well,

And piled the bricks of clay into the sky:
The ziggurat of {{p|Ur}} began its slow
And patient climb; {{c|1920|Inanna}}'s temple, high;
The first of kings, who came their crowns to know;

The first of scribes were trained; the first priests made
The temples holy; and the cities spoke
{{p|Sumerian}}, alone, and, unafraid,
{{c|1921|Akkadian}}, {{p|Semitic}}, of the folk.

{{c|1907|J1}}: the desert; and the camel; and
The poem, long before the pen at all,
Within the dry, the trackless, open sand;
{{c|1908|J2}}: the river; city; and the call

Of tablet and of scribe, whose careful fears
And joys set down the spoken word; and they,
Together, they are {{c|1876|J}}, through all the years,
And the {{p|Semitic}} world; and this, today,

Is all the chapter: the {{p|Near Eastern}} sign,
Through six millennia of layered reign,
The token and the proof of one long line
Of civilized succession, and its train;

The house of {{c|1876|J}}, of the {{p|Near East}}, the line
From {{c|1834|Adam}} unto {{c|977|Abel}}, and through {{c|308|Seth}};
The {{c|1876|J}} men wrote it first; they wrote it fine;
They wrote it down, and write it still, with breath.

And when a modern {{c|1876|J}}, who can't forget,
{{p|Israeli}}, {{p|Saudi}}, {{p|Yemeni}}, or one
{{p|Syrian}}, finds a fascination yet
In writings that his grandfathers had done,

It is an echo of what he will keep
And carry: written sign of signed descent,
Whose first inscriptions, pressed in clay, lie deep
In crescent-land, where all mankind's ascent

Began, at founding of the mind. And so,
{{c|1876|J}}: the {{p|Semitic}}; and the writing's store,
Which all the world still reads; and, far below,
The tablets lie in clay, as long before,

Beneath the crescent's ancient sky, where they
Were pressed by hands that wrote it first, and plain;
And there the chapter closes, on its clay,
Where all the tablets of the {{c|1876|J}} remain.


# Chapter 138: H, L, T — The Indus Valley

Three houses share the {{p|Indus}}: {{c|1874|H}}, and {{c|1878|L}},
And {{c|1886|T}}; not near in blood, but in one land
They built one people's cities, and they dwell
Together in the valley that they planned.

{{p|Harappa}} and {{p|Mohenjo-daro}} stood,
{{p|Dholavira}}, {{p|Rakhigarhi}}: the stream
Of {{p|Indus}} and {{p|Saraswati}}, the good
Brown water ran, and fed the farmer's dream.

Two thousand years their cities stood and grew,
With forty thousand souls in each, and more;
The streets were laid in grids, and ran straight through,
And faced the four directions, door by door.

The bricks were one in size, the weights were one,
The drains ran hidden under street and lane,
And no one built so well beneath the sun
For three millennia, nor would again.

The houses had their water, and the baths
Were great and public, holy, and were clean;
And on the seals, and on the market paths,
Their writing ran, in signs that all had seen.

They spoke the speech the {{p|Dravidian}} south
Still speaks today, the mother of its tongue;
Their names were spoken by the mother's mouth,
Their songs were sung, as all good songs are sung.

Their god was {{x|Pashupati}}, lord of beasts,
Who sat in yoga, horned, upon the seal;
And he is {{c|1340|Shiva}} now; their bathing feasts,
Their goddess and their lingam, where men kneel.

The {{c|1923|Priest-King}} in his robe of trefoil stars,
The {{c|1924|Dancing Girl}} in bronze, with hand on hip,
The terracotta mothers, and the jars,
The seals of trade upon the merchant ship.

Of India's houses, {{c|1874|H}} is the great,
The largest, {{c|1925|Haplogroup H}}; and his hand
Built {{p|Mohenjo-daro}}'s streets, set the weight,
And lit the lamps, and sealed the goods of land.

And {{c|1878|L}}, of {{c|1926|Haplogroup L}}, is the strong
In the south and west, {{p|Dravidian}} kin;
His sons went to the {{p|Caucasus}} along,
And {{p|Central Asia}}'s steppes they settled in.

And {{c|1886|T}}, of {{c|1927|Haplogroup T}}, took the sea,
The sailor house, whose ships went far and wide
To {{p|Arabia}}, the {{p|Swahili}} quay,
The {{p|Horn of Africa}}, and the far tide.

He joined the {{p|Indus}} to the {{p|Arab}} shore,
And to the {{p|Horn}}, in one long loop of trade,
Before the kings, and many years before
Their realms arose; and so the bond was made.

Then {{p|Saraswati}} dried, and the monsoon
Shifted its rains, and slowly, year by year,
The cities emptied, not at once, but soon
The people scattered, far, and far, and near.

They did not die, but scattered to the plain,
And stayed, and mixed, and in {{p|Karachi}} still,
{{p|Mumbai}} and {{p|Delhi}}, walk their sons again,
Their sons, of {{c|1874|H}} and {{c|1878|L}} and {{c|1886|T}}, who fill

The whole subcontinent from shore to shore;
Their cities sleep, their streets are laid in stone,
Their god sits on the seal, as long before,
And still their blood is in the nation's bone.

So honor {{c|1874|H}}, and {{c|1878|L}}, and {{c|1886|T}}, the three
Who built the {{p|Indus}} cities, grid and bath,
The seal, the weight, the drain, the trade by sea,
And left their sons to walk the long-worn path.


# Chapter 139: N — The Uralic Peoples

And {{c|1880|N}} walked north. While from the house of {{c|1929|NO}}
His brothers turned to eastward rice and rain,
{{c|1880|N}} went the other way, through ice and snow,
Into {{p|Siberia}}'s long, frozen plain.

Through taiga winters, through the tundra's white,
To where the reindeer graze, the world's far rim,
He walked; the {{p|Urals}} and the {{p|White Sea}}'s light,
From {{p|Bering Strait}} to {{p|Baltic}}, all knew him.

The forest dweller, fisher of the lake
Whose ice he cut, the herder of the deer,
He spoke the tongue {{p|Uralic}} peoples make,
And keep, and speak, and pass from year to year.

And still today, where all of {{p|Europe}} speaks
The tongues of other houses, {{c|1880|N}} has kept
His own: in {{p|Finland}}, by the {{p|Baltic}}'s creeks,
In {{p|Estonia}}, where his fathers slept.

The {{p|Sami}} herd their reindeer in the snow
Of {{p|Lapland}}; and the far {{p|Samoyeds}} still roam
{{p|Yamal}}'s long shore, where all the cold winds blow,
And keep the speech of {{c|1880|N}}, and keep their home.

And in the heart of {{p|Europe}}, far from kin,
The {{p|Magyars}} speak it, fifteen million strong;
Their fathers rode from {{p|Great Hungary}}, in
The {{p|Urals}}' reach, and brought their tongue along.

Their nearest kin, on the {{p|Ob River}}'s banks,
Two thousand miles to east; and yet the tongue
Held whole, among the other peoples' ranks,
As island in the sea, and still is sung.

And {{c|1931|Väinämöinen}} is their singer old,
The ancient wizard, eldest of the wise;
{{c|1932|Ilmarinen}}, smith, who forged the bold
{{p|Sampo}}, the mill of grain and salt and prize.

The {{p|Sampo}} grinds out grain, and salt, and gold;
And in {{p|Karelia}} the songs are sung
Of these, the heroes and the gods of old,
The {{p|Kalevala}}, sung in the northern tongue.

So honor {{c|1880|N}}, who walked into the cold,
Whose {{c|1933|Haplogroup N}} is the reindeer line,
The forest's fisher, singer, and the old
Unconquered speech, still spoken, still his sign.


# Chapter 140: O — Rice Agriculture and East Asia

While {{c|1880|N}} walked north into the taiga's snow,
His brother {{c|1881|O}} walked south, and southeast, down
To river valleys where the waters flow,
The {{p|Yangtze}} and the {{p|Yellow River}}'s brown.

And there he made the paddy: low wet ground,
Flooded with care, the water held in hand,
Where rice, the water-grain, was sown and found
To feed ten times the mouths of the dry land.

As {{c|1873|G}} made wheat upon the Crescent's field,
So {{c|1881|O}} made rice; the second farming came
From him, and all the {{p|Asian}} lands would yield
The grain he grew, and carry still his name.

At {{p|Hemudu}}, at {{p|Liangzhu}}, and the shore
Of {{p|Majiabang}}, the first farmers stood
Some seven thousand years ago, and more,
And raised their villages of reed and wood.

From there the rice went north, where millet grew
Upon the {{p|Yellow River}}'s northern plain,
And south to {{p|Vietnam}} and {{p|Thailand}}, through
{{p|Cambodia}}, and filled the deltas' grain.

And east to {{p|Korea}} and {{p|Japan}} it came,
Where sons of {{c|1850|D}}, the {{c|1934|Jōmon}}, long had dwelt;
And from the meeting rose the {{c|1935|Yayoi}} name,
And in one people both their bloods were felt.

Five tongues are carried in the house of {{c|1881|O}}:
{{p|Sino-Tibetan}}, {{p|Austronesian}} speech,
{{p|Austroasiatic}}, {{p|Kra-Dai}}, and slow
And {{p|Hmong-Mien}} of the highlands, out of reach.

On the {{p|Yellow River}}, under {{p|Shang}}'s kings,
The scribes cut signs on bone and on the shell;
And from those signs the written {{p|Chinese}} springs,
Still written now, unbroken, read as well.

The longest written thread of humankind,
Four thousand years, the same land and the same,
The bowl of rice, the table, intertwined
With all the generations of his name.

And {{c|1881|O}}'s sons took to the sea from {{p|Taiwan}},
Through {{p|Philippines}} and {{p|Indonesia}}'s isles,
Out on the wide {{p|Pacific}}, on and on,
In outrigger canoes across the miles.

By star and swell and flight of birds they steered
To {{p|Samoa}}, {{p|Tonga}}, {{p|Tahiti}}'s far,
{{p|Hawaii}}, {{p|Easter Island}}, and appeared
At last in {{p|New Zealand}}, beneath the star.

The {{p|Maori}}, the {{p|Hawaiians}}, and the rest,
{{p|Samoans}}, all are {{c|1881|O}}'s, who crossed the land,
And then the largest ocean, east and west,
Till each far island knew the sailor's hand.

So honor {{c|1881|O}}, the paddy-builder, he
Who gave the rice, the script, the sail, the oar;
{{c|1937|Haplogroup O}}, the house that, by the sea
And river, feeds a quarter, and yet more.

---

# Taurus (6宮) - Days 141-168


# Chapter 141: P at Baikal — Paikal

In the deep {{p|Siberian}} winter came
{{c|1938|Haplogroup P}}, unto {{p|Lake Baikal}}'s shore,
The deepest lake on earth, and of the same
Old crack the earth had opened long before.

Twenty-five million years the rift grew wide,
A mile and more in depth, and filled with rain;
A fifth of all earth's water fresh inside
That single crack, beneath the taiga's reign.

There swim the omul and the nerpa seal,
The only seal that lives where waters freeze;
The {{p|Evenki}} and the {{p|Buryat}} kneel
And beat the shaman's drum beside its seas.

And here came {{c|1882|P}}, the father of the two,
Of {{c|1883|Q}} and {{c|1884|R}}, called {{c|1939|Paikal}} by the lake,
Whose fathers, since the strait, had wandered through
{{p|Eurasia}}'s length; and here they paused, to take

Their breath beside the ice, and ask: which way?
Two answers came. The first was east, to walk
The dry land of {{p|Beringia}}, which lay
Dry then, where now the strait's cold waters talk.

And those who walked it east were {{c|1883|Q}}, and they
Crossed to the {{p|Americas}}, and then spread
From the {{p|Aleutians}} all the long, long way
Down to {{p|Tierra del Fuego}}, far ahead.

The {{p|Inuit}}, and the nations of the south,
The peoples of that whole new world, are {{c|1883|Q}}'s,
And carry him in blood, and in the mouth
Of all their elders telling the old news.

The second answer was the west: to turn
And run back on the road the fathers came,
Through {{p|Central Asia}}, to the grass, to learn
{{p|Pontic-Caspian}} steppe; and {{c|1884|R}} his name.

{{c|1884|R}} is the boomerang, the line that went
As far as it could east, and then came back;
And all of {{p|Europe}}, {{p|India}}, are sent
Of {{c|1884|R}}, his sons, who walk along his track.

And near {{p|Irkutsk}}, at {{p|Mal'ta}}, lay a child,
Four years of age, of {{c|1884|R}}'s house, near its root,
Still at {{p|Baikal}}; and in his blood were filed
Both roads at once, the seed and the far fruit:

The {{p|Navajo}} and {{p|Cherokee}} are kin
To him, the {{p|Inca}} too, and in the west
{{p|Lithuanian}} and the {{p|Swede}}: within
That buried child both roads already rest.

The lake is there today; the taiga lays
Its snow upon the shore; the drums are played
Beside the water; through the ice, always,
The nerpa rise to breathe in ice's shade.

So honor {{c|1882|P}}, who stood upon the ice
And watched his sons go into dusk, the two:
{{c|1883|Q}} to the east, {{c|1884|R}} west; and both suffice
To people half the world, as now they do.

{{c|1939|Paikal}}, the deepest water, and the stone
Of the crossroads, where one line went both ways;
The stars, the ice, the silence, and alone
The father, in {{p|Siberia}}'s long days.


# Chapter 142: Manu and Yemo — R and the Yamnaya

And {{c|1884|R}} came back. From {{p|Lake Baikal}}'s cold shore
He turned and walked the long road to the west,
Across the taiga, and the {{p|Urals}}, for
The sea of grass, where he would come to rest.

From the {{p|Carpathians}} to the {{p|Altai}}, wide,
The {{p|Pontic-Caspian steppe}}; there he stayed,
And there his sons were born, and at his side
His two sons grew, the house that {{c|1884|R}} had made.

His sons were {{c|1940|Manu}} and {{c|1941|Yemo}}, the twins,
The houses {{c|1928|R1a}} and {{c|1942|R1b}};
And here the story of the world begins,
When {{c|1940|Manu}} offered {{c|1941|Yemo}} up; and he

Was slain, the first of all; and then the whole
Of the world's order rose from {{c|1941|Yemo}}'s frame:
His head became the sky, the sun's bright bowl
His eyes, and moon; his bones, the mountains came;

His blood, the rivers; and from him the kind
Of every man: the priest came from his head,
The fighter from his chest, and, so designed,
The farmer from his loins, the land to tread,

The servant from his feet; the cattle, too,
Came from his flesh; and so the world was made
From that first sacrifice, and it holds true:
The order of the world from {{c|1941|Yemo}} laid.

The north calls {{c|1941|Yemo}} {{c|1944|Ymir}}, and it calls
{{c|1940|Manu}} {{c|1943|Mannus}}; {{p|India}}'s {{c|1945|Yama}} died
The first of men, and rules the dead's dark halls,
And {{c|1940|Manu}} there outlived the flood's great tide.

And on the steppe they tamed the horse; and then
A man on horseback crossed in one bright day
What walking took a week; the herds, the men,
The wars, now moved with speed none could gainsay.

And so the {{p|Yamnaya}} rose, riders, those
Who herded cattle on the grass, and raised
The {{p|kurgan}} mounds above their dead in rows
On the {{p|Pontic-Caspian}} lands they grazed.

And out they rode, in every way they went:
West to {{p|Europe}}, {{c|1942|R1b}} to the west,
{{c|1928|R1a}} to the east, as they were sent,
Brought {{p|Corded Ware}} and {{p|Beaker}}, and the rest.

And so the men of {{p|Europe}} stand in three:
The house of {{c|1875|I}} below, of {{c|1873|G}} between,
Of {{c|1884|R}} above; {{p|Sardinia}}, by sea,
Keeps {{c|1873|G}}, and in the north the {{c|1875|I}} is seen.

South, through {{p|Central Asia}}, {{c|1928|R1a}} rode
To {{p|India}} with chariot and song,
And with the house of {{c|1874|H}} and {{c|1878|L}} abode,
And they were one, the {{p|Vedas}}' holy throng.

There it became {{p|Sanskrit}}, and in {{p|Iran}}
{{p|Avestan}}; and {{p|Tocharians}}, far east,
In {{p|Tarim}}'s sands, the farthest of the clan,
Left red-haired dead, and kept the steppe's old feast.

And half of all who live, today, still speak
The tongue of {{c|1884|R}}, from {{p|Ireland}} to {{p|Nepal}}:
The {{p|Romance}} tongues, {{p|Germanic}}, {{p|Slavic}}, {{p|Greek}},
{{p|Armenian}} and {{p|Celtic}}, Persian, all.

To {{p|Cucuteni}}'s painted towns there came
The riders; and the farmers' daughters wed
The sons of {{c|1884|R}}, and in one house, one name,
The steppe and the old {{p|Europe}} both were bred.

So honor {{c|1884|R}}, the boomerang, who came
Back from the east, and tamed the horse, and rode;
And honor {{c|1940|Manu}}, {{c|1941|Yemo}}, and their name,
The twins, the sacrifice, the world's first code.


# Chapter 143: E — Returns to Africa

And {{c|1861|E}} came back. {{c|1947|Haplogroup E}} had crossed
The {{p|Bab al-Mandab}} once with {{c|1851|Noah}}'s band,
And wandered {{p|Eurasia}}, but was not lost:
He turned, and walked back to his fathers' land.

His brothers, {{c|1850|D}} and {{c|1849|C}} and {{c|1862|F}}, went on,
To {{p|Japan}}, to {{p|Tibet}}, the far-off lands,
To {{p|Australia}}, the steppe; but he was gone
Back south, alone of all the outbound bands.

North from {{p|Yemen}}, to the {{p|Levant}} he came,
Then south again through {{p|Sinai}}, past the sea
At {{p|Suez}}, into {{p|Egypt}}, and the same
The green {{p|Nile Valley}}, where his sons would be.

And then across the whole {{p|Sahara}}, green
In those days, lakes and rivers, grass and game,
Where sand lies now; and all the lands between
He filled, from west to east, and gave his name.

{{p|North Africa}}, the west, the east, he filled,
And took the river valleys and the plain,
The grass, and all the lands, as he had willed;
And there his house grew great, and there would reign.

He did not find the land an empty place:
The houses that had never left were there,
The {{c|1836|A}} and {{c|1842|B}}, the {{c|1837|San}} and {{c|1838|Mbuti}} race,
In {{p|Kalahari}} sands and forest air.

They kept the desert and the forest's deep,
And {{c|1861|E}} the grass; and of the men today
In {{p|Africa}}, the most are his, to keep
His house, from north to south, in every way.

His {{p|Bantu}} sons{{fn|The house E-V38, also called E1b1a.}} rose where the two lands meet,
{{p|Cameroon}} and {{p|Nigeria}}, and spread
Their tongue to east and south, on many feet,
Till half the continent spoke what they said.

{{p|Swahili}}, {{p|Zulu}}, {{p|Kikuyu}}, the speech
{{p|Kinyarwanda}}: all are of one tongue,
First {{x|Proto-Bantu}}, spoken in the reach
Of that small homeland when the house was young.

And in the north his other houses dwell:{{fn|E-M81 among the Berbers; E-M78 in Egypt and the Horn.}}
The {{p|Berbers}} of {{p|Morocco}} and the sand
Of {{p|Libya}}, {{p|Algeria}} as well,
{{p|Tunisia}}; the {{p|Egyptians}} of the land

By the {{p|Nile}}; the {{p|Ethiopians}}, too,
{{p|Eritreans}}, {{p|Somalis}} of the {{p|Horn}};
And {{c|1861|E}} and {{c|1876|J}}, the houses old and true,
Share {{p|Afroasiatic}}, sisters born.

His sons were the {{p|Egyptians}}, who of old
Raised up the pyramids, and to the sun
Gave disks, and gods with heads of beasts, and told
The soul's long journey when its life was done.

And far across the sea, in lands today
Of the {{p|Americas}}, his sons are found,
And there, too, {{c|1861|E}} has made his house and way,
And stands upon that far and foreign ground.

So honor {{c|1861|E}}, who walked away and came
Back home, the one whose road went out and in:
The door swung both ways; and the house's name
Is {{p|Africa}}'s, where all of us begin.


# Chapter 144: Malta — The Oldest Temples

And now the builders of the temples rise,
The first of them, a people without name;
They kept no writing, but beneath their skies
They raised their gods' first houses all the same.

On a small dry isle in the middle sea,
{{p|Malta}}, some few thousand farmers at most
Raised temples out of limestone, standing free,
The oldest on the earth, before the host

Of {{p|Egypt}} piled its pyramids, before
The ziggurats of {{p|Sumer}}, and ahead
Of {{p|Stonehenge}}: they began, in days of yore,
Thirty-six hundred B.C.E., and spread

For {{p|Ġgantija}} and {{p|Ħaġar Qim}}, and for
{{p|Mnajdra}} and {{p|Tarxien}}, out of bedrock's hold
They cut out blocks of fifty tons, and bore
Them with no wheel or metal, strong and bold.

They left no name for themselves, or for one
Of any gods they served; and what they keep
Is stone and sherd and bone, and, one by one,
The little figures, seated or asleep:

The {{p|Fat Lady}}, broad of hip and of thigh,
In clay and limestone, singular in art
In {{p|Europe}}'s {{p|Neolithic}}, the reply,
{{p|Malta}}'s idiom, to an older heart:

The mother {{c|1900|Marija Gimbutas}} found
Beneath Old {{p|Europe}}, ere the horsemen came;
{{p|Venus of Willendorf}} on other ground;
{{p|Cucuteni-Trypillia}}'s clay: the same

Great mother, and the same unbroken line.
But nowhere else did that devotion raise
Such stone. Look at the temples' own design,
The shape they kept through all their building days:

Paired lobes along a central passageway,
A kidney or a clover in the plan,
The entrance on the long axis; they lay
Before each room the uprights lintels span:

The trilithon, a thousand years ahead
Of {{p|Stonehenge}}. The carved spirals on the walls,
The plant, the beast, the pillar-pairs that lead
As gateways of the world; and in the halls,

Figurines, ash of the ritual fire,
The bones of offered beasts beneath the floor.
A thousand years the isle fed the choir
Of builders. Then the builders were no more.

Then, near twenty-five hundred B.C.E.,
The temples stood, and none would tend them more;
No war, no burning, and no enemy;
So ended temple-building, and its lore.

The {{x|Bronze Age}} settlers who came later on
Kept no remembrance of the builders' name;
The isle, ringed by the sea, was spent and gone:
Its soil worn thin, its forests felled for flame

And moving stone, until the land that fed
Some thousands of the builders could not feed
Them more; not with a bang, they starved or fled,
Or thinned away, in slow decline and need.

The temples stood upon the windy rise
Four thousand years, empty, without a stir,
And stand there still, beneath the island skies,
And are, today, the very thing they were.

So honor them, the first ones in the line
After {{p|Göbekli Tepe}}, where hunters came
To gather at the stones; here, at the shrine,
The settled farmer laid his harvest's claim.

Foraging gave way to the field; the feast
Gave way to the god's standing house of stone;
Here, for the first time known, a people ceased
To keep back anything; their surplus, grown

Each year, went to the temples, till the land
Gave out. No palace and no city wall,
No fortress: only temples, by each hand.
They built for their gods, and that was the all.

The temple, then, is elder than the town,
As at {{p|Göbekli Tepe}} it had been shown,
Greater for thousands of years; none laid down
A purer bond of faith to work in stone.

In one narrow sense, they were most devout
Of any people in the human line;
And so the warning: if the work runs out
Ahead of field and harvest, then the shrine

Devours the hands that raise it. The wrong
Is not the temple; building can outrun
The ground beneath it; and the isle, ere long,
Was stripped, its trees and fields and harvest done.

Small island, fervent faith, the building spree,
And then the crash, and then the island's fall:
{{p|Malta}} was first, a warning, as we see,
That few who came thereafter heard at all.

Was this a tragedy, or was it great?
Both, without laughter and without a blame;
And each of them, the two, has equal weight;
And so we tell them both, and both the same:

The temples splendid, and the builders dead;
Their gods remembered now by none who live;
The sacred turned to ruin; in its stead
The ruin turned memorial. They give

Us all we have: the stones upon the hill,
The spirals and the lobes, the wind that blows
Along the empty corridors; and still,
In {{p|Valletta}}, glassed, the {{p|Fat Lady}}'s pose.

Honor them: builders who built past their store;
The priests who led the work; the women's hands
That shaped the mother out of clay; the corps
Of farmers whose surplus fed stone, till lands

Ran out: the whole people that set the shrine
Above itself, and perished by the choice.
{{p|Malta}}: first temple people in the line
Since {{p|Göbekli Tepe}}; the first warning voice.

The first loss: in the human age, the first
Civilization whose remembered name
Is gone, its people scattered and dispersed,
With none of all who live its stones to claim.


# Chapter 145: The Old Kingdom — Pyramids at Giza

While {{p|Malta}} spent itself upon its isle,
A greater people on a greater stream
Began to build, along the {{p|Nile}}'s long mile,
At such a scale as none had dared to dream.

The sons of {{c|1861|E}} had dwelt beside the {{p|Nile}}
Long ages: {{p|Badari}}, {{p|Naqada}}'s clay,
Their pots, their copper, and the signs whose style
Grew into hieroglyphs; and on their way

They joined the {{p|Two Lands}} under one, the thin
Long valley, and the {{p|Delta}}'s spreading fan,
Thirty-one hundred B.C.E.; and in
That union, {{c|1960|Menes}}' kingship then began.

And {{c|1960|Menes}} is {{c|1961|Narmer}}, shown on the stone
Of his great palette, first of them to reign;
And then the scribes, the god-king on his throne,
The tax, the grain, the order of the plain.

Then {{c|1962|Djoser}} at {{p|Saqqara}} built the first
Great house of stone, the {{p|Step Pyramid}}, made
By {{c|1963|Imhotep}}, the builder, priest, well-versed
In healing, who was honored and obeyed.

A tomb laid flat, then raised in stages high,
Two hundred feet, and fifteen acres wide,
The first great work of stone in years gone by,
The sign of all to come, the builders' pride.

And then {{c|1964|Sneferu}} raised three: at {{p|Meidum}} one
That fell in part; {{p|Bent Pyramid}}, whose slope
Was changed midway; the {{p|Red Pyramid}}, done
Smooth-sided, true, the first fulfilled great hope.

And then his son, {{c|1965|Khufu}}, at {{p|Giza}} raised
{{p|Great Pyramid}}, four hundred eighty feet,
Two million stones and more, his name thus praised,
The tallest work of human hands complete.

Its faces true to north and east and west,
The King's and Queen's rooms, the Gallery's height,
The shafts that point to stars; and, at the crest,
The soul of the dead king would take its flight

Up through the stone, to join the northern stars
That never set, a star himself on high;
The pyramid his road, and nothing bars
The king, once dead, from climbing to the sky.

His son, {{c|1966|Khafre}}, built the second, and set
On higher ground, so both seem equal-tall,
And carved the {{p|Sphinx}}, the lion-man, that yet
Looks to the rising sun, and guards them all.

{{c|1967|Menkaure}} built the third and smallest; three
{{c|1965|Khufu}}, {{c|1966|Khafre}}, {{c|1967|Menkaure}}, there they stand,
The most known works of all humanity,
Still standing, after all, upon the sand.

The pharaoh is a god, {{c|1968|Horus}} in flesh;
And, dying, he becomes {{c|1166|Osiris}}, lord
Of the dead, judge of souls; his son, afresh,
Becomes {{c|1968|Horus}}; and so the throne's restored.

And so the pyramid is not a tomb
Alone, but cosmic order's very frame:
Built right, the king will rise and stars will bloom;
Built wrong, the world itself would fall to shame.

For twenty years his thousands worked the stone,
Not slaves, but fed and paid and healed, and sent
From every village, each crew named and known,
And then went home again, their service spent.

"{{c|1965|Khufu}}'s Drunkards," "{{c|1965|Khufu}}'s Friends," so they wrote
Their names upon the blocks, with jest and pride;
The quarries, copper mines, the grain, the boat,
The tax, the scribes, the first state far and wide.

But after {{c|1967|Menkaure}} the work grew less,
The later pyramids grew small and low;
The nomarchs rose; the king's strength, in distress,
Grew weak; and drought came, and the flood's great flow

Failed, as it never had; and famine then
Came; the {{p|Old Kingdom}} broke, and fell, and lay
In pieces, under rival kings and men;
And {{p|Akkad}}, in that drought, fell the same way.

The pyramids at {{p|Giza}} stand today,
Their faces weathered, all their casing gone;
And still at sunset, gold and orange, they
Glow as they glowed when {{c|1965|Khufu}}'s crews looked on.

So honor them: the god-kings and the stone,
The scribes, the crews who built and then went home;
The house of {{c|1861|E}}, who made the {{p|Nile}} his own,
And raised the first great works beneath the dome.


# Chapter 146: The Akkadian Empire

While pyramids were rising at the {{p|Nile}},
Across the {{p|Sinai}} and the desert sand,
Between the rivers, in another style,
The first of empires, ruled by command,

Of {{c|1969|Sargon of Akkad}}. Before his day
The cities stood apart, each with its wall:
{{p|Uruk}}, {{p|Ur}}, {{p|Lagash}}, {{p|Kish}}, and on their way
{{p|Umma}}, {{p|Nippur}}, and {{p|Eridu}}, and all,

Each with its king, its god, its watered field;
And they had made the writing pressed in clay,
The wheel, the bronze, the sixty that would yield
The hours and the angles we use today.

Their kings were {{c|1971|lugal}}, {{c|1972|ensi}}; and they fought
And traded, and one city ruled the rest
A while; and {{c|1913|Gilgamesh}} at {{p|Uruk}} wrought,
And {{c|1973|Lugalzagesi}} held {{p|Sumer}} best.

But none could hold for long. Then {{c|1970|Sargon}} came:
His mother laid him in a basket made
Of reeds, upon the river; with no name,
And a gardener raised him in the shade.

He rose as cupbearer to {{p|Kish}}'s king,
And then was king himself; his name, the true,
The rightful king; and he began to bring
The cities under him, and {{p|Akkad}} too,

And {{p|Elam}} to the east; and to the north
{{p|Syria}}, {{p|Anatolia}}, the shore
Of the great {{p|Upper Sea}}, where he went forth
And washed his weapons, as none had before;

And in the {{p|Lower Sea}} he washed them too,
The {{p|Persian Gulf}}; and none had ruled so wide;
And so the first empire came and grew,
And {{p|Akkad}} rose upon the river's side.

He reigned for fifty-six years; and his tongue,
{{p|Akkadian}}, of {{c|1876|J}}'s house, then became
The common speech; {{p|Sumerian}} was sung
Less and less, though it kept its sacred name.

His daughter, {{c|1974|Enheduanna}}, at {{p|Ur}}
Was {{c|1975|Nanna}}'s priestess; and she was the first
Whose name we know of all who wrote; and her
Great hymns to {{c|1920|Inanna}} still are rehearsed.

The {{p|Exaltation of Inanna}} sings
The goddess of both love and war, and still
Is read today; the daughter of the kings
Was the first author, writing by her will.

His sons, {{c|1977|Rimush}}, {{c|1978|Manishtushu}}, reigned,
And both met risings, and were slain; and then
His grandson {{c|1979|Naram-Sin}} the summit gained,
And named himself a god among all men,

The first who did it living; and, made known
On his great stele, he climbs up the height,
A god in war, his foes beneath him thrown,
The sun and stars above him, burning bright.

But {{c|1979|Naram-Sin}} laid waste {{c|1984|Enlil}}'s own shrine
At {{p|Nippur}}; and the gods, in wrath, called down
{{p|Gutians}} from the {{p|Zagros}} on his line,
And drought besides, on every field and town.

His son {{c|1980|Shar-Kali-Sharri}} fought in vain;
It fell; the {{p|Gutians}}, a mountain band,
Ruled for a hundred years with little gain,
Till {{p|Uruk}}, then {{p|Ur}}, drove them from the land.

Of {{c|1970|Sargon}} came the form of rule: the host
Of standing soldiers; governors per land;
One tongue, one weight, one road from coast to coast,
One tax, the {{c|1981|King of the Four Quarters}}' hand.

And {{c|1970|Sargon}} is remembered still, the king
Who rose from nothing, foundling, to the throne;
His capital, great {{p|Akkad}}, is a thing
Whose place is hidden; but his name is known.

So honor {{c|1970|Sargon}}, first to rule them all,
{{c|1974|Enheduanna}}, first to sign her song,
And {{c|1979|Naram-Sin}}, the god-king, and his fall,
And {{p|Akkad}}, first empire, lost, yet strong.


# Chapter 147: Stonehenge

Far on an isle at {{p|Europe}}'s western shore,
Before a word was written there, there rose
On {{p|Salisbury Plain}}, a stone work, and more:
{{p|Stonehenge}}, the ring of stones in ordered rows.

Three thousand years before the Common Age
It started as a ditch and bank, a round
Of three hundred and thirty feet, a stage
Of wooden posts upon the sacred ground.

The sons of {{c|1875|I}} and {{c|1873|G}} began it, those
Of hunters and of farmers, and they brought
The bluestones from {{p|Preseli}}, where they rose
In {{p|Wales}}, a hundred fifty miles, and wrought

A double circle of them at the heart,
Each two to four tons, eighty stones in all,
On sledge and log and raft, by strength and art,
Across the hills and coast, and raised them tall.

In twenty-five hundred B.C.E. came
The sarsens, twenty-five tons each, from north
Some twenty miles; and thirty, in one frame,
Held up a ring of lintels, joined henceforth;

And five great trilithons, a horseshoe, stood
Inside the ring; and tenon, mortise, cut
In stone, as carpenters would work in wood;
The lintels curved, the perfect circle shut.

And all of it was set to face the sun:
Midsummer's dawn above the {{p|Heel Stone}} rose,
Midwinter's sun set, when the year was done,
Between the greatest trilithon, to close.

And in that time the {{p|Beaker}} people came,
Of {{c|1942|R1b}}, who brought the steppe's own speech;
They took the isle, and kept the work the same,
And added to it, and enlarged its reach.

The bluestones, set in oval, they arranged
In the horseshoe, two thousand B.C.E.;
The people of the isle were new and changed,
And yet the work went on, as all could see.

Then, fifteen hundred B.C.E., the last
Of building ceased, and it was left complete,
The ditches silting, and some great stones cast
Down by the years, beneath the wind and sleet.

It was the center of a sacred land
Of mounds and henges, of the dead, the sky,
The ancestors, the year; from every hand
Of all the isle and over sea they'd lie

In death beside the stones, their ashes laid
Within its ring; the place that all agreed,
Above all others, where the work be made,
The axis of their world, and of their creed.

The temple first: the sacred place made one
The scattered people round it; and the new,
The {{p|Beaker}} folk, kept on the work begun,
And knew it holy, and they kept it too.

It stands on {{p|Salisbury Plain}}; and the sun
Of winter sets between the uprights still;
At solstice, crowds still gather, everyone,
To watch the sun rise there above the hill.

So honor them: the ones who moved the stone
From {{p|Wales}}, who raised the sarsens, and the new
Who kept the work, and those whose ashes, sown,
Lie in the ring; and all the pilgrims, too.

{{p|Stonehenge}}: the ring of stones, the solstice sign,
The calendar that still tells time today,
The work that outlived builders, tongue, and line,
And stands upon the plain at close of day.


# Chapter 148: Minoan Crete

While {{p|Stonehenge}} weathered on its windy plain,
And {{p|Egypt}} rose again from its dark years,
Upon an isle amid the middle main
A palace people reached their height: their spheres

Were {{p|Crete}}, the largest island of the sea
{{p|Aegean}}, and the {{p|Minoans}} were their kind,
Who wrote in {{p|Linear A}}, their own, free
From any other tongue that men could find.

From nineteen hundred B.C.E. they grew,
And flourished till the fifteen-hundreds came;
{{p|Knossos}}, {{p|Phaistos}}, {{p|Malia}}, {{p|Zakros}} too,
The palaces that held their wealth and name.

They had no walls; the palaces arose
Straight from the land, unguarded, open, free;
Their fleet kept them, and in the sea, their foes
Could never reach them: masters of the sea.

And on their walls the frescoes moved with life:
The dolphins, octopus, and flying fish,
Wild goats and lilies, crocus, and the knife
Of saffron-gatherers, and every wish

Of bull-leapers, priestesses, and the lines
Of bearers, offerings; and how they cared
For sea and land, the beasts, the plants, the vines,
And light-wells lit the halls, and air was shared.

At {{p|Knossos}} water ran, both hot and cold,
And flushed away, four thousand years ago;
Fifteen hundred rooms, many-storied, old,
Around a central court, ran to and fro,

A labyrinth, where corridors would wind
With no one axis; and the bull was there
On every altar, horns of every kind,
And in the maze, the {{c|1990|Minotaur}}'s own lair.

The mother goddess with her snakes was theirs,
In open bodice, holding up the two;
And priestesses, not priests, led all the prayers,
And her young consort died, and rose anew.

This was the old {{p|Europe}}'s great mother, kept
Upon an island, safe within the sea,
Through all the years when other peoples slept,
The fairest work of all the {{x|Bronze Age}} free.

And far they traded: {{p|Egypt}}, where they bore,
The {{c|1992|Keftiu}}, their gifts before the throne;
The {{p|Levant}}, {{p|Anatolia}}, the shore
Of {{p|Cyclades}} and {{p|Greece}}; and theirs alone

Was the {{p|Aegean}} for some hundred years,
A lake of {{p|Crete}}: the oil, the wine, the tin,
The copper, cloth, and pottery; their peers
Were none, so rich the palaces within.

Then, fifteen hundred B.C.E., there came
The fire of {{p|Thera}}, northward, far away,
The greatest burst of mountains, and its flame
Blew out the island's heart into the bay,

And left the crescent of {{p|Santorini}};
The ash fell over {{p|Crete}} and over all,
The wave struck at the northern shore; the sea
Rose, and the ports and fields came down to fall.

The palaces went on a while, and then,
Wounded, they faltered; {{p|Mycenaeans}} came,
The sons of {{c|1942|R1b}}, the mainland's men,
And took {{p|Knossos}}, and wrote, in their own name,

In {{p|Linear B}}, their {{p|Greek}} tongue, instead;
Yet the {{p|Minoan}} way was not undone,
But taken in, and in the new house bred,
The bull, the goddess, and the maze, as one.

The frescoes on the walls still show today
The bull-leapers, the saffron, and the sea,
The dolphins in the light-wells at their play,
The island's people, as they used to be.

So honor them: the palaces unwalled,
The mother and her snakes, the bull, the ships,
The priestesses, the saffron, and the called
{{p|Minoan}} tongue, still sealed upon their lips.


# Chapter 149: Yamnaya — The Steppe Breaks Europe

West of the steppe there lay a farming land,
The {{p|Cucuteni-Trypillia}}'s domain,
{{p|Romania}}, {{p|Moldova}}, and the grand
Black earth of {{p|Ukraine}}'s wide and fertile plain.

Seventeen hundred years their towns had stood,
The greatest of the {{p|Neolithic}} west,
{{p|Talianki}}, {{p|Maidanetske}}, of wood
And clay, with fifteen thousand souls, the best.

And every sixty years or eighty, they
Would burn their towns, as was their sacred rite,
And build anew upon fresh ground; and day
By day, their walls in painted spirals bright.

Their pottery was finest of them all,
Thin-walled, in red and white and black, with lines;
They knew the mother goddess, and no wall
Was built about their towns, nor war's designs.

In thirty-five hundred B.C.E. rode
The {{p|Yamnaya}} out of the east, the sons
Of {{c|1884|R}}, with bronze axe, horse, and wagon's load,
And came upon the towns of the old ones.

The sons of {{c|1884|R}} took wives from the old land,
The daughters of the goddess and the clay;
And so the towns were built no more; the hand
That painted spirals turned another way.

The corded ware, the battle-axe of stone,
The single grave, the rider's bones laid down;
The house of {{c|1884|R}} now held the land alone,
And of the two, one people and one crown.

The mother of the hearth, the goddess, wed
The father of the sky, and in his hall
She kept her rite; the spiral and the thread
Were woven with the wheel, one house for all.

Their tongue became the tongue of all the land,
And theirs the speech that {{p|Europe}} speaks today:
{{p|Celtic}}, {{p|Germanic}}, the {{p|Italic}}, and
The {{p|Slavic}} and the {{p|Baltic}}, all one way.

The {{p|Corded Ware}} went north; the {{p|Beaker}} west,
{{p|Iberia}}, to {{p|Britain}}, {{p|Ireland}}'s shore;
By twenty-five hundred, all of the rest
Of {{p|Europe}}, to the far {{p|Atlantic}} shore.

And others of the riders went to south
And east, to {{p|Anatolia}}, {{p|Iran}},
And on to {{p|India}}; from mouth to mouth
Their speech went with them, all the way they ran.

{{c|1928|R1a}}, {{c|1942|R1b}}, the fathers' line,
Are now the most of {{p|Europe}}'s men, and found
In {{p|India}} and in {{p|Iran}}; the sign
Of billions, {{p|Yamnaya}}'s, the whole world round.

And every {{p|European}} bears the two:
The mothers of the painted towns, the clay,
The goddess; and the riders, fathers, who
Came from the steppe; and both are there today.

So honor both: the towns that burned and rose,
The spiral and the goddess and the pot;
And {{p|Yamnaya}}, the horse, the wheel, and those
Who rode, whose speech the world has not forgot.


# Chapter 150: The Yellow Emperor

And east, along the {{p|Yellow River}}'s flow,
The house of {{c|1881|O}} had farmed since ancient days,
And slow, as yellow loess comes to grow,
They grew to one, by slow and patient ways.

Their founder, {{c|1999|Huangdi}}, of the yellow ground,
The {{c|1998|Yellow Emperor}}, the earth's own lord,
In twenty-seven hundred, he was crowned,
And taught them all the arts, and held the sword.

He made the bow, the arrow, and the cart,
The pots, the calendar, and in the war
The chariot that pointed south; the art
Of healing, in the {{p|Huangdi Neijing}}'s lore.

His wife, {{c|2000|Leizu}}, found silk: a cocoon fell
Into her tea, and as she drew it out,
The thread unwound, and wound, and wound as well,
And all the silk of {{p|China}} came about.

He fought {{c|2004|Chiyou}}, the rebel, bronze of head,
With horns, at {{p|Zhuolu}}, and he won the day,
And joined the tribes along the river's bed
Into one people, under his own sway.

With {{c|2005|Yandi}}, the Flame Emperor, he's one:
He is the father of the {{p|Han}}, who say
They are the children of {{x|Yanhuang}}, each son,
And keep him as their father to this day.

Before him were the {{p|Three Sovereigns}}: the first,
{{c|733|Fuxi}}, who taught the net, the fire, the food,
And the eight trigrams, the {{p|bagua}}, well-versed;
And {{c|2006|Nüwa}}, serpent-bodied, and her brood,

Who made the people out of yellow clay,
And when the heavens cracked, she patched the sky
With five-hued stones she melted on that day;
And {{c|2007|Shennong}} too, the {{c|2008|Divine Farmer}}, high

Of heart, who tasted every plant to see
Which fed, which healed, which killed; and so he taught
The farm, the herbs; and died at last when he
Took one too strong for all the cures he wrought.

With {{c|1308|Abraham}} and {{c|1940|Manu}}, so is he
The third of the {{x|Three Ancestors}} of all,
The fathers of mankind, the root, the tree
From which all peoples living grow up tall.

And every house that ruled the {{p|Yellow}} land
Claimed him as father; and his tomb today
In {{p|Shaanxi}} receives, at {{p|Qingming}}, the hand
Of those who rule, who come to bow and pray.

From him the script came down; on bone and shell
The {{p|Shang}} would cut it, and it is still read;
No other people's writing, kept so well,
Has run so long, and never once was dead.

So honor {{c|1999|Huangdi}}, of the yellow earth,
Who gave the arts, and joined the tribes in one,
The father of the {{p|Han}}, and of the birth
Of all mankind, beneath the yellow sun.


# Chapter 151: Neo-Sumerian Empire and Abraham

The {{p|Gutians}} were driven out; then rose
{{p|Ur}}, and {{c|2011|Ur-Nammu}} took the throne, and reigned;
He founded Ur's Third Dynasty; and those
Whose {{p|Sumer}} was restored, its might regained.

He made the oldest law; and long before
{{c|1919|Hammurabi}}'s, three centuries, the fine
Was most of it; but death was there in store
For murder, theft, and rape, the broken line.

He raised the {{p|Ziggurat of Ur}}, the stair
That climbs to {{c|1975|Nanna}}'s shrine, the moon-god's own,
The greatest temple of the land; and there
It stands today, in part, its tiers of stone.

Then {{p|Sumer}}'s writing flowered, the last time:
The {{p|King List}}, from before the flood, was made,
And {{c|1913|Gilgamesh}} grew longer, line and rhyme,
Before the old {{p|Sumerian}} would fade.

In this world {{c|1308|Abraham}} was born, in {{p|Ur}},
Called {{c|2012|Abram}} then; his tongue was of that land,
{{p|Akkadian}}; he saw the tower stir
The sky, and trade go out on every hand.

His father, {{c|2013|Terah}}, made the temple's gods
In images; and one day the son broke
What the shop made; and father, son, at odds,
Strove for the household's altar and its smoke:

Who keeps the rite: the shop that served the moon,
Or the son, who would light the flame himself,
With no carved go-between; and late or soon
The house was broken, image, shrine, and shelf.

Then {{p|Ur}} fell: {{c|2014|Ibbi-Sin}}, its final king,
Saw {{p|Amorites}} come from the desert sand,
And drought and famine; provinces would spring
Away from him; then {{p|Elam}}'s fighting band

Came down from {{p|Susa}}, sacked and burned {{p|Ur}}, bore
Off {{c|2014|Ibbi-Sin}} in chains to {{p|Susa}}; then
Did {{c|2015|Ningal}} weep for {{p|Ur}}, and evermore
Her {{p|Lament}} mourned her scattered folk and men.

And so then {{c|2013|Terah}} and his house went north,
For {{p|Ur}} was burned, along {{p|Euphrates}}' stream,
To {{p|Haran}}, on the trading road, and forth
No more; for {{c|2013|Terah}} died there, as a dream.

And there the call to {{c|1308|Abraham}} was heard:
To leave his country and his kin, and go,
And leave his father's house, at {{c|472|God}}'s own word,
To the land that he would be shown, and know.

He came, by road, to {{p|Sanliurfa}}'s plain,
Beside the hill where {{p|Göbekli Tepe}} lay,
The oldest temple, older than all reign;
{{c|1520|Melchizedek}} met him there on the way,

The priest-king, {{c|2017|George Gobeklius}}, the one
Of all the priests of that old temple-hill
Whose line ran back to when it had begun
With those who raised the pillars, and who still

Blessed {{c|1308|Abraham}}; and he gave to him then
A tithe; and so the oldest priesthood passed
Its blessing to the father of the men
Of the one {{c|472|God}}, from first of all to last.

Then south he went, to {{p|Canaan}}: {{p|Shechem}}, then
To {{p|Bethel}}, to the {{p|Negev}}; and he went
To {{p|Egypt}} in a famine, and again
Came back; from {{c|2016|Lot}}, his nephew, his way bent;

He rescued {{c|2016|Lot}} out of the four kings' hand;
He made the covenant with {{c|472|God}}, and won
The promised land; and on the mountain stand
He nearly gave up {{c|635|Isaac}}, his own son;

And died at a hundred seventy-five,
And in {{p|Machpelah}}'s cave, at {{p|Hebron}}, lay
Beside his {{c|2018|Sarah}}; and his sons alive
Would carry on his house from that same day.

His house was {{c|1876|J}}, of {{c|1907|J1}} and {{c|1908|J2}},
The desert and the city, joined in one;
For {{c|634|Ishmael}} became the {{c|1907|J1}}, the true
{{p|Arabian}} line; and {{c|635|Isaac}}, the son,

{{c|1908|J2}}, and {{p|Israel}}'s twelve tribes; and all
Who keep the one {{c|472|God}}'s faith are of his line,
He who heard, at {{p|Haran}}, his {{c|472|God}}'s own call,
And took the blessing of the oldest shrine.

So honor {{c|1308|Abraham}}, who fled from {{p|Ur}},
The burned, and met the last priest of the hill,
And took the blessing he would there confer,
The father of the one {{c|472|God}}'s faith and will.


# Chapter 152: Hammurabi — Law and the Old Babylonian Empire

When {{p|Ur}} had fallen, in the years since then,
{{p|Mesopotamia}} would break apart;
The {{p|Amorites}}, {{p|Semitic}}-speaking men,
Had trickled in, and came to play their part

Across the region as the ruling class;
{{p|Amorite}} kings took crowns in town on town,
{{p|Tigris-Euphrates}}' vale; and it would pass
That they held sway there, all the valley down.

Down in the south {{p|Isin}} and {{p|Larsa}} fought
For supremacy; {{p|Mari}}, in its spheres,
{{p|Eshnunna}}, {{p|Assur}}, each one, as it sought,
Carved out the north and east among their peers.

One small {{p|Amorite}} city-state, unknown
For long, began its rise: {{p|Babylon}}'s name
Is {{c|2020|Babilim}}, the {{p|Akkadian}}, known
As "Gate of {{c|472|God}}"; and long it stayed the same,

Was a provincial center, modest, long;
Its {{p|First Dynasty}}, near the time when we
Count nineteen hundred, came and made it strong;
Its sixth king made it an empire: he,

{{c|1919|Hammurabi}}. He held the throne about
Seventeen ninety-two, for forty-two
Years, to seventeen fifty; and throughout
Decisive, as his long reign carried through.

His first decades made sure, at home, his hold;
With neighbors he made allies, through the art
Of diplomacy; and, as kings of old,
Reformed the rule, laid temples; for his part

He led canals across the land. A king
By {{p|Mesopotamian}} kingship's ways,
Patient, methodical in everything;
Then, in his reign's second half, in those days,

He struck. A run of swift campaigns brought down,
One after one, the rivals: {{p|Larsa}} fell,
{{p|Eshnunna}}, {{p|Mari}}; and his realm, his crown,
By his reign's end, would come to grow and swell,

Larger than any realm since on the throne
{{c|1969|Sargon of Akkad}} sat, and long before;
He joined {{p|Tigris-Euphrates}} as his own,
By {{p|Babylonian}} rule, and no more

Torn; {{p|Old Babylonian}} rule was born.
His name is known today not for his war,
But for the law code, written, and not torn,
The {{p|Code of Hammurabi}}, which he bore:

Two hundred eighty-two laws, on a tall
Stele, seven and a half feet, whose face
Of black diorite, standing over all,
Took in {{p|Akkadian}} the wedge-marks' trace.

It stood in {{c|2021|Marduk}}'s temple; in the sun,
Of public places through the realm, as planned,
So citizens could see it, every one,
Their rights and obligations, understand.

And at the crown, {{c|1919|Hammurabi}} looks down,
And stands before the sun-god, {{c|2022|Shamash}}, lord
Of justice, and receives the law, the crown
Of law, from whose own hand the law is poured:

The king receives it from the hand divine,
The law as gift, not his own work, but sent
From heaven's will, the first in a long line,
Transcribed from heaven, as the heavens meant.

The god will give the law; the king will bring
It down to earth, the messenger; and all
Obey it, for the law's a sacred thing,
A cosmic order, which outranks the call

Of any human might or human sight.
And what the {{p|Code}} contains: the law laid clear,
{{p|lex talionis}}, made explicit, right,
"An eye for an eye," as its words appear:

If someone blinds another, his own eye
Is lost in kind; if one should break a bone
In another's body, his own, thereby,
Is broken: so the law is set in stone.

The punishments are graded, too, by class:
For nobles, more; for commoners, less weighed;
And harm to slaves, in law, would come to pass
As damage done to property, and paid.

It was, in its own day, a new display:
The law in writing, posted, town by town,
Throughout the realm, and there for all, the way
For every reader to read it, set down;

It checked the judges' arbitrary hand,
And magistrates'; protections, too, it made:
False charges drew a penalty; it planned
That witnesses must testify, and weighed

The evidence; for women, too, conveyed
Protections: marriage contracts; a set course
In divorce, and inheritance; and laid
On business, too, its comprehensive force:

Commercial contracts, partnerships, and shares,
The debts, and liability, and pains
For damage; and for all of these, it bears
A comprehensive frame, which it sustains,

The working of a complex urban place,
A whole commercial order, and its ground;
And it is of the oldest, in the race
Of codes, in human hands preserved and found

In full. {{c|2011|Ur-Nammu}}'s law code came before,
By three hundred years; {{p|Lipit-Ishtar}}'s, made
By {{p|Isin}}'s king; but {{c|1919|Hammurabi}}'s, more
Complete, preserved, is foremost, and is weighed

As the most whole of all. And it has passed
Its sign to every later code of law;
And still, today, its mark is holding fast:
Each written, public code, that all men saw.

And {{c|1919|Hammurabi}}, {{c|1308|Abraham}}'s own kin,
His cousin: both were {{c|1876|J}}, {{p|Semitic}} men;
Both came of {{p|Amorite}} migrations, in
The land reshaped, and both descended then

From one {{p|Semitic}} pool of forebears, spread,
Once {{p|Ur III}} had fallen, through the lands;
Two cousins of one time, of one house bred,
One tongue, one region, one moment, two hands.

Both, after {{p|Sumer}}, are the figures, then,
Of the {{p|Semitic}} rise within the land,
{{p|Mesopotamia}}'s; and both, as men,
Began traditions that would long, long stand.

And there's a lesson in the contrast, too:
{{c|1308|Abraham}} is a nomad, and he went
Out of the city, wandering it through,
And left its walls behind him for the tent;

While {{c|1919|Hammurabi}}, city-king, would build
The walls, and codify the urban law;
From {{c|1308|Abraham}} a faith, as heaven willed,
From {{c|1919|Hammurabi}}, law, which cities saw.

One's legacy, the worship of one god,
Whom none can see; the other's, the decree
That binds the city's people, and its rod;
Two ways civilization came to be.

Two cousins, where {{c|1907|J1}} and {{c|1908|J2}} part,
Each on another path: one with his sheep
Goes south, and seeks the desert's very heart;
The other reigns where brick-built ramparts keep

The city, gate-of-god. One shall become
Monotheism's patriarch; the code
The other's, which men copied; and the sum:
Both men who matter, each upon his road.

{{c|1919|Hammurabi}}'s empire did not last:
Succession struggles weakened {{p|Babylon}}
Within a generation, once he'd passed;
His son, {{c|2023|Samsu-iluna}}, then took on

Rebellions through the realm. Down in the south
The provinces seceded; and instead,
Where marshes spread, at the {{p|Persian Gulf}}'s mouth,
The {{p|Sealand Dynasty}} rose up, and led.

Then, in fifteen ninety-five B.C.E.,
{{p|Hittites}}, {{x|Indo-European}}, came down
From {{p|Anatolia}}, by their decree,
And raided {{p|Babylon}}, and sacked the town;

They carried {{c|2021|Marduk}}'s statue off; and down
Went {{p|Babylon}}'s great might, which none could mend;
And all the {{p|Old Babylonian}} crown
Was broken, though the statue, in the end,

Came back; a dynasty, the {{p|Kassites}}, came
To power; four centuries they would hold
The land, in looser rule, and not the same;
And {{p|Babylon}} remained a city, old,

Its age of rule was over; but the code,
His legacy, would last, and long, past all
The realm's collapse; was copied, read, and showed,
And studied, cited, after the realm's fall;

{{p|Mesopotamian}} kings, later, said
That they were his own legal heirs; the schools
Of scribes would teach his code, and it was read,
A text, a written text, of written rules;

And through the {{p|Near East}}, buried in the ground,
Its copies, from the later times, remain;
He'd done what {{c|1970|Sargon}} did, a template found
For later kings, but in law's own domain:

{{c|1970|Sargon}}, the first of emperors; and he,
{{c|1919|Hammurabi}}, the prototype of law,
The legislator; and, as time would see,
The realm fell; but the law outlived its awe.

And now it stands inside the {{p|Louvre}}, where
A traveler may stand and read it, keen,
As it once was: {{p|Akkadian}}, laid bare,
Cut in cuneiform, so clear and clean,

In the black diorite, the laws comprised,
Two hundred eighty-two, by which the whole
Of his realm stood in order, organized
And standing under his own just control.

The text's still legible; and of the great
Old monuments, it is among the best
Preserved of all the {{p|Near East}}; and its weight,
Its laws, still reach the codes of all the rest,

The modern nations' codes, and every one,
Tied still by chains of text and thought today.
{{c|1919|Hammurabi}} of {{p|Babylon}}, the son
Of {{c|1876|J}}, and {{c|1308|Abraham}}'s own kin; the way,

The {{p|Old Babylonian}} house's head
And emperor, the one through whom it flowed,
And {{p|Mesopotamia}}'s law, which led
To its first synthesis: the famous code.

And from that day it passed to every land,
And then through them to us, here, in our day.
The bearded king on black stele will stand
Before the sun-god, taking, as he may,

The law from him. The law is still to read;
The king, too, though the realm did not live on;
Black diorite still holds, and holds indeed,
{{c|1919|Hammurabi}}, the {{p|Code}}, and {{p|Babylon}}.


# Chapter 153: The Middle Kingdom

And {{p|Egypt}} rose again: the land had split,
{{p|Herakleopolis}} the north held, and south
{{p|Thebes}} slowly grew; and drought had weakened it,
And for a hundred years, from source to mouth,

The river ran divided; till, at last,
{{c|2025|Mentuhotep II}}, the mighty {{p|Theban}} king,
Defeated all the north, and made it fast
To one again: the {{p|Middle Kingdom}}'s spring.

For three centuries and a half it stood,
