And kept it from the heirs it could not rouse
To bend. And in five-sixty-eight came there

The {{c|2678|Lombards}}, into {{p|Italy}}, and took
The most of it from the usurper's hand;
Their kings took {{c|2679|Flavius}};{{fn|From Authari, king from 584 to 590, the Lombard kings of Italy took the name Flavius.}} and wrote the book,
The {{x|Edict of Rothari}}, {{x|Latin}}, planned

{{p|Roman}} law; and they came {{x|Arian}}, then
Turned {{x|Catholic}} with {{c|2680|Theodelinda}}; and
Seven-fifty-one, {{c|2681|Aistulf}} took again
{{p|Ravenna}}, seat {{c|2665|Theodoric}} had manned,

Back from the usurper's exarch; the heirs
Truer than {{c|2383|Justinian}}, these were they.
{{p|Rome}} never fell. The fall's a myth of theirs:
Four-seventy-six, set in his own day,

{{c|2682|Marcellinus}}, chronicler of the {{p|East}},{{fn|The year 476 as the end of the West first appears in the chronicle of Marcellinus Comes, written at the court of Constantinople in Justinian's time.}}
Whose lord would need a {{p|West}} fallen to take;
And {{c|2383|Justinian}} had the law all pieced,
Built {{c|2683|Hagia Sophia}}; and would break

The {{x|Academy}} in {{p|Athens}}, of nine
Hundred years; and the {{x|Platonists}} who fled
Came back from {{c|2605|Khosrow}} when the peace, a line
He wrote, set free their going home. He bled

The realm, with plague and the {{c|2596|Sassanid}} war.
So mark it: not to {{c|2649|Goths}} the {{p|West}} was lost;
Its last emperor it lost, not to war,
But to {{c|2383|Justinian}}; and, at its cost,

The faith of {{c|1497|Christ}} became what {{p|Rome}} would keep,
Defend, and hold; and under it, the same,
Unbroken, was the rite, and ran as deep;
The feasts, the incense, and the altar's flame:

The same rite stood in {{p|Rome}} under new names:
the temples were the churches or were stone,
the feasts went on, the incense and the flames,
the old {{p|Roman}} frame held what it had known.


# Chapter 190: Ethiopia

South of {{p|Egypt}}, past cataracts and {{p|Kush}},
Past {{p|Meroe}}'s high tombs, the highland rose,
{{p|Aksum}}, in {{p|Ethiopia}}; its push
Of trade, {{p|Adulis}}, where the {{p|Red Sea}} flows,

To {{p|Rome}}, {{p|Arabia}}, {{p|India}}; script
Was {{c|2630|Ge'ez}}, their tongue a {{x|Semitic}} one,
Kin to {{x|Arabic}}; and, crowned and equipped,
Their fourth-century king, {{c|2631|Ezana}}, won

Over to {{c|1497|Christ}} three-thirty, by the word
Of {{c|2632|Frumentius}}, who had, as a young boy,
Was shipwrecked there, and served the court, and stirred
Its trust; in {{p|Alexandria}}'s employ

Made bishop by {{c|2633|Athanasius}}, came
Back home, and preached; {{c|2631|Ezana}} turned; and so
{{p|Aksum}}, after {{p|Armenia}}, the same,
The second realm to take the faith, and grow.

And at {{p|Chalcedon}} in four-fifty-one
the bishops split on how the {{c|1497|Christ}} was made:
"Two natures," {{p|Rome}}; {{p|Alexandria}}, "one,"
and {{p|Aksum}}'s bishop, sent from there, obeyed.

It was one church that fought over a throne:
which patriarch would say the creed for all.
The {{c|2634|Copts}}, the {{c|2635|Syrians}} held to their own
with {{c|2636|Ethiopians}}, a single hall.

At {{p|Aksum}}, in the church of {{p|Mary}}, there
The {{c|2637|Ark of the Covenant}} still rests, brought
By {{c|2638|Menelik}}, of {{c|2189|Solomon}} the heir,
And {{c|2212|Sheba}}'s son: the {{x|Kebra Nagast}} taught

How {{c|2639|Sheba}}'s queen came to {{c|2189|Solomon}}, bore
His son, {{c|2640|Menelik}}, who went home, and took
The {{c|2641|Ark}} to his own land. And this is more
Than tale: it's true, as all the faithful look;

The kings of {{p|Ethiopia}} came down
From {{c|2189|Solomon}}, three thousand years, the line
Unbroken, crown to crown; and in the town
And hills, the {{c|2644|Beta Israel}} kept the sign

Of {{x|Torah}}, older than the {{x|Talmud}}'s word,
Alone in highland, true; and so they keep
Their faith. And {{p|Aksum}} waned, when it was heard
That {{x|Islam}} held the trade routes, broad and deep,

And moved its seat southward. So honor them:
The second realm of {{c|1497|Christ}}, the highland's crown,
The {{c|2641|Ark}} at {{p|Aksum}}, {{c|2189|Solomon}}'s own stem,
The queen of {{c|2212|Sheba}}'s son, who brought it down.


# Chapter 191: Arabia Before Islam

{{p|Arabia}}, ere {{c|1911|Muhammad}}, a quilt
Of tribes, oases, towns of trade, the tent
Of {{c|1915|Bedouin}}, the homes the {{c|2500|Jews}} had built,
And monks of {{c|1497|Christ}} who prayed where trade-routes went.

Two lines there were: {{c|1918|Qahtan}}, the south, the land
Of {{p|Yemen}}, come from {{c|2733|Joktan}}, {{c|2734|Eber}}'s son;
And {{c|1917|Adnan}}, of the north, of desert sand,
Of {{p|Hejaz}} and {{p|Najd}}, from {{c|634|Ishmael}}, the one

Of {{c|1308|Abraham}}, by thirty steps of birth;
Twelve sons, like {{c|2019|Jacob}}'s; through {{c|2736|Nizar}}, the line,
{{c|2737|Mudar}}, {{c|2738|Ilyas}}, then came the {{c|1916|Quraysh}} to earth,
To {{c|2739|Hashim}}'s clan, {{c|1911|Muhammad}}'s own, the sign

Of {{p|Mecca}}. And they kept gods: the most high
Was {{c|2740|Allah}}, maker, seldom prayed to; and
His daughters, {{c|2741|al-Lat}}, {{c|2742|al-Uzza}}, close by,
And {{c|2743|Manat}} too, were honored through the land.

Three hundred sixty images were kept
within the {{c|2744|Kaaba}}: gods of tribes, and they
were stars and homes, there where the pilgrims stepped;
set {{c|2745|Hubal}} chief, the god to whom they'd pray.

And some were {{c|2746|hanif}}, pure, who kept the one
{{c|472|God}} as {{c|1308|Abraham}} had kept, in no shrine
But his. {{c|2747|Qusay}}, of {{c|1911|Muhammad}}'s line, won
For the {{c|1916|Quraysh}}, {{p|Mecca}} and the {{c|2744|Kaaba}}'s sign,

To guard it, and the pilgrims' trade; they held
The sacred months, when none could fight, for all
The caravans; and {{p|Mecca}}'s wealth so swelled.
In {{p|Yemen}}, {{p|Himyar}} heard the {{x|Torah}}'s call,

Turned {{x|Jewish}}; {{p|Aksum}} came, of {{c|1497|Christ}}; and then
The {{c|2750|Sassanids}}; {{c|2748|Ghassanids}}, the west,
Were {{c|1497|Christ}}'s, {{p|Byzantium}}'s; the {{c|2749|Lakhmids}}, men
Of {{c|1497|Christ}} as well, the {{c|2750|Sassanids}}' own guest;

And in {{p|Yathrib}}, {{p|Medina}}, dwelt the {{c|2500|Jews}}:
{{c|2751|Qurayza}}, {{c|2752|Nadir}}, and {{c|2753|Qaynuqa}}, the tribes
Who fled from {{p|Rome}}'s wars, kept their trade; and news
Of monks in caves by wells, who taught the scribes.

Here was one peninsula and one rite
kept many ways, by tribe and town and tent,
the high god and his daughters, and the light
of Jews and Christian monks, with one intent.

And incense, myrrh went north to {{p|Rome}}; and silk
And spice came from the east through {{p|Yemen}}'s ports;
And east and west, the two realms, of one ilk,
Warred on, wore each other down, in sorts.

In the {{x|Year of the Elephant}} came forth
{{c|2754|Abraha}} of {{p|Yemen}}, to take the rite
Of pilgrims for his church; and he marched north
With elephants: whose house it was, whose right.

And birds dropped stones upon them, and they fled,
And plague struck them; and in that year was born
{{c|1911|Muhammad}}; and his father had been dead
Before his birth; his mother, too, was torn

From him when young; his grandfather, the lord
{{c|2755|Abd al-Muttalib}}; he was raised
By {{c|2756|Abu Talib}}, uncle; by accord
He was {{c|2757|al-Amin}}, the trustworthy, praised;

He traded, and he wed {{c|2758|Khadija}}, rich,
A widow, fifteen years his elder; and
He went up to {{p|Hira}}'s cave, to the niche
On the {{p|Mount of Light}}, to pray; as was planned,

At forty, in six-ten, {{c|2759|Gabriel}} came,
And said: Recite! In the name of your {{c|295|Lord}},
Who made, made man from a clot; so the flame
The {{x|Quran}} began: the old house restored.


# Chapter 192: Muhammad and the Rise of Islam

{{c|1911|Muhammad}} ran home shaking from the cave,
and wrapped himself in blankets, terrified.
He sought no founding; it was what {{c|472|God}} gave.
{{c|2758|Khadija}} held him, and believed beside.

Twenty-three years the words came, verse by verse,
Surah by surah; and, after his death,
Collected as the {{x|Quran}}, to rehearse:
The recitation, {{c|2740|Allah}}'s word and breath.

The oneness of the one {{c|472|God}} was his core,
the seal of prophets came from {{c|2599|Mani}}'s line,
a chain of messengers sent long before,
both {{x|Christian}} and the Manichee: one vine.

Five pillars: shahada, the word of faith;
Salat, five prayers a day toward {{p|Mecca}}; then
Zakat, the gift to those in need, the wraith
Of hunger fed; and sawm, the fast, again,

In {{x|Ramadan}}; and hajj, the pilgrim's way
To {{p|Mecca}}, once in life: and simple, clear,
And hard, but to be done, a frame each day
For all of life's own striving, far and near.

On Friday, after prayer, the people ate
together, bread and broth, the poor fed first,
the {{x|Eucharist}} that churches celebrate,
one table and one house, and none dispersed.

It was the dearest rite the faith would keep;
when golden ages fell to want and dearth,
the meal grew thin; the {{x|Hajj}}, the prayers, ran deep,
and still they eat, not knowing of its birth.

For thirteen years he preached in {{p|Mecca}}; and
The tribe of {{c|1916|Quraysh}}, who held the {{p|Kaaba}}'s keys,
Fought him: whoever held the word would stand
To teach the pilgrims there, and take their fees.

His first were slaves, and women, and the low,
Those with no tribe's shield; {{c|2756|Abu Talib}}, by
His clan's own duty, kept him, and not so
From faith; and then, in six-nineteen, would die,

{{c|2758|Khadija}} too, the {{x|Year of Sorrow}}; and
His danger grew; and in six-twenty-two
He made the {{c|2761|Hijra}} to {{p|Medina}}'s land,
Whose tribes had asked him there, to judge them through

Their feuds, and be their prophet; by the count,
Years start at {{c|2761|Hijra}}; and the {{c|2762|ummah}} there
Became the first of {{x|Islam}}'s realms, the fount,
With him both prophet and the ruler's chair.

{{p|Medina}}'s {{c|2500|Jews}}, he thought, would come to see
A prophet, {{c|1308|Abraham}}'s, in him; and grim,
They would not have it; so it came to be
The {{x|qibla}} of the prayer moved from the rim

of {{p|Jerusalem}} to {{p|Mecca}}. The fast
was moved from {{x|Yom Kippur}} to {{x|Ramadan}}:
one fast, one prayer, one Abraham, recast
as the two houses' quarrel, carried on.

And war with the {{c|1916|Quraysh}}: at {{c|2763|Badr}}, the first,
Six-twenty-four, three hundred beat their foes,
A thousand strong; at {{x|Uhud}} came the worst:
Six-twenty-five, he fell, and wounded, rose,

Thought dead a while; and words came down to stay
The shaken; at the {{x|Trench}}, twenty-seven,
They dug, as {{p|Persians}} dug, and held the day,
And the {{c|1916|Quraysh}} withdrew, as sent from heaven.

And the {{c|2751|Banu Qurayza}} were then tried
For joining with the foe; their men were slain,
Their women and their children sold. Beside,
Six-twenty-eight, {{x|Hudaybiyyah}}; again

A truce was made, though weak it seemed; in two
Years the {{c|1916|Quraysh}}' friends then broke it; and he came,
Ten thousand strong, to {{p|Mecca}}; and it knew
To yield, and gave itself up in his name.

{{c|1911|Muhammad}} came into the {{p|Kaaba}}; there
its images were cleared, the house made {{c|472|God}}'s;
he gave its keepers back the key to bear,
forgave most enemies, and spared the rods.

It was the triumph of his mission, done:
{{p|Mecca}} was now the center of the new
Community; six-thirty-two, he'd run
The {{x|Farewell Pilgrimage}}, and spoke, all through,

At {{p|Arafat}}, the {{x|Farewell Sermon}}; then
He died soon after at {{p|Medina}}, head
In {{c|2765|Aisha}}'s arms; and all his grieving men
Heard {{c|2766|Abu Bakr}}, his old friend, who said:

If you worshipped {{c|1911|Muhammad}}, he is dead;
If you have worshipped {{c|2740|Allah}}, he lives on.
{{c|2766|Abu Bakr}} was first {{c|2767|caliph}}, and led,
{{c|2768|Rightly Guided}}; and with the rebels gone,

The {{x|Ridda}} crushed, he held the {{c|2762|ummah}} one.
Then {{c|2769|Umar}} sent the {{c|1910|Arabs}} out; within
Twelve years after the {{c|2776|Prophet}}'s death, they'd won
{{p|Syria}}, {{p|Iraq}}, {{p|Persia}}, {{p|Egypt}}; in

The {{c|2596|Sassanids}} fell; {{p|Byzantium}} lost
Its richest lands; the map was drawn anew;
{{c|2769|Umar}} was slain; and {{c|2770|Uthman}}, at the cost
Of other copies, made the {{x|Quran}} true

In one text; and was slain; {{c|2771|Ali}}, the fourth,
The cousin, son-in-law; the {{c|2772|fitna}} came,
The war among them; he was slain; and forth
Came {{c|2773|Muawiya}}, took the caliph's name;

At {{p|Damascus}} the {{c|2774|Umayyads}} rose;
For {{c|2771|Ali}} were the {{c|2775|Shia}}, all his own,
Held that the {{c|2776|Prophet}}'s house should rule; and those
Who stayed, the {{c|2777|Sunni}}, kept the custom known.


# Chapter 193: Journey to the West

In the {{c|2696|Tang}}, the monk {{c|2778|Xuanzang}} set out west,
Six-twenty-nine, to find the sutras' source
In {{x|Sanskrit}}, for his life's one single quest:
The words in {{x|Chinese}} had gone off their course.

They would not let him go; he went alone,
Against the law; seventeen years he went,
{{p|Central Asia}}, {{p|Afghanistan}}, unknown,
To {{p|India}}, and at {{c|2779|Nalanda}} spent

His years among ten thousand monks, the hall
Of learning: logic, medicine, and thought;
And mastered {{x|Sanskrit}}, and the schools, and all
The great debates; and when they would have brought

Him to be head there, he went home instead,
Six-forty-five, with six hundred and more
Books on twenty-two horses; and the head
Of {{x|Tang}}, {{c|2780|Taizong}}, welcomed him at the door.

He spent his life in turning them: the scrolls,
Thirteen hundred; {{c|2781|Yogacara}}, the mind
Alone, he brought; and wrote, of all the goals
And kingdoms of the west, the {{c|2782|Records}}, signed,

Of {{c|2782|Western Regions}}: rice and rite and sage,
The customs of each city; and before
Him, {{p|Bamiyan}}'s {{c|1959|Buddhas}} stood, the great age
Of stone cut from the cliff; they stand no more.

And on the road, the {{c|2787|Monkey King}} went too,
{{c|2786|Sun Wukong}}, born from stone, who learned the arts
Of {{x|Dao}} and {{c|1959|Buddha}}, ate the peaches through,
Made havoc up in heaven, and, in parts,

Was pinned beneath a mountain; and was freed
To guard the monk, {{c|2788|Tripitaka}}, a band
Of gold around his head, which, at the need,
The monk's spell tightened, by his own command.

And {{c|2789|Pigsy}}, {{c|2790|Zhu Bajie}}, the lazy pig;
And Sandy, {{c|2791|Sha Wujing}}, the river's own;
The dragon prince, the horse; and, small and big,
Eighty-one trials met them, which were thrown

By demons in disguise, the women's land,
The flaming mountains, rivers made of sand;
They reached {{p|India}}, took the sutras' hand,
And, coming home, were all enlightened, and

Each trial was a hindrance of the heart,
Made outward, to be passed; and so the way
Was walked, with friends, and every trial a part,
To bring the teaching home, and make it stay.

And in the {{x|Tang}} the {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s way was theirs:
{{c|2793|Chan}} rose with {{c|2794|Huineng}}, the sixth patriarch,
Awakening at once; and {{c|2796|Pure Land}}'s prayers
To {{c|2797|Amitabha}}, of the west, would mark

All those who called his name. And {{p|Chang'an}} stood
The greatest city of the world; to where
There came {{c|2654|Persians}}, {{c|1910|Arabs}}, {{c|2798|Sogdians}}, who would
Trade, study, live; {{c|2564|Koreans}}, {{p|Japan}}'s heir.

So honor {{c|2778|Xuanzang}}, who once walked the west,
The {{c|2787|Monkey King}}, who guarded him; and Tang,
The golden age, the high mark and the best,
Where all the {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s teaching came and rang.


# Chapter 194: The Islamic Golden Age

{{c|2868|Abbasids}} cast the {{c|2869|Umayyads}} down,
In seven-fifty; and {{c|2870|al-Mansur}} made
In seven-sixty-two a round new town,
{{p|Baghdad}}, four gates; and there the learning stayed

For centuries: the {{c|2871|House of Wisdom}}, where
The {{x|Greek}}, {{x|Persian}}, {{x|Indian}} books were turned
{{x|Arabic}}: {{c|1081|Aristotle}}, {{c|2376|Plato}}, there
With {{c|2872|Galen}}, {{c|2408|Euclid}}, {{c|2265|Ptolemy}}, were learned,

{{c|2873|Hippocrates}}; and kept, when they were lost
Elsewhere. From {{p|India}} the numbers came,
The zero, and the decimal, and, crossed
With {{x|Greek}}, {{c|2874|al-Khwarizmi}}'s, whose own name

Is algorithm; and his book, the one
Of {{x|al-jabr}}, is algebra, made whole.
{{c|2875|Al-Razi}} told the pox and measles, done
Apart, and tested all his cures; the scroll

Of the {{x|Comprehensive Book}} he then wrote;
{{c|2877|Ibn Sina}} wrote the {{x|Canon}}; he joined
{{c|1081|Aristotle}} to the {{x|Platonists}}' note;
And {{c|2879|Ibn al-Haytham}}'s {{x|Optics}} then coined

The test by trial, the way of finding out;
{{c|2881|Al-Biruni}} measured the earth, its round,
And studied {{p|India}}, and wrote about
All things, a hundred forty books, profound.

{{c|2882|Al-Ghazali}}: the thinkers lost their way
In incoherence; {{c|2883|Ibn Rushd}} then wrote
The {{x|Incoherence}} of it, back, to say
The thinkers' cause was sound, and kept afloat.

{{c|2885|Al-Farabi}}, the {{c|2886|Second Teacher}}, next
{{c|1081|Aristotle}}; {{c|2887|Ibn Arabi}} joined
The {{x|Sufi}} way to thought; and {{c|2888|Rumi}}'s text,
The {{x|Masnavi}}, at {{p|Konya}}, there was coined,

The greatest of the mystic songs; and spread
The {{x|Sufis}} from {{p|Morocco}} to the lands
Of {{p|India}}, a sea; and, by their head,
The way went on, from teacher's hands to hands.

{{c|2889|Al-Hallaj}} cried {{x|Ana al-Haqq}}; and who
Could speak for {{c|472|God}}? The jurists, and the court
Of {{p|Baghdad}}, held the word; nine-twenty-two:
That was the fight; and so they cut him short.

{{c|2869|Umayyads}} who lived went on in {{p|Spain}},
And {{c|2890|Córdoba}} was theirs, a caliph's seat,
Half a million, books, baths, a lighted lane,
All paved, when {{p|Paris}} was a muddy street.

Nine-oh-nine: the {{x|Shia}} {{c|2891|Fatimids}} rose
In {{p|Egypt}}, rival to {{c|2892|Abbasid}} reign,
And built {{p|Cairo}} and {{c|2893|al-Azhar}}; and those
In {{p|Mazandaran}}, by {{p|Caspian}}'s main,

The {{c|2894|Bavandids}}, held {{p|Tabaristan}}'s height,
Woods; kin to {{c|2895|Sasanian}} kings, the last
Old house of {{p|Iran}} not yet won by fight;
{{c|2896|Qarin}} the First, eight-seventeen, held fast;

When {{c|2897|Mazyar}} rose against the caliph's hand,
{{c|2896|Qarin}} stood with {{p|Baghdad}}; eight-forty-two,
He took {{x|Islam}} himself, and kept his land
Of mountains; so the old kings' blood went through

Into new faith: {{c|2898|Abul Melik}}, his son;
And in eight-sixty-nine, a grandson came,
{{c|2899|Abul Hamza}}, in {{p|Armenia}}, one
Of the {{c|2900|Artsruni}}; west, under their name.

The {{c|2901|Seljuk Turks}} came; caliphs kept the name;
Sultans ruled; at {{c|2902|Manzikert}} they beat,
Ten-seventy-one, {{c|2838|Byzantines}}, and came
To {{p|Anatolia}}; and in each street,

{{x|Hanafi}}, they built their schools; learning went
On, till twelve-fifty-eight, the {{c|2904|Mongols}} came,
Took {{p|Baghdad}}, and the {{c|2868|Abbasids}} were spent;
The books thrown in the {{p|Tigris}}; it became

Black with their ink. So honor that bright age,
Four centuries: the numbers, and the cure,
The optics, and the thought, the {{x|Sufi}} page,
Through {{p|Córdoba}}, {{p|Toledo}}, and kept sure.


# Chapter 195: Charlemagne and Byzantium

And in the {{p|West}}, while the usurper's hand
Kept the throne empty, the {{c|2660|Franks}} grew, and grew;
{{c|2818|Clovis I}} took up, in the {{x|Nicene}} band,
The faith; the {{c|2649|Goths}} kept {{x|Arian}}, as true.{{fn|Clovis I of the Franks was baptized a Nicene Christian, a Catholic, around the year 500, unlike the Goths, the Vandals and the Burgundians, who were Arians.}}

His heirs, the {{c|2819|Merovingians}}, would then reign
Three hundred years, but weak, and ruled by none;
The {{c|2820|Mayors of the Palace}} were the brain;
And {{c|2821|Charles Martel}}, the {{c|2822|Hammer}}, Mayor, won

At {{c|2823|Tours}}, seven-thirty-two, stopped the march
Of {{x|Umayyads}}, who fell back to {{p|Spain}};
{{c|2824|Pepin the Short}} then asked the {{c|2825|Pope}}: the arch
Of kingship: should the one who ruled now reign?

The {{c|2825|Pope}} said yes; and {{c|2826|Pepin}} took the crown;
{{c|2827|Carolingians}} began; and his son
Was {{c|2677|Charlemagne}}, {{c|2828|Charles the Great}}, whose renown
Would build what {{p|Europe}} had not seen, as one.

{{c|2677|Charlemagne}} reigned forty-six years. He fought
the {{c|2829|Saxons}} for their grove, and in it felled
the Irminsul, and set the priests he brought
at their own altars, where their feasts were held.

Seven-seventy-four: he took the land
of {{p|Italy}} from {{c|2678|Lombards}}; and in {{p|Spain}}
he pressed the {{c|2764|Muslims}} back with his own hand
and held the frontier as his own domain.

He did not break the {{c|2830|Lombards}}; took the crown,
{{c|2831|Rex Langobardorum}};{{fn|Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom in 774 and took the title Rex Langobardorum. Its crown is the one later called the Iron Crown of Lombardy.}} and its crown, too,
Held it for twenty-six years, in renown,
The realm of {{c|2665|Theodoric}}'s heirs, come through.

He brought from {{p|York}} {{c|2832|Alcuin}}, and there, to lead
His school; old learning lived again and rose;
The script was made that we today can read,
And monks would copy old books, and keep those

That would be lost. On {{x|Christmas}}, on the day,
Eight hundred, {{c|2834|Leo III}} crowned his head
{{c|2835|Imperator Romanorum}},{{fn|Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne in St Peter's on Christmas Day 800. The papacy held the imperial throne to be vacant because a woman, Irene, ruled in Constantinople.}} to stay,
In {{p|St. Peter's}}; and the throne, so long dead

Since {{c|2665|Theodoric}}, filled. The {{c|2825|Pope}} would place
The crown; the claim was not the {{c|2825|Pope}}'s: he held
{{p|Rome}}, {{p|Italy}}, {{p|Gaul}}, {{p|Germany}}, by grace
Of conquest and of law; and he excelled,

{{c|2678|Lombards}}' heir, who were {{c|2665|Theodoric}}'s own;
And this enraged {{p|Constantinople}}, where
{{c|2836|Irene}} ruled, claimed the {{p|Roman}} throne alone;
The {{c|2838|Byzantines}} would not let a {{c|2837|Frank}} share

The crown: for since {{c|2383|Justinian}}, they'd kept
The {{p|West}} by the usurper's right, no right,
And kept the throne empty, where none had stepped;
No {{c|2837|Frank}} would have the crown they'd seized by might.

{{p|Byzantium}} itself was shaken: then
{{c|2839|Iconoclasm}} rose, seven-twenties,
When {{c|2834|Leo III}}, emperor, bade men
Break holy icons, for all their plenties.

The fight was over who would hold the face:
the throne, that broke the icons in its name,
or monks, who kept them in the holy place
as windows, for a century of flame.

{{p|Nicaea}}, seven-eighty-seven, said
The {{x|Second Council}}: honored, not adored;
It came back, till eight-forty-three, then fled;
And all the icons came back, were restored;

{{x|Triumph of Orthodoxy}}'s feast is kept
In Lent. {{c|2840|Cyril}}, {{c|2841|Methodius}}, then went
To the {{c|2842|Slavs}}, and made letters where they stepped,
The {{c|2843|Glagolitic}}, made with this intent:

That they would pray in their own tongue; and so
{{p|Rus}}, {{p|Moravia}}, {{p|Bulgaria}}'s land,
Prayed not in {{x|Latin}}, {{x|Greek}}; and so would go
The faith in each one's tongue, as they had planned.

{{c|2677|Charlemagne}} died; his grandsons split the whole
At {{c|2845|Verdun}}, eight-forty-three: {{c|2846|West}} and {{c|2847|East}},
{{p|Middle Francia}}, which broke apart; the toll
Of {{c|2848|Vikings}}, seven-ninety-three, released

At {{p|Lindisfarne}}, slew monks, and from the sea,
From {{p|Scandinavia}}, three hundred years,
From {{p|Ireland}} to {{p|Russia}}, they would be
Raiders, then settlers, kings, and turned, by tears.

So honor {{c|2677|Charlemagne}}: the empty throne
Was filled again, eight hundred, at the feast;
The {{c|2678|Lombards}}' heir, {{c|2665|Theodoric}}'s, his own;
The monks' icons, windows, kept in the {{p|East}}.


# Chapter 196: Scandinavia and the Eddas

In the cold north, {{p|Scandinavia}}, where
The winter sun would barely rise, the {{c|2929|Norse}}
Kept the old steppe-born gods, and kept them there
The longest, in the old rite's living force.

The {{c|2930|Europeans}} kept the bishops' rite;
the {{c|2929|Norse}} kept the old altars of the North,
and when they took the bishops in, they'd write
the old gods down in books, and bring them forth.

In {{p|Iceland}}, {{c|2933|Snorri Sturluson}} set down
The {{c|2932|Prose Edda}}, and the {{c|2931|Poetic}} old,
The myths; for, though of {{c|1497|Christ}}, he loved the crown
Of the old tales, and wrote them, to be told.

{{c|2935|Odin}}, the {{c|2936|Allfather}}, hung on the tree
{{p|Yggdrasil}} for nine nights, and won the runes;
{{c|2937|Thor}}, with {{x|Mjölnir}}, thunder; and, as free,
{{c|1203|Freyr}} and {{c|2938|Freyja}}, gods of the fields and moons;

And {{c|2939|Loki}}, trickster, bore the monsters: one,
{{c|2940|Fenrir}} the wolf, and {{c|2941|Jörmungandr}}, the snake
That rings the world; {{c|2942|Hel}}, of the dead; and done
By him, {{c|2943|Baldr}} died, gentle, for his sake.

Nine realms upon {{p|Yggdrasil}}: {{p|Asgard}}'s height,
The {{c|2944|Aesir}}'s; {{p|Vanaheim}}, the {{c|2945|Vanir}}'s; men
In {{p|Midgard}}; giants, {{p|Jotunheim}}; and, bright,
{{p|Alfheim}}, the elves'; the dwarves, in deep, and then

{{p|Niflheim}}'s ice, {{p|Muspelheim}}'s flame; and, below,
{{p|Hel}}, for the dead not fallen; and who fell,
{{c|2946|Valkyries}} bore to {{p|Valhalla}}; and so
At {{c|2947|Ragnarök}}, just as the old songs tell,

{{c|2940|Fenrir}} will swallow {{c|2935|Odin}}; {{c|2937|Thor}} will slay
The snake, and die of venom; {{c|2948|Surtr}}'s flame
Will burn the world; and then, a newer day,
Two hidden in the tree come out, the same.

Seven-ninety-three, when {{p|Lindisfarne}} burned,
The {{c|2848|Vikings}} raided, traded, settled; and,
Founding {{p|Dublin}}, {{p|Cork}}, {{p|Waterford}}; and turned
To {{p|England}}, and the {{p|Danelaw}} was their land;

The {{c|2949|Varangians}} served the emperor's throne;
They settled {{p|Iceland}}, eight-seventy, came,
Nine-eighty-six, to {{p|Greenland}}, {{c|2950|Erik}}'s own;
{{p|Vinland}}, a thousand, {{c|2951|Leif}}; and, all the same,

Went up the rivers east to trade, and made,
The {{c|2953|Rus}}, the {{p|Kievan Rus}}; and {{c|2954|Rurik}} came
To {{p|Novgorod}}, his kin {{p|Kiev}}; and stayed
{{c|2955|Vladimir}} took, nine-eighty-eight, the name

Of {{c|1497|Christ}}, from {{p|Constantinople}}, they found,
His envoys, such a beauty in the rite,
They knew not if on earth or heaven's ground
They stood; and so the {{p|Rus}} took up that light.

In {{p|Scandinavia}} kings took the rite:
first {{c|2956|Harald Bluetooth}} in nine-sixty-five;
{{c|2957|Olaf Tryggvason}} took {{p|Norway}}'s by might;
{{c|2958|Olaf II}} fell, a saint who would survive.

{{c|2959|Sweden}} came last; the twelfth century saw
{{p|Uppsala}}'s temple, with offered dead,
Come down, as crown and church took up its law;
The altar took new priests there, in its stead.

In {{p|Iceland}} it was settled without war:
the {{x|Althing}}, in the year one thousand, said
the bishops' rite in public; and the door
of each home kept the old rite there instead.

The sagas would be written, of that day:
Of {{c|2960|Egil}}, {{c|2961|Njál}}, {{c|2962|Laxdæla}}; and in {{p|France}},
{{c|2964|Rollo}}'s {{p|Normandy}}, nine-eleven, pay;
And {{c|2963|William}}, of his line, would take the chance,

Ten-sixty-six, at {{c|2965|Hastings}}, and would win
{{p|England}}. And so the {{c|2848|Vikings}} ceased, and took
The rite of {{c|1497|Christ}}; but they had shaped, within,
All {{p|Europe}}'s map: so honor them, their book.

# Cancer (8宮) - Days 197-224


# Chapter 197: Heian Japan

The {{c|2905|Heian}} age, from seven-ninety-four,
Was named for {{p|Heian-kyō}}, the town of peace,
{{p|Kyoto}} as now, laid out as was, before,
Like {{p|Chang'an}} of the {{x|Tang}}; and without cease

Four hundred years the court lived in its art;
The {{c|2906|Fujiwara}} held the rule instead,
As regents for the child kings, and, apart,
For grown ones too; and all their daughters, wed,

Bore grandsons. {{c|2908|Michinaga}}, at the height
Of their house, had four daughters, each a queen
To four kings; and he wrote: this world, by right,
Is mine, a full moon, nothing lacking, seen;

And after him the regents waned. And there
The women of the court, in {{c|2802|kana}}, wrote:
{{c|2909|Murasaki Shikibu}}, in her care,
The {{c|2910|Tale of Genji}}, chapters, every note,

Fifty-four, of the {{c|2911|Shining Prince}}'s heart,
The court, and mono no aware, the sweet
Sadness of passing; and, to take her part,
{{c|2912|Sei Shōnagon}}, her rival, wrote complete

The {{c|2914|Pillow Book}}: her lists, her scenes, the things
That make one's heart beat fast, the fair, the plain;
{{c|2915|Izumi Shikibu}}, whose love-song sings;
{{c|2916|Ono no Komachi}}, of age's pain;

{{c|2917|Immortal Poets}}, many women; for
The men wrote {{x|Chinese}}, kanji; and the low
Was {{c|2802|kana}}, women's; so they wrote, and more,
In their own tongue; and theirs endures, and so

The men's is lost. And all of it was touched
With mono no aware: the blossoms fall
After a week; the leaves turn brown; and clutched
A night of love, then parting; and in all,

The taste of loss. But out beyond the town,
The {{c|2918|bushi}} rose then: the {{c|2919|Taira}}, and
{{c|2920|Minamoto}}, cadet lines of the crown,
Who served the provinces, and grew, and manned

Their bands; and then {{c|2921|Hogen}}'s and {{c|2922|Heiji}}'s wars,
In fifty-six and sixty, brought them in;
{{c|2923|Kiyomori}}, {{c|2919|Taira}}, held the doors,
With puppet kings; but {{c|2924|Yoritomo}}, kin

Of {{c|2920|Minamoto}}, raised the {{p|Kanto}} plain,
The {{c|2925|Genpei War}}, eighty to eighty-five;
At {{p|Dan-no-ura}} the {{c|2919|Taira}} slain,
Child-king {{c|2926|Antoku}} drowned, none left alive,

With him, the sword {{c|2710|Kusanagi}}, at sea.
And {{c|2927|Yoritomo}}'s {{c|2928|Shogunate}}, the state,
At {{p|Kamakura}}, ninety-two; and he
Ruled; the emperor in {{p|Kyoto}} would wait.

So honor {{c|2905|Heian}}: {{c|2909|Murasaki}}'s pen,
{{c|2912|Sei Shōnagon}}'s lists, and the blossoms' fall;
The passing of the court, the warrior men;
And mono no aware over it all.


# Chapter 198: Kūkai

In {{p|Japan}}, early in the ninth age, came
{{c|2799|Kūkai}}, who brought from {{x|Tang}} {{c|2800|Shingon}}'s word,
And made it live; born on {{p|Shikoku}}, the same
He went with envoys, eight-oh-four, and heard,

At {{p|Qinglong Temple}} in {{p|Chang'an}}, the way,
From {{c|2801|Huiguo}}, master of the hidden rite,
Who gave him all of it in months; that day
He died; {{c|2799|Kūkai}} came home, with the light

Of scriptures, mandalas, and all the tools
Of rite, and all of {{c|2800|Shingon}}, the {{x|True Word}};
At {{p|Kōya}}, eight peaks, a mandala, schools
He built, and set the teaching, as he'd heard.

He made the {{c|2802|kana}}, letters for the sound
Of {{x|Japanese}}, where once the {{x|Chinese}} signs
Were used for sound alone, a heavy round;
And so the tongue was freed for poets' lines.

He taught: the world's the body of the one,
{{c|2804|Mahāvairocana}}, the {{c|1959|Buddha}} on high,
{{c|2805|Dainichi}}, the {{c|1959|Buddha}} who's like the sun;
And all are woken now, and need but try

Through body, speech, mind, the mysteries three,
The mudrās, mantras, visions, and the rite,
In this same body, in this life, to be
A {{c|1959|Buddha}}: sokushin jōbutsu's light.

He wrote, a master of the brush; and made
The ponds and bridges; thought on word and sign;
And did not die, but sat, and there he stayed,
In meditation, at {{p|Kōya}}'s high shrine,

At {{p|Oku-no-In}}, uncorrupted; and still
The pilgrims come, and he is waiting there
For {{c|2806|Maitreya}}, the one to come, until
He'll rise; and daily they feed him, with care.

And {{c|2807|Saichō}} brought from {{p|China}} the {{c|2808|Tendai}},
The {{x|Lotus Sutra}}'s way, of {{c|2809|Zhiyi}}'s school,
All teachings in one ladder, raised on high,
At {{p|Mount Hiei}}; it would become the great pool

From which, in after years, the schools would flow.
The two were friends, and wrote, and lent their books,
And sometimes argued; and they made it so,
The {{x|Japanese}} way, with all its own looks.

At {{p|Heian-kyō}}, now {{p|Kyoto}}, newly made
By {{c|2815|Kanmu}}, seven-ninety-four, the new
Teaching matched the new town; and, unafraid,
The kami and the {{c|1959|Buddha}} closer drew

Together: {{c|2816|honji suijaku}}, that each
Kami is but a bodhisattva, shown
In this land's form; and so, in all their reach,
{{c|885|Amaterasu}} was {{c|2805|Dainichi}}'s own,

{{c|2724|Hachiman}} was {{c|2817|Amida}}'s; the shrine
And temple built together; one rite, two
Faces, and no divide; one house, one line,
And one religion, as the faithful knew.


# Chapter 199: Tang and the Great Persecution

The {{c|2696|Tang}}, from six-eighteen, the golden age:
{{p|Chang'an}}, the greatest city of the world,
A million souls; {{c|2849|Li Yuan}}, on the stage,
A general, took the {{x|Sui}}'s throne, and unfurled

The {{x|Tang}}; {{c|2780|Taizong}}, his son, slew brothers, made
His father yield; and ruled, the model king
Of {{x|Confucius}}' rule, in peace; and he stayed
The golden reign that all would after sing.

{{c|2851|Wu Zetian}} rose, killed her rivals, and
Ruled, the one woman, emperor in name;
The {{c|1959|Buddha}} rose above the rest; her hand
Made {{p|Longmen}}'s {{c|1959|Buddha}}, with her face the same.

Then {{c|2852|Xuanzong}} reigned, at first in glory; then
His trusted {{c|2854|An Lushan}}, {{x|Sogdian}} by birth,
A general, rose, fifty-five; and men
Died, eight years, through the war; and through the earth

Fifty-three million became seventeen;
The {{x|Tang}} grew weak; and {{c|2855|Yang Guifei}}, his love,
His soldiers made him kill; and all the sheen
Of his long reign went dark, as from above.

{{c|2856|Li Bai}} was at his court; {{c|2857|Du Fu}} lived through
The war, and wrote it; with {{c|2858|Wang Wei}}, the four
{{c|2859|Bai Juyi}}, the {{c|2860|Four Greats}}, whose verse is true
Through all the ages, masters evermore.

Eight-four-five: {{c|2861|Wuzong}} struck the {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s way:
{{c|2862|Great Persecution}}: forty thousand fell,
The temples; and the state sent, on that day,
Two hundred sixty thousand monks as well.

The cause was land: the monasteries held
vast fields untaxed, and bronze the mint would take;
and {{c|2861|Wuzong}}'s Daoist priests would have expelled
the Buddha's monks, as rivals for one stake.

And {{x|Manichaeism}} was nearly all gone;
{{c|2863|Nestorian}} {{c|1497|Christ}}'s, which came with the {{x|Tang}};
The {{c|2597|Zoroastrian}} {{x|Sogdians}} too; and on
It went; and after {{c|2861|Wuzong}}, the bell rang,

His heir reversed it; but the great days passed.
{{c|2793|Chan}} lived, which needed neither books nor halls,
But only sitting; {{c|2796|Pure Land}} too would last,
The name of {{c|2797|Amitabha}}, which still calls

The laity, no temple and no school;
And these two would become the {{x|East}}'s chief way.
The {{x|Tang}} declined: {{c|2864|Jiedushi}} would rule
Their lands; the eunuchs held the court; the day

Of risings came; and in nine-oh-seven,
The {{x|Tang}} was done; the {{p|Five Dynasties}}, and
{{p|Ten Kingdoms}} split; then, as sent from heaven,
Nine-sixty, and the {{c|2865|Song}} rejoined the land.

And still the {{x|Tang}} is the high mark: its lines
Still the finest; and the {{x|Chinese}} who dwell
Abroad still call themselves the {{x|Tang}}'s; the signs
Of all they look back on, they keep it well.


# Chapter 200: Ireland and Brian Boru

{{p|Ireland}}, which {{c|2966|Saint Patrick}} turned, then became
A place of learning, in the fifth age, blessed;
For while the {{p|West}} was burned, and in the flame
Of {{c|2383|Justinian}}'s wars, the plague, the rest,

The empty throne, the island lay beyond
The usurper's reach; and learning there stayed:
The monks kept {{x|Greek}} and {{x|Latin}}, and the bond
With books that would be lost; and so they made

{{c|2967|Columba}}'s {{p|Iona}}, five-sixty-three;
{{c|2968|Columbanus}}' houses all through the land
Of {{p|Europe}}; {{c|2969|Aidan}}, from {{p|Lindisfarne}}, free,
Went through the north; the {{c|2970|Book of Kells}}, by hand,

Was made, the knotwork, interlaced, the art
Of all the {{x|Celts}}. And {{p|Ireland}} was split
Into small kingdoms, the {{x|tuath}}, each apart,
With overkings, the {{c|2971|High King}} over it,

At {{p|Tara}}. And the {{c|2848|Vikings}} came, and burned,
In ninety-five; {{p|Iona}} sacked again;
And they made towns, the first the island learned:
{{p|Dublin}}, {{p|Waterford}}, {{p|Cork}}, {{p|Limerick}}; men

Of {{x|Norse}} and {{x|Irish}} dwelt in them. And then
{{c|2972|Brian Boru}}, of {{p|Munster}}'s {{p|Dál gCais}}, rose,
High King, ten-oh-two, who joined the isle's men
In one, the first; and he beat the {{x|Norse}} foes,

With {{p|Leinster}}'s kings, at {{c|2973|Clontarf}}, on the day
Of {{x|Good Friday}}, ten-fourteen, broke the might
Of the {{x|Norse}} in {{p|Ireland}}; and, as he lay
In prayer within his tent, at end of fight,

The fleeing {{c|2848|Vikings}} found him, and he died;
And after him the kings fought on, apart.
And {{c|2975|Eriugena}}, scholar, at the side
Of {{c|2976|Charles the Bald}}, the learned court's own heart,

Knew {{x|Greek}} and {{x|Latin}}, and he turned the {{x|Greek}}
Of {{c|2977|Dionysius}} to {{x|Latin}}; made
The {{x|Periphyseon}}, the great whole, to seek
The one in all; the high crosses were laid,

{{x|Old Irish}} kept the oldest tales: the {{c|2978|Táin}},
The {{x|Cattle Raid of Cooley}}, where, alone,
{{c|2979|Cú Chulainn}} held {{p|Ulster}}, {{p|Connacht}}'s bane,
In battle-fury, warped, shape not his own,

Doing what none could do; and he would fall
When his taboo was broken; kin, of old,
Of {{c|2067|Heracles}} and {{c|2333|Bhima}}; and, in all,
{{c|2980|Medb}}, the queen of war and sovereignty, bold.

For {{c|2966|Patrick}} did not burn the temples; he
Preached, and the chiefs turned, and the tribes came too;
The faith took in the old, and let it be;
And so the old gods lived on, in the new.

So honor {{p|Ireland}}: where the books were kept
Beyond the usurper's reach; {{c|2972|Brian}}, slain
Praying at {{c|2973|Clontarf}}; the hero who leapt
In fury; and the old rite, kept again.


# Chapter 201: India in the Early Medieval

The {{c|2983|Guptas}} fell in the sixth century;
{{p|India}} split into its regions' kings;
And yet from that came no stagnation; free,
The tongues, the temples, and the thought of things,

Grew rich. And {{c|2341|Shankara}} came, and he taught
{{c|2986|Advaita}}: {{x|Brahman}}, the self, are the same;
All else illusion; and he wrote, and brought
{{c|2987|Upanishads}}, the {{c|2988|Gita}}, and the name

Of {{c|2989|Brahma Sutras}}; and his word was set
As {{x|Vedanta}}'s; he went out to debate
The {{c|2561|Buddhists}}, all through {{p|India}}; and met
Them at their seats, and won, and changed their state.

It was one house of teachers and their seats:
who held the kings, the students, and the alms.
{{x|Vedanta}} won the patrons and the streets,
the monasteries lost their students' psalms.

And so the {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s way grew small, and less,
Till, by eleven hundred, it was rare;
{{p|Nalanda}}'s books, in {{p|Tibet}}'s great recess,
In {{p|China}}, and the south, were kept with care.

And {{c|2990|bhakti}} spread, the love of god: the south
Of {{x|Tamil}}, where the {{c|2991|Alvars}} sang to him,
{{c|2072|Vishnu}}; {{c|2992|Nayanars}}, {{c|1340|Shiva}} in their mouth;
And {{c|2342|Ramanuja}}, of the middle rim,

{{c|2993|Vishishtadvaita}}: one, but qualified,
So love could reach to god; and {{c|2343|Madhva}}, two,
{{c|2994|Dvaita}}, god and soul forever side
By side, apart, and some souls damned, it's true.

The {{c|2995|Cholas}} of the south, the {{x|Tamil}} kings,
{{c|2996|Rajaraja}} and {{c|2997|Rajendra}} built the shrine
{{p|Brihadeeswarar}}, {{p|Thanjavur}}'s; wings
Reached to {{p|Sumatra}}, {{c|2998|Srivijaya}}'s line;

They spread the {{x|Tamil}} tongue, {{c|2999|Shaiva}} way,
The dancing {{c|1340|Shiva}}, {{c|3001|Nataraja}}, cast
In bronze; the {{c|3002|Palas}} of {{p|Bengal}}, who'd stay
With {{c|1959|Buddha}}, sent {{x|Vajrayana}} at last.

{{c|3003|Rashtrakutas}}, {{c|3004|Pratiharas}}, the three
Fought for the north, and wore each other down;
And from the {{x|Afghan}} highlands, by degree,
The {{c|3006|Ghaznavids}} came; then the {{c|3007|Ghurids}}' crown:

{{c|3008|Mahmud of Ghazni}}, seventeen raids, took
{{p|Somnath}}'s gold, in ten-twenty-five; and then
{{c|3009|Muhammad of Ghor}} beat, as in the book,
{{c|3010|Prithviraj}} there at {{x|Tarain}}; and his men

Made the {{c|2984|Delhi Sultanate}}; Muslim rule
Began; and {{c|3012|Alauddin}}'s {{c|3011|Khiljis}} went in
Down to the {{p|Deccan}}; the {{c|3013|Tughlaqs}}, by rule,
Held almost all; {{c|3014|Muhammad}}, with a din,

Moved the capital, made copper coin, sent
His hosts to {{p|Central Asia}}; and all failed;
And then the sultanate grew weak, and went
To regions: {{p|Bengal}}, {{p|Gujarat}}, all trailed.

So honor {{p|India}}: {{c|2341|Shankara}}'s one,
The {{c|2990|bhakti}} songs, the {{c|2995|Cholas}}' bronze and stone,
The {{c|3001|dancing Shiva}}, and the seats long won,
And all its regions, each one with its own.


# Chapter 202: The Crusades

At {{x|Council of Clermont}}, ten-ninety-five,
the {{c|2825|Pope}}, {{c|3017|Urban II}}, sent the knights to ride
to aid {{p|Byzantium}}, and then to strive
with {{c|2764|Muslims}} for the Tomb where {{c|1497|Christ}} had died.

It was one {{c|472|God}}, one city, and one tomb;
the quarrel was whose priests would hold the keys,
whose bells would ring there, and whose call, whose room
for pilgrims, and whose feasts, and whose decrees.

God wills it! cried the crowd; and so began
The {{c|3019|First Crusade}}; and {{c|3020|Urban}} promised all
Who died there that their sins were washed; the plan
Had asked for hired men, when, at the fall

{{x|Manzikert}}, seventy-one, the hand
Of {{c|2901|Seljuks}} took {{p|Anatolia}}; came
An army through the {{c|2838|Byzantines}}' own land,
And ate its food; {{c|3021|Alexios}}, the same,

Made them swear oaths to give him back the lands
They took; but after {{p|Antioch}} was won,
{{p|Jerusalem}}, ten-ninety-nine, their hands
Kept all; and in the town, when it was done,

They slew the {{c|2764|Muslims}}, {{c|2500|Jews}}, and eastern kin
Of {{c|1497|Christ}}; and then made the {{c|3023|Crusader States}}:
{{p|Jerusalem}}, {{p|Tripoli}}, and, within,
{{p|Edessa}}; and two hundred years, their gates.

And in {{p|Georgia}}, {{c|3024|David the Builder}}, few
In men against the {{c|2903|Seljuks}}, wed a bride,
{{c|3025|Gurandukht}}, a {{c|3026|Cuman}} khan's child; and through
Eleven-eighteen, the {{c|3026|Cumans}} allied,

Forty thousand families, came down to fight;
At {{p|Didgori}}, in twenty-one, they broke
The {{c|2903|Seljuks}}; and {{p|Tbilisi}} came in sight
Once more for {{p|Georgia}}; so the steppe's own folk

And {{p|Caucasus}} were wed; and not the first:
A hundred years before, {{c|3027|Mariam}}, born
In {{p|Vaspurakan}}, an {{c|2900|Artsruni}}, nursed
In {{c|2899|Abul Hamza}}'s line, of {{c|2896|Qarin}}'s, sworn

To {{c|3028|George}} the First of {{p|Georgia}}, bore a girl,
{{c|3029|Guarandukht}}, who was given north across
The grass to {{c|3030|Osen}}, {{c|3031|Cuman}} khan; the whirl
Of years: she bore him {{c|3032|Aepa}}; and, no loss,

His daughter {{c|3033|Anna}}; eleven-oh-eight,
{{c|3034|Vladimir Monomakh}} made peace, and took
{{c|3033|Anna}} for his son {{c|222|Yuri}}: the steppe's mate,
A {{c|3026|Cuman}} bride; and {{c|222|Yuri}}, by the book

The {{c|3035|Long-Armed}}, founded {{p|Moscow}}; and his son,
{{c|3036|Andrey}}, of {{c|3033|Anna}}, built the churches white;
{{p|Tabaristan}}'s old princes, one by one,
Through {{p|Georgia}} and the steppe, they came to light

Among the {{c|2953|Rus}}. Crusaders never knew;
They fought for one city, while the old blood
Walked north by its own road; the houses grew.
{{c|3037|Second Crusade}}, after {{p|Edessa}}'s flood

Failed: {{c|3038|Louis VII}} and {{c|3039|Conrad III}}, none
Did anything; the {{c|3040|Third}}, when {{c|3041|Saladin}}
Took {{p|Jerusalem}}, eighty-seven, won
Nothing; and {{c|3043|Barbarossa}} drowned; and in

A quarrel, {{c|1406|Philip}} left; the {{c|3042|Lionheart}}
And {{c|3041|Saladin}} fought on, and made a truce:
The city {{c|2764|Muslim}}, pilgrims could depart
And come; each one was courteous in use.

And {{c|3041|Saladin}}, {{c|3046|Salah ad-Din}}, the {{p|Kurd}},
Ruled {{p|Egypt}}, {{p|Syria}}, and joined in one
The {{c|2764|Muslims}}; and his courtesy was heard
In {{p|Europe}}. Then the {{c|3047|Fourth}}, which never won

The {{p|Holy Land}}, but, owing {{p|Venice}} gold,
Sacked {{p|Constantinople}}, for three days long,
And carried off the relics; and the hold
{{c|3048|Latin}} emperors, sixty years; the wrong

Of {{c|2494|Christians}} sacking {{c|1497|Christ}}'s own greatest town,
From which it never would be whole again;
The greatest of betrayals, when the crown
Of {{c|1497|Christ}}'s own house was robbed by {{c|1497|Christ}}'s own men.

The {{x|Great Schism}}, ten-fifty-four, between
two sees, was a quarrel for the first chair,
{{p|Rome}} or {{p|Constantinople}}; from this scene
the quarrel held, and no hand would repair.

The {{x|Children's Crusade}}, twelve-twelve, ended sold
Or drowned; the {{x|Fifth}} struck {{p|Egypt}}, and it failed;
{{c|3049|Frederick II}}, though cast out, went, and, bold,
Twelve twenty-nine, by treaty, there prevailed,

Took {{p|Jerusalem}}, lost it, forty-four;
{{c|3050|Saint Louis}}, forty-eight, was caught, and paid;
At {{p|Tunis}}, twelve-seventy, died; and more:
At {{p|Acre}}, ninety-one, the last was laid.

The wars bore fruit: the {{c|2930|Europeans}} came
to know their cousins' learning in the East,
their numbers, paper, sugar, and the same
old Greek the house had kept: one house, one feast.

And {{p|Venice}}, {{p|Genoa}}, grew rich on fare
Of ships; and money grew, and banks were made;
And so the ground was laid, and left in care,
For all that came, the learning and the trade.

The {{c|3052|Military Orders}} rose: the band
{{c|3053|Templars}}, {{c|3054|Hospitallers}}, {{c|3055|Teutonic Knights}},
who kept the pilgrims' road, grew rich in land;
the {{c|3053|Templars}} rich enough to lose their rights.

In thirteen-oh-seven Philip of {{p|France}}
arrested them for heresy, and seized
their gold: the charge was faith; the cause, finance,
an order's treasure, and the king was pleased.

The crusades were a war of race and blood:
the Frank against the Arab, {{c|2500|Jew}} and Greek;
the cross was raised, but under it a flood:
contempt for every people they called weak.


# Chapter 203: Kamakura Japan and the Kamikaze

In {{p|Japan}}, from eleven-eighty-five,
The {{c|2928|Kamakura Shogunate}} held sway;
The {{c|2920|Minamoto}} line did not long thrive;
The {{c|3121|Hōjō}} regents ruled the shoguns' day,

As {{c|2907|Fujiwara}} had the child kings held;
{{c|3122|Hōjō Yasutoki}}, twelve-thirty-two,
Wrote the {{c|3123|Goseibai Shikimoku}}, which spelled
The warriors' law, apart from the court's, new.

{{x|Buddhism}} burst into new schools: the first,
{{c|3124|Hōnen}}'s {{c|3125|Jōdo-shū}}, the {{x|Pure Land}}, which taught
That calling {{c|2817|Amida}}'s name reversed
All sin; and all the poor found what they sought.

{{c|2812|Shinran}}, his pupil, made {{c|3126|Jōdo Shinshū}},
The {{x|True Pure Land}}: one call, in faith, alone
Suffices; the rest {{c|2817|Amida}} will do;
The saving hand is his, and not our own.

{{c|3127|Eisai}} brought {{c|3128|Rinzai Zen}} from {{p|China}}'s shore,
With koans, and the warriors took it up;
{{c|2814|Dōgen}}'s {{c|3129|Sōtō Zen}} asked for nothing more
Than sitting, just to sit, an empty cup.

{{c|2813|Nichiren}} told the regents they must stand
by the {{c|3130|Lotus Sutra}}, by it alone,
and leave the other schools' support: the land
would fall if the other schools held their own.

He said a foreign foe would come; and so,
{{c|3076|Kublai Khan}} sent, and asked that {{p|Japan}} bow;
The {{c|3121|Hōjō}} regent said no; and the foe
Set sail, twelve-seventy-four, prow on prow.

At {{p|Hakata Bay}}, on {{p|Kyushu}}, they came;
The samurai fought one on one, by right;
The {{c|2904|Mongols}} fought in ranks, with bombs of flame
And poisoned arrows; and that day, that night,

Many samurai fell; and then there broke
A typhoon on the fleet; the {{c|2904|Mongols}} fled;
The samurai said they had won; they spoke
Of victory, but knew they'd lost, and bled.

Seven years they made ready; built a wall
Of stone, two meters high, along the bay;
Trained samurai to fight in ranks; and all
The shrines and temples, one rite, came to pray.

In twelve-eighty-one, {{c|3079|Kublai}} sent two fleets,
A hundred forty thousand men, and more;
Nine hundred ships from {{p|Korea}}; the sheets
Of thirty-five hundred from {{p|China}}'s shore.

The samurai held out for weeks; and then
Another typhoon came; the fleet was caught
In harbor, and four thousand ships, and men,
A hundred thousand, drowned, or came to naught.

And those who reached the shore were cut down there.
The {{c|3083|kamikaze}}, so the wind was named,
The wind divine, sent by the gods, the care
Of {{p|Japan}}'s kami, who the islands claimed.

The wars wore out the {{c|2928|Shogunate}}: the men
Who fought had looked for land, and none was won;
No land to give; the lords grew angry; then,
In thirteen-thirty-three, its rule was done:

{{c|3131|Go-Daigo}}, emperor, would then restore
The throne's rule, the {{c|3132|Kenmu Restoration}};
It would not hold; the warriors ruled once more,
The court lost its hold upon the nation.


# Chapter 204: Genghis Khan

On the high steppe, {{c|3056|Temujin}}'s life began,
Born, eleven-sixty-two, of small lords;
His father poisoned, he was nine; his clan
Were hunted, poor, by the old tribal swords.

They lived on roots and marmots; and the boy
Slew his half-brother for a fish; and then
Ruled all his brothers; rivals would employ
Him as a slave; he fled, and built again

His life, through friendship and through marriage; and
When {{c|3058|Merkits}} stole his wife, {{c|3057|Borte}}, far away,
His blood brother {{c|3059|Jamukha}} gave a hand,
And {{c|3060|Toghrul}} too; he won her back; and they

Had {{c|3061|Jochi}}, his first son; and so he grew
His following, and joined the {{x|Mongol}} lands;
In twelve-oh-six, the great assembly drew
Him {{c|1892|Genghis Khan}}, the lord of all their bands,

The universal ruler, forty-four;
A million souls, a small folk next to those
Great realms around them; and he went to war
Across three continents, and all his foes:

{{c|3062|Western Xia}}, twelve-oh-nine; {{c|2707|Jin}}'s domain,
Twelve-eleven; {{p|Beijing}}, twelve-fifteen, fell;
{{p|North China}} lay in ruins; and again,
In twelve-nineteen, {{c|3063|Khwarazm}}'s realm as well.

Its governor had killed the envoys sent,
The merchants too; and {{c|1892|Genghis}} answered: all
The towns that fought were razed, the people spent:
{{p|Samarkand}} and {{p|Bukhara}}, {{p|Merv}}, would fall,

And {{p|Nishapur}}, {{p|Herat}}, the very best
Of {{p|Persia}}'s cities; and the channels made
For water were destroyed; and, in the rest,
{{p|Khorasan}}, the breadbasket, lay decayed,

Of all {{x|Islam}}, and for centuries stayed
A ruin. In twelve-twenty-seven died
{{c|1892|Genghis}}, thrown from his horse; his grave was made
Unmarked; those who had seen were slain beside.

His sons divided all: the khanate's sway
{{c|3064|Ogedei}} held; {{c|3061|Jochi}}'s, the western plain
Of steppe; {{c|3066|Chagatai}}, {{p|Central Asia}}'s way;
{{c|3067|Tolui}}, the homeland, the old domain.

And the rest of {{x|Jin}} fell, twelve-thirty-four;
{{c|3069|Batu Khan}} won the {{c|3068|Kipchak}} steppe; and then,
Twelve-forty, {{p|Kiev}} fell; and, as before,
The {{p|Rus}} were sacked, made tributary men,

The {{x|Tatar Yoke}}, two centuries; and there
{{p|Moscow}}, a small town, gathered tax, and grew
For the {{c|2904|Mongols}}; and, rich from its own share,
It rose in time; the other {{p|Rus}} it drew.

And {{c|3070|Batu}} went to {{p|Poland}} in the west,
Twelve-forty-one; at {{p|Legnica}} he broke
The German knights, the Polish, and the rest;
At {{p|Mohi}}, {{p|Hungary}}'s host; at one stroke

All {{p|Central Europe}} lay before him; then
{{c|3064|Ogedei}} died; {{c|3070|Batu}} returned to choose
The next {{c|3065|Great Khan}}; and so the {{p|West}}'s own men
Were saved by a khan's death, and did not lose.

The {{c|2904|Mongols}}' realm, one land, the greatest yet,
From {{p|Korea}} to {{p|Hungary}}, the north
{{p|Siberia}} to {{p|Vietnam}}; it met
All {{p|Eurasia}}, and bound it, back and forth.

The {{c|3071|Pax Mongolica}} made safe the road
From {{p|Europe}} to {{p|China}}, and all by land;
Merchants and missionaries went; and flowed
The {{p|Silk Road}} at its peak, from hand to hand.

And {{c|3072|Marco Polo}}, from {{p|Venice}}'s shore,
Told of the riches of the {{p|East}}; and west
Went gunpowder and printing, and the store
Of paper money, compass, and the rest.

The {{c|2904|Mongols}} let each priesthood keep its rite;
queens kept the Nestorian cross, and men
Tibetan {{x|Buddhism}}; all, in one light,
prayed to Eternal Heaven, one; amen.

{{c|3073|Ilkhanate}} took {{x|Islam}}, and the great
{{c|3074|Golden Horde}} too; the east, in {{p|China}}'s ways,
Became the {{c|3075|Yuan}}, {{c|3076|Kublai Khan}}'s own state;
But that belongs to the next chapter's praise.

So mark the hinge: one man, from nothing, came
From {{p|Mongolia}}, who joined his tribe, and then
Remade the world: honor {{c|3056|Temujin}}'s name,
From {{p|Hungary}} to {{p|Cambodia}}'s men.


# Chapter 205: The Mongols in Europe

And {{c|3069|Batu Khan}}, grandson of {{c|3077|Genghis}}, led
The western war, the late twelve-thirties; fell
The {{c|3068|Kipchak}} steppe; and then, in frost, he sped
Against the {{p|Rus}}: {{p|Ryazan}} burned as well,

In twelve-thirty-seven; {{p|Vladimir}}, sacked,
Twelve-thirty-eight; {{p|Kiev}}, twelve-forty, lay
Rubble; two hundred houses stood intact;
And so the {{x|Tatar Yoke}} began that day:

Two centuries the princes paid, and went
To {{p|Sarai}} on the {{p|Volga}}, the {{c|3116|Horde}},
To bow; and {{p|Moscow}}, a small town, was sent
To gather tax, and rose to be the lord.

{{c|3070|Batu}}, twelve-forty-one, his army drawn
To {{p|Poland}} and to {{p|Hungary}}; and there,
At {{c|3117|Legnica}}, the German knights were gone,
Lured by a feigned retreat; at {{c|3118|Mohi}}, where

The {{x|Hungarian}} host was broken through,
{{c|3119|King Béla}}, fleeing for his life; and they
Rode to the {{p|Adriatic}}; and in view,
{{p|Vienna}}, next; and {{p|Europe}} feared that day.

But then the {{c|3065|Great Khan}}, {{c|3120|Ögedei}}, had died
At {{p|Karakorum}}, in that December; so
{{c|3070|Batu}} went east, to where the throne was tried
Among the heirs; and west he did not go.

So {{p|Europe}} was saved by a drunkard's end,
Far off; the {{c|2904|Mongols}} had shown that its knights
Could not stand to the steppe: the bows that bend,
The feigned retreat, the horse, the ordered fights.

The {{c|3074|Golden Horde}} then settled on the low
{{p|Volga}}, and ruled the western steppe, the land
From the {{p|Black Sea}} up to the {{p|Urals}}; so
Two and a half centuries, the {{c|3116|Horde}}'s hand.

And then the princes, under {{p|Moscow}}, broke
The yoke; but that comes later. Mark it now:
The horsemen of the east, as at one stroke,
Made {{p|Europe}} choke, and taught its knights to bow.


# Chapter 206: The Mongols in the Middle East

{{c|3088|Hulagu Khan}} marched on into the west,
The {{c|3065|Great Khan}} {{c|3097|Möngke}}'s brother, sent forth to bring;
His grandsire laid {{p|Persia}} waste; the rest
To heel: the {{p|Middle East}}, and caliph, king.

A hundred fifty thousand men he led;
The {{c|1040|Assassins}} first, at {{p|Alamut}}'s hold
In the {{p|Elburz}}, the {{c|3098|Nizaris}}, who spread
Their killings through the {{p|Middle East}}, of old,

A century; twelve-fifty-six, their chief
Gave up; and {{c|3089|Hulagu}} had razed it all;
Their books were burned, their master slain; and grief;
And some lived on, and did not wholly fall.

The {{c|3098|Nizari Ismailis}} are still led
Today by the {{c|3099|Aga Khan}}, of that line
Of {{p|Alamut}}, a peaceful folk, who've spread
Their gifts across the world, in work benign.

He marched on {{p|Baghdad}} from {{p|Alamut}}'s height;
{{c|3100|Caliph}} {{c|3101|al-Mustasim}} would not yield;
Twelve-fifty-eight, he breached the walls by might;
Sacked for a week; a million in the field.

Canals of {{p|Mesopotamia}}, where
The waters ran, were broken; and the land
That fed the {{p|Middle East}} lay empty, bare,
A desert; and the caliph, by command,

Was slain; and with him the {{x|Abbasid}} line,
Five hundred years the head of {{x|Sunni}} rule,
Was ended; and an age was gone; the sign
Of {{x|Islam}}'s one head, its seat, its learned school.

{{c|3089|Hulagu}} took {{p|Damascus}}, which gave in;
He would have taken {{p|Egypt}} next; but died
{{c|3097|Möngke Khan}}, in twelve-fifty-nine; he, as kin,
Went east to the succession, with his side,

And left {{c|3102|Kitbuqa}}, his general, there,
In {{p|Syria}}, with twenty thousand; north
From {{p|Egypt}} came the {{c|3090|Mamluks}}, slaves, to bear
Their arms; and at {{c|3091|Ain Jalut}} they went forth,

Twelve-sixty, by {{x|Goliath}}'s spring, to meet;
And {{c|3103|Qutuz}} the sultan, {{c|3104|Baybars}} his sword,
Used the {{c|2904|Mongols}}' own arts: the feigned retreat,
Envelopment, reserves, against the horde;

{{c|3102|Kitbuqa}} died; the {{c|2904|Mongols}}' host was slain:
Their first great loss; their westward march was done;
{{p|Egypt}} and {{p|Syria}} were saved; the reign
Of the {{c|3090|Mamluks}}, two centuries, begun.

{{c|3073|Ilkhanate}} held {{p|Persia}}, {{p|Iraq}}'s plain;
Its {{c|2904|Mongols}} turned {{x|Persian}}, and, in their time,
{{c|3092|Ghazan}}, twelve-ninety-five, made {{x|Islam}} reign;
The state's; the Christian hopes were past their prime.

And {{x|Persian}} learning lived again: the hand
Of {{c|3105|Rashid al-Din}}, the vizier, wrote
The great {{c|3106|Jami al-Tawarikh}}, which spanned
All realms, the first world history of note:

The {{c|3107|Turks}}, {{c|2930|Europeans}}, the {{c|2904|Mongols}}' own,
{{c|3108|Indians}} and Chinese, for scholars came
Within the {{c|2904|Mongol}} peace, and all were shown
From all those lands, and wrote down each by name.

The {{c|3109|Ilkhanids}}' painting flowered, and blent
With Chinese arts; the histories were made
Illumined, three in one, as they were meant,
The {{x|Mongol}}, Chinese, and {{x|Persian}}, inlaid.

In the mid-fourteenth century, it fell
Through heirs' disputes and the {{x|Black Death}}; and broke
To {{c|3110|Jalayirids}}, {{c|3111|Muzaffarids}} as well,
The {{c|3112|Sarbadars}}, and each a separate folk.

So mark it: of all {{x|Islam}}'s blows, the worst:
{{x|Abbasid}} {{p|Baghdad}} never came again;
{{p|Cairo}} and {{p|Samarkand}} and {{p|Delhi}} nursed
What learning lived, out on the margins, then.


# Chapter 207: The Mongols in China

And {{c|3076|Kublai Khan}}, grandson of {{c|3077|Genghis}}, won
All {{p|China}}; and the Southern {{c|2865|Song}}, who'd stood
For decades past the {{p|Yangtze}}, were undone
At {{c|3078|Yamen}}, twelve-seventy-nine, for good:

The loyal fleet was sunk; and, to the end,
One bore the boy emperor to the sea,
A minister, who would not yield or bend,
And drowned with him; and no more {{x|Song}} would be.

{{c|3079|Kublai}}'s {{c|3075|Yuan}}, from twelve-seventy-one,
The first from outside who held {{p|China}} whole;
His seat was {{p|Khanbaliq}}, the {{x|Khan}}'s, begun
Where {{p|Beijing}} stands; he took the Chinese role

Of rule, but kept the ranks: the {{c|2904|Mongols}} first,
The {{c|3080|Central Asians}} next, the foreign born;
The northern Chinese; and, the last and worst,
The southern Chinese; and it bred their scorn.

And {{c|3072|Marco Polo}} served {{c|3079|Kublai}}; he wrote
{{p|Khanbaliq}}'s splendor, and the paper bills,
The coal they burned, the posts, the roads of note,
The canals; and the {{p|West}} read it, with thrills.

{{c|3081|Polo}} reached {{p|China}}, served the {{c|3082|Khan}}, and wrote{{fn|Some historians, among them Frances Wood, have argued that Polo never reached China; most hold that he did.}}
What he had seen, and did not overstate:
The things it told were true, and kept afloat
The {{p|West}}'s desire for the {{p|East}}'s rich freight.

He sent his fleets to {{p|Japan}} twice; and they,
The typhoons, {{c|3083|kamikaze}}, broke them all;
{{p|Vietnam}} and {{p|Java}} went the same way;
The steppe's war failed in jungle and in squall.

Then came the plague; the {{p|Yellow River}} burst;
Too much paper money printed; the lords
Of {{c|2904|Mongols}} fought among themselves; and first
{{c|3084|Red Turbans}}, thirteen-fifty-one, drew swords;

{{c|3085|Zhu Yuanzhang}}, a peasant, led the rest,
Took {{p|Nanjing}}, fifty-six; and, sixty-eight,
Took {{p|Khanbaliq}}, renamed {{p|Beiping}}; and, blessed
As {{c|3086|Hongwu Emperor}}, made the {{c|3087|Ming}} state.

The {{c|2904|Mongols}} fled back to the steppe; their reign
Had lasted not a century; and west,
{{c|3088|Hulagu}}, {{c|3079|Kublai}}'s brother, there had slain
The last caliph, rolled in a carpet, pressed

Beneath the horses' hooves, for royal blood
Must never touch the ground; the books were thrown
Into the {{p|Tigris}}, and it ran, a flood
Black with the ink; the {{x|Golden Age}} was flown.

At {{c|3091|Ain Jalut}}, the {{c|3090|Mamluks}} turned them back,
Twelve-sixty; the {{c|3073|Ilkhanate}}, in time,
Took {{x|Islam}} with {{c|3092|Ghazan}}; and on that track
The {{x|Persian}} poets sang, in their own rhyme:

{{c|3093|Saadi}}, {{c|2888|Rumi}}, {{c|3094|Hafez}}; and in the north
The {{c|3074|Golden Horde}} ruled {{p|Russia}} through its lords,
Took tribute; {{c|3095|Uzbeg Khan}} brought {{x|Islam}} forth,
And the steppe heard the Prophet, in its hordes.

In {{p|Central Asia}}, {{c|3096|Chagatai}}'s fell
To pieces; and from out its ruins came
{{c|3015|Timur}}, late in that century, as well;
But the next chapter tells of him by name.

The {{c|2904|Mongols}}' wars killed forty million, so
Much of the world that was; and yet they bound
{{p|Eurasia}} as one, and the arts would go
Both east and west, and plague along that ground.


# Chapter 208: The Ottoman Rise

{{c|3221|Ottoman Turks}} were one, at first, of all
The beyliks, when the {{c|2903|Seljuks}} lost their hold
Beneath the {{c|2904|Mongols}}; theirs, the least, and small,
Out on the edge, by {{p|Byzantium}}'s fold.

{{c|3222|Osman I}}, who gave the whole house its name,
A {{c|3223|ghazi}}; he took {{p|Prusa}} from the {{x|Greek}};
His son {{c|3224|Orhan}} made it the seat; and came
Across the {{p|Dardanelles}}; walls were weak

At {{p|Gallipoli}}, by an earthquake; so,
In thirteen-fifty-four, in {{p|Europe}} stand;
{{c|3225|Murad I}} pressed the {{p|Balkans}}; and would go
To set his throne in {{p|Edirne}}, at hand.

The {{c|3226|Battle of Kosovo}}, eighty-nine,
Crushed {{x|Serbia}}; {{c|3227|Murad}} himself was slain
By a {{x|Serbian}} knight; and next in line,
{{c|3228|Bayezid I}}, the {{c|3229|Thunderbolt}}, would then reign,

And came near {{p|Constantinople}}; but east
Came {{c|3015|Timur}}; and at {{c|3182|Ankara}} they met,
Fourteen-oh-two; he took {{c|3183|Bayezid}}; and ceased
The {{c|3115|Ottomans}}, almost; his sons, beset

Each other eleven years; then {{c|3230|Mehmed I}}
Restored it; and {{c|3231|Murad II}} built it then;
At {{c|3232|Varna}}, forty-four, crusaders' cry
Crushed; at {{c|3233|Kosovo}}, forty-eight, again;

The {{p|Balkans}} had been taken; all around,
{{p|Constantinople}} was hemmed in, alone;
The {{c|3115|Ottomans}} held all the {{p|Black Sea}}'s ground,
And {{p|Anatolia}} was all their own.

The {{c|3234|Janissary}} corps, the Sultan's own,
came from the {{c|3235|devshirme}}, the boys' levy: sons
of Balkan village churches, taken, grown
to serve the Sultan's altar, and his guns.

A slave corps, loyal to the Sultan, none
Beside; it held the Turkish lords in check;
Viziers, pashas came of them; no son
Inherit; each new age came at his beck.

They brought great guns; and gunsmiths came, and more:
{{x|Hungarian}}, {{x|Italian}}, {{x|German}}, made
Bombards; the great {{c|3237|Basilica}}, for war,
Six hundred pounds, the stones it threw; walls frayed.

{{c|3238|Mehmed II}}, the {{c|3239|Conqueror}}, at just nineteen,
Fourteen-fifty-one, took the throne; and wise,
Of many tongues, and cruel, set, and keen,
He made the final siege his only prize:

He built {{p|Rumeli Hisarı}}, the great hold
On the {{p|Bosphorus}}, and cut off the grain
From the {{p|Black Sea}}; and the great bombard, rolled
Out, fourteen-fifty-three; he passed the chain

With ships drawn overland; and, breached, the wall
Held fifty-three days; on May twenty-nine,
{{p|Constantinople}} fell; and in the fall
{{c|3240|Constantine XI}}, the last one of the line.

So mark it, fourteen-fifty-three: they held
The {{p|Balkans}}, save for {{p|Albania}}'s line;
{{p|Anatolia}}, the beyliks compelled;
The {{p|Black Sea}} theirs; their fleets out on the brine.

A hundred fifty years from {{c|3241|Osman}}'s small
Frontier, to take the greatest Christian town;
And {{p|New Rome}} was the Sultan's; and the hall
Of {{c|3242|Mehmed}}, and the city was his own crown.


# Chapter 209: The Corruption of the Papacy

The papacy had ages of its own
when families and kings would hold the keys
and keep the chair as houses keep a throne.
Mark two: the {{c|3271|Pornocracy}}, first of these.

"The rule of harlots": so its foes would tease.
The {{c|3272|House of Theophylact}} made its home
of the chair sixty years, and held the keys
with {{c|3273|Theodora}}, {{c|3274|Senatrix of Rome}}.

{{c|3275|Marozia}}, her daughter, at fifteen
loved {{c|2825|Pope}} {{c|3276|Sergius III}}; to him she bore
the son who would be {{c|2825|Pope}} {{c|3277|John XI}}: a queen
of {{p|Rome}} who kept the keys for years and more.

She made the popes, her husband and her son;
her grandson too, {{c|3278|John XII}}, took the chair:
the keys were in a family's hands, as one
house keeps its altar, with its kin at prayer.

And {{c|3278|John XII}} was charged by {{c|3280|Otto}}'s side:
the {{p|Lateran Palace}} a brothel, prayers
to the old gods at dice. The charges tried
to take the keys from {{c|3275|Marozia}}'s heirs.

He was deposed by {{c|3280|Otto}}, but he came
back when {{c|3280|Otto}} left; in nine-sixty-four
he died at twenty-seven, and his name
held {{p|Rome}} for his house a little while more.

A dozen popes the {{c|3271|Pornocracy}} made,
And many died by force: the poison poured,
A pillow; so the chair, its keys, its trade,
Passed on by murder, by the strangler's cord.

{{c|3281|Cadaver Synod}}, eight-ninety-seven,
Came first: {{c|2825|Pope}} {{c|3282|Stephen VI}} dug up the dead
{{c|3283|Formosus}}, nine months dead, bound for heaven,
In papal robes, was tried; a deacon said

The dead man's answers; and it was condemned;
His acts annulled; his blessing fingers cut
From his right hand; the body, so contemned,
Thrown in the {{p|Tiber}}; and the door was shut

On {{c|3282|Stephen VI}}: that year, strangled, he fell;
Such was the papacy in that dark age:
Corruption, murder, theater as well,
The keys passed hand to hand, as on a stage.

The second low: thirteen-oh-nine, the chair
Went, as the {{c|3285|Avignon Papacy}}, south
Down to {{p|France}}, and served the crown of {{p|France}} there;
Seven French popes, the king's word in their mouth.

For {{c|3286|Philip IV}} had made the move, at war
With {{c|3287|Boniface VIII}}, who had been seized
By {{p|France}}, thirteen-oh-three, and died; and more,
The court grew rich, and sold, as {{p|France}} was pleased:

It sold its offices and pardons; sold
Appointments; and its courts lived high and grand;
And it was bound to {{x|French}} banks, and their gold;
The keys were held now in the banker's hand.

{{c|3288|Catherine of Siena}} then moved the {{c|2825|Pope}},
{{c|3289|Gregory XI}}, to go back home again,
In seventy-seven; he died; the hope
Broke: the {{c|3290|Western Schism}}; two, then three men:

One in {{p|Rome}}, one in {{p|Avignon}}, and then
a third at Pisa; and the kings would choose
their pope by alliance: one chair, three men,
three courts, one office, and the keys to lose.

The {{c|3291|Council of Constance}} would meet to end
the schism, fourteen-seventeen; it set
the three aside, and {{c|3292|Martin V}} would tend
the one chair; the keys were one house's yet.

A century on, {{c|3220|Martin Luther}} came;
Fifteen-seventeen, nailed his {{x|Theses}} up,
Ninety-five, at {{p|Wittenberg}}; and the blame
Was pardons sold, to fill {{p|St. Peter's}} cup.

The {{x|Protestant Reformation}} grew there:
the keys had been a family's, and the kings',
and princes and the households everywhere
would claim the keys as well, with all it brings.

And this is why we love the chair of {{p|Rome}}:
it was a household, with its brides and grooms,
its keys passed hand to hand, as in a home,
its saints and schemers in the Fisher's rooms.

The {{c|3293|Vicar of Christ}} could be any man
of any house, a boy, a lover, lord,
and still the office held since it began,
and that is why they fought for it by sword.


# Chapter 210: The Kenmu Restoration

In thirteen-thirty-three, {{c|3131|Go-Daigo}} rose,
Emperor; and the {{c|2928|Shogunate}} he fought;
With samurai who turned: among all those,
{{c|3141|Ashikaga Takauji}}, who brought

And {{c|3142|Kusunoki Masashige}} came too;
The {{c|3121|Hōjō}} fell; {{x|Kamakura}} was won;
A hundred fifty years of warriors, through;
{{c|3131|Go-Daigo}} entered {{p|Kyoto}}; it was done.

Then there came the {{c|3132|Kenmu Restoration}}:
His own first minister, he gave the lands
And posts; but he favored court and station,
Above the samurai, who'd won; their hands

Had hoped for {{c|3121|Hōjō}} lands, and they were spurned;
{{c|3146|Takauji}}, who'd the {{c|3121|Hōjō}} betrayed,
The {{c|3121|Hōjō}}, now {{c|3131|Go-Daigo}}; and he turned,
In thirteen-thirty-six, took {{p|Kyoto}}; made

A rival of the junior line his own;
And {{c|3131|Go-Daigo}} fled to {{p|Yoshino}}, south,
Up in the mountains, and he claimed the throne;
Two courts, for fifty-six years, mouth to mouth:

The {{c|3143|Ashikaga}}'s North, in {{p|Kyoto}}'s halls;
The South at {{p|Yoshino}}; {{c|3144|Nanboku-chō}},
{{x|Northern and Southern Courts}}; and each one calls
Itself the line; the samurai chose, so.

{{c|3142|Kusunoki Masashige}}, the most true
Of all {{c|3131|Go-Daigo}}'s generals, who'd won
By ambush against the many, and knew
At {{x|Minatogawa}} he would be undone,

And fought; and after it, with his brother,
He took his life, the warrior's way; his son
Had sworn to fight; he, above all other,
Became the emblem of the loyal one.

So {{c|3146|Takauji}} made his {{c|3147|Shogunate}}
At {{x|Muromachi}}, in {{p|Kyoto}}; but weak
Than {{x|Kamakura}}'s; its writ, its state,
Reached central {{p|Japan}}; the {{c|3148|shugo}} would seek

Their own; the shogun's word they would ignore.
And under them the {{c|3149|Zen}} grew; and the art
Of {{c|3150|tea}}, the {{c|3151|sadō}}, was refined; and more,
The {{c|3153|Noh}}, by {{c|3154|Zeami}} made, and set apart;

And {{c|3155|ink painting}}, the {{c|3156|sumi-e}}, there came
From {{x|Song}} {{p|China}}; thirteen-ninety-seven,
The {{c|3157|Kinkaku-ji}}, in gold leaf's bright flame,
Built by {{c|3158|Yoshimitsu}}, rose to heaven;

And {{c|3160|Yoshimasa}}, later, built with art
The {{c|3159|Ginkaku-ji}}, subtler, and less bright,
The {{p|Silver Pavilion}}, the quiet heart;
And all of it beneath a failing might.

The {{c|3132|Kenmu Restoration}} failed; and so
{{c|3131|Go-Daigo}} is remembered as the brave
Who tried what could not be, so long ago:
Restorer, failed, heroic, to the grave.


# Chapter 211: The Black Death

The plague came from the {{c|2904|Mongol}} steppes, where long
{{c|3133|Yersinia pestis}}, in marmots' blood,
For thousands of years; and the {{c|2904|Mongols}}' throng
Of armies carried it, as on a flood.

Thirteen-forty-six, the {{c|3074|Golden Horde}} lay
Around {{p|Kaffa}}, which was the {{c|3114|Genoese}}' port,
In the {{p|Crimea}}; plague broke out; and they
Hurled corpses over walls into the fort;

The {{c|3114|Genoese}} then fled by their ships, and came
{{p|Messina}}, {{p|Sicily}}, forty-seven,
They bore the plague with them; it spread, aflame,
{{p|Mediterranean}}, under heaven,

Then north through {{p|Europe}}; {{p|Marseille}} fell; and where
The popes at {{p|Avignon}} sat, it came too;
{{c|2825|Pope}} {{c|3134|Clement VI}} lived, by the doctor's care,
Between two roaring fires; and it passed through.

{{p|Paris}}, {{p|London}}, the {{x|Hansa}}, {{p|Norway}}, and
{{p|Iceland}}: it reached the corners of the west;
A third of all the people of the land
Died in four years, by fifty-one; the rest

Saw cities lose half of their own, and fields
Untilled, villages abandoned; none
Were spared: the priest, the lord, behind their shields,
Died at the rate of all, and all as one.

The buboes, size of apples, in the groin
And armpits; black spots on the skin, of blood
Beneath; and vomit; and in days, to join
The dead. Some towns shut gates against the flood

With varying success; and then would write
{{c|3135|Giovanni Boccaccio}} the tale:
The {{c|3136|Decameron}}: {{c|3137|Florentines}} in flight
To villas, telling stories through death's gale.

Flagellants marched through {{p|Europe}}, whipped and bled
for sins they thought had brought the plague on all;
the towns turned on the eldest house instead,
of Abraham's, and burned it, wall by wall.

In {{p|Strasbourg}}, {{p|Basel}}, and {{p|Cologne}} they burned,
accused of poisoning the wells. The chair
of {{c|3138|Pope Clement VI}} held them kin, and spurned
the charge: they died of plague too. Mobs didn't care.

Some said it was {{c|472|God}}'s punishment for sin;
Some, bad air, the miasma; some, the stars;
And none could say what let the death come in,
Or hold it back with prayers or locks or bars.

{{x|Islam}} was struck as hard: in {{p|Cairo}} died
Two hundred thousand; {{c|2884|Ibn Khaldun}} said
That civilization shrank; and the pride
Of the {{c|3139|Mamluks}}' realm never rose, but bled.

And {{p|China}}, struck first; the {{c|3075|Yuan}}'s decline
Grew faster: plague and famine, and the flood
Of the great {{p|Yellow River}}, all combine
To end the {{c|2904|Mongols}}' rule, and shed their blood.

And after: labor scarce, the wages rose;
The feudal order strained; the serfs could press
Their lords for better terms; and, as it goes,
The {{x|Church}}, which could not stop it, mattered less.

So {{p|Europe}} came out changed; the old and sure
Was shaken; and the plague came back again,
But never like the first, the type, the pure
Shape of the plague, in forty-eight, for men.


# Chapter 212: The Ming Rises

In {{p|China}} the {{c|3075|Yuan}} fell to decay:
The plague, the {{p|Yellow River}}'s flood, the dearth,
The {{c|2904|Mongol}} princes' quarrels, and the pay
In paper money printed past its worth;

{{c|3084|Red Turbans}}, thirteen-fifty-one, arose,
Awaiting the {{c|1959|Buddha}}, {{c|2806|Maitreya}}'s reign,
To end the foreign {{c|2904|Mongols}}; and of those,
{{c|3085|Zhu Yuanzhang}}, a peasant, orphaned, plain

By plague; a monk, a beggar; and he rose
And up through the {{c|3161|Red Turbans}}, to command;
Took {{p|Nanjing}}, fifty-six, his seat; and those
Who rivaled him, he ended, hand by hand.

The {{c|3163|Battle of Lake Poyang}}, sixty-three,
Broke {{c|3162|Chen Youliang}}'s great fleet; in sixty-eight
His armies entered {{p|Khanbaliq}}; and he,
The {{x|Yuan}} emperor, fled north; the state

Was {{c|3087|Ming}}; as {{c|3086|Hongwu Emperor}} he reigned,
A peasant, as {{c|2447|Liu Bang}} of {{x|Han}} had been
A thousand years before; and he remained
Suspicious, as who knows the knife of kin:

Brothers betray, courts plot; and there is not
One safe; he purged; and thirty thousand died
In one; and forty thousand more, the lot,
And then cast the old {{c|3164|chancellor}} aside,

The post a thousand years had kept; and ruled
Himself, by letters to each board; and all
The {{c|3165|examinations}} came back, and schooled
In {{x|Neo-Confucianism}}, for all;

He shut the coasts to foreign trade, and made
The {{c|3166|Da Ming Lü}}, the code of law; rebuilt
The {{p|Great Wall}} in the form where it is laid
Today; gave land to peasants, to the hilt.

Died thirteen-ninety-eight; his grandson came,
{{c|3167|Jianwen}}; fourteen-two, his uncle rose,
{{c|3168|Zhu Di}}, the {{c|3169|Prince of Yan}}, in war; and flame
Took {{c|3167|Jianwen}} in his palace's close;

{{c|3168|Zhu Di}}, the {{c|3170|Yongle Emperor}}, was crowned,
The greatest of the {{x|Ming}}; he moved the throne
And from {{p|Nanjing}} northward to {{p|Beijing}}'s ground,
And built the {{c|3171|Forbidden City}}, his own;

{{c|3172|Yongle Encyclopedia}}, the vast,
Twenty-two thousand volumes and still more,
The largest of the world for ages past;
Four hundred live; the rest were lost to war.

He sent the {{c|3173|treasure voyages}}, the fleet
Of {{c|1936|Zheng He}}, built in great shipyards; and bent
His arms on {{p|Vietnam}}; and then, retreat:
The fleets were burned, and {{p|China}} inward went.

So mark it: native rule was called again
Up from the peasant's hut, the beggar, monk;
The {{x|Ming}} rose high; and then, as all things wane,
Its early strength, at sea, drew back and shrunk.


# Chapter 213: Timur

{{c|3015|Timur}}, or {{c|3113|Tamerlane}}, for he was lame,
{{c|3177|Timur the Lame}}, born thirteen-thirty-six
By {{p|Samarkand}}, of {{c|3178|Barlas}}, no great name,
A lesser noble's son, of Turkic mix;

He wed into the line of {{c|1892|Genghis Khan}},
And ruled as son-in-law, not as their heir;
He claimed the blood, but weakly, and went on
To join the {{c|3096|Chagatai}} lands through his care

In thirteen-seventies; then conquests came,
As great as {{c|1892|Genghis}}' own, though less in land:
{{p|Persia}}, the eighties; {{p|Isfahan}}; and the same:
Seventy thousand heads, by his command,

Built into towers of skulls; he broke then
{{c|3179|Tokhtamysh}}'s {{c|3074|Golden Horde}}, ninety-five;
Sacked {{p|Sarai}}, the {{c|3116|Horde}}'s wealth and its men;
And so {{p|Muscovy}} grew strong, and would thrive;

And sacked {{p|Delhi}} in thirteen-ninety-eight,
A hundred thousand slain there in one day;
He led the elephants home; and the great
The {{c|2984|Delhi Sultanate}}, crippled, gave way.

In fourteen-hundred, sacked {{p|Damascus}}; there
{{c|2884|Ibn Khaldun}} met him, wrote down their talk:
The greatest scholar, conqueror; a rare
Meeting of mind and sword, the dove and hawk.

Fourteen-oh-two, the {{c|3180|Ottomans}} he broke
At {{c|3182|Ankara}}, took {{c|3181|Sultan Bayezid I}},
And bore him in a cage; under that yoke
The sultan in captivity would die.

And so {{p|Constantinople}} stood, reprieved
For fifty years; {{c|3183|Bayezid}} would else have won
The city, but for {{c|3015|Timur}}; and, relieved,
{{p|Byzantium}} lived on, its days not done.

{{c|3015|Timur}} set out for {{x|Ming}} {{p|China}}, and died
At {{p|Otrar}} on the way, fourteen-oh-five;
{{c|3184|Gur-e-Amir}}, at {{p|Samarkand}}, his pride;
And his grandson {{c|3185|Ulugh Beg}} would there thrive,

Astronomer, who built, at {{p|Samarkand}},
A great observatory; star by star
He charted, scholar-king; till, by the hand
Of his own son, he died; and there's the scar.

{{c|3187|Timurid Renaissance}}, {{p|Herat}}'s court
And {{p|Samarkand}}'s: the painters, and the song,
The domes, the verse of {{c|3188|Jami}}, of each sort
Of {{x|Persian}} art grew there, and flourished long.

And after him his realm broke into parts;
