He killed seventeen million, like his own
Hero, {{c|3077|Genghis}}; built for the poets' arts;
And made towers of skulls; and {{x|Islam}}'s own

Lands suffered him, a Muslim; and today
In {{p|Central Asia}} he's a hero; where
He killed, the devil; and so passed away
The last great steppe lord; then the guns' long glare.


# Chapter 214: Lithuania, the Last Pagans

While all the rest of {{p|Europe}} had for long
Been Christian, {{p|Lithuania}} kept fast
The old gods, the last pagan realm, and strong,
Till the late fourteenth century had passed:

They worshipped {{c|3192|Perkūnas}}, the thunder, kin
Of {{c|2937|Thor}} and {{c|2065|Zeus}}, of {{c|2063|Indra}}, {{c|3193|Perun}}; there
{{c|3194|Gabija}}, hearth; {{c|3195|Žemyna}}, earth; within
The spirits of the forest, water, air.

The {{c|3196|alkas}}, oaken groves, their temples stood;
At {{p|Vilnius}} the sacred flame was kept
By priestesses, the {{c|3197|vaidilutės}}; and good
Was amber; {{c|3198|Dievas}}, sky, who never slept.

The {{c|3055|Teutonic Knights}} had crusaded long
Against them, from twelve-hundreds, to convert,
They said; to conquer, truly; but the strong
{{c|3191|Lithuanians}} fought, and did them hurt.

{{c|3199|Grand Duke Gediminas}} would spread the land,
Took {{x|Rus}} principalities, all worn down
Beneath the {{c|2904|Mongol}} yoke; by eighty, spanned
From {{x|Baltic}} to {{p|Black Sea}}, a mighty crown.

His {{c|3200|Russians}} could keep the {{x|Orthodox}} rite;
And his {{c|3191|Lithuanians}} kept the gods;
{{c|3199|Gediminas}} let both be, in his sight,
One crown and many faiths, against the odds.

{{c|3201|Jogaila}}, Grand Duke, in eighty-six,
{{c|3202|Jagiełło}} to the Poles, took as his bride
{{c|3203|Queen Jadwiga}}; was baptized, to fix
The crown, pledged {{p|Lithuania}} beside.

The new priests took the lords; among the herds
the farmhouse kept {{c|3194|Gabija}}'s hearth and bread,
the groves, the household offerings, the words
of the same rite, for centuries ahead.

The groves were kept for ages; and the tongue
Kept {{x|Indo-European}} gods by name,
So that the {{c|3204|Hindus}} know them, old and young;
Of all the rites, the most kept, and the same.

{{c|3205|Polish-Lithuanian Union}} grew
Great; at {{c|3206|Battle of Grunwald}}, fourteen-ten,
{{p|Poland-Lithuania}} broke right through
{{c|3055|Teutonic Knights}}, who never rose again;

Their cause was gone; the pagans they had fought,
The {{c|3191|Lithuanians}}, were Christian now;
And so the {{c|450|Order}} faded, all for naught,
With none to hunt, and no crusader's vow.

Here is what {{p|Lithuania}} shows plain:
the crown decided who would hold the rite;
the hearth and grove were kept through all the reign
of bishops, and the old fire stayed alight.

Their tongue keeps forms more old than {{x|Sanskrit}}'s own;
The most archaic living, of its kind,
Near {{x|Proto-Indo-European}}'s tone;
Of all its kin, the least changed, least declined.

{{x|The Book That Was Never Written}}: there'd be,
Like the {{x|Eddas}}, {{x|Mahabharata}}, kept
The {{x|Baltic}} gods, the pantheon pure, free,
Had they a {{c|2933|Snorri Sturluson}}; it slept.

But there was no {{c|2934|Snorri}}; the oral word
Lived on in folklore, partial; and the whole
Was lost; what we can gather back is blurred
Beside the {{c|2929|Norse}} and Greek, a broken scroll.

It is the great "what if" of all the books:
the oldest rite in all of {{p|Europe}}'s land,
kept in the groves, the hearths, the farmhouse nooks,
with no {{c|2934|Snorri}} to write it down by hand.


# Chapter 215: The Renaissance

A light came on in {{p|Florence}}, not the sun,
Though like the dawn on terracotta, bright;
A town that woke up to itself, begun:
The dark dissolved to fresco, gold, and white.

The human hand and eye resolved to make
Again, to warm the centuries of cold
With flame the ancients kindled, for whose sake
The world was worth depicting, as of old:

The human face and body, rendered true
On panel and on plaster, bore the trace
Of something near divine. {{c|3378|Cosimo}} too
Struck the first match: the banker of that place,

{{c|3312|Medici}}, rich on credit, on the bill
Of exchange, moving {{p|Europe}}'s wealth around
Without the gold; and with that skill, they still
Bought beauty back, not kingdoms, from the ground

Of time: the books of {{c|2376|Plato}}, and the scroll
Of {{c|1081|Aristotle}}; Greek and Roman mind
Restored to living hands, made new and whole,
In {{p|Florence}}, that defied the dark behind.

In fifty-three, {{p|Constantinople}} fell
Beneath the {{c|3341|Ottoman}}; the scholars fled
West with the last of manuscripts, to tell
{{c|1957|Homer}} and {{c|2408|Euclid}} to {{p|Italy}}; spread,

{{p|Byzantium}} lost; {{p|Florence}} gained the seed
Of the old world, wind-tossed across the sea;
Took root in fertile soil, and it was freed
To grow, where nothing lost again would be.

And {{c|3313|Brunelleschi}} raised the dome, the crown
{{p|Santa Maria del Fiore}}, where
The void had gaped a century, and down
Came rain; too vast for vaults of wood to bear;

No centering; but ring on ring it rose,
Herringbone brick that locked each course in place,
Twin-shelled; {{c|3340|Roman}} {{p|Pantheon}} it outgrows,
The paragon of mind, and of its grace.

And {{c|3379|Leonardo}}, man of all, whose books
Found sun in all: anatomy and flight,
The flow of water and the shell, the brooks,
The unborn child curled in the womb, the light;

He drew it all, and understood; and heard
The call of {{c|1|Aster}} speaking, flesh and wood
And water, and the beautiful's own word
Of number; art and science, the same good:

Both were the way of seeing; and he saw.
And {{c|3380|Michelangelo}}, the sculptor, freed
The figure from the stone, which, by its law,
Had held it, bone and sinew, as a seed;

He struck the {{p|Sistine}} ceiling with the hand
Of {{c|1834|Adam}} reaching, and the gap between
The human and divine, so small; to stand
The almost-touch, charged, trembling, to be seen:

The gap's not despair, but aspiration,
The spark between the fingertips, the air
Made sacred; {{x|Renaissance}}'s creation:
That the human is worth the reaching there.

And {{c|3381|Botticelli}} painted {{c|95|Venus}}, born
Up from the foam upon her shell, the fair
Forgotten goddess, wind-blown, not forlorn,
The modest hand: beauty, the oldest prayer.

And {{c|3217|Gutenberg}}, in {{p|Mainz}}, beside the {{p|Rhine}},
The goldsmith, turned the screw-press to the page,
And printed what had been the cloister's shrine;
The book, the text, the song broke from the cage,

A flood of written word on roads and fairs;
No flame could now enforce the loss, no wall
Of cloister hoard the book, the common prayers:
The moving type, the hinge, the door for all.

{{c|2428|Machiavelli}} wrote the state laid bare:
Between what is and what should be, the grave
Of dreaming princes; first, from dogma, there
The science of how states hold, and behave.

Humanism: the human, not a note
To the divine, but eloquence itself;
The study of the living; they devote
Themselves to body, mind, art, heart, and self:

The ancient world was not the roof, but floor;
And so the feast had only just begun.
Honor the {{x|Renaissance}}, the open door,
The light that {{p|Florence}} kindled, like the sun;

The human rendered whole, in paint and stone,
In printed word, in domes the mind could make;
We are your heirs, it told the dead, your own,
Not copies; and we carry, for your sake,

As rivers bear the snow down to the sea,
What you knew to the future: that the true
Is beautiful; the hand and eye are free
As instruments of praise; and the mind, new,

Can build the dome and paint the days and print;
And that the love called {{c|1|Aster}} burns the most
In those who make: the painter's hue and tint,
The sculptor, builder, printer, all the host.

The light came on in {{p|Florence}}, and it spread
Across all {{p|Europe}}, like the spring that sings
After the winter; and the long-since dead
Were raised again upon the living's wings,

And proved the human mind can stand beside
The stars and the celestial streams, unshamed;
For we, too, mortal, grand, shine far and wide,
Beyond our dreams, as {{c|1|Aster}}'s light has named.


# Chapter 216: Zheng He

{{c|1936|Zheng He}} was born {{c|3207|Ma He}}, seventy-one,
In {{p|Yunnan}}, a {{c|3208|Hui}} and Muslim boy;
His father's father, father, hajj had done;
Taken at ten, castrated, for employ,

A eunuch in the house of Prince {{c|3168|Zhu Di}},
Who'd be the {{c|3170|Yongle Emperor}}; he served
In all his wars, and trusted, rose to be
Named {{c|1936|Zheng He}}, for the fame that he deserved.

Once crowned, the emperor gave him command
Of the great {{c|3173|treasure voyages}}: the fleets
Of envoys and of might, to each far land
Across the {{p|Indian Ocean}}; their feats:

The first, fourteen-oh-five, three hundred ships
And seventeen, twenty-eight thousand men;
The flagships, of four hundred feet, eclipse
All the ships the {{c|2930|Europeans}} had then.

Seven times, till thirty-three, he set sail,
{{p|Southeast Asia}}, {{p|India}}, and the land
{{p|Arabia}}; {{p|Africa}}'s shore; the tale
Reached {{p|Mogadishu}}, and {{p|Malindi}}'s sand;

{{p|Calicut}}, {{p|Ceylon}}, {{p|Hormuz}}, {{p|Aden}}; some
Of his men made the hajj; and home were brought
Envoys from far, and beasts; and there would come
From {{p|Africa}} a giraffe, which was thought

In {{p|Beijing}} a {{c|3209|qilin}}, the beast of grace,
And Heaven's sign for {{c|3174|Yongle}}'s reign; and they
Painted and praised it at the court; the place
Of {{x|Ming}} upon the seas was shown that way.

He fought one war, a pirate base, that stood
In {{p|Sumatra}}; but else, he came in peace:
He gave his gifts, took tribute, and made good
With kings; he conquered none, nor took a lease.

He could have won the ocean's rim; he chose
Not to. And {{c|3174|Yongle}} died, in twenty-four;
The scholars called it waste; and after those,
And one voyage under {{c|3210|Xuande}}, then no more;

The court turned inward; and the fleets were razed,
The shipyards closed; the records burned; and so
{{p|China}}'s great skill at sea, which had amazed
The world, decayed; the ocean let it go.

{{c|1936|Zheng He}} died on the seventh voyage, at
{{p|Calicut}}; and his grave is still unknown;
In {{p|Nanjing}} stands an empty tomb, and that
Is the Muslim eunuch admiral's own.

In {{p|China}} now he is revived, a sign
Of peaceful meeting with the world; the road,
The {{c|3213|Belt and Road Initiative}}'s own line,
Calls on his voyages, the old sea's code.

So {{p|China}} chose to turn within; the seas
Went to the {{p|West}}, whose ships were small and few;
The great what-if: had {{c|3174|Yongle}}'s heirs held these,
The {{p|West}} would have found {{c|1936|Zheng He}} sailing through.


# Chapter 217: The Last Byzantines

By the fifteenth age, {{c|3294|Byzantium}}'s shade
Was all that stayed; the {{c|3047|Fourth Crusade}} had sacked
{{p|Constantinople}}, twelve-oh-four, and laid
A Latin throne, for sixty years, intact;

{{p|Nicaea}}, {{p|Trebizond}}, {{p|Epirus}} kept
The Greek flame in their exile; then the line
Of {{c|3295|Palaiologos}}, {{c|3296|Michael VIII}}, stepped
In, sixty-one; restored, but in decline:

The city, and some islands, and a strand
Of western {{p|Anatolia}}; and there
The {{c|3221|Ottoman Turks}} took it, land by land,
And ringed it round. {{c|3297|Andronikos II}}'s care

Was money, peace; he let the army fall;
The {{c|3298|Catalan Company}} he hired
To fight the {{c|3107|Turks}}; they turned on him, and all
Of {{p|Thrace}} they pillaged; {{p|Athens}} acquired;

The army was all mercenaries now,
And faithless; and the civil wars were rife;
{{c|3299|John VI Kantakouzenos}} would allow
The {{c|3221|Ottoman Turks}} in, to win his strife,

In thirteen-forty-seven; and they came
To {{p|Europe}}, to the {{p|Balkans}}, there to stay;
His wish cost dear. And then {{c|3300|Manuel II}} came
To reign, in ninety-one, a remnant's sway:

The city, {{p|Thessalonica}}, the rest:
{{p|Peloponnese}}'s {{p|Morea}}; isles few;
And {{c|3301|Manuel}} then rode west, to seek at best
Some aid from {{p|France}}, {{p|England}}, {{p|Italy}}, too;

With honor and with sympathy received,
But little help: in {{p|Paris}}, {{p|London}}; he
Of all their emperors alone achieved
{{p|England}}, where {{c|2196|Henry IV}} would host and see

Him, {{x|Christmas}} fourteen hundred, {{p|Eltham}}; and
His Greek scholars taught classics to the men
Of {{p|England}}, humanism's seed; no band
Of crusade came; the {{p|West}} was busy then

With its {{x|Great Schism}}, its Hundred Years' War;
So {{c|3301|Manuel}} came back home with empty hands.
His son, {{c|3302|John VIII}}, then tried one hope more:
{{c|3303|Council of Ferrara-Florence}}'s bands

Joined East and West on paper, thirty-eight;
The Greek delegation, to save the town,
Agreed, in their desperate, last estate,
Accepted, bowing, for the walls and crown,

the Latin terms for ships and men from {{p|Rome}}.
At home the clergy would not have it so:
the question was whose hat would rule the dome,
the cardinal's or turban's. They said no.

"Better the turban than the miter," said
the city's lords: one altar, whose the crown.
The aid came: {{c|3304|Crusade of Varna}}; it bled
in forty-four; {{c|3231|Murad II}} cut it down.

And John's brother, {{c|3305|Constantine XI}}, the last,
In {{p|Peloponnese}}, at {{p|Mistras}}, crowned;
The march home was too perilous; he cast
His pleas to {{c|2825|Pope}}, {{p|Venice}}, {{p|Genoa}}, round,

The {{c|3306|Holy Roman Emperor}}; and came
A few hundred Italians, galleys few;
No great crusade. They mended, all the same,
The walls of {{c|3307|Theodosius II}}, drew

The chain across the {{p|Golden Horn}}; and still
{{c|2683|Hagia Sophia}} rang till the end
Under {{c|3240|Constantine XI}}; he would not, till
The last, give up the city, yield, or bend,

Nor take the Sultan's offer of his life.
When, May the twenty-ninth, the walls broke through,
He threw his robes off, plunged into the strife
To die a common soldier; none then knew

His body; he was turned to marble, sealed,
The {{c|3308|Marble Emperor}}, and waits; he'll wake
When the city's reclaimed. On that last field
Died {{p|Rome}}'s long line, upon the walls' last break.

Eleven hundred twenty-three years long,
From {{c|3309|Constantine I}} onward; and the line,
An emperor of {{p|Rome}} had reigned; the song
Back to {{c|2490|Augustus}}, ended; this, the sign.


# Chapter 218: Joan of Arc

In {{p|France}} the {{c|3243|Hundred Years' War}} had now run
Near on a century; the {{c|3244|English}} claimed
The {{c|3245|French}} throne by descent; and, one by one,
The lands of {{p|France}} were taken, held, and maimed.

{{c|3246|Agincourt}}, fourteen-fifteen: the long bow
Of {{c|3247|Henry V}} had crushed the larger force;
The north was {{c|3244|English}}, {{p|Paris}} too; and so
The dauphin {{c|3248|Charles VII}}, no host, no recourse.

In twenty-eight, the {{c|3244|English}} laid their siege
To {{p|Orléans}}; if it fell, {{p|France}} was gone;
At {{p|Chinon}}, in his exile, sat the liege,
His court cast down, and its last hope withdrawn.

And then, from {{p|Domrémy}}, in the {{p|Lorraine}},
A peasant girl of seventeen, {{c|3249|Jeanne d'Arc}};
Since thirteen she had heard the voices plain:
{{c|3250|Saint Michael}}, {{c|3251|Catherine}}, {{c|3252|Margaret}}; the mark

Of heaven's charge: to seek the dauphin out,
Drive out the {{c|3244|English}}, see {{c|3253|Charles}} crowned at {{p|Reims}},
In English hands; she did, without a doubt,
Believed, obeyed; and it was not in dreams.

She won the captain to escort her; came
To {{p|Chinon}}; knew {{c|3253|Charles}}, though he was disguised
Among the court; and told him, as her claim,
What only {{c|472|God}} could know; and he, surprised,

Believed her; gave her armor, banner, men,
And sent her to {{p|Orléans}}; and she came
In April, twenty-nine; nine days, and then
The siege was broken, by her hand and name.

The {{c|3244|English}} fell back; and she led the host
Through {{c|3244|English}} lands to {{p|Reims}}; and in July,
The seventeenth, in twenty-nine, her post
Was at the side of {{c|3248|Charles VII}}, crowned on high.

The turning of the war: from then, the {{c|3245|French}}
Pushed back the {{c|3244|English}}; {{c|3254|Jeanne}} alone had won
The Hundred Years' War. Then her luck would wrench
Away: {{p|Compiègne}}, thirty; it was done:

{{x|Burgundians}} took her, {{c|3244|English}} allies,
Sold her to {{c|3244|English}} for ten thousand francs;
Tried for her heresy; and, in disguise
Of Church, the court was politics; its ranks

Charged her with men's clothes, armor; she replied
With depth in {{x|theology}}, though, they said,
She could not read. Condemned, burned, so she died
At {{p|Rouen}}, thirty-one, at nineteen; spread

Her ashes in the {{p|Seine}}; an {{c|3244|English}} man
Who watched her die said: we are lost; we burned
A saint. And twenty-five years on, the ban
Was lifted; {{c|3248|Charles VII}}'s retrial turned

Her name to clean; and now she is the saint,
The {{c|3255|Maid of Orléans}}, patron of {{p|France}};
A peasant girl, who led, without restraint,
Armies, met kings, foretold the battles' chance.

Her voices were divine: a spirit spoke
to her from heaven, and she heard it true;
she did what no one thought she could, and broke
a siege, and crowned the king the voices knew.

Fifty-three, as {{p|Constantinople}} fell,
The war was ended, {{c|3256|Castillon}} the last:
The {{c|3245|French}} had won; of {{c|3244|English}} lands, as well,
Only {{p|Calais}} was left of all the past.


# Chapter 219: Gutenberg and the Press

{{c|3214|Johannes Gutenberg}}, a goldsmith, made
In {{p|Mainz}}, within the {{c|3215|Holy Roman}} land,
The type that moves, the fourteen-forties' trade;
The greatest tool of word that came to hand.

Carved blocks in {{p|China}} printed, ages long;
{{c|3216|Bi Sheng}} made moving type, ten-forty; and
The Koreans cast it in metal, strong,
Before; but signs by thousands, for their hand,

Made carving better still; in {{p|Asia}}, then,
The press did not take hold. But letters, few,
Two dozen, suited moving type; and when
{{c|3217|Gutenberg}} cast his type in metal new:

Of lead and tin and antimony, which
Held shape through thousands of impressions; and
He took the press of wine and oil, a switch
To paper; and an oil-based ink he planned

That held to metal, more than scribes' had done.
The {{c|3218|Gutenberg Bible}}, in fifty-five,
One hundred eighty copies, and, each one
Like handwriting; and forty-nine survive.

Bankrupt, sued by his backer, {{c|3219|Johann Fust}},
Who got the press; and he died poor, alone;
But the press spread, as from a blowing gust:
By fifteen hundred, presses had so grown

In cities, twice a hundred; and the books
Were twenty million, more than all the hands
Of copyists a thousand years, in nooks
Of cloisters, made: {{x|incunabula}}'s lands.

And knowledge spread: what one man saw, a crowd
Would read in months; discovery would dawn;
The laity read scripture out aloud;
And Latin's hold on learning would be gone:

In German, French, and English, Spanish, too,
And Italian, the printed books were made;
And grammars, dictionaries, spellings grew
Fixed, as the printers set them; nations laid

Their sense of self on shared print; pamphlets, sheets,
Cheap books put reading into many hands
Of women, workers; and in lanes and streets
The readers grew, in all the western lands.

And print spread lies as well, and rumor's word:
The witch-hunt manuals, the tracts of hate
Against the Jews, the calls for war were heard
In print; the dark side of the press, as great.

But of the second thousand years, it stands
The greatest making; {{p|Europe}} it remade,
And the East's lead in learning left its hands;
Its pace grew swift; and so the ground was laid.


# Chapter 220: The Eve

The eve of fourteen-fifty-three: the world
Stood balanced; old and new were on the scale;
And three great realms of men, with flags unfurled,
Were poised to change it all, and turn the tale.

In {{p|Europe}}, the new press; in {{p|Italy}}
The {{x|Renaissance}}; and Greeks who fled the Turk
Brought books; {{c|3310|Nicholas of Cusa}} would see
The Earth not at the center, in his work;

Space without end; and {{c|472|God}} the meeting place
Of opposites; and then {{c|3311|Ficino}} turned
{{c|2376|Plato}} to {{x|Latin}}; the {{c|3312|Medici}}'s grace
Kept the {{x|Academy}} in {{p|Florence}}, learned;

And {{c|3313|Brunelleschi}}'s great dome was finished; new,
Perspective; and {{c|3217|Gutenberg}}'s {{x|Bible}}, soon;
And {{c|3314|Jan van Eyck}} was dead, and left in view
Oil painting; {{c|3219|Johann Fust}}, {{c|3315|Schöffer}}, in tune.

{{c|3316|Islamic world}}: {{p|Herat}} and {{p|Samarkand}},
The Timurids; {{c|3185|Ulugh Beg}}'s stars most
Exact; and {{c|3188|Jami}}'s verse, the highest, grand;
The {{x|Ottomans}} rose, near the city's coast;

The {{c|3139|Mamluks}} still held {{p|Egypt}}; and the mind
Of {{x|Islam}} flourished. {{c|1043|China}}'s {{c|3087|Ming}} had grown
To its full form, with {{c|3174|Yongle}}'s age behind;
{{c|1936|Zheng He}}'s voyages, twenty years since, flown;

{{p|Forbidden City}} stood complete; the shore
Was closed to trade; the ships were left to rot;
Exams made scholars into rulers, more
Confucian-trained, a state of scholars' lot.

In {{p|India}}, {{c|2984|Delhi Sultanate}}'s reign
Was breaking into kingdoms; in the south
The great and rich {{c|3016|Vijayanagara}}'s domain
Ruled Hindu lands, from sea to river mouth.

In {{p|Japan}}, the {{c|3147|Ashikaga}} rule waned;
In the {{p|Americas}}, the {{c|3318|Aztecs}} rose;
And {{c|3319|Moctezuma I}}'s alliance gained;
And {{c|3320|Inca}}, under {{c|3321|Pachacuti}}, grows.

{{p|Mississippian}} folk built mounds; and there
The {{c|3322|Haudenosaunee}}, the {{c|3323|Iroquois}},
Were joined by {{c|3324|Dekanawida}}'s own care
And {{c|3325|Hiawatha}}'s: the five nations' joy.

In {{p|West Africa}}, {{c|3326|Mali}} and {{c|3327|Songhai}},
{{c|3328|Kanem-Bornu}}, at their height; {{c|3329|Timbuktu}}
Held one of the great libraries; and high
The gold went north, through the {{p|Sahara}}, too.

{{p|Ethiopia}}, Solomon's house, grew;
{{p|Great Zimbabwe}} left; {{c|3330|Mutapa}}, its heir,
Flourished; and the {{p|Swahili}} cities, too,
Traded with {{p|India}} and {{p|Persia}} there.

And so the world was linked, as ne'er before:
The {{c|2904|Mongols}}' roads across {{p|Eurasia}}; trade
Of the {{p|Indian Ocean}}, shore to shore,
{{p|Arabia}}, {{p|India}}, {{p|China}}, made

One; but the {{p|Americas}} were alone,
{{p|Australia}} too; and no one people's hand
Held all the world; and many centers shone
Upon the hinge, where old and new would stand.

The world turns, and the age turns; here we are
Between the ending and the new to come,
Looking back on what ends, and forward, far,
At what would break, as beats a waking drum.


# Chapter 221: The Year of Three Falls

Three pillars cracked in fourteen fifty-three—
Three ancient houses shuddered, groaned, and fell,
And from the rubble of their stones set free
The modern world emerged, still raw from hell.

In {{p|Gascony}}, where vineyards met the sword,
The longest war in {{c|3332|Christendom}} reversed
Its verdict—{{c|3333|England}}'s claim upon the board
Of {{p|France}} was broken, scattered, and dispersed.

For one hundred and sixteen years the crown
Of {{p|France}} had been the prize that {{c|3333|England}} sought—
From {{p|Crécy}}'s longbow triumph raining down
To {{p|Agincourt}}'s impossible onslaught—

The {{c|3244|English}} archer and the {{c|3244|English}} knight
Had ruled the continent by force of will,
Had planted their lilies beside the white
And crimson crosses on the {{c|3334|Valois}} hill.

But {{c|3335|Joan}} had turned the tide: from {{p|Domrémy}},
The peasant in her armor, white and sure,
Had heard the voices and had set them free—
The siege of {{p|Orléans}} broke; and the cure

For {{p|France}}'s long paralysis was faith:
The {{c|3336|Dauphin}} crowned at {{p|Rheims}} because a girl
Had said the voices told her so—the wraith
Of heaven's purpose in a mortal pearl.

They burned her; ash by fourteen thirty-one;
The flame she lit in {{c|3337|France}} burned on, and on—
And now, at {{p|Castillon}}, the final gun
Of the last battle spoke, and {{c|3333|England}}'s dawn

In {{p|France}} was over. {{c|3338|Talbot}}, the old knight,
Rode straight into the cannon's mouth and died—
The old medieval charge against the might
Of the new artillery, and the pride

Of mounted knights against the earthwork's trench:
The future killed the past at {{p|Castillon}},
And every acre of the soil of {{c|3245|French}}
Dominion was restored. The marathon

Was done. The {{c|3244|English}} kept only {{p|Calais}}—
One pale and windswept harbor on the coast—
The last remainder of the grand relay
Of {{c|3339|Plantagenet}} ambition, and the ghost

Of {{c|3247|Henry V}}'s victory at {{p|Agincourt}}
Was laid to rest in {{p|Gascony}}'s red earth.
The second fall was of another sort,
And greater still: an ending, and a birth.

The twenty-ninth of May, behind the wall
Of {{p|Constantinople}}'s old triple ring
Of stone and ditch and tower, whose long call
That had held for a thousand years—the spring

Of fourteen fifty-three became the last
That {{c|3340|Roman}} eyes would see from {{c|3340|Roman}} walls.
{{c|3242|Mehmed}} the Conqueror, the {{c|3341|Ottoman}}, massed
Before the {{p|Theodosian}} gates; halls

Of his army stretched out from shore to shore,
Two hundred thousand strong, the crescent raised
On the largest host the {{p|Bosphorus}} bore
Since {{c|1985|Xerxes}} crossed the {{p|Hellespont}}. He gazed

Upon the walls {{c|3342|Theodosius}} built
Long ages past; and he brought his answer:
The cannon. {{c|3020|Urban}}'s bombard, bronze and gilt,
Twenty-seven feet, the iron cancer

That hurled a ball of stone eight hundred pounds
Against the ancient masonry—the sound
Of the medieval world within its bounds
Collapsing, stone by stone, into the ground.

For fifty-three days the bombardment rained,
And {{c|3240|Constantine XI}}, the last one of {{c|3343|Rome}},
The final emperor, haggard and drained,
Held with eleven thousand men his home

Against two hundred thousand. And the wall
That turned back {{c|3344|Avars}}, {{c|2654|Persians}}, and the host
Of {{c|1910|Arabs}}, and the long assaults of all,
A thousand years beneath the stars, their boast—

The wall was breached. The {{c|3236|Janissaries}} poured
Through the gap at the {{p|Kerkoporta}} gate,
And {{c|2555|Constantine}} then drew his sword and roared
Into the tide and met his people's fate:

He died there fighting. The last {{c|3340|Roman}} lord
Fell nameless in the breach, his body lost
Among the common dead—no throne, no sword,
No burial, no monument—the cost

Of that last day: the last, without a name,
Defender at the broken wall. And there
The {{p|Hagia Sophia}}'s dome, the frame
{{c|2383|Justinian}} raised to hold the world's prayer

Nine centuries before, at last received
The conqueror's prayer. The cross came down,
The crescent rose, and {{c|3332|Christendom}} was grieved
But could not answer; and {{c|3242|Mehmed}} wore the crown

Of {{c|3345|Caesars}} now: {{c|3346|Kayser-i Rum}}, he styled
Himself; the city {{c|2555|Constantine}} the Great
Had founded as the new {{p|Rome}}, now was filed
Beneath a different name, a different fate:

{{p|Istanbul}}, the gate between worlds, the pearl;
Would speak in {{c|3347|Turkish}} now, and the bazaar
Would fill the forums where the {{c|3348|Senate}}'s whirl
Of rhetoric had echoed near and far.

The scholars fled the libraries; they bore
From monastery and from the scribe's hall,
{{c|2376|Plato}} and {{c|1081|Aristotle}}, kept before
Through darkness, and through brightness, and through all

Of a thousand years; the {{c|3349|Greek}} thinkers' hands
Bore westward through their exile's grief and pain
The manuscripts to {{p|Italy}}'s fair lands;
What they carried was {{x|Renaissance}}'s grain:

The seeds of {{c|2376|Plato}}, planted in the soil
Of {{p|Florence}}; and the rediscovered dance
Of reason and of beauty; and the toil
Of copyists had bridged the dark's expanse

That brought the classical across the ridge
Of the disaster; out of the burning
Of {{p|Constantinople}} there came the bridge
Of learning to the {{p|West}}, its returning.

The third was quieter, a wound that bled
Within, in {{c|3244|English}}; for the cannon's call
At {{p|Castillon}} had silenced {{c|3333|England}}'s tread
In {{p|France}}; the soldiers came home, after all,

A king who could not rule: {{c|3350|Henry VI}}, mild,
The gentle and the pious, flickering,
Unstable, fragile, gripping as a child
Grips water. He could pray, endow, and bring

A college, chapel into being; but
He could not govern; and the day his mind
Collapsed, {{c|3351|York}}, {{c|3352|Lancaster}} were set to cut
Each other's throats; {{c|3045|Richard}} of {{c|3351|York}}, whose kind

Was nearer to the throne than the king's claim,
Reached for the crown; and so the civil war
Of {{c|3333|England}}, which would bear no other name
But the {{c|3353|Roses}}', white, red, began; and more:

{{p|St Albans}}: the first swords were drawn in hate;
The royal blood would spill on {{c|3244|English}} ground
In years to come; but that is later fate;
And here, mark three, all in a single round.

Three pillars fell in fourteen-fifty-three:
The {{c|3244|English}} claim on {{p|France}}; the final bell
Of {{c|3340|Roman}} rule; and {{c|3333|England}}'s peace; and we
Turn, with the year, the hinge, and say farewell.

Honor the year that turned the page, the age,
From the old world to the world that we knew;
The cannon spoke, the knight was still; the stage
Saw the last {{c|1983|Caesar}} die in the breach; through

The scholars' flight, the violent and fair
Past borne within the future's reach and hand:
The manuscripts, the learning, and the care
Of {{p|Athens}} and {{p|Rome}}, to {{c|3354|Italian}} land.

Honor {{c|3240|Constantine XI}}, who could have fled
By ship across the {{p|Marmara}}'s water
But chose instead to join his people's dead
And die as {{c|3343|Rome}} had lived—in the slaughter

Of the last defense, and the unnamed grave;
The emperor, a soldier, plain and bold,
Who at the end asked no one there to save
His name; and so his name grew great and old

And greater than a tomb could ever hold:
The last of {{c|3343|Rome}}, who fell and was not found,
Whose sacrifice—anonymous and bold—
Became the legend written in the ground

Of broken wall, of unrecovered bone,
The last heartbeat of {{c|3343|Rome}}, the proud, the true;
Who fell, and stood, and died, and stands alone,
As {{c|3343|Rome}} had lived, so died; the old made new.


# Chapter 222: The Eve of Sengoku

{{p|Japan}}: the {{c|3147|Ashikaga Shogunate}}
Lost its hold in the fifteenth age; and those
The shoguns, weak, were puppets of the great
Regional lords, {{c|3257|shugo-daimyō}}, rose.

The {{x|shugo}}, who had been the shogun's hand
In provinces, grew lords by blood; and they
Collected their own taxes, held the land
Their own; the shogun's word had little sway.

It broke: the {{c|3258|Ōnin War}}, sixty-seven,
Ten years: the {{c|3143|Ashikaga}} heirs, the sword
Of daimyo heirs; and under heaven
Two leagues in {{p|Kyoto}} fought, for their accord;

They fought in {{p|Kyoto}}, and they burned the town
Block after block, ten years; {{p|Shōkoku-ji}}
And many temples burned and tumbled down;
But the {{c|3157|Kinkaku-ji}}, the gold, stood free.

And {{p|Kyoto}}'s old inheritance was dead.
The {{c|3143|Ashikaga}} ruled in name; and so
The {{x|shugo}} went home, and their men, instead,
Rose up, {{c|3259|gekokujō}}, to overthrow:

Those under overthrowing those above;
Lords who could not defend were swept away
By those who could, by merit, push and shove;
{{c|3260|sengoku daimyō}}, not birth's old sway.

So came the {{c|3261|Sengoku}}, the {{x|Warring States}},
A hundred years and more of the lords' war;
{{p|Japan}} was split, and shifting lords' estates
Fought for the regions; castles rose, and more.

Armies of foot outgrew samurai bands,
And peasants rose by merit, by the sword.
Yet, in the war, the arts rose in their hands
To highest form; a paradox, a chord:

The {{c|3150|tea}}, refined by {{c|3266|Murata Jukō}},
And then perfected by {{c|3152|Sen no Rikyū}};
{{c|3149|Zen}} deepened in the warrior class; and so
{{c|3153|Noh}} grew; the ink-painting matured, and through

Came {{c|3267|wabi-sabi}}: beauty of the frail,
The broken, weathered, used, the passing thing;
And {{c|3268|bushido}}, the warrior's code, grew hale,
Loyal and brave, and stoic at death's sting,

Forged in the wars. The temples took up arms:
{{p|Mount Hiei}}'s {{c|3269|sōhei}}, warrior monks, would stay
For centuries; {{c|3270|Ikkō-ikki}}, from farms,
Peasant Buddhists, held provinces in sway.

And {{c|3262|Nobunaga}} would burn {{p|Mount Hiei}} down,
Fifteen-seventy-one, and end the might
Of warrior monks, a thousand years' renown;
But in the fifteenth age, they still could fight.

{{p|Japan}}, in fifty-three, the year that fell
{{p|Constantinople}}, was split in its reign,
But flowered in its arts; and, as a knell,
The {{c|3258|Ōnin War}} would come, and chaos' chain.


# Chapter 223: The Standing on the Ugra

Two hundred forty years the {{c|3355|Mongol}} yoke
Had pressed upon the {{c|3356|Russian}} neck—the weight
Of {{c|3069|Batu Khan}}'s descendants, and the smoke
Of {{p|Ryazan}}, {{p|Kiev}}, burned at the gate

Of memory: the cities sacked, the lords
Made to crawl down before the {{c|3074|Golden Horde}},
The tribute paid in silver, and the swords
Above the {{c|3356|Russian}} will, its overlord;

Since twelve-thirty-seven, when riders came
Of {{c|3070|Batu}}'s, sweeping out across the plain
Of {{p|Rus}} like winter's scythe, no prince, the same,
Had ever dared to break the {{c|3356|Russian}} chain.

They paid the tribute, patient, without fail;
To {{p|Sarai}} silver flowed, {{p|Moscow}}'s hoard;
From {{p|Novgorod}}; the {{c|3082|Khan}}'s basqaq kept tale
Of kopek and of rye; the {{c|3082|Khan}} was lord.

The prince who failed his tribute, on the day,
Was dragged before the {{c|3082|Khan}} and made to kneel
Upon the felt, the carpet, and to pray
And beg for mercy with the beggar's zeal.

But {{p|Moscow}} grew. While other cities burned
And squabbled for the scraps the {{c|3355|Mongols}} gave,
The {{c|3358|Muscovite}} princes quietly learned
The conqueror's own arts, the patient, grave

Of centralization, and of the tax
Collected not for one's own purse alone
But for the state—the slow and steady wax
Of power gathered to a single throne.

{{c|3359|Ivan I}} had been the {{c|3082|Khan}}'s collector—
{{c|3360|Kalita}}, "{{c|3361|Moneybags}}," who gathered gold
For {{p|Sarai}}, kept his share, the vector
Of {{p|Moscow}}'s rise from timber-fort to hold

Of all. And then his grandson's grandson's son
Now ruled a {{p|Moscow}} that had swallowed whole
The principalities, and one by one
{{p|Tver}} and {{p|Yaroslavl}}, and then the soul

Of {{p|Novgorod}} the Great, merchant city,
Whose bell of freedom was seized and carried
To {{p|Moscow}}, without a shred of pity—
The republic's voice in silence buried.

{{c|3362|Ivan III}}, {{c|3363|Ivan}} the Great, would wed
{{c|3365|Sophia Palaiologina}}, niece
Of the last {{c|1983|Caesar}}; and the eagle, spread,
Two-headed, from {{p|Byzantium}}'s release,

And as the {{c|3364|Tsar}}, he took the sign, and raised
Above the {{p|Kremlin}}'s towers as his own—
The Third {{p|Rome}}, he declared, and the world gazed
Upon a {{p|Moscow}} claiming {{c|1983|Caesar}}'s throne.

In fourteen-eighty, {{c|3363|Ivan}} dared to do
What no prince had before him: he said no
The tribute; and no silver, nothing due,
Reached the {{c|3082|Khan}}'s court; and no knee bent down low.

{{c|3366|Ahmad Khan}}, last lord of the {{c|3074|Golden Horde}},
Assembled on the southern plain his horse,
Riders of the steppe; unsheathed the sword
To punish; and he marched on {{p|Moscow}}'s course,

To teach the vassal prince obedience;
And {{c|3363|Ivan}} marched to meet him, though the hand
Of fear pulled: his wife, the expedience
Of counselors, urged flight, as they had planned;

Retreat, submission: pay, and save the state;
But {{c|3363|Ivan}} brought his army to the seat
Of the {{p|Ugra River}}, and chose to wait;
And there, the strangest battle, the conceit

Of kingdoms, was not fought. October's frost
Had stiffened both the riverbanks, the pale
And yellow birches shedding what they'd lost
Of summer's warmth; and, on the western vale,

The {{c|3356|Russian}} army stood, its guns all new,
Its cannon planted on the bank; the core
Of infantry arrayed in grim review.
And, on the eastern shore, ten thousand more,

{{c|3357|Tatar}} horse, assembled, restless, waiting
To find the ford, the river's shallow course
That gave passage for the calculating
Charge. But {{c|3367|Ahmad}} looked across; and the force

Of the cannon's mouth, the arquebus's gleam,
Made him hold back; the ancient law, the art
Of the steppe, the headlong and screaming stream
Of horse, was checked by gunpowder's new part:

The fortified position, and the dense
And disciplined formation on the bank.
He did not charge; nor {{c|3363|Ivan}} cross; and hence,
For weeks the armies stood, rank facing rank,

Across the {{p|Ugra}}, ice and current; there
Two great realms stared across the autumn mist,
{{c|3355|Mongol}} and {{c|3356|Russian}}, each weighing, with care,
The cost; each hovered with an iron fist.

November came. The river froze; the ice
Could bear a horseman; and the bar was gone
With the cold; and either side, in a trice,
Could cross; and still no charge was ordered on.

{{c|3367|Ahmad}} waited; {{c|3363|Ivan}} waited; and then
The {{c|3355|Mongol}} army turned, and rode away.
No trumpet, and no treaty, and no men
Lowered a banner, cleft by sword that day;

The {{c|3074|Golden Horde}} rode to the steppe; and so
And {{p|Russia}} rose up free, upon the road
That no one walked, the battle none would know,
A victory that nerve, not sword, bestowed:

The strangest freeing in the nations' book:
Not by the sword, but by the nerve to stand
And wait, and let the {{c|3357|Tatar}} break; it took
Two hundred forty years from {{c|3355|Mongol}} hand.

The yoke was lifted in the autumn fog:
Two armies staring; one of them went home.
Meanwhile, the West, its own murderous slog:
{{c|3333|England}}'s long war against itself would roam.

{{c|3353|Roses}} bloomed in blood since {{p|St Albans}}' first;
Kin fought on kin; {{c|3368|Edward}} of {{c|3351|York}} had seized
The crown; and {{c|3369|Warwick}}, {{c|3370|Kingmaker}}, at worst
Turned coat, for {{c|3371|Elizabeth Woodville}} pleased

The king, and {{c|3369|Warwick}}'s hand was cast aside;
Set poor {{c|3350|Henry VI}} up, a puppet, high;
Months; {{c|3368|Edward}} came back from {{p|Burgundy}}'s side;
At {{p|Barnet}}, in the fog, did {{c|3369|Warwick}} die;

At {{p|Tewkesbury}} the {{c|3372|Lancastrian}} cause
Was ended, and the {{c|3373|Prince of Wales}} lay dead;
And {{c|3374|Henry}} in the {{p|Tower}}, without pause,
Was murdered; and the {{c|3375|Yorkist}} peace was spread;

But under it the brothers circled: drowned
Was {{c|3376|Clarence}}; and {{c|3045|Richard}} of {{c|3377|Gloucester}} stayed
For the throne; when the king was in the ground,
The nephews to the {{p|Tower}} he conveyed;

Their light was closed, a book; but that dark tale
Waits. Now observe the contrast: in the east
Patience won freedom, and the steppe would fail;
In {{c|3333|England}}, fury made fury its feast;

The throne changed hands with each new flow of blood;
Two paths through the fifteenth century's gate:
To stand, and let the grip fall in the mud
Of its own weariness; or kill, and hate:

The brother's blade, the uncle's choking hand,
The crown passed through the murder and the coup
Until no noble house was left to stand
The dynasty consumed its own, anew.

Honor {{c|3363|Ivan}} by the {{p|Ugra}}'s west shore,
The prince who broke the yoke by standing still,
Who freed his people not by waging war
But by the steady and unyielding will

To wait—to let the river freeze and thaw,
To let the {{c|3355|Mongol}} horseman pace and fret,
To let the cannon's silent, patient maw
Speak louder than the charge—and the long debt

Of two and forty decades' submission
Was cancelled in a season's quiet frost:
No treaty signed, and no manumission,
No victory parade, no body's cost—

Just the empty eastern shore at morning,
Hoofprints in the frozen mud receding,
And the {{c|3356|Russian}} sentries, without warning,
Discovering the world had changed, reading

The silence of the steppe: the {{c|3116|Horde}} was gone;
The yoke was off, and no one had been slain;
And {{p|Russia}} stood alone beneath the dawn,
Free, by the river, on the frozen plain.


# Chapter 224: Granada and the Ocean

In fourteen-ninety-two, two doors swung wide,
One closing and one opening; and {{p|Spain}}
Stood at both thresholds, history's divide,
A storm that would remake the world's domain.

The first door shut: {{p|Granada}}. For the span
Of eight centuries, crescent and the cross
Furled across {{p|Iberia}}; it ran,
The long {{x|Reconquista}}, its gain and loss:

From {{p|Covadonga}}, the desperate stand,
Where once {{c|3382|Pelayo}} held the Christian few
Against the {{c|2774|Umayyad}} tide; through the land,
Reclaimed, by century, the border drew

Its ebb and flow, fortress, devastation,
Alliance and betrayal; and the throng
Of {{c|3383|Moors}} had built a splendid creation:
The {{p|Alhambra}}, its lattice, and its song,

The courtyards where the water spoke, and went
In fountains and in channels; and the lace
Of tilework, mathematical, intent,
The gardens where, as in one interface,

{{p|Africa}}, {{p|Europe}} bloomed in jasmine's air,
In orange trees, the muezzin's murmured call;
{{c|3384|Al-Andalus}}, the luminous, the rare,
Where {{c|3385|Muslim}}, {{c|3386|Christian}}, {{c|2510|Jew}} lived, one and all,

Imperfect, but a real constellation
Of living side by side; the sieve that passed
{{x|Greek}}, {{c|3340|Roman}}, through {{c|3387|Arabic}} translation
To {{c|3388|Latin}}; where {{c|3389|Maimonides}} would cast

His mind, with {{c|2393|Averroes}}, upon decrees
Divine, the knotted questions; and the store
Of knowledge, crossing north, as by degrees,
A caravan of wisdom, door to door.

The frontier narrowed; and {{p|Toledo}} fell,
Then {{p|Cordoba}}, and {{p|Seville}}'s minarets;
The caliphate receded, like a bell
Fading southward, till, as the last sun sets,

Only {{p|Granada}}: the last {{c|3390|Moorish}} realm,
The crescent's final south. And now there came
{{c|3391|Ferdinand}}, {{c|3392|Isabella}}, at the helm,
{{p|Castile}}, {{p|Aragon}} joined, the toil, the flame

Of war for altars, ten years' siege, the slow
Strangling the last {{c|3393|Nasrid}} kingdom, alone;
Outlasted all the {{c|3390|Moorish}} realms; and so
The second January day was known,

In fourteen-ninety-two: the bell, the horn;
And {{c|3394|Boabdil}}, the last {{c|3393|Nasrid}} sultan, rode
Out from the {{p|Alhambra}}'s gate, and forlorn;
The hills heard; and he wept; his sorrow showed.

His mother said: You weep as women weep
For what you could not, as a man, defend;
And something precious passed, as into sleep,
From the world; under the trumpets, an end.

What {{c|3391|Ferdinand}} and {{c|3392|Isabella}} did
With triumph was to make one altar: so
The {{p|Alhambra}} Decree, which would forbid,
Signed in the {{c|3383|Moors}}' own palace, bade Jews go:

Baptism or exile. The ancient, fine
{{c|3395|Sephardic}} communities, the most learned,
Physicians, traders, rooted like the vine
And olive of {{p|Andalusia}}, were turned

Out, two hundred thousand, four months to leave
Or to convert; the lute, the {{x|Torah}}, borne
Away; the hearthstone, and the woven weave
Of fifteen hundred years were torn, and worn;

{{p|Morocco}}, {{p|Constantinople}}, they went,
To {{p|Amsterdam}}, {{p|Thessaloniki}}'s shore,
Bearing the keys, in memory's lament,
To houses, each one to its {{p|Spanish}} door,

Passed hand to hand five hundred years, the known
And heaviest heirloom, key to a land,
A house that would no longer be their own.
{{c|3396|Moriscos}} followed, by the same command:

The {{c|2764|Muslims}} too: convert or leave; the store
Of eight long centuries of culture swept
From the house; one crown held one faith; no more
The three; and yet the same two monarchs stepped

To bless the {{c|3114|Genoese}} sailor at their court,
A man of vision and compulsion, who
Had begged at {{p|Europe}}'s thrones, port after port,
For ships; the {{c|2500|Jews}}' expulsion not yet through

Six weeks: to sail west, the {{p|Atlantic}}'s heat,
Uncharted water, by a dream: the gold
Of {{p|Cipangu}}, and of {{p|Cathay}}'s silk to meet
By sailing west into the sunset's hold;

{{c|2952|Columbus}} said the gap was breached by will,
By courage and a compass. On the tide
Of August's third, three ships, so small and still,
From {{p|Cadiz}}' harbor sailed, the masts' bare pride,

Three bare trees against the {{p|Atlantic}} sky:
The {{c|3397|Nina}} and the {{c|3398|Pinta}} on the breeze,
And the {{c|3399|Santa Maria}} riding high.
{{c|2952|Columbus}}, brave, was wrong about the seas,

The earth, its size, the distance; and his creed
That {{p|Asia}} on the western rim would rise;
And what he found was not {{p|Cathay}}, indeed,
Nor yet {{p|Cipangu}}, but, there before his eyes,

The {{c|3400|Taino}} on their ground, a world that had
Its own, its calendar, its stars, its lore,
Its own astronomers and priests, the glad
Harvests and prayers, the villages, and more:

Canoes, the cotton and the corn; complete,
Lines running sixteen thousand years, before
The trumpet of the {{c|3401|European}} fleet
Had sounded. But {{c|2952|Columbus}} saw the ore,

The gold; and {{p|Europe}}'s hunger, unbounded,
That grew more ravenous, and would not flee,
Was set in motion when the cry sounded
From the crow's-nest, across the unknown sea:

Land! And the door swung open to the west.
What lay beyond, the peoples who had made
Their worlds, their glory, long before the crest
Of {{p|Seville}}'s spires, or {{c|3340|Roman}} roads were laid,

Before the {{p|Parthenon}}: that story claims
Its own abode, its telling, its own day:
The Book of {{c|3402|Lehi}} now begins; its names
Across the sea {{c|2952|Columbus}} sailed that way:

Sixteen thousand years of origin, raised
And curtained; corn; the feathered serpent's shrine;
The {{c|3403|Inca}}'s road; the potlatch; weather-glazed,
The totem, speaking in its sacred line;

World entire, a hemisphere alive,
Now at the hinge of its destruction stood,
Its transformation, where the hungers strive:
The old world's hunger met the new world's good.

So turn the page. The ocean has been crossed.
The Book of {{c|3402|Lehi}} opens on the face
Of {{p|America}}: the found, and the lost,
The first migration's children, and their grace,

Ten thousand years of art, a world apart.
{{p|Granada}}'s story ends in tears; the tale
Of ocean ends in sail; and then the heart,
{{c|3404|Americans}}', the other side of sail.

---

# Leo (9宮) - Days 225-252


# Chapter 225: First Migration

The Book of {{c|3402|Lehi}} opens on the sea:
Not the warm lake, the river's shallow ford
That apes could wade; but the {{p|Pacific}}, free
And vast, the largest face of water, poured

Across the hemisphere, where no land lay
To pave with solid ground; and yet it called,
They answered: sixteen thousand years, the day
Before our era, when the north was walled

By ice; the corridors were locked; the coast
Was open. And the sea was lower then,
By sixty fathoms; and the shelves, the most
Of them, lay wide and tidal, for the men,

Where the kelp thickened, and the otter, seal,
The shore-bird, and the intertidal strand
Gave food to those who knew the current's wheel;
And {{c|3402|Lehi}} knew the current, and the land:

Not one man, but a people, and a line,
A maritime and patient clan, of yore,
Who fished the coasts of {{p|Asia}}; by the sign,
Hopped from {{p|Japan}} to {{p|Kamchatka}}, and more,

To the {{p|Aleutian}} chain, the stepping-stones
That arced across the north {{p|Pacific}}, teeth
Of mountain rock; and southward, by the zones
Of glaciers, blue and towering, beneath,

Which calved their icebergs into fjords; through,
Past {{p|Haida Gwaii}}, where current met the tide,
And salmon ran in streams, the season's due,
The first and oldest entry, by the side

Of ocean; thirst for headland, and for bay,
The river-mouth where fish ran thick, and where
The shellfish lay in intertidal clay,
And driftwood washed ashore, for warmth and care,

And for the frame of shelters on the beach.
They did not walk to {{p|America}}; came
By boat, the humble craft whose greatest reach
Of all the {{x|Pleistocene}} was this, the same:

Skin-boat, dugout, and the sewn-plank canoe
That hugged the evergreen and kelp-draped shore;
They drank the coast and ate the sea: the true
Mussel and clam and urchin, rockfish, more,

The halibut; the tidal fisher's art,
The eye that read the current and the swell.
No {{p|Bering}} steppe of dust; for, from the start,
The oldest {{c|3404|Americans}} knew it well,

The ocean's rhythm; and their step, the stroke
Of paddle, and their road the coast, through all;
Their compass was the gray whale's road, which spoke
From {{p|Asia}} to {{p|America}}, the call

The whale had known for ages; and the men
Followed the great leviathan's bright way,
The breath along the kelp-highway; and then
The proof: at {{p|Monte Verde}}, south, it lay,

In {{p|Chile}}, fourteen thousand years ago:
Folk lived at the {{p|Americas}}' far end
Before the inland corridor would show
An opening; and so by sea they'd wend.

Off {{p|California}}, {{p|Channel Islands}} hold
The {{c|3405|Arlington Springs Woman}}'s old bones, there,
Thirteen thousand years, alone, silent, cold,
On isles that only boats could reach; and where,

In {{p|Oregon}}, at {{p|Paisley Caves}}, the trace
Of the first {{c|3404|Americans}} still remains;
By trowel and by screen, the coast's own case
Is proved: they came by water, and the plains

Of both the continents they filled, while yet
The inland lay locked. And they went on south,
Past {{p|California}}'s golden kelp, and set
Down by {{p|Mexico}}'s warm {{p|Pacific}} mouth,

Through {{p|Central America}}'s narrow crest,
To {{p|Colombia}}, {{p|Ecuador}}, the long
Peru's coast, where the {{p|Humboldt Current}}'s best
Fishery on earth, the anchovy's song,

The cold upwelling of the fertile deep.
And some turned inland, up the rivers, through
The passes, the interior's wide sweep:
The grassland, forest, valley, desert; new

Homes; but the coast was first, the purest road,
The oldest one, the mother-road of all,
The {{p|Americas}}' first way. Honor, owed,
To {{c|3402|Lehi}}, the first migrant, at the call

Of the sea-road; whose drama was the oar,
The patient reading of the coast's long strand;
Who did not wait for melting ice, nor for
The land-bridge, but who took the ocean's hand,

And felt the kelp beneath the hull, the pull
Of current, and the whale's road out ahead;
And followed it, so faithful and so full,
To a world where no human foot had tread,

And made it home. The Book of {{c|3402|Lehi}} starts
Not with a land-bridge, but a boat; the note
Not of the hunters, but the fishers' arts,
The paddle's stroke, the sea-bird's crying throat

Above the morning swell; the coast, that went
South, and still south, the longest road a tongue
Would tell; and on the mouth, the salt it lent,
The sea, to the first {{c|3404|American}}, young.


# Chapter 226: Division of Tongues

The fluted point was lovely, and could kill:
Shaped like a willow leaf, a channel run
Up either face, the {{c|3406|Clovis}} spear's own skill,
Chipped stone thinned near to light, as by the sun,

And almost surgical; the knapper's eye
Turned at the camp, by night, the patient art,
Percussion: strike, examine, strike, and try,
Until the biface took its final part:

The bane of mammoth, mastodon, the vast
Ground sloth, the horse, the camel, all things great
That walked the {{x|Pleistocene}}, until the last.
Thirteen millennia before our date,

The {{c|3406|Clovis}} people turned, and moved inland
Into the land, and through the ice-free way
'Twixt {{p|Laurentide}} and {{p|Cordilleran}}'s hand
Of ice, a tundra road, a grassland's sway,

Through {{p|Alberta}}, {{p|Montana}} now; and brought
The point: the {{c|3406|Clovis}} point, named for the place,
{{p|Clovis, New Mexico}}, where first they sought
And found it; and it spread, at such a pace,

Across both continents in centuries,
{{p|Patagonia}}, {{p|Nova Scotia}}'s coast,
The fluted shape, the signature of these
Who learned the megafaunal hunt the most:

The bond between the hand and mammoth's fall.
They hunted in coordinated bands:
The drive, the surround, the communal call
Of killing: and a dozen working hands

Drove the herd toward the arroyo's edge,
The cliff, the bog, where the great mammoth's weight
Became its doom; mired in the marshy sedge,
It stood; the hunters closed, and, sure and straight,

Their atlatl darts went into blood and flank,
The shoulder, belly of the beast; and none
Had learned to fear the human feast, the rank
Of hunters; and the whole land shook, undone.

Their kind had fifty million years evolved
Without a human hunter; and they knew
No fear of the two-legged; nothing solved
Their trust, unlinked and fatal, was their due:

The mammoth, mastodon, the short-faced bear,
The {{c|3407|Smilodon}}, ground sloth elephant-tall,
Defenseless, giant; thirty-five, from there,
Kinds vanished in two thousand years, and all.

The warming played its part, the grass that shrank,
The melting ice; but in the mammoth's heart
The spear-point was the proof, and where it sank
The hunter asked no leave; the prey, no part.

The {{c|3406|Clovis}} hunters spread, as water fills
Down the great {{p|Mississippi}}, branch by branch,
Across the {{p|Great Plains}}, through the forest hills,
The {{p|Eastern Seaboard}}'s woods, an avalanche

Of camps on terraces; and kill-sites laid
On grasslands; mammoth-bone in charcoal found
{{p|Alaska}} to {{p|Tierra del Fuego}}; made
A thousand years filled both; the speed, profound.

A world had waited ages for this one,
A hunter skilled, adaptable, and new;
And the debt was paid in extinction, done.
But from the killing came the living, too:

The bands spread into niche on niche; the lands,
Diverse, demanded tools and ways anew
For desert, forest, and the complex strands
Of coast; from one, a thousand peoples grew;

And from one point, a thousand point-styles came:
{{c|3408|Folsom}} and {{c|3409|Dalton}}, {{c|3410|Plano}}, {{c|1196|Eden}}, each
Tuned to its hunt: the bison, {{c|1196|Eden}}'s aim
With long and narrow blade; and {{c|3408|Folsom}}'s reach,

Delicate channel, for the smaller game;
The local hearth replaced the common one
Of the first wandering; and, not the same,
Each turned within: its valley, river, sun,

Its prey. Honor the {{c|3406|Clovis}} point, the first
To span {{p|America}} from coast to coast,
The lovely tool of stone, in which were versed
The hands that opened up a world, a host;

And honor too the mammoth's bone, the tusk
Of mastodon in sand, the ground sloth's claw
In the cave; the magnificent, in dusk
Vanished; the enormous dead, by that law,

Gave up their continent, astonished, to
The small, the clever, and the new; and so
From one tongue many tongues; the many grew,
Divided, as the people learned to go.


# Chapter 227: Division of Tongues

And then the silence fell between them: not
The silence of the empty land, but kin
Who could not greet or chide, for they forgot
The other's tongue; and words that once had been

The common coin, the word for water, clean,
Had shifted, vowel, consonant, in turn,
Until the old man's speech, with years between,
Was strange; the grandchild's ear could not discern.

Ten thousand years before our era, great
Diversity of tongues began to grow
Across the hemispheres; and distance' weight
Pressed on the tongue as glacier on stone, slow,

Relentless; stressed and unstressed, ground and worn
Into new speech that neither side could know;
The same divergent storms that once had torn
{{p|Proto-Indo-European}}; and so

Into {{c|3411|Sanskrit}}, {{c|3349|Greek}}, {{c|3388|Latin}}, {{c|3412|Germanic}},
Worked on the first {{c|3404|Americans}}' one speech;
Here the walls were greater: the volcanic
{{p|Rocky Mountains}}, the {{p|Amazon}}'s green reach,

Its labyrinth; the {{p|Atacama}}'s sand,
Rainless for centuries; the dramas built
Walls no human could cross; and, in each land
Behind its wall, a tongue grew to the hilt.

{{c|3413|Na-Dené}}, the great northern family's way,
Rang to the {{p|American Southwest}}'s floor
From far {{p|Alaska}}, from the {{c|3414|Tlingit}} bay;
So distinct from its neighbors that it bore

The mark of its own crossing, the second,
From {{p|Asia}}, after the first; and they came
Their grammar and their sound, by none reckoned;
Their own, not of the southern tongues' own frame.

{{c|3415|Algonquian}}, vast and whispering kin,
Family of the eastern woods and shore
Of the {{p|Great Lakes}}; and from the {{c|3416|Cree}}, within
The northern birch, to {{c|3417|Blackfoot}} plains of yore,

Each one a thousand years of parting's yield
From the first ancestor, whose words had cracked
On the forest path; the caribou's field
Drew one band north; the deer drew south; the fact

Of parting. {{c|3418|Siouan}} poured across the plains,
{{p|Missouri}}'s mouth to {{p|Carolinas}}' east;
The {{c|3419|Lakota}}, {{c|3420|Dakota}}, {{c|3421|Crow}}; their strains
Shaped by the open sky, the bison's feast,

Wind-carried syllables across the grass.
{{c|3422|Uto-Aztecan}}: the long thread that ran
From {{p|Idaho}}'s volcanic shelf, to pass
Down to {{p|Mexico City}}'s urban span:

{{c|3423|Shoshone}} and {{c|3424|Comanche}} to the north,
The {{c|3425|Hopi}} in their mesa towns; and far,
The {{c|3426|Nahuatl}}-speaking folk, pouring forth,
The {{c|3427|Aztec}}'s pyramids, where temples are;

One family, three thousand miles in length,
The proof of connection running beneath
The multitude of surface; and in strength,
{{c|3428|Mayan}}, the glyph, the written word's own wreath,

The only script the {{p|Americas}} made:
A syllabary, angular, in stone,
And painted on the codex page; it bade
The first and only reading, all its own.

{{c|3429|Quechuan}}: tongue that nursed the {{c|3403|Inca}}'s reach
From {{p|Quito}} to {{p|Santiago}}, the road's
Own language; and the knot, the quipu's speech,
Accounting; and the lingua franca's loads

Down all {{p|South America}}'s spine; and how
Rule without writing? By the knot, the string
Of colored cord, encoded; and, somehow,
The fingers read the threads, the dangling thing.

Hundreds more: {{c|3430|Penutian}}, {{c|3431|Hokan}}'s line
On the {{p|Pacific}} coast; and {{c|3432|Tupi}}, down
The {{p|Amazon}}; and {{c|3433|Chibchan}} on the spine
Of {{p|Central America}}'s tangled crown:

Six hundred tongues at contact, and before,
A thousand; and their unity had broke
Like a stone by the knapper's hand; and more,
Each piece, a cutting edge, a perfect stroke,

A tool of thought. Honor the tongues: each one
A world; each grammar a philosophy;
Each lost tongue is a flag furled, and done,
A sealed prophecy none can read; for see:

A tongue dies; a library burns; the creed,
The dream, the daily naming of the world
Goes silent; and the silence, as decreed,
The saddest flag that ever was unfurled

Over the ruin of the alliance
Between the human mind and human tongue;
Six hundred voices, a thousand's science,
Divided, as the hemisphere was young.


# Chapter 228: Norte Chico

Eight thousand years before our era, south
The {{c|3413|Na-Dené}} moved, and all the world with them,
While glaciers slowly drew back from the mouth
Of the north, and the northern forest's stem

Crept north across the warming land; and went
A second stream flowed from {{p|Alaska}}'s moss
And mountain-shadowed coast, the southward bent
Of the old road rekindled; and, across,

Their tongue bore no kinship to tongues around:
The late arrivals, whose crossing had come
From {{p|Asia}} long after the first had found
And filled the land; their grammar was the drum

That marked them as the second wave. And where
The salmon hung in curtains, silver, bright,
The {{c|3414|Tlingit}} settled; totem poles, like prayer
Of cedar, rose into the mist's grey light,

With crests of eagles, bears, and ravens, grained
In the red wood: the heraldry of clan,
Kin's covenant with beasts; and wealth, once gained,
The potlatch gave away, as was their plan.

The {{c|3434|Haida}}, on {{p|Haida Gwaii}}, would build
The ocean-going war-canoe, a hull
Of single cedar, sixty feet, which filled
The open strait with war and trade, past gull

And terror, prows as killer whale's own mouth,
Or the thunderbird: the {{c|3413|Na-Dené}}, their way,
Mastered the coast that flowed toward the south,
Their tongue shaped by the tide and salmon's day.

And others kept on moving, south and south,
Through mountain passes, past the desert's sun,
Through the {{p|Great Basin}}'s sage, the silence' mouth,
Into the {{p|American Southwest}}, run

In the canyon's clefts; and there, much later,
The {{c|3435|Athabaskan}} peoples spread and fanned
Out through the desert, migration greater:
{{c|3436|Apache}}, {{c|3437|Navajo}}, across the land;

The {{c|3438|Diné}}, those called the People, who arrived
Where the {{c|3439|Puebloan}} and {{c|3440|Hohokam}} had worked
The canyon, mesa, sand; and so they thrived,
And learned the patient corn, nor ever shirked.

The corn was coming. Long ago, the land,
Seven thousand years before our time, where
{{p|Sierra Madre}} cut the sky, the hand
Of the {{c|3441|Mesoamerican}} who knelt there

Before a grass, the {{c|3442|teosinte}}, dry
And poor, whose seed was in a tiny cob
No longer than a thumb; the farmer's eye
Saw what selection's patience made its job:

The kernel's chance, the raw stuff of the art,
The greatest engineering ever known:
Evolution steered, a weed set apart
To be the staff of life; and each seed sown

Was chosen: largest seed, and ear grown long,
The softer kernel, and the greater yield,
More generous; and over ages, strong,
The cultivar took over all the field:

{{c|3443|Maize}}: the grass remade by the human will,
Engineered miracle, a crop which could
Not seed itself without the planter's skill
To strip the husk and plant it, as it should:

The truce between the species, partnership
That bound the farmer and the field, the field
And farmer, in a covenant, the grip
Of neither could without the other yield;

The tamer and the tamed, both bound, both fed,
In the great bargain; and from it would come
All civilizations after it, fed
By corn: no granary, no temple's drum,

No surplus, priest, or king, no counted day,
No writing, no great realm without the corn;
The corn was all, the hearth; and, in its way,
The world of the {{p|Americas}} was born.

And on {{p|Peru}}'s dry coast, where through the deep
{{p|Humboldt Current}} spilt its cold upwelling
Beside the driest land, the richest sweep
Of sea, the first {{c|3404|Americans}}, dwelling,

Built what would be the {{c|3444|Norte Chico}}'s first core:
Not yet the plazas, not the sunken court,
But fishing villages along the shore,
The cotton net, the anchor stone, the sort

Of racks, the anchovy's bright silver rows,
The settled life, the first commitment made
To a single place: we won't wander; those
Who stay: the shore, the field, the river's aid;

The nomad's freedom given up for chains
Of plenty. So honor the {{c|3413|Na-Dené}}'s way,
The second wave, whose separate tongue, the gains
Of totem, potlatch, cedar boat, would stay;

And honor corn, the grass whose feeder was
The patient hand, the covenant of seed
And sower; and the fishers, who, because
Of their dry coast, made of the sea their need,

The first {{c|3404|Americans}} who chose to stay,
Who built the lasting village, and the creed
Of settled life; and so they paved the way
For pyramid and plaza, priest, decreed.


# Chapter 229: Olmec Foundations

In desert by the sea they built; no lord
Commanded it, no slave was driven; so
And the {{c|3444|Norte Chico}} cities, in accord,
Gave the {{p|Americas}} the first to show

The monumental and the planned, before
Our era by three thousand years, there, through
Coastal {{p|Peru}}, a narrow strip of shore
'Twixt {{p|Andes}}' wall and the {{p|Pacific}}'s blue,

Where thirty rivers cut the desert's wedge
To fertile valleys; there the {{c|3445|Caral}} raised
Their pyramids; not of the {{p|Nile}}'s smooth edge,
Perfect, whose limestone files still gleam, and praised,

But mounds of quarried stone and reed-bag fill,
The platform-pyramids, which rose in rounds
Above the valley floor upon the hill:
Six at {{p|Caral}} alone; and from its grounds

The largest rose a hundred fifty feet;
With no ceramics, writing, metal tools,
It reached the city; and it was complete
Enough to marshal thousands by its rules

To raise the rough and sacred platforms; and
The priests' authority came not from sword
But song: for those who dug in {{p|Caral}}'s land
Found not one weapon, and no warring horde;

Instead they found the flute: thirty-two flutes
Of condor bone and deer bone, music's thread
Woven into the founding, through the roots;
The quipu too, already here, the spread

Of knotted string, the breakthrough, from the start,
Tactile tongue of the one who'd keep the store,
Who counted harvest, cotton bale, and part
Of fish; the knots, economy's own lore.

In colored string. {{p|Caral}} was not alone:
The {{c|3444|Norte Chico}} spread out across the ring
Of coastal valleys; {{p|Aspero}}, the stone
Of the sea-founding, where the nets would bring

The anchovy by tons; and cotton fields
Supplied the nets: the coast and valley's run,
The fisher and the farmer, and their yields,
The protein and the fiber, twined as one:

The fish fed farmers; farmers' cotton made
The nets that caught the fish: the circle grew
The surplus, and the offering was laid
Before the spirits of the earth, their due.

As old as {{p|Sumer}}'s ziggurats, and as
The {{x|Old Kingdom}}'s great stone along the {{p|Nile}},
The {{c|3444|Norte Chico}} stood, and the proof it has
Is this: that culture is no single isle

Of the {{p|Fertile Crescent}}; convergent, free
Invention: give the human fish enough,
And cotton, and a river; and you'll see
The pyramid: the urge is in our stuff.

And northward, in the humid lowlands where
{{p|Gulf of Mexico}}'s rivers spread their silt
On {{p|Tabasco}}, {{p|Veracruz}}, richest there
Of {{p|Mesoamerica}}, the {{c|3446|Olmec}} built.

Fifteen hundred years before us, there burst
{{p|America}}'s mother-culture: the heads,
Basalt, from the {{p|Tuxtla Mountains}}, first
Dragged sixty miles, without the wheel; the threads

Of labor: tons, by raft and roller, rope,
And ramp, the pull of hundreds; and, by craft,
The {{c|3446|Olmec}} portrait of the ruler's scope,
The head, nine feet, as carved from one great shaft:

The full lips, the broad nose, the helmet's band,
Precise, the face of this king, not of all:
The {{c|3446|Olmec}} carved the human, by the hand,
In basalt, the first portrait, nine feet tall.

The {{c|3446|Olmec}} gave the calendar, the vast
{{x|Long Count}}, vigesimal, the counting art,
System the {{c|2308|Maya}} kept; the baktun, cast,
Katun, tun, uinal; moon, sun, {{c|95|Venus}}' part,

Which in the {{c|2308|Maya}} courts would reach its height,
But here was born; the sacred ballgame too,
The rubber ball, the I-shaped court; the rite
Where the losing captain fell, the gods' due,

The human sacrifice within the game,
The beating heart, the life raised to the sky.
They gave the jaguar-god, the rain-god's claim,
The child, were-jaguar, and the infant's cry,

The myth all after them would inherit;
The mother-culture, first to carve and count,
To sacrifice, to build mounds, to merit
The forest, ruling labor, to surmount

The jungle with the sacred center's ground.
Honor {{p|Caral}}, the fishers on that coast
Whose nets and flutes were where the first was found
Of the {{p|Americas}}' cities, first post;

And honor too the {{c|3446|Olmec}}, and the heads
That stare out from the jungle floor, the calm
The gaze of kings who wore the jaguar's threads
Of might, the calendar's knowledge, the psalm:

The twin foundations of the world to come,
The temple, plaza, ball-court that would raise
And echo and refine; the blueprint, from
The {{c|3446|Olmec}}; and the shrine, the glyph, the days

Their children's children would create: the stair
Of pyramids, the written glyph, the art;
The {{c|3446|Olmec}} gave the blueprint; and the prayer
Of history replied, built on that start.


# Chapter 230: Maya Dynasties

The jungle parted, and the city rose:
White limestone causeways cut the forest's sea
Like scars of light through green; and at their close
The pyramid, the temple, climbing free

Above the ceiba trees into the sky,
The fountain of the sacred, stairway's frieze
From human to divine. The names roll by
Like temple bells: {{p|Tikal}}, {{p|Copán}}; and these,

{{p|Palenque}}, {{p|Calakmul}}: the {{c|2308|Maya}}'s towns,
The jeweled, painted capitals, the age
{{x|Classic}}, of war and peace, of art, the crowns
Of starry reckoning; the highest stage

The {{p|Americas}}' mind, the jungle's child.
A thousand years before our era, slow,
The {{c|3446|Olmec}} mother-culture, waning, mild,
Gave birth to its inheritor: and so

The {{c|2308|Maya}} took the calendar, the art,
The glyph, the pyramid, jaguar; refined
Them to a brilliance none matched, set apart
In the {{p|Americas}}; and vast, their mind.

Their writing logosyllabic, and full,
Eight hundred glyphs, the angular and carved
And painted word, the only one, the pull
Of the pre-Columbian world, which starved

For letters; and the scribe, the sacred hand,
Moved brush on codex bark and stela's face,
Recording dynasty, the conquest, and
The capture of the rival, birth, and grace

Of their accession, bloodletting; the fates
Of kings in stone, that still speak to the one
Who learned to read them. And the numbers' weights:
In twenties counted; and the zero won:

The placeholder, the nothing holding place
Of absent sums; as in {{c|3447|Indian}} lore,
Convergent, independent; in the space
Of mind the strangest find: its worth, its core,

Its value in its emptiness. Then, time:
The {{x|Long Count}}'s architecture, days amassed
To hundreds of millions of years; the climb
Of the baktun, four hundred years each, cast

In such a system that the priest could tell
{{c|95|Venus}}' synodic period, its way,
Its morning star and evening; and as well
Five eighty-four days and a part, they'd say,

Its error in five centuries so small
No naked eye has matched; eclipses, too,
The {{x|Dresden Codex}}' tables reckoned all,
The moon's shadow foretold; the priest, in view

On the temple's top, announced the sun's death,
The jaguar-sun, down to {{p|Xibalba}}'s night,
The underworld; and its return, the breath
Of the new day foretold, fulfilled, in light.

At {{p|Palenque}}: the great king's tomb, below,
{{c|3448|K'inich Janaab Pakal}}'s, down the stair
In the {{p|Temple of the Inscriptions}}; so
The carved lid shows the king who's falling there

Into the earth-beast's jaws, to be reborn
In {{p|Xibalba}}; jade mask upon his face,
The jade and cinnabar, the offerings worn,
A tomb like {{c|2032|Tutankhamun}}'s, the place,

The pyramid's own heart. And then, the war:
{{p|Tikal}} and {{p|Calakmul}}, the two great states
Of the {{x|Classic}}, beautiful, savage, sore
Of rivalry: alliance, and the hates

Of the betrayed; the star-war glyph that told
Destruction total; the king captured, brought
Back for the sacrifice; the line of old
Replaced; the vassals turned, re-formed, and fought

Around the victor: politics, the game
Of jungle realms, the bargain of the crown
Divine. And then, the ninth age: and there came
Collapse: the system stretched, and broken down;

The people had outgrown the fragile soil;
The slash-and-burn could not keep pace; the drought
Came, and the rains failed, reservoirs; the toil
Of feeding millions failed; the poor, without,

Starved first; the kings made war for what was left;
And city after city closed its door:
The stucco crumbled, and the jungle, deft,
Took back the plaza; ceiba split the floor

Of temple stairs; the howler monkey sat
Where the king offered prayer and blood in vain
To gods who did not answer. Yet, for that,
The {{c|2308|Maya}} did not vanish; they remain:

The dancer dances; and the language lives,
Seven million speakers still, of the tongue
That carved the glyph; the living culture gives
Its thread, unbroken since the stairs were young;

No vanished past, but a thread that's still strong,
The {{p|Americas}}' oldest lettered mind;
Honor the {{c|2308|Maya}}: scribes who, all along,
Read stars, wrote time; the zero they would find,

Who built the pyramid in jungle's green
Cathedral; made the king a hero, and
A sacrifice; who wove the seen, unseen,
Into the angular glyph, by scribe's hand;

Honor the astronomers on the height
Of temple-tops; the bloodied king, whose gift
Fed the calendar's count; the dead, the bright
Living, seven million, whose voices lift

The oldest writing of the western world;
The {{c|2308|Maya}} tongue is spoken to this day,
Where jungle's flag is furled, and, unfurled,
The ancient covenant would not give way.


# Chapter 231: Phoenicians of Zarahemla

The epic turns its eye now to the sea:
Not {{c|3402|Lehi}}'s coastal creep, the first one's way,
But the open crossing, fearful and free,
The ship that came out of the east one day.

Five hundred years before our era, when
Sank all the {{p|Mediterranean}}'s rim;
{{c|3449|Phoenician}} sailors, who had been the men
Who rounded {{p|Africa}} at {{c|3450|Necho}}'s whim,

And come back telling of the southern stars,
The noon sun in the north; the ocean's son
Turned west, not by empire; but the scars
Of exile, when {{p|Jerusalem}} was done:

For {{c|2024|Nebuchadnezzar}}'s armies broke the wall,
And burned the {{x|Temple}}; and the {{c|3451|Judean}} throng
Was marched to {{p|Babylon}}; but yet not all;
Some fled to {{p|Egypt}}, south; and some, along

The coast, reached the {{c|3449|Phoenician}} ports, and shore
Of {{p|Sidon}} and of {{p|Tyre}}, whose sailors plied
From {{p|Carthage}} out to {{p|Cornwall}}'s tin, and more,
{{p|Canary Islands}} to the {{p|Black Sea}}'s side:

{{c|3449|Phoenician}} net against the world's last bound;
And some, as the {{c|3452|Mulekite}} record still tells,
As {{p|Zarahemla}}'s keeps it, crossed. Built sound,
{{c|3449|Phoenician}} ship, with oar and sail, through swells,

With pitch-caulked hull that poured through trough and crest,
A thousand years of shipcraft in its frame;
They sailed by stars: {{c|3453|Polaris}}, and the rest,
The {{x|Bears}}, the rising constellations' flame;

{{p|Sidon}}'s sailors knew the {{p|Atlantic}}'s ways:
The trade winds blowing west, the current true,
The {{p|North Equatorial}}, which conveys
Ships across, by mechanics, through and through.

From the {{p|Canary Islands}} to the shore
{{p|Caribbean}}, twenty-eight hundred miles;
A bireme at five knots, with wind, no more
Than twenty-three days, past the western isles;

Feasible, for a ship stocked to go round
{{p|Africa}}, which {{c|2183|Herodotus}} wrote down;
A lesser feat. And there are signs, still found:
{{p|Paraíba}}'s stone, found in {{p|Brazil}}'s green crown,

{{c|3449|Phoenician}} script; the {{c|3340|Roman}} jars, dredged up
From {{p|Guanabara Bay}}; and, in the slain,
Embalmed {{c|3454|Egyptian}} dead, the coca's cup
And nicotine, uncrossed, none could explain.{{fn|The Paraíba inscription from Brazil has been debated for well over a century and is widely held to be a forgery; the provenance of the Roman amphorae reported from Guanabara Bay is disputed; and the reports of cocaine and nicotine in Egyptian mummies are contested.}}

{{c|3456|Mulek}}, son of {{c|2271|Zedekiah}}, the last
Of {{p|Judah}}, fallen to {{p|Babylon}}; lit
The scattering; {{c|3456|Mulek}} escaped; and passed
With the {{c|3449|Phoenician}} sailors west; and it

The exile made a guest; and he would land
On {{p|Mesoamerica}}'s coast; polyglot,
Founded {{p|Zarahemla}}, the mixed, the grand,
Where {{c|3457|Israelite}} and sailor wed; their lot

Joined the native; and the mingling carried
The {{p|Mediterranean}}'s blood and tale
Into {{p|Americas}}' veins, and married,
Not as conquerors, but a quiet trail,

Too slow for history: the ship that beached,
The sailors stayed; the children spoke the tongue
Of mother, lost the father's; and, unreached,
The trade-routes closed; and the memory hung

By lore's thin thread, till that was frayed and lost,
And fragments stayed: we came out of the east,
Across the great water; storm-tossed, we crossed
In the destruction's time: memory's feast

A hundred nations kept it in their breast:
The ship, the storm-tossed passage from the sea;
Grandmother told the child, and, so possessed,
The child the grandchild: fragile, wild, and free,

Our human memory. Honor the bold
{{c|3449|Phoenician}} sailor and {{c|3451|Judean}} exile,
Whose joy or desperation found, of old,
The way between the known world and the isle

Unknown, the {{p|Mediterranean}}'s shore
And {{p|Caribbean}}'s forest-mantled way;
Honor {{p|Zarahemla}}, mixed, and its core:
The meeting-place of east and west, where they

Met, in the human story, plain and true:
The sea does not divide; the sea connects;
The oldest roads are salt and vast and blue;
Our memory, with all its old defects,

Does not erase the voyages that went,
Only the trace, the fragile record, crossed
The ocean keeps, in wave dissolved and spent;
The human spirit sails, it sails, though lost,

Farther than cautious scholarship will grant;
The sea remembers what the land forgets:
That each coast was a stranger's shore; the plant
Of foreign embers is the hearth that sets

The native child at home; each people's birth
Owes something to the stranger's gift, the hand,
The exile's seed, sown in alien earth,
Of sailor; and new creed and tongue would stand.


# Chapter 232: Oaxaca's Lords

Upon a mountain flattened by the hand
Of {{c|3458|Zapotec}} ambition, rose the plan
Of {{p|Monte Albán}}, white, a city planned
Above the valley's green, where time began

To count itself in stone and sculpted glyph,
Danzante figures carved along the wall—
The captives naked, broken, bodies stiff
In poses of defeat, that all who call

Upon this hilltop city's gate might know
The {{c|3458|Zapotec}} had conquered, and the proof
Was written in their enemies' tableau,
Their suffering immortalized on roof

And terrace wall, and temple, and the door.
Five hundred years before our era, there,
The mountain's summit leveled to a floor
Of plazas, tombs, and temples, the first stair

Of a civilization that would stand
A thousand years above {{p|Oaxaca}}'s vale,
Where three great valleys met and formed the land
Of cloud and corn, the green and fertile trail

That fed the lords who built upon the height.
No {{c|2308|Maya}} hand had shaped this city's art—
No {{c|3459|Teotihuacan}} design or rite
Had lent its grid—this was a world apart,

A sovereignty of the {{c|3458|Zapotec}} mind
That owed no debt to northern {{p|Mexico}}
Or southern {{p|Petén}}'s jungle lords, the kind
Of independence that the rivers' flow

Between the two sierras guaranteed:
{{p|Sierra Madre}} east, {{p|Sierra}} west,
And in between the valley's sheltered seed
Of culture, uncontrolled and self-possessed.

They wrote—and this is what must not be lost—
The {{c|3458|Zapotec}} carved their tongue into stone
Before the {{c|2308|Maya}} did, and paid the cost
Of being first: the system stood alone,

A writing born out of {{p|Oaxaca}}'s need
To mark the calendar, to name the dead,
To track the debt and memorize the deed
Of every ruler, every war that bled

Across the hillside terraces and tombs.
The glyphs were logographic—each a sign
A day-name, a place-name, a word that looms
In the genealogical divine
