Record of who begat whom, and of who
Held power in which generation's chain—
The {{c|3458|Zapotec}} lord's authority grew
From ancestry: the living must maintain

The covenant the ancestors had sealed,
And every tomb beneath the plaza floor
Was an ancestor whose might, unconcealed,
Still flowed on upward through the temple's door

Into the living ruler's sacred right.
And in the valley's eastern arm there rose
A second people, masters of the night
Of genealogy—the {{c|3460|Mixtec}}, those

Whose painted books would prove the most complete
Surviving record, since the world began,
Of the {{p|Americas}}: the deerskin's sheet
Unscrolled to show a thousand years of clan

And kingdom, marriage, war, and sacrifice,
Each figure painted in the codex style:
The profile face, calendrical device
Of birth-names, the elaborate compile

Of every lord and lady, every throne.
{{c|3461|Codex Nuttall}} tells the tale of {{c|3462|Eight Deer}}—
{{c|3463|Jaguar Claw}}, he the conqueror whose own
Ambition nearly unified the sphere

Of {{c|3460|Mixtec}} kingdoms into one domain:
He won eleven cities, took the name
Of {{c|3464|Toltec}} royalty, and his campaign
Of marriages and murders built a frame

Of might such as {{p|Oaxaca}} had not seen—
Till his foes conspired, plotted, and seized
The conqueror himself, and the machine
Of his ambition stopped, and they appeased

The ancestors with {{c|3462|Eight Deer}}'s sacrifice.
The record lived; the codex kept the chain
Of each alliance, each cast of the dice
That marriage was in {{c|3460|Mixtec}} rule: the gain

Of one lord's daughter for another's son
Was not mere love but sovereignty transferred,
And every painted wedding scene had won
Or lost a kingdom—and the painted word

Of codex was the law, the proof, the seal
Of royal birth, authority, the ground
The genealogy that would reveal
On which a rightful government was found,

Required in the {{c|3460|Mixtec}} world of law.
{{p|Monte Albán}} declined; in the ninth age
Its plazas emptied, and the final thaw
Of {{c|3458|Zapotec}} unity left a stage

Of rival towns across the valley's downs,
And into those fragments the {{c|3460|Mixtec}} came—
Not as conquerors bearing spears and crowns
But as sons-in-law who married their claim

Into the {{c|3458|Zapotec}} high nobles' line,
The interweaving of two ancient bloods
That blurred the boundary and the design
Of who was {{c|3458|Zapotec}} and who the floods

Of {{c|3460|Mixtec}} genealogy had brought—
Two peoples woven into one estate,
Their cultures braided in the thread they wrought
Of gold and turquoise, jade and the ornate

And dazzling metalwork that {{c|3460|Mixtec}} hands
Produced—the finest goldsmiths of the age,
Whose lost-wax castings rivaled any land's
Achievement, every pendant a small stage

Of miniature perfection, every ring
A sermon in the craft of patient fire.
Honor the lords of {{p|Oaxaca}}—the string
Of {{c|3458|Zapotec}} and {{c|3460|Mixtec}} that aspire

To heights above the valley's green embrace,
Who wrote their language first upon the stone,
Who painted on the deerskin every face
Of every ancestor, and kept the bone

And record of their line through all the age—
Who owed no northern lord, no southern king
Their sovereignty, who wrote upon the page
Of their own mountain the remembering

Of everything they were: the self-made crown
{{p|Oaxaca}}'s lords, who built upon the hill
A city that could look upon the brown
And fertile valley with the ancient will

Of those who know exactly who they are,
And where they came from, and whose blood they bear—
The genealogists who read each star
Of ancestry and found their purpose there.


# Chapter 233: Andean Precursors

Before the {{c|3403|Inca}} raised their sun-crowned throne,
Before the royal roads stretched east and west,
Four kingdoms laid the deep foundation stone
On which the {{p|Andes}}' final lord would rest.

For nothing rises from the empty air—
The greatest reign is but the heir of all
The smaller realms that had been planted there
Before it, and the {{c|3403|Inca}}'s golden hall

Was built upon the floor that {{c|3465|Moche}} had poured,
That {{c|3466|Nazca}} drew, that {{c|3467|Wari}} organized,
That {{c|3468|Tiwanaku}}'s temple-builders stored
With sanctity—and each had memorized

A portion of the {{x|Andean}} plan. South—
Along the coastal desert's barren shelf
Where rain has never fallen and the mouth
Of every river is a thread of self-

Contained fertility between the sand—
The {{c|3465|Moche}} rose: and {{p|Sipán}}'s warrior-priest clan,
Whose tombs would yield the richest contraband
Of gold and silver that the {{p|Andes}}' span

Of buried centuries would ever show.
The {{c|3469|Lord of Sipán}} went down to his grave
With gold and turquoise, copper's burnished glow,
A retinue of those who could not save

Themselves from honor: guards, attendants, wives,
Interred beside him, the sacrificial
Cost of their rule, all measured out in lives,
Ultimate credential and official

Proof that {{c|3465|Moche}} lordship did not end at death.
And then the pottery: the stirrup-spout
Ceramic portrait heads that catch the breath
Of every modern eye: each face devout

Or laughing, warlike, sickened, old or young,
Each vessel was a portrait from the life
Of someone real; and there's no other tongue
Of clay has spoken with such lifelike fife

And naturalism: the {{c|3465|Moche}} potter's wheel
Turned out the faces of a people's race
In terra cotta truth, the common weal
Of a whole people, captured in the grace

Of clay: the blind man, runner, and the priest,
The warrior with his captive on a rope,
The couple in their love, wholly released
From modern prudishness; and so, the scope

Of {{c|3465|Moche}} art was all the scope of {{c|3465|Moche}} life;
No human thing escaped the potter's skill.
And south, along the desert, where the knife
Of drought has stripped the land of green, until

No green thing lives upon the pampa's floor,
The {{c|3466|Nazca}} drew their lines. Upon the stone
And gravel of the {{p|Nazca}} plateau's shore
Of nothingness, they traced the overblown

And vast geometry of the divine:
The hummingbird, the spider, monkey's curl,
The condor, its wings spread in endless line
Against the brown—each figure's sprawl and swirl

Invisible from ground level, the scale
So vast that only from the sky above—
Or from the mountains' edge—the full detail
Reveals itself: a spider drawn with love

Across three hundred meters of the plain.
Why draw what human eye could never see
From standing height? The desert's dry domain
Preserved the question: was the gallery

For gods who gazed from heaven? For the dead
Who walked the lines in spirit? Or the act
Of drawing was itself the prayer said—
The making was the rite, and the abstract

And walking meditation through the dark
Of moonlit desert nights, the faithful feet
That traced the monkey's tail and left their mark
Upon the pampa's hot and stony sheet?

The {{c|3466|Nazca}} kept their reason with the dust.
And east, above the desert, on the height
Of cold plateau, the highland's upward thrust,
The altiplano's feast of sky and light

Meets {{p|Titicaca}}'s sacred, lake-deep blue;
There the {{c|3468|Tiwanaku}} built their holy seat.
At thirteen thousand feet, where thin air drew
The breath of pilgrims laboring to meet

Their god; the {{p|Gate of the Sun}} was carved there,
A single block of andesite, the face
Of the great {{c|3470|Staff God}}, weeping, starved, who'd stare
In ecstasy, rays streaming into space

From the divine head like the condor's crown—
The pilgrims came from each {{x|Andean}} vale,
From coast and jungle, and each highland town,
To bring their offerings along the trail

That led to {{p|Tiwanaku}}'s sacred core.
This was no capital of war, no sword;
The {{c|3468|Tiwanaku}} ruled by the temple's lore,
By pilgrimage, by holiness outpoured

That radiated outward, all about,
Out from the sacred center like a hymn:
The peoples of the {{p|Andes}} felt devout
Before the {{c|3470|Staff God}}'s gaze; and the thin, dim,

High altiplano air, oxygen-lean,
Became the proof of spiritual height—
The closer to the sky, the more was seen
Of the divine, the closer to the light.

And {{c|3467|Wari}}, organizer of the way,
Took {{c|3468|Tiwanaku}}'s highland faith, and showed
The state could spread it wider, and could lay
Beyond the pilgrim's reach, the building road:

The {{c|3467|Wari}} built the roads, the terraced hill,
The centers that the {{c|3403|Inca}}, without guilt,
Would take as theirs; the relay-runner's skill,
The storehouses along the way, all built;

The clay of {{c|3403|Inca}} rule was mixed, the frame
Already shaped and set out to be dried;
The {{c|3467|Wari}} built; the {{c|3403|Inca}}, when they came,
But glazed and filled it, and it was supplied.

Honor four mothers of the mountain throne:
{{c|3465|Moche}} the artist, and {{c|3466|Nazca}} the mystic,
And {{c|3468|Tiwanaku}} the holy, and the stone
Of the altar, {{c|3467|Wari}} the logistic

And the pragmatic builder of the road—
Four pillars underneath the {{c|3403|Inca}}'s crown,
Four kingdoms that had each already showed
A portion of the answer: set it down

That nothing rises from the empty air,
That each great golden age stands on the ground,
The labor of the ones who planted there
The seed, and what the later age had found.


# Chapter 234: Mound Cities

The earth itself was architecture: no
Quarry gave stone on {{p|Mississippi}}'s plain,
No limestone cliff, no granite ridge; and so
The land gave soil: the basket-load, the grain

Of clay, the human back, the human hand,
The patient piling, day on day, a slope,
A million baskets, rising from the land,
No pyramid of stone, but earth; the scope

Of labor, muscle, and the weight of loam.
And first, in the {{p|Ohio}} country's hills,
There the {{c|3471|Adena}} built their mounds: the home
Of the dead; but more than graves or landfills:

The mound was what the land itself would yield
When people sculpt the earth to sacred form:
The conic mound, the earthen ring, the field
Enclosed and ritual, kept from the storm,

A meeting-place where living met the dead.
The {{c|3472|Hopewell}} came, two thousand years ago;
Ambition quickened, and the trade-net spread,
Till {{c|3472|Hopewell}} held the {{p|Great Lakes}}' copper glow,

Obsidian from {{p|Yellowstone}}'s far lands,
And mica from the {{p|Appalachian}} floor,
Shells from the {{p|Gulf of Mexico}}'s warm sands,
And silver from {{p|Ontario}}'s cold store:

A net across the continent, that brought
Its luxuries to the {{p|Ohio}}'s graves:
The dead with half a continent's wealth, wrought
Copper cut into falcons; and the waves

Of obsidian knapped to paper-thin,
The mica mirrors, polished to reflect
The ancestor's own face, the link, the kin
Between the living and the circumspect

And watchful dead who lay beneath the mound.
The mounds grew rich; and, on {{p|Ohio}}'s height,
And the {{p|Great Serpent Mound}} upon its ground,
Thirteen hundred feet of earth, all coiled tight,

A serpent swallowing an egg, the sun,
The world: its meaning is a dozen tales;
The serpent is beyond dispute: and done
By hand, the earth-work on the wooded vales.

And then, the city: {{p|Cahokia}} rose
Beside the {{p|Mississippi}}, where the stream
Met the {{p|Missouri}}, {{p|Illinois}}: and those
Three rivers' junction, fertile as a dream,

The richest ground in all the northern land,
The soil the corn required; this was the realm
Of maize, from the {{x|Mesoamerican}} hand
Of wisdom, that came north; and at the helm

A surplus such as north had never known;
From that surplus, {{p|Cahokia}}, its crown:
By year one thousand, twenty thousand, grown
Where {{p|East St. Louis}} is, a teeming town,

As great as {{p|London}} in that age, no less;
The largest north of {{p|Mexico}}; and there,
When corn and river and ambition's press
Joined; and a city rose from mud and air:

{{p|Monks Mound}}, the center, a hundred feet high,
Of earth in terraced stages, base as wide
As {{c|1965|Khufu}}'s {{p|Great Pyramid}}; to the sky
The chief's great hall: the hierarchy's pride

Of rank on the {{p|Mississippi}}; the chief
On top, set on the summit, as decree
Of strata, made of earth and height, belief
In rank. And then {{p|Woodhenge}}: the posts, to see

The equinox's light, the solstice dawn,
Red cedar in a ring, the debt of sun
Each season marked; the calendar was drawn
In ceremonies tied to where it spun

Upon the eastern ridge; for those who need
To know the year are cities. And then, when
By twelve hundred, it was over: the seed
Thinned out; the mounds fell silent; and again

The {{c|3473|Mississippian}} way, like a wind,
Scattered to south and east, in chiefdoms, where
At {{p|Moundville}}, {{p|Etowah}}, the mounds were pinned
In smaller towns; the idea was there:

The earth could be the monument they meant:
The soil beneath the feet, when cured and wrought
By human labor and by long intent,
Could rise as high as any stone that's brought.

Honor the mound-builders: {{c|3471|Adena}}'s clay,
And {{c|3472|Hopewell}}, {{c|3473|Mississippian}}; the hands
That carried up a million loads, the way
With no wheel, beast, or iron; yet their lands

Were crowned with monuments that still endure,
Still rise above the {{p|Mississippi}}'s plain,
Still testify, immovable and sure,
That earth itself, when shaped by human pain

And purpose, is the oldest building made:
Not stone imposed upon the ground, but ground
Itself, lifted by will, collective, laid
And made into the sacred, mound by mound,

To hold the dead, to hold the chief above
The people's gaze; the soil beneath the tread
Of those who built with nothing but their love
Of land they stood on, raised it overhead.


# Chapter 235: Desert & Cliffs

The desert teaches everything or none:
Those who came to the {{p|Southwest}}'s burning floor
Of canyon, mesa, silence, and the sun,
'Twixt {{p|Rockies}} and {{p|Sierra Madre}}'s door,

Found little given freely; and the rain
Fell rarely; and the teacher of all things
That live spoke stern: Adapt or perish; plain,
No third way. Three peoples heard what that brings,

And each wrote its own essay of the sand
On how the human mind, when unafraid
Of hardship, turns the wasteland green: the land
First, of the {{c|3440|Hohokam}}, canal and spade,

Where {{p|Phoenix}} spreads its asphalt grid today;
But fifteen hundred years before, they drank
The river: {{c|3440|Hohokam}} had found the way
Of irrigation, bank by channeled bank:

Hundreds of miles of hand-dug channels led
The {{p|Salt}} and {{p|Gila}} Rivers' snowmelt, poured
To corn and squash and cotton in the bed
Of the {{p|Sonoran}} furnace; clay-lined, stored

Against the seepage; and the desert, made
By human labor into garden ground,
Was the {{c|3440|Hohokam}}'s quiet gift; no shade
Of pyramid, of temple; but they found

The desert's harshness pardoned; and they drew
Water from riverbed to field; the yield
Far more than the bare desert ever grew
Fed many, that the dry land could not shield.

They built their ball courts too: the rubber game
That {{p|Mesoamerica}} invented, played
In the {{p|Sonoran}} heat, the drama, same
Of cosmos; thought came northward, in the trade

Along the trails from {{p|Mexico}} to these
Dry lands; for cultures are not islands; hands
Pass on the thought. And second, in the trees,
The {{c|3474|Mogollon}} of the high mountain lands,

Between the desert and {{p|Mogollon Rim}},
The potters, with their {{c|3475|Mimbres}} ware, the rare
Black-on-white, with a line so sure and trim,
So spare, so absolute, so full of care:

Of fish and crane and rabbit, figures, bold
And playful, dancing on the bowl; each one
A scroll of nature, to the essence told:
One line, the wing; one curve, the river's run;

One dot, the eye: the potter knew that all
Could be reduced to essence, perfect, dry,
The living form abstracted. At the fall
Of the potter, the finest bowl, to die,

Was killed: a hole punched through the painted clay
To free the vessel's soul, to go below
The floor beside the dead; and so, the way
Of art for life and death: and both would show

The beauty that outlived the potter's day.
And third, the greatest, in ambition, scale:
The {{c|3476|Ancestral Puebloans}}, and then their way
Of {{p|Chaco Canyon}}'s monumental tale:

In sandy wash below the canyon's stage
Of rock and sage, the {{c|3477|Puebloans}} would then show
What gathered human will could build, the gauge
Of the unlikely: houses, row on row,

{{p|Pueblo Bonito}}, with six hundred rooms,
Four stories, fitted stone, the largest host
In {{p|North America}}; and as it looms,
{{p|Chaco}}, no town, but something else: a post

Of ceremony, gathering, a crown
Of roads that met upon the canyon's floor:
The roads ran straight, thirty feet wide, cut down
Through mesa-tops, for ritual, and more:

Not roads for trade, but for the sacred way,
Like {{c|3466|Nazca}} lines laid out upon the land,
Aligned to solstice, equinox's day,
The pilgrims' paths, as drawn by sacred hand.

{{p|Mesa Verde}}: cliff-dwellings carved below
The sandstone overhangs, the rooms of stone
Where rock withheld the rain's destructive flow,
Sheltered beneath the canyon wall alone:

{{p|Cliff Palace}}, with a hundred fifty rooms,
Hung in the rock-face like a nest, and reached
By handholds, safe from summer's sun that dooms,
Defensible, from western winds unbreached,

Engineered comfort in the cliff's embrace.
The rains grew less; the thirteenth age brought drought
That settled like a judgment on the place:
The water failed; the corn's demand ran out

Beyond the sky's gift; the arithmetic
Of land that cannot feed its people; so
South, east they went; the cities emptied quick;
The heirs went to the {{p|Rio Grande}}, below,

Bearing what cliff and canyon had bestowed:
The kiva's sacred roundness underground,
The corn-dance and the rain-prayer, which was owed
To ancestors; the people, wise and sound,

Who built upon the hardest earth, and when
Its patience ended, did not die, but sought
Rebirth in gentler land. Honor the men
And women of the desert, all they wrought:

The {{c|3440|Hohokam}}, {{c|3474|Mogollon}}, {{c|3439|Puebloan}}: they
Proved that the desert is no empty space,
But classroom; and its lesson, to this day,
Is written on the canyon's weathered face:

The hardest land produces the most art,
That scarcest water teaches deepest care,
That people of the margins hold the heart
Of civilization in the dry air.


# Chapter 236: Norse in Vinland

The longship cut the fog like a gray blade
Through the gray water; and the {{c|2929|Norse}} aboard
Could smell the land before the land displayed
Itself: the pine, the resin, unexplored,

The forest that no {{c|3401|European}} axe
Had touched; and first, peering into the mist,
Gripping the prow, stood {{c|3478|Leif}}, whose father's tracks
Were exiled: {{c|3479|Erik}}, from {{p|Norway}} dismissed,

To {{p|Iceland}}; and from {{p|Iceland}}, by its law,
For killing a man, fled to {{p|Greenland}}'s ice;
And from that ledge, the westward ocean's draw
Called out; to the {{c|2929|Norse}}, no edge would suffice

To stop them. In the year one thousand, came
{{c|3480|Bjarni}} {{c|3481|Herjulfsson}}'s report of new land
Beyond the ocean, blown off course; the same
Three coasts, wooded and flat, but never manned;

And {{c|2951|Leif Erikson}} crossed the space between
The seeing and the landing; and he sailed
With thirty-five; the autumn winds, serene,
Of the {{p|North Atlantic}}, for them prevailed,

And brought them first to {{p|Helluland}}, the slab
Of stone, the barren, flat, and glacial shore
Of {{p|Baffin Island}} as it is now, drab,
No timber and no welcome; and they bore

On past it. Then to {{p|Markland}}: forest, coast
Of {{p|Labrador}}'s dense spruce, and timber there
That {{p|Greenland}}'s treeless colony would most
Need; but {{c|3478|Leif}} pressed on south, the season fair,

Until the coastline gentled, and the air
Grew milder; streams were thick with salmon, great
Beyond the {{c|2929|Norse}} experience; and there
Wild grapes grew on the shore, and gave, as freight,

The land its name, {{p|Vinland}}: the wine-land, coast
Where frost came late, the grass grew lush; and so,
Said {{c|3478|Leif}}, is what a {{c|3482|Norseman}} wants most;
They built their camp, the longhouse, forge aglow,

The smithy where the bog-iron was worked
To nails at {{p|L'Anse aux Meadows}}, the tip
Of {{p|Newfoundland}}; the proof in the sod lurked
A thousand years, until released its grip:

The ring-headed bronze pin; the spindle-whorl
That proved that women came; the iron slag;
A settlement whose very bones unfurl
{{p|Scandinavia}}'s name, as on a flag.

They wintered there; they met the {{c|3483|Skraelings}}, those
Strangers, the coast's own people, whose dark line
Against the trees was the first meeting, close,
{{c|3401|European}}, {{c|3484|American}}: a sign

Not of conquest, but trade: the red cloth spread
For furs; the milk that frightened those who had
No cattle; but the peace was glass; and dead
Were eight of nine by {{c|3485|Thorvald}}, made it bad,

{{c|3478|Leif}}'s brother; and the {{c|3483|Skraelings}} came amain
With arrows; and then {{c|3485|Thorvald}} fell: the first
{{c|3401|European}} by {{c|3484|American}} slain:
The first blood of the long transaction, cursed.

And so the {{c|2929|Norse}} withdrew: not in a rout,
Not driven screaming to the ships, but slow:
The practical assessment, cost and doubt:
{{p|Vinland}} too far, too many {{c|3483|Skraelings}}; so

The line to {{p|Greenland}} stretched beyond the bar
Of what the colony could justify;
They left; the grass grew back; the longhouse, far,
Rotted in sod; the land went on, its sky

Its own, its history its own; the touch
Of the future had brushed upon its shore.
This was not conquest, plague, the cross, the clutch
Of sword; it was a briefly opened door

That shut again: the {{c|2929|Norse}}, the prelude, played,
That history denied: too small to force
A change, a touch too brief, too slight, that made
No lasting wound, a meeting, in the course

At the edge of two worlds; a single pin
Beneath the sedge is what the years preserved.
But mark this well: the land, and all therein,
Was never empty; nor the undeserved

And passive background were the {{c|3483|Skraelings}}: they
Were the coast's plenty, people of the shore
For thousands of years there, and had no way
Needing no finding; and, upon their floor

Ancestral, outlived the {{c|2929|Norse}} by staying.
Honor {{c|3478|Leif}}, son of exiles, who pushed west
The known world's edge, courage not decaying
In ice-age seas; but honor more the rest:

The {{c|3483|Skraelings}}, who had watched the {{c|2929|Norse}} at ease
From the trees, and held the shore long after
The longships left, the forge went cold; and these,
Constant-hearted people, with their laughter,

Who needed no one's sail upon the sea
Of their horizon to confirm the land
Was real, and theirs, and home, as it would be;
Their own, beneath their feet, upon their sand.


# Chapter 237: Eskimo-Aleut Expansion

A third migration, and the last: the gate
Of {{p|Beringia}} was drowned, the broad plain
Submerged beneath the melted glaciers' weight
And risen sea; but on the {{p|Arctic}}'s main,

The passage lay open to those who had
The means and will: the frozen ocean's road
Was not a wall; and from {{p|Alaska}}, clad
In furs, a thousand years ago, there strode

The {{c|147|Thule}}, across the world's own top; its night
Of {{p|Arctic}} winter held no fear for those
More than the warm savanna's noonday light
For warmer folk; they mastered, as one knows,

The kayak: skin and bone, the single seat
Of walrus-hide on driftwood frame; the boat
Most intimate, the hunter wore complete,
Sealed by a drawstring skirt about the throat,

The man and vessel one; and when the wave
Rolled the kayak over, he did not drown,
But, as the water wished, would so behave,
Roll back up: the {{c|3486|Eskimo}} roll, the crown

Of trust between the body and the craft.
The umiak: the open boat, the freight
Of women and the camp, broad, fore and aft,
Of tents and tools and children, and the weight

Of cached provisions; where the kayak was
The sword, the umiak the shield, the load,
And stable platform. And the sled, because
Of the {{c|147|Thule}} and their dogs, the winter road

Across the sea-ice, in the freezing fog,
The driver on the runners, and the team
Of huskies bred to pull: the human, dog,
Ten thousand years of taming, its extreme

And final test; without the dog, no home
Was possible: the living engine. And
The igloo: from the snow itself, a dome,
The very thing that kills, turned shelter's hand;

The frozen enemy, turned warm with breath,
Insulation in the substance of cold:
Some forty blocks of wind-packed snow, from death
A shelter, spiraled inward, and, behold,

A house built swiftly, that in spring would melt
And leaves no scar upon the land; the hand
Of ingenuity laid flat, that felt
The ice, and said: Here too; here, I will stand,

Even in coldest place, the killing dark,
I'll make a home. And then the whale, the vast
Bowhead, leviathan, the {{c|147|Thule}}'s ark
Of plenty: one could feed a village, cast

Through a whole season; blubber, rendered oil
For lamps that burned the polar night; the bone
That framed the house when driftwood failed the toil;
The baleen's springy plate, as tool, alone

Served for the metal that they lacked: the whale
Was the estate on which the pact was made
With frozen sea. From the umiak's rail,
Six hunters, sinew line, the toggling blade

Of the harpoon that turns beneath the mass
Of blubber, holds; the sealskin float paid out
By patient hunter on the water's glass,
The whale dives, and tires, and dives, without

Its sleep and blood, till the great beast succumbs,
And one whale's body feeds the waiting shore.
East from {{p|Alaska}}, as the season comes,
The {{c|147|Thule}} opened the {{p|Arctic}}, door on door:

{{p|Beaufort Sea}}, the {{p|Archipelago}}'s maze
Of islands; {{p|Hudson Bay}}'s enormous bound;
The {{p|Labrador}} coast's fog, and the fjords' haze
Of {{p|Greenland}}'s west; in four centuries, crowned

The continent, three thousand miles of ice;
And where they settled, the {{c|3487|Dorset}} went down:
The {{c|3487|Dorset}}, there before, whose quiet price
Of lonelier tradition held the crown

Of {{p|Arctic}} for a thousand years: no dog,
No bow, no open boat; their mastery
Was small, lone hunter's skill; and in the fog
Of {{c|147|Thule}}'s dogs and bows and crews at sea,

The {{c|3487|Dorset}} froze to margins and to lore
Of the {{c|3488|Inuit}}, who still call them {{c|3489|Tunit}}:
Gentle giants, strong, the old ones, before,
Who could not keep the new world's pace, or fit,

And vanished from the ice. Honor the last
Great wave, the {{c|147|Thule}}, who paid the {{p|Arctic}}'s price,
Accepted its impossible, and cast
The kayak's shell, trained dogs, spiraled the ice

To dome, chased whale through swell, and made a home
Of frozen dark: the proof that there's no place
So hostile on this planet that the loam
Of human mind and will cannot find space

To live there: not to merely just survive,
But prosper, hunt, and sing, and pray, and raise
The children, keep the ancestors alive
In stories: those who looked out on the glaze

Of ice, and did not turn away, but said:
This too can be traversed; this too, our land;
And we will learn. And so the {{c|147|Thule}} would spread
Across the world's own crown, with sled and hand.


# Chapter 238: The Redeemer

In each land comes a figure, one who bears
The weight of heaven's message on his back,
Who walks among the broken and repairs
The covenant the people let go slack,

Who teaches, and who suffers, and who goes
Away, who promises to come again;
And then the people, left behind, compose
The scripture of departure; and the pain

Of absence is the engine of the faith.
Two figures now, two continents apart,
Two centuries apart; and yet the wraith
Of one same archetype beats at the heart

Of both: the {{c|3490|Redeemer}}, he who descends,
Who teaches peace, who builds the law, who goes
Before the mission ends; whose leaving lends
The deepest awe the people ever knows.

In {{p|Tula}}, which the {{c|3464|Toltec}} would erect,
In central {{p|Mexico}}; and there, below,
Where warrior-columns, grim, stand to protect
The legend, over history, would go:

A man: {{c|3491|Ce Acatl Topiltzin}}, born
On {{x|One Reed}}'s day, the priest-king, in the cause
Of the {{c|3492|Feathered Serpent}}: wind, breath, the morn
Star, {{c|3493|Quetzalcoatl}}, whose rising and whose pause

As evening star, meant death and life in one
Arc of the sky; who wore the quetzal's green
Feathers in the temple's dark; as the sun,
He bore the name of culture's gift, the sheen:

The corn, the calendar, the arts of peace,
The writing and the wisdom of the scribe;
The {{c|3464|Toltec}} culture's gift, and its release
Of human culture from war's bloody tribe.

{{c|3494|Topiltzin}} taught that human sacrifice
Was an abomination; that the floor
Be clean of the obsidian's device;
That butterflies and flowers, and no more,

Were offerings the {{c|3492|Feathered Serpent}} sought;
The human and divine were bound, their prayer
Of beauty, not of blood. For what he taught,
{{c|3495|Tezcatlipoca}}'s priesthood, standing there,

Reaching for the one altar, with the glass
That smoked, its god's own face, would not allow
The flowers; and they would not let them pass,
But plotted on the priest; and they, somehow,

Brought him a mirror: his own face, diseased
And old; the terror of his mortal fate
Undid him; and with pulque made drunk, they seized
His shame, and barred him {{p|Tula}}'s throne and state.

He walked east, the sea his last desire,
And at the {{p|Gulf}}'s edge, weeping and bereft,
Set himself free: burned upon a pyre{{fn|The sources give both endings: in one, Quetzalcoatl burns himself and his heart rises as the morning star; in the other, he sails east on a raft of serpents.}}
His heart became the morning star; and left,

He sailed away, the raft's light growing dim
Upon the eastern ocean's rim; and both
Are so: he promised to return; of him
The age would come again; and, by that oath,

The world would learn of flowers and not blood.
Then north, a thousand miles, two ages on,
A figure came across the water's flood:
The {{c|3498|Peacemaker}}, remembered; and, as dawn,

The {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}} know him: the root
Of their own constitution; in the light
Of longhouse embers, sacred, resolute,
He came across {{p|Lake Ontario}}'s night,

From the north shore, a stranger, who forsook
His {{c|3499|Huron}} people; and he found the five
At war: the {{c|3500|Seneca}}, {{c|3501|Cayuga}} shook,
{{c|3502|Onondaga}}, {{c|3503|Oneida}}, {{c|3504|Mohawk}}; strive

Not against strangers, but each other: score
On score of blood-feud; for a brother, son
Killed to avenge; revenge's endless war
Ate nations from within; and he, the one,

The {{c|3498|Peacemaker}}, he offered grief's release:
The {{x|Great Law}}: the {{c|3505|Great Law of Peace}}, the law,
{{x|Gayanashagowa}}, the great league of peace:
Five nations by one oath, beneath the awe

Of one roof: each its hearth and its domain;
But all the five-fold matters, as they fell,
Were settled at {{p|Onondaga}}, the main
And central flame, where fifty sachems dwell,

The royaneh, deliberating the law:
The path of the unanimous; the right
Of the clan mothers, who could so withdraw
A chief who ruled unwisely; and the might

Of women over men's ambition; both
Held voice; and war required consent of all.
He planted the {{c|3506|Great White Pine}}, there, the oath,
The {{x|Tree of Peace}}, and, under it so tall,

The five-fire longhouse, laid out east to west:
The {{c|3504|Mohawk}}, keeper of the eastern door;
And {{c|3500|Seneca}}, the west; the center, best,
{{c|3502|Onondaga}}, the keeper of the lore

Of law; beneath the roots, the hatchet, sunk,
The war-club, buried, that no hand should take;
The arrow snapped; beneath the pine's great trunk,
The nations, freed, the blood-feud's chain would break.

And then the {{c|3498|Peacemaker}} departed. Like
{{c|3494|Topiltzin}}, the refrain the same: the one
Who, broken-hearted or fulfilled, will strike
West, or into the sky, his teaching done,

And leaves the law and the behest to keep
It burning, as a light upon the coast;
The people choose the teaching, or the deep
Violence they were asked to lose, its ghost.

Two {{c|3507|Redeemers}}: one of feathers, one pine;
One of the pyramid, one of the floor
Of longhouse; one, the morning star's design;
One planted the tree, and closed the war's door;

The pattern of the world: the teacher came
And healed; his banner, raised, and then withdrawn;
And what reveals itself is still the same:
The covenant is fragile; peace lives on

Only by choosing it each day; the law
Is only as strong as the will of those
Who say, We will keep it. Honor, with awe,
The {{c|3490|Redeemer}}, who carries heaven's throes,

Its aching weight, and sets it down before
The dreamer and the warrior; says: create
A world of flowers, not blood; law, not war;
The planted tree, whose branches, in their state

Of peace, shelter the nations, who lay down
Their weapons, choose the harder path: the pact
Of the healed and shared, the never-grasped crown
Of might; and this is the {{c|3490|Redeemer}}'s act,

His testament: I came, I taught, I leave;
And what you build without me is the proof
Of whether you believed. Now you must weave
The peace yourselves, beneath the planted roof

Of the tree, by the law I gave; the star
Of morning rises, and the pine will grow;
The longhouse warmth is kept for those who are
True to the teaching; choose the flower, so,

Not the blade; choose the council, not the war;
Choose the covenant the {{c|3490|Redeemer}} made,
And he will come again; but not before
You keep the peace without him, unafraid.


# Chapter 239: The Fall of Tenochtitlan

The city rose out of the lake, a prayer
Answered in stone and floating garden-ground:
{{p|Tenochtitlan}}, jewel beyond compare,
Where {{c|3508|Huitzilopochtli}}'s children, crowned,

Did not resist the beauty, but had built
It into causeways on the water, arched,
And aqueducts whose arches split the gilt
Of morning; each quarter hummed and marched

With trade, a hundred thousand lives: the plume,
The feather, obsidian blade, the bean
Of chocolate, and the cotton of the loom;
Two hundred thousand souls lived there, between

Its walls, more than in any {{p|Europe}}'s town
At that same age; from {{p|Chapultepec}}'s spring,
Clean water fed the fountains coming down
To plazas where the priests and merchants' ring

Went on, where architects would plan the feasts
Of carving: serpent, eagle, sun; and there
The skull-rack's grim accounting; for the priests'
City was not undone by squeamish care:

Tribute of {{c|3509|Triple Alliance}}'s wars
Fed the realm's hunger and the altar's need;
And {{c|3510|Moctezuma}} ruled from polished floors,
The absolute and guaranteed, decreed

Lord of the {{c|3511|Mexica}}; {{p|Texcoco}} and
{{p|Tlacopan}} beside him, three cities' chain
In one alliance; and the markets, spanned
At {{p|Tlatelolco}}, wider than the main

Of {{p|Salamanca}}; sixty thousand fed
Its dance of trade: the jaguar pelt, the plume
Of quetzal, gold and jade and turquoise spread,
Vanilla, rubber, copal, and the loom,

The lapidary's and the goldsmith's art;
The {{c|3512|Spaniards}}, later, swore they'd never seen
In any {{p|Europe}} market such a mart;
And the chinampas, floating gardens, green

On woven reed upon the lake, where grew
The maize and squash and amaranth, the soil
So engineered, the most productive, through
The hemisphere; and so their keepers' toil

Fed a realm. Then, the sails: fifteen-nineteen;
{{c|3513|Hernán Cortés}} then stepped ashore, with his horse;
And the {{c|3514|Totonacs}} told, as they had seen,
The {{c|3511|Mexica}}'s ways, gave the lever's force:

The tributary peoples, ground beneath
The {{c|3509|Triple Alliance}}'s heavy rack
Of flower-war and tax, would so bequeath
Their hatred to the stranger; and the crack

Was this: {{c|3496|Cortés}} did not conquer it alone;
He broke the {{c|3511|Mexica}} with their own foes,
Alliance turned against itself, the bone
Of realms. Then {{c|3510|Moctezuma}}, as signs rose,

Would hesitate: was this {{c|3493|Quetzalcoatl}}, come
Back from the eastern sea, as was foretold,
The {{c|3492|Feathered Serpent}}? Or an envoy, from
Some distant lord? And while he weighed, and told

The omens, signs, {{c|3496|Cortés}} advanced, and he laid
The {{c|3401|European}} purpose through the lines
Of {{c|3511|Mexica}} diplomacy, a blade
Through silk. They met on causeway, by the shrines:

{{c|3510|Moctezuma}} in his jade and in gold,
The feathered headdress, all the grand display;
And {{c|3496|Cortés}}, in rusted iron, grim and cold,
Unwashed, his handful, weak in number; they

Were armored in the certainty that {{c|472|God}}
And gold were one pursuit. Then, the slaughter;
And on the {{c|3515|Noche Triste}}, through the causeways trod
The {{c|3516|Spanish}}, driven bloody through water;

But they returned; they always would return,
With the {{c|3517|Tlaxcalan}} allies, who'd destroy
Their ancient foes, the {{c|3511|Mexica}}; he'd learn
The lesson realms all fear, the subject's ploy:

The subjects' hate is the invader's gift.
And an ally too small for eye to see,
{{c|3518|Cocoliztli}}, plague, terrible and swift,
Ran on before {{c|3516|Spanish}} boots: smallpox, free,

Silent, needing no sword; it moved along
The causeways, markets, palace, and the hut
Of the gourd-worker, through the weak and strong;
And forty in a hundred fell, were cut,

The {{c|3511|Mexica}}, before a single pike
Had breached the citadel. The siege then came:
Eighty days of starvation, thirst, the strike
Of cannonade; the causeways cut, the same

Waters held by brigantines he made
From lakeshore wood; {{c|3519|Cuauhtémoc}}, the last
Tlatoani, fought on his knees, and stayed
In rubble, till the city, boneyard, passed

Into surrender's silence: no more drums
From the great temple's height, no market's sound,
No laughter in the plazas; and there comes
Colonial night. In the ruin, found,

A scribe, {{c|3520|Mormon}}, the keeper of the trust
Of record, and gathered memory's hope:
The painted books, the codices from dust
Of kings, the genealogies, the rope

Of knotted calendar, the count of days,
The feasts, the names of gods, from ages past;
And fled north to the mount, the desert's maze,
Hid from the conqueror, buried to last.

The record slept beneath the earth, a seed,
A stratagem of rebirth, long delayed.
Honor {{p|Tenochtitlan}}, whose roads lead
Across the world the sword would break and fade,

But could not make the memory unmanned:
The chinampas, and all the chocolate trade,
The serpent and knife, the calendar stand
Of stone, the jade-green mask; all of it laid

In soil, and waiting for the day the hoard
Of the old record-keeper's found once more,
And the long toil of forgetting's restored
To light; the city rises, as before;

And so the memory no conquest's might
Could ever make undone, returns to dwell
In its old home, the city of the light
Upon the lake, alive in those who tell.


# Chapter 240: The Four Quarters Fall

From {{p|Cusco}}'s navel ran the four roads' span:
And north to {{p|Chinchaysuyu}}'s coastal heat,
South, {{p|Collasuyu}}'s {{p|Altiplano}} clan,
East to {{p|Antisuyu}}'s green jungle beat,

And west to {{p|Cuntisuyu}}'s desert shore;
The {{c|3403|Inca}} realm stretched on the mountain's spine,
Volcanic, from {{p|Ecuador}}; its stone core
To {{p|Chile}}, stone and rope, one voice's line:

The {{c|3521|Sapa Inca}}, {{c|3522|Inti}}'s son, divine,
Lord of the land the condor touched; the state
Ten million souls, without a written sign;
The {{c|3523|Quechua}} kept their records in the weight

Of quipu's knotted cords, whose colors spoke:
Red for war, white for silver, yellow, gold;
And each knot's place the census, and the yoke
Of levy: bushels in the storehouse, told,

The soldiers for the campaign, and the days
Of labor that each ayllu owed the state;
The quipucamayoc read the strings, as phrase
Is read from {{c|3401|European}} printed plate.

The {{c|3512|Spaniards}} burned threads where memory dwelt;
For the knots kept the dead; and who would hold
The dead, the friars held, was theirs; they dealt
The {{x|Andean}} past to silence; the old

Ten thousand years of record to the flame.
Before the flame, the roads: the {{c|3403|Inca}}'s way
Ran forty thousand kilometers' frame,
Of chasqui runners, relay, day by day,

{{p|Quito}} to {{p|Santiago}}'s latitude:
Fresh fish from coast, still new, two days to reach
The {{c|3521|Sapa Inca}} at his altitude
Of mountains; and the bridges, each by each,

Of rope, swayed over gorges, through the clouds.
The terraces, carved in the mountainside
Like stairways for the gods; and in their crowds
The crops climbed up the altitudes, applied:

Maize low, and quinoa in the middle,
Potatoes on the top; and, high up there,
The height was solved as one solves a riddle;
And chuño, freeze-dried in the mountain air,

Pressed by the peasant's foot, the first of food
Made to be stored, for decades, in the state's
Warehouses, kept against the famine's mood;
So that the {{c|3403|Inca}} hunger's yearly rates

Were lowest in the land. {{c|3321|Pachacuti}},
The {{c|3524|Earth-Shaker}}, ninth {{c|3521|Sapa Inca}}, built
This wonder, turning, as a king's duty,
Small {{p|Cusco}} to a realm; and, with the tilt

Of stone, remade the capital; and raised
{{p|Machu Picchu}} on granite clouds; the throne
Of {{c|3403|Inca}} with the sun, the sun-god praised,
Made one. Then came the war of brothers: grown,

{{c|3525|Huáscar}} in the south, {{c|3526|Atahualpa}} north;
The realm was smothered in its civil war;
The cruel timing: thirty-two brought forth
{{c|3527|Pizarro}}'s {{c|3516|Spanish}} column, greed before,

{{p|Cajamarca}}: a hundred sixty-eight
Against eighty thousand, it came to pass:
For {{c|3526|Atahualpa}} walked in, there, in state,
Unarmed, on golden litter, through the mass

Of crowd; and the friar {{c|3528|Valverde}}'s word
Of faith, the {{x|Bible}}, the demand to yield,
Was offered; to his ear he held it, heard
Nothing, and cast it down; and so was sealed

The made-up insult: and {{c|3527|Pizarro}} gave
The signal; cannon roared; the horse broke through
The panicked crowd; and there was none to save
The unarmed: seven thousand dead; and, too,

In thirty minutes; {{c|3526|Atahualpa}}, dragged
From his fallen litter, and his world's walls
Collapsing inward, as a temple, sagged
Beneath its dome. The ransom room: his halls

He filled with gold as high as man could reach,
And twice with silver: twenty-four tons' weight
Of sun-metal, the masterworks; and each
The labor of a thousand hands; their fate:

{{c|3527|Pizarro}} melted them, destroyed the plans
And genealogies of gold, for bars
Of bullion; then he killed the king; the clan's
Hope, garroted where {{p|Cajamarca}}'s stars

Shone on the plaza; {{c|3526|Atahualpa}} chose
Baptism's hardness over flame; the line
Since {{c|3529|Manco Cápac}} first emerged from those
Caves of {{p|Pacaritambo}}, cut, its spine.

The roads fell silent. Tambo and the store
Were emptied; and the quipu, by the priests,
Were burned in heaps; and so, forevermore,
The terraces went fallow; at their feasts,

The lords fed on {{x|Andean}} silver, bone;
The {{c|3530|mita}}, once communal, freely owed,
Became the brutal draft, the forced, the known
Labor in {{p|Potosí}}'s mines, from which flowed

The silver of {{p|Seville}}'s cathedrals; eight
Million died. Honor the four quarters' name,
{{p|Tawantinsuyu}}, the knotted cord's state,
The road through cloud and dew, the terrace, frame

Of storehouse, and the lord of sun, whose gold
Could not buy life from those who worshipped it;
The engineering, patient, broken, bold,
When strangers came with horses and false writ;

The quipu's language died in flame; the cries
Of the last {{c|3521|Sapa Inca}} swallowed by
The conqueror; the terraces still rise;
The roads remain; potato climbs the high

Mountainside with quinoa; and the rain
Of {{x|Andean}} sky waters what no sword
Could take: the knowledge of the soil, the grain,
The memory outlives the foreign lord.


# Chapter 241: The Northern Fires

The silver called them north: in forty-six,
When {{p|Zacatecas}}' veins of ore were struck,
The {{c|3516|Spanish}} hunger, and the politics
Of bullion, drove the frontier on, and stuck

Beyond the settled {{c|3511|Mexica}} domain,
Into the lands the {{c|3531|Aztecs}} never ruled:
The dry sierras and the open plain,
Where those the {{c|3511|Mexica}} had called, and schooled

As {{c|3532|Chichimeca}}, called the dog-folk, so,
Barbarians of the north, looked from high
From mesa and from cliff, the crown below
Of {{p|Spain}} draw near their hunting grounds, and nigh.

Not these the allied {{c|3533|Tlaxcalans}}, who lent
Their arms to {{p|Spain}} at the bishop's behest;
These were the hounds of the steppe, never bent:
The {{c|3534|Caxcanes}}, {{c|3535|Zacatecos}}, and the rest:

The {{c|3536|Guachichiles}} and {{c|3537|Guamares}}, of the bow,
The arrow, and the mesquite hills, who knew
Each canyon and arroyo's flow, and so
Could vanish like the wind in sand; and through

They would not yield one league of country, where
The sun revolved in its relentless arc.
The {{c|3538|Mixtón War}} broke first, in forty: there,
From {{p|Mixtón}}'s fortified peñol, the dark

And steepest crag, the {{c|3539|Caxcan}} warrior's cry:
{{c|3540|Tenamaxtli}} raised it; the frontier's bar
Collapsed: the missions fell, the settlers fly,
The mining camps were burned; and, near and far,

They swept {{p|Nueva Galicia}}'s land,
Until the viceroy learned no force could hold;
He called {{c|3541|Pedro de Alvarado}}'s hand,
The {{c|3531|Aztecs}}' conqueror, veteran, old,

Who rode north with his cavalry and pride:
At {{p|Nochistlán}} he met the {{c|3534|Caxcanes}}' stands;
Rough slope; and there, beneath his horse, he died,
Crushed, the conquistador, and all his bands

Undone by warriors rolling stones from heights,
With a ferocity that none could shrink
In {{c|3516|Spanish}} chronicles, with all their slights;
They knew this was no war for tribute's clink,

Or trade, but on the ground of all their world:
The land, the hunting ground, the sacred hill,
The right to live as desert's hand had curled
Them, free, to vanish, and return, and kill.

{{c|3542|Antonio de Mendoza}} then came
With the largest army {{p|New Spain}} had seen,
Fifty thousand, {{c|3427|Aztec}}, {{c|3517|Tlaxcalan}}, flame
With {{c|3516|Spanish}} iron; and the siege between

The mountain strongholds broke at {{p|Mixtón}}; so
The desert's lord was subdued, but for now;
The embers scattered; and the war would grow
From each spark of {{c|3544|Mixtón}}'s defeat, and how

The {{c|3543|Chichimeca War}}, four decades long,
From fifty on to ninety, and it bled,
The longest colonial war, the strong
Resistance of the north; the silver's thread,

The road that carried {{p|Zacatecas}}' ore
Down south to {{p|Mexico City}}'s abode.
The {{c|3536|Guachichiles}}, the fiercest, painted, bore
Red blood-root's dye; their archery, a mode

Near to perfection that the desert knew:
An arrow each second, and they would ride
The stolen horse bareback, and, aiming, slew
Their chosen targets from the gallop's stride;

The {{c|3532|Chichimeca}} learned the horse as fast
As {{c|3516|Spanish}} learned to fear the midnight raid,
The ambush and the war-cry; trains were cast
In flame; haciendas fell; the road was made

A corridor of dread, where the escort
The arrow's target; and the dead outweighed
The ore that reached the port; and, of the sort
That breaks the bone of armies, war was laid

Which {{p|Spain}} could not win by the sword alone:
The frontier was too vast; and so the crown
Tried what the sword could not: the peace that's grown
By purchase; and the missionary's gown,

The food and clothing given; and the slow
Seduction of the mission and the ranch,
The measured flow of colonists; and so
Loyal {{c|3533|Tlaxcalans}} planted, branch on branch,

With {{c|3532|Chichimeca}}, keepers of the same
Altar in settled villages, the sung
And gentle persuasion's aim; and it came:
It worked, in part; the frontier calmed, among

The tribes; not conquered, but they had agreed:
They rose when provocation made them fight,
And took the peace when peace kept what they'd need:
The land, the hunt, and freedom from the might

Of mission's call: its altar and its bell.
Honor the {{c|3534|Caxcanes}} on their peñol heights,
The {{c|3536|Guachichiles}}, the desert's stealth; as well,
The {{c|3535|Zacatecos}}, {{c|3537|Guamares}}, and their fights:

Peoples whom no empire ever tamed,
Who held the north for fifty years; the crown
Against the richest on the earth, who claimed
No kingdom but the canyon, nor renown,

Whose spears were of the desert's own design:
The thorn, the stone, the arrow, and the will
To stand; and the unconquered's simple sign
Is to be here, upon the land, here still,

Which conquerors passed through, but never held:
The silver went south; miners came and went;
But from the mesa's edge the view, unquelled,
Remained the {{c|3532|Chichimeca}}'s own, unspent.


# Chapter 242: The Wampanoag's Bargain

Before the ship, the plague: sixteen-sixteen,
Three years before the {{c|3545|Pilgrims}} ever came
To {{p|Plymouth}}'s rock, there streamed, a thing unseen,
The {{c|3546|Leptospira}}, the terrible, the same

Through {{p|Patuxet}}, {{p|Namasket}}, and the shore
Of the {{c|3547|Wampanoag}}; and so, when it passed,
A whole people's silhouette was no more:
Nine out of ten were dead. The bones were massed

Unburied where the villages once had stood;
The cornfields overgrown; no smoke would rise
From longhouse fires; the epidemic could
Do what no foe had done; before their eyes

The coast was emptied, villages collapsed,
Where {{c|3244|English}} would call it {{p|New England}}. Then
{{c|3548|Massasoit}}, sachem, as the plague elapsed,
{{c|3549|Ousamequin}}, {{c|3550|Yellow Feather}}, the men

Of the {{c|3547|Wampanoag}}'s small remnant still held,
And did the math: a thousand left, no more;
The {{c|3551|Narragansett}}, spared, would see them felled,
Their rivalry's last word, unless the score

Could be restored. And then the ship arrived:
A hundred two, half-starved, and unprepared,
Shivering on {{p|Cape Cod}}; and few survived
December; and by spring, not half were spared.

And {{c|3548|Massasoit}} saw not threat but giving
Of chance: a counterweight, to set aright
{{c|3551|Narragansett}} threat; and of the living,
{{c|3552|Tisquantum}}, {{c|3553|Squanto}}, strangest in his plight:

Kidnapped by {{c|3244|English}}, sold to {{c|3516|Spanish}}, fled
Through {{p|London}}, and returned to find his own,
Bones on the beach, the village's whole dead,
{{p|Patuxet}}'s people, all of them; alone,

He walked the emptied ground, and chose to teach
The strangers how to live upon this land:
Where herring flows for fertilizer; each
Berry that cures the scurvy; bark, at hand,

That cuts the fever; not from love, but pure
Pragmatism, calculated: his own
Were gone; the {{c|3545|Pilgrims}} were the only, sure,
Hands that might remember {{p|Patuxet}}'s known

Dawn, and might work the land. In twenty-one,
{{c|3548|Massasoit}} and Governor {{c|3554|Carver}} swore:
Neither shall harm the other's daughter, son;
If one's attacked, the other's arms restore

Its peace: a mutual defense; the art
Of the sachem's diplomacy, unfurled
With statesman's skill, who knew from the first start
The {{c|3244|English}} needed him; their fragile world

Was resting on the {{c|3547|Wampanoag}}'s own grace.
The autumn feast, the {{c|3244|English}} thanksgiving,
Was no free friendship, no naive embrace,
But a formal meal of nations living

Each by the other: ninety warriors came
With {{c|3548|Massasoit}}, five deer as tribute laid;
A three-day feast; alliance sealed; the same
Not as the fairy tale for schoolrooms made,

But clever, careful negotiation
Of two who needed each other, and knew
That each one's life, and each one's own nation,
Hung on the balance; and the balance, true,

Held for {{c|3548|Massasoit}}'s life, four decades' time,
Of gifts, of diplomacy, and the plan
That kept the {{c|3244|English}} in their place; the climb
Of the {{c|3547|Wampanoag}}, rebuilt, then began.

The math was changing: each new face that came
Upon the ships was hungry for the land;
More {{c|3244|English}}, always more; each town, the same,
Advanced the line, and acres' great demand

Wore patience down: the cattle trod the corn
Unfenced; the {{c|3244|English}} law replaced the court
Of sachems; and the pact's own children, born
In the widening gap, were taught, in short,

The treaty was a gift, and not a trade;
The {{c|3108|Indians}} the guests, and not the hosts;
And seeds of the betrayal, so, were laid
In soil where the {{p|Patuxet}} dead, the ghosts,

Still whispered to the corn. Honor the one,
{{c|3548|Massasoit}}, the {{c|3550|Yellow Feather}}, he who
Chose stranger over isolation; done,
Held his shattered people together, through

The diplomatic art; who knew from start
The {{c|3244|English}}; and, instead of war, when few
They were, he might have won, chose, as the part
Of wisdom, the alliance; and it drew

His nation through a generation more,
And sowed the bitter harvest: his own son
Would reap what patience sowed; the feast, the war
Would turn to flame; but that is yet undone.

For now the feast is held, the corn is shared,
Two nations eat beneath the autumn sky,
The horn of harvest's plenty is declared,
And makes the bargain sweet, as time goes by.


# Chapter 243: Metacom's Fire

The son recalled what the father let go:
{{c|3555|Metacom}}, whom the {{c|3244|English}} {{c|1406|Philip}} named,
As if a king needed their name to show
His sovereignty; the sachem's line, the famed,

The son of {{c|3548|Massasoit}}, who watched the long
Forty years of the father's plan undone:
Each promise botched, each border crossed, each wrong
Court of the sachem overruled; and one

By one the hunting grounds cut short, the fence,
The cow, the freight of {{c|3244|English}}, and their claim
That {{c|472|God}} had cleared the land for them, and hence
The plague itself was {{x|Providence}}'s flame

Cleared {{p|Jerusalem}} for the chosen; and
The {{c|3447|Indian}}, the {{c|3556|Canaanite}}, to cede
By the divine command. And on a strand,
In seventy-five, of their land, indeed,

The {{c|3547|Wampanoag}} were penned; alive, but few;
And his own brother, {{c|3557|Wamsutta}}, was dead
In {{c|3244|English}} custody: a justice drew
On the convenient suspect with its lead,

And burned like coal in {{c|3555|Metacom}}'s own chest;
Three {{c|3547|Wampanoag}} men hanged at {{p|Plymouth}}, tried
By {{c|3244|English}} law: of sovereignty, the test
Was failed: a foreign court could judge, decide

And kill the sachem's people; and the pact
Was not just smudged, but blotted out; and stripped
All pretense. {{c|3555|Metacom}} chose war, in fact,
No reckless raid, but careful, well-equipped

Alliance, by a statesman's skill: {{c|3558|Nipmuck}},
And {{c|3559|Pocumtuck}}, {{c|3551|Narragansett}}, and more,
{{c|3560|Abenaki}}: a dozen nations' pluck,
A net to strangle, ere they grew, the shore

Of colonies; and, in seventy-five,
{{p|New England}} burned: first {{p|Swansea}}; and then came
{{p|Brookfield}}, {{p|Deerfield}}, and {{p|Springfield}}'s mill, alive
With flame; and {{p|Northfield}}, {{p|Hatfield}}, all the same:

Twelve of the region's ninety towns destroyed,
The battle spread throughout the forest ground
And greens, {{p|Connecticut}} to coast; the void
Of war the {{c|3244|English}} had never yet found:

No war, per head, has killed more of their own:
One in ten colonists, dead or displaced;
And {{c|3561|Indigenous}} losses deeper; grown
By the next ship, the {{c|3244|English}} were replaced;

But {{c|3555|Metacom}}'s alliance was the last
Of each nation's fighting strength. {{c|3562|Great Swamp Fight}}:
December, bitter cold; the {{c|3244|English}}, massed
With {{c|3563|Mohegan}} allies, found at last, despite

The frozen marsh, the {{c|3551|Narragansett}} hold
In {{p|Rhode Island}}'s cedar swamp, a walled isle
Where families camped: women, children, old;
The merciless assault, with fire, the while

The people slept, burned wigwams; the pyre
Of the burning village turned the war's tide:
{{c|3551|Narragansett}} lost their heart, entire,
The nation, cost of having been allied

With {{c|3555|Metacom}}. And still they fought; and through
The winter, seventy-six, raids went on;
The colonists were caught, for the foe knew
Each trail, each ford, each ambush-hollow, gone

Into the forest; even {{p|Boston}} feared
That it might follow {{p|Springfield}} into ash.
But spring brought hunger; the alliance, sheared,
Unraveled: {{c|3504|Mohawk}} raids, disease's lash;

Blockade denied them powder; and the pride
Of nations scattered: some surrendered, some
Fled north to {{c|3560|Abenaki}}, {{c|3245|French}}'s side;
And {{c|3555|Metacom}} was hunted, as the drum

Of his war broke. August, seventy-six:
The swamp at {{p|Mount Hope}}, where he had been born,
The last betrayal, and the hunter's fix:
{{c|3564|Alderman}}, of the {{c|3565|Pocassets}}, a sworn

Ally of the {{c|3244|English}}, who shot him there
Beneath his fathers' sky; and debts were paid
In the worst coin: they quartered him, laid bare
The body, hacked the head off, and displayed

The head upon a pike at {{p|Plymouth}}'s gate
For twenty years, the grinning trophy, dread,
Of the colonial rule, rising, great;
His wife and son were sold as slaves; the thread

Of {{c|3548|Massasoit}}'s own line, the grandchild, south
To {{p|Caribbean}}, to {{p|Bermuda}}'s fields
Of sugar; and the treaty's final mouth
Spoke its last spell, most cruel of its yields.

So honor {{c|3555|Metacom}}, the son who saw
What his father chose not to see, who read
The treaty's hidden flaw, and, by its law,
Rose against certain ruin; who, instead,

Burned all {{p|New England}} and had nearly won;
Who proved the dispossessed had earned the right
To fight upon their country, in its sun;
Whose severed head, on {{c|3566|Plymouth}}'s pike, the sight,

Was the price paid, resistance of the dead
And living, 'gainst the colony's device:
The land taken by law and sword; instead
The plow for people; {{c|3555|Metacom}}, the price,

Broke the colonist's safety, and the vow
That {{c|3447|Indian}} was a vanishing shade:
He showed that shadow had its teeth; and how
The forest and the meadow, unafraid,

Would not surrender what beneath them lay
Without the fight that shakes the world awake.
The son remembered; and, from that far day,
The woods kept his memory, for his sake.


# Chapter 244: The Kachina Underground

For eighty years the {{c|3567|Pueblo}} peoples bore
It all, since {{c|3568|Oñate}}'s iron boot had crossed
{{p|Rio Grande}}, ninety-eight; the friars' war
Ground sacred dances down; and, at the cost,

The kivas sealed with stone; the masks were burned
Of the kachinas, {{p|Taos}} to {{p|Hopi}}'s town;
The forced conversion's labor, as it turned,
Fell on the {{c|3567|Pueblo}} backs, dragged up and down

The timbers for the churches, day by day;
The friars' altars to the one god built
Atop the buried kivas; but the way
Of the rain-prayer and corn-song, without guilt,

Went on, whispered, hidden from the friar;
The {{c|3567|Pueblo}} peoples bore it all along
Mesa-patient; but the well grew drier;
The drought came: in the seventies, the strong

Relentless failure of the sky to rain;
The {{c|3516|Spanish}} tribute-corn, which none could pay,
The starving towns; {{c|3436|Apache}} raids, the bane
Of weakened missions; and the whip's harsh sway,

The friars' answer, violence that rose,
Of men who blamed the drought on kiva sin:
Kachinas, the rain-rite, the dance that goes
On, hidden, in the kiva's fold within;

In seventy-five, the {{c|3516|Spanish}} then seized
Some forty-seven healers, and hanged three,
To break the spirit's stand; but, not appeased,
{{c|3569|Popé}} of {{p|Ohkay Owingeh}} rose up: and he

Had been among the whipped: the scars he bore
On his back, the text that urged the rising:
And knotted cords, like stars, were sent before
From {{p|Taos}} to the {{p|Piro}}, the devising

Encoded in the fiber: loose one knot
Each day; and when the cord is smooth, then rise.
August the tenth, sixteen-eighty: the lot
Of twenty-four pueblos, beneath the skies,

To the kachina's drums, rose up as one;
The {{c|3516|Spanish}}, caught 'twixt sky and stolen land;
The {{c|3567|Pueblo}} fury, burning like the sun,
Burned down the mission doors on either hand:

And each church, {{p|Taos}} down to {{p|Isleta}}, razed;
And twenty-one {{c|3570|Franciscans}} killed, the cost
Of eighty years of whip; the settlers, dazed,
To {{p|Santa Fe}}; the governor's grip, lost

On {{p|New Mexico}} dissolved, like the clay
In the acequia's flood. They ringed the town:
Two thousand warriors, {{p|Santa Fe}}; the way
Of water cut; the last stand, sallies, down

Out from the palace, bought the time alone
To gather settlers, flee, and go south,
Lonely, humiliated, to the bone,
Down the {{p|Rio Grande}} to {{p|El Paso}}'s mouth

Of dust; the {{c|3567|Pueblo}} stood upon their land
The first time in eighty years. {{c|3569|Popé}} then said:
Undo all: go wash, by the river's hand,
Baptism off; take the old name instead,

The true name the kachinas know; the track
Of {{c|3516|Spanish}} road, the mission's frame, the bell
Of iron, destroy them all; and give back
The kiva to the dancers, who would tell

The rain-prayer to the cloud, the corn, the earth.
Twelve years of freedom, the old ways restored,
The ceremony born again; the dearth
And inner strife: {{c|3569|Popé}} was a tyrant lord;

The unity the rising asked could not
Be sown in peace; the pueblos quarreled; drought
Continued; raids increased; and freedom's lot,
Too fragmented to hold, at last gave out.

{{c|3571|Diego de Vargas}} in ninety-two
Returned; the reconquest's mold had changed:
No chargers through the plaza, no mass slew
Of executions; things were rearranged:

The {{c|3567|Pueblo}} had proved that they could expel
The foe outright; the {{c|3516|Spanish}} came to treat,
Not by the sword: with amnesty as well,
Lighter tribute; and, cornerstone, complete:

The tolerance of all the {{c|3567|Pueblo}} rite:
Kachinas would still dance; the kivas stay;
The old religion's way would not, despite
The mission, be its bane; the price to pay,

Unspoken compromise; the reconquest
Was possible; the {{c|3567|Pueblo}} kept their prayer,
Their skies, their gods; conversion, at its best,
Was surface; and beneath, the altar there

Of {{x|Christian}} faith, and the {{c|3572|Franciscan}}'s plea,
Kachina danced; the corn-prayer, wreathed, would rise
From the unconquered kiva, rising free,
Into the clouds. Here the victory lies:

Not in the twelve years' freedom's shrouds alone,
But in the stubborn life that followed; for
Kachinas dance today in {{p|Zuni}}'s own,
In {{p|Hopi}}, {{p|Acoma}}: the sacred core

The {{c|3516|Spanish}} cruelty could not erase,
Because one generation proved it could
Be erased; that proof was the leverage, base
Of bargaining that kept, beneath the wood

Of the conqueror's church, the sacred, kept,
And living, underneath the roof, alive;
The rite was hidden there, and never slept;
The old ways, in the new, would still survive.

So Honor {{c|3569|Popé}}, the scarred medicine man
who knotted the cord of the {{c|3567|Pueblo}} soul
and in one August dawn untied the plan
of eighty years, and took the altar whole:

who proved the kiva and the church were one
house, and the one who keeps the rite is who
can hold it; so kachinas, in the sun,
still dance in plaza and in kiva too:

the prayer, the mask, the rain, the corn, the bread
of the same altar, kept before the cross
and after it, and every morning fed
by the land that remembers its own loss.


# Chapter 245: The Great League Cracks

The {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}} played this before:
The People of the {{c|3573|Longhouse}}, whose old law,
Confederate, was older than the door
Of any church, the colony, the raw

{{p|New England}}'s towns; and the {{c|3574|Five Nations}}, then
Six, {{c|3575|Tuscarora}} joining, in twenty-two,
Who knew the {{c|3401|European}}'s weakness: men
And there were two kinds, {{c|3245|French}} and {{c|3244|English}}; through

The wood between, a shared hate; and the creed,
{{x|Catholic}} and {{x|Protestant}}; the fur, the land;
And played the one against the other's need,
A hatchet balanced on its edge, at hand:

Lean to the {{c|3245|French}}, the {{c|3244|English}} wedge would press;
Lean to the {{c|3244|English}}, and the {{c|3245|French}} supplied
{{c|3576|Algonquin}} foes with guns; and, nonetheless,
With both and neither, they would be allied,

{{c|3325|Hiawatha}}'s sons, whose {{x|Great Peace}}, the law,
Threaded the needle where none could pass through:
The raw and brilliant statecraft, without flaw,
Of life between the realms; and well they knew

{{x|Covenant Chain}}: the metaphor they made
With {{c|3244|English}}: link by link, respect, the bond
Of conference; the wampum belt was laid
At {{p|Albany}}'s stockade; and, from beyond,

The {{c|3323|Iroquois}} diplomat knelt to none,
But called the governor brother, not child,
Not subject, but the equal partner; one
Who overturned assumption, proud and wild:

We are not subjects; we are your allies;
The chain kept polished, each corroded link
Revised at council, as each season flies,
Or the alliance rusts, and peace will sink.

And for a century the game would burn:
The double-crossed, the double-courted, sat
At the continent's hinge; and in their turn
Nor {{c|3337|France}} nor {{p|Britain}} could advance, but that

The {{c|3573|Longhouse}} held the {{p|Great Lakes}}' key, the gate
Of the {{p|Ohio Valley}}, and the fur
Trade's arterial flow; and then, the weight
Of war that would decide it all would stir:

In fifty-four, a young {{c|3577|Virginian}}, named
{{c|3578|Washington}}, would bring the war's first shots, slung
From the {{p|Ohio}} forest's ambush, framed:
The {{c|3245|French}} and {{c|3447|Indian}} War; and its tongue

Not {{c|3245|French}} nor {{c|3447|Indian}}, but global war
That {{p|Europe}} called the {{x|Seven Years}}, the soul
The continent at stake; and, as before,
{{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}} steered from pole to pole:

The {{c|3504|Mohawk}} leaning {{c|3244|English}}; to the {{c|3245|French}},
{{c|3500|Seneca}}; {{c|3579|Confederacy}}, apart,
To stay above the fray; but at the trench
The {{c|2930|Europeans}} bled each other's heart;

But the game changed: the middle's balanced sky
Was closing. {{c|3580|William Johnson}}, England's man,
Who married {{c|3504|Mohawk}}, spoke their tongue, the eye
Within the longhouse, pulled them to the plan

Of {{c|3581|British}} cause; neutrality was breached.
At the {{p|Battle of Lake George}}, {{c|3582|Hendrick}}, old
The {{c|3504|Mohawk}} sachem, the alliance preached
Into the battle's forge; and, in the cold

{{c|3245|French}} volley, fell; the first price, paid in blood
By {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}}. The {{c|3581|British}} won;
{{p|Treaty of Paris}}, sixty-three, the flood:
{{c|3337|France}} ceded all of {{p|Canada}}; was done

{{p|Ohio Valley}} opened; and the {{c|3245|French}}
Alliance the western nations needed
For balance, was torn from them like a wrench;
{{c|3561|Indigenous}} peoples woke, unheeded,

To find their counterweight was broken, clean:
{{c|3583|Pontiac}} understood it first, war chief
Of {{c|3584|Ottawa}}, whose coalition, keen
And terrible, burst forth beyond belief

The {{p|Great Lakes}}, sixty-three: {{p|Fort Detroit}}'s siege;
And {{p|Fort Michilimackinac}} was taken
By lacrosse game: the warriors, for their liege,
Hid weapons in the sport; the fort, shaken,

Fell to the war-club at the goal; and eight
Were captured; and like {{c|3555|Metacom}}'s, the soul
Of the same resistance, refusal's weight
To yield new order its terms and control:

Without the {{c|3245|French}}, the {{c|3581|British}}, unrestrained,
Would take the acres west. And then the line:
The {{c|3585|Royal Proclamation}}, then ordained,
In sixty-three, the {{p|Appalachians}}' sign:

No settlement beyond the crest; the west
Reserved; a distant king's intent, who knew
{{c|3561|Indigenous}} alliance was the best
Thread of the realm's stability; and through

Defiance of the boundary, came war.
The colonists ignored the line, and crossed;
The day the {{c|3573|Longhouse}} feared, had feared before,
When neither needed them: the balance lost,

And neither honored now the wampum's plan.
Honor {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}}, the {{c|3586|Great League}},
Whose diplomacy held, since it began,
The continent in balance; the intrigue

Of covenant, the chain kept polished bright,
Masterwork of statecraft, in the shifting
Of forest's light; and when it broke outright,
It did not vanish, but went on, lifting

The {{c|3573|Longhouse}}: still it stands; the fire still burns
At {{p|Onondaga}}; and the battered whole
To council, never once adjourned, returns;
The {{x|Great Peace}}, which no crown's frown could control,

A covenant the nations earned between
Themselves; the law was here before the ships;
It stays, as patient as the longhouse, seen
In wampum's purple veins and steady grips.


# Chapter 246: The Guarani War

Deep in the continent, where rivers ran
Unnamed by {{p|Europe}}, braided through the wood,
And the red earth gave what it gave, the plan
Of no empire: the {{c|3587|Guarani}} stood,

In the conquest's darkest, desperate time,
And built a thing no crown had planned, an art:
A commonwealth of music, and the chime
A city shaped like prayer; and, at its heart,

The sacred and the practical entwined.
The {{c|3588|Jesuits}} came, black-robed, with the cross
And gospel forged in {{p|Rome}}; but, as designed,
Their flame was not just {{p|Europe}}'s creed; for loss

Was in the jungle, where the hunters roamed,
The {{c|3589|Bandeirantes}} riding out in their greed,
From {{p|Sao Paulo}}'s frontier, the wolves, who foamed
For {{c|3587|Guarani}} bodies, chained, sold to feed

The market; and the missions gave the rare
And strange: a wall to keep the hunted free
From brutal market of the slavers' lair;
Reductions rose, some thirty towns, to be

Along the {{p|Parana}} and {{p|Uruguay}},
Where the {{c|3587|Guarani}} lived behind the door
Of covenant that held the wolves at bay.
They built in stone; they carved the saints, and more,

With hands that knew the forest's older gods;
And in baroque facades, the mission frame,
The jaguar's eye peered out, against the odds,
Through {{x|Christian}} stone; the violin, too, came:

{{c|3587|Guarani}}, whose fathers sang to spirits
Of forest, filled the church with music's key
That {{p|Europe}}'s courts would envy, its merits:
A people who had taken, and set free

What the conqueror offered, and transformed
It into what the conqueror forsook:
A beauty no crown's will had ever formed;
A hundred thousand souls, in towns; the book,

The printing press, the hospital, the school;
Elected councils underneath the crown
Of a far king, but governed by the rule
The {{c|3587|Guarani}} helped shape and keep; the town

They farmed the yerba, raised the herds, and dwelt
Between the forest and the realm's far edge,
A world where no whip on a slave was felt;
Imperfect, paternal, and strange: a pledge,

Amid sin's hemisphere, the nearest thing
To justice in its range; and so they stayed
A century and half; then came the sting:
The diplomats, who lines on maps had laid

On land they'd never walked; the {{x|Treaty}}'s claim
That bore {{p|Madrid}}'s name, seventeen-fifty,
Traded the territories, a card game:
{{p|Spain}} gave {{p|Portugal}} the land, so thrifty,

Seven missions east of {{p|Uruguay}}'s guard
To {{p|Lisbon}}'s crown; a province drawn in ink;
The cost, some thirty thousand lives, the hard
Dice of diplomacy, which did not think.

Move, they said. Abandon what you have built:
The churches, workshops, herds, the orchards, graves
Beneath a century of prayer and silt;
Obey the kings who never saw these waves.

And they refused; and {{c|3590|Sepe Tiaraju}}
Rose from {{p|Sao Miguel}} to defend the land
No treaty signed in {{p|Europe}} could undo,
A warrior with a prophet's fire in hand:

This land {{c|472|God}} gave us; and no king may sell
What the {{c|3591|Creator}} granted; we require
No {{c|3401|European}} license here to dwell.
And so the war began, with bows, and ire,

With clubs and faith, against the joined array
Of two empires, the unholy pact
Of {{p|Spain}} and {{p|Portugal}}, who marched that day
Together, crowns whose missionaries' act

Had built these towns, and came to disallow
What their priests made. The {{c|3588|Jesuits}} were split:
Some said to fight, and some to bow; and now
Some wept in wooden booths, and prayed, but it

Brought no miracle. At {{p|Caibaate}}, in fire,
Some fourteen hundred fell within a day
Against musket and the cannon's choir,
The arithmetic of gunpowder's sway

Against the courage of the dispossessed.
And then {{c|3592|Sepe}} fell: a lance-thrust stopped his breath,
On the eve of the final battle; blessed
And cursed, the warrior took his rest in death

In the red earth that he would never yield.
The missions burned; the churches that had held
The violins, looted; and in the field
The cattle ran, now wild, by none compelled,

Upon the pampa's grass. The scores of song,
The libraries, the presses, shattered, brass
And type; the {{c|3587|Guarani}}'s republic, long,
Dissolved like fog along the river's glass.

Then, sixty-seven, the last blow was dealt:
The {{c|3588|Jesuits}} expelled, the last to go
In the wreck of what looked like heaven, felt
From outside as a dream of what could grow

If guilt could build a wall between the greed
Of conquest and its charity; but thrones
And realms will never tolerate the creed
Of commonwealths that answer none; the stones

Of the reductions crumbled; on the floor
Of forest the red walls sank, overgrown
With vine and orchid; and the jaguar's roar
Reclaimed the nave where violins had shone;

The {{c|3587|Guarani}} scattered to woods and plains;
Experiment in justice, all undone
By the same crowns that once had forged its chains.
Honor the {{c|3587|Guarani}}, who, in the sun,

Built in the wilderness, with stone and song,
A thing no crown could dream of, as they made
A world where the enslaved, refusing wrong,
Sang their own, not the master's, unafraid;

Who took the violin and made it weep
In {{c|3587|Guarani}}, a sacred tone, a sound
That neither {{p|Madrid}} nor {{p|Lisbon}} could keep.
Honor {{c|3590|Sepe Tiaraju}}, he who found

The word to say: No to the treaty's line,
And the decree; who chose the river's flow
And the red earth, above the knee's decline:
The missions fell; the music did not go.

It lives in each refusal to be moved,
In each people's own unextinguished cry:
This land is ours; this truth needs not be proved;
The red earth keeps it, as the years go by.


# Chapter 247: The Great League Broken

Oldest democracy: before the quill
Of {{c|3593|Jefferson}} had scratched its founding creed,
Before the {{c|3244|English}} colonists would fill
The parchment rolls with liberty's bright seed,

{{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}} had already made
A union of five warring nations' strife,
A {{x|Great Law}} spoken underneath the shade
Of the white pine, the {{x|Tree of Peace}}'s life,

Rooted in {{p|Onondaga}}'s earth, where came
{{c|3594|Deganawidah}}, the {{c|3498|Peacemaker}}, from
Across the waters, and he changed the name
Of blood-feud into peace: and five; then, come

{{c|3504|Mohawk}}, {{c|3503|Oneida}}, {{c|3502|Onondaga}}, old,
{{c|3501|Cayuga}}, {{c|3500|Seneca}}; then, the long walk
Of the {{c|3575|Tuscarora}} up the north, to hold
The league: condolence covenant, and talk,

Not war; where fifty chiefs sat in the ring,
And the clan mothers chose who would speak for
Each nation, and could strip a faithless king
Of antlers. Women held the fire; and more,

The longhouse stretched from sunrise: and the guard,
The {{c|3504|Mohawk}} kept the east; and at the west
{{c|3500|Seneca}}, {{c|3595|Keepers}} of the door, and hard
Between, bound by the wampum belts, the rest

Who told the peace, the protocol, the art
Of consensus: no nation overruled,
No war without the council's word; each part
Must speak; the oldest way the many ruled.

But now the {{c|3244|English}} colonies revolt
Against their king; and, underneath the pine,
There came the war, divided, as a jolt,
Asking the {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}} to sign

One side. The {{c|3404|Americans}} first sent men
Who spoke of brotherhood: stay neutral, stand
Aside; a family quarrel; and then
The {{c|3596|Six Nations}}, then, need not lend their hand

Between a father and his sons. But then
The {{c|3581|British}} came with muskets, blankets, guns,
And promises, and argued, once again:
The rebels want your land, whatever runs

Of brotherhood they speak; their settlers press
The frontier, hand by hand; and, as a yoke,
The longhouse country shrinks; the crown, no less,
Has drawn a line; the {{x|Proclamation}} spoke

In sixty-three: no settling, by decree,
West of the {{p|Appalachians}}; choose the throne,
The line holds; choose the rebels, and you'll see
The settlers' flood take all of what you own

Between the {{p|Mohawk Valley}} and the sweep
Of western streams. And {{c|3597|Thayendanegea}} chose:
{{c|3598|Joseph Brant}}, the {{c|3504|Mohawk}} war chief, schooled deep
In {{c|3599|Eleazar Wheelock}}'s halls, where those

Of {{p|Connecticut}}'s corridors had fed
The crown's tongue to a boy: he chose the king,
Not from a servile love, but from what's said
Reckoning settlers the more deadly thing

Than a far monarch's glove. To war, with {{c|3600|Brant}},
{{c|3500|Seneca}} and {{c|3501|Cayuga}} went; and drew
{{c|3502|Onondaga}}'s keepers toward the grant
Of the {{c|3581|British}} side; but the {{c|3601|League}} cracked through:

Both the {{c|3503|Oneida}} and {{c|3575|Tuscarora}} chose
{{c|3484|American}} alliance; other way:
Of calculation: that the end of those
Beside the victors would be spared that day.

The {{x|Great Law}}: by consensus; force on none
Who disagreed. But could the council hold
When half its nations fought the other one?
Condolence broke; the rot, the war, the mold

Of {{c|3602|Europe}}'s war, within, split seam from seam
Of the longhouse. {{p|Oriskany}}'s grim day:
{{c|3503|Oneida}} fought the {{c|3504|Mohawk}} in the steam
Of August's ambush; brothers, in the fray,

Killed brothers for the kings' and rebels' name,
Of {{c|3401|European}} quarrel, not their own;
The {{c|3586|Great League}}'s children burning in the flame,
The quarrel's pebbles crushing the old stone

Of oldest peace. Then came the burning time:
{{c|3578|Washington}} sent his generals, his tone
As cold as {{p|Valley Forge}}'s winter rime:
Total destruction, devastation, known

By {{c|3603|Sullivan}} and {{c|3604|Clinton}}, as they marched
Through the {{c|3500|Seneca}} and {{c|3501|Cayuga}} land:
Scorched earth; and forty towns were burned and parched,
The orchards cut, the corn destroyed by hand

In granaries; the children born that fall
Were born to famine. Not a battle, but
A world destroyed by system: longhouse, all
Collapsed, the cattle slaughtered, and each hut

In smoke, in seventy-nine. And the name
The {{c|3500|Seneca}} gave {{c|3578|Washington}}, his own:
{{c|3605|Town Destroyer}}: a prophecy, the same
Passed on to each president, and so known.

The war ended; the {{c|3581|British}} lost; the peace
Was signed at {{p|Paris}}; and no word was found
For the {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}}: no release
Of sovereignty; the {{c|3581|British}} ceded ground

Not theirs to cede, {{c|3596|Six Nations}}' hunting land,
Drawn on a foreign map, a foreign page,
Erased them. And the {{c|3503|Oneida}}, who'd stand
Beside the rebels, bleeding at each stage,

Were cast aside as coldly; and, ere long,
Their land shrank from six million acres to
A fragment, by the {{c|3484|American}} wrong,
Ingratitude, that proved what {{c|3600|Brant}} knew true:
