It did not matter which side they would choose;
The settler wanted land, and land alone,
And neither crown nor congress would refuse
The frontier's hunger. {{c|3600|Brant}} led north his own

Up to {{p|Grand River}}, in the {{c|3581|British}} land,
A reservation, granted for the worth
Of their alliance: scant proof, close at hand,
That loyalty to crowns buys home on earth.

{{p|Onondaga}}'s fire dimmed, but did not die;
The council yet would meet beneath the dome
Of longhouse sky; the white pine, patient, high,
Would shelter those who keep the law at home

And speak the {{x|Law}}; but the {{c|3586|Great League}} he'd made,
{{c|3594|Deganawidah}}, from an older war,
Was broken by a newer; and the shade
Of peace that held five nations, as before,

Was shattered by the crowns, whose own caprice
Could break a continent and call it blessed.
Honor the {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}}, whose peace
Was built before republic was impressed

In {{c|3602|Europe}}'s lexicon; who spilt their blood
On both sides of a foreign, savage war,
And learned that no alliance in the flood
Of crowns would save the people from the store

Of settlers and surveyors digging graves
Where longhouses had stood. The fire still burns;
The council meets; the {{x|Great Law}}, as it saves,
In the clan mothers' memory, returns,

Who choose the chiefs; and the white pine still grows,
Forever, over {{p|Onondaga}}'s flame;
The oldest peace, though any new war blows,
Kept by the mothers of the clan, the same.


# Chapter 248: The Sun Reborn

The name returned like thunder from the tomb:
Two hundred years since {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}},
The last {{c|3403|Inca}}, was strangled in the room
Of captive stone in {{p|Cuzco}}, since the new

And {{c|3516|Spanish}} order sealed the serpent's mouth
And crowned itself in blood upon the throne
Of {{c|3607|Tawantinsuyu}}; and all the south
Had learned to grieve in silence and alone.

But the name never died; in valleys, where
The quipu's knotted cord still whispered, hid,
In mountain rallies, through the {{c|3523|Quechua}} air,
The tongue no {{c|3516|Spanish}} strangling ever rid,

The prophecy of {{c|3608|Inkarri}} was sung:
The severed head would grow a body, wrought
From living mountain stone; the {{c|3403|Inca}}, young,
Return, to set the world aright, as taught:

The pachakuti, the reversal, dawn
That fills the overturned and bitter cup.
{{c|3609|Jose Gabriel Condorcanqui}}, drawn
From {{p|Tinta}}, in the freezing heights, came up,

A kuraka, a headman, in between:
He gathered all the mita's crushing tax
From his own people for the crown; and seen,
By day, the obraje's cruel weaving racks

Where {{c|3523|Quechua}} women wove till bleeding hand
Could hold no more. He traced his line, and said
Of royal blood, from the last {{c|3403|Inca}}'s strand,
Through the last's daughter, by the mountain fed,

Unsunk by time. He wrote {{p|Lima}}, {{p|Madrid}},
He begged for law's artillery, the plea
Of the corregidor: forced work, forced bid,
Tribute; the repartimiento's decree

That each soul buy the {{c|3516|Spanish}} merchant's wares:
Buy what you need not at three times the price,
Or learn the whip. The courts, in their affairs,
Said nothing; the petitions melted, ice

In bureaucratic shade, a system built
To profit from the pain. And so he chose
The other way: November four; the guilt
Of the dying eighty, its embers' close:

Seized {{c|3610|Arriaga}}, the corregidor,
Paraded through {{p|Tungasuca}}'s square,
And hanged him from the gallows; and, no more
Petitions; and there rang through mountain air

The name that he claimed: {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}},
The Second, the serpent reborn, the sun
Returned to burn the {{c|3516|Spanish}} realm all through,
The pachakuti finally begun.

The {{p|Andes}} rose, from {{p|Cuzco}} to the height,
From altiplano's frozen breath to plain
Of valleys; sixty thousand rose to fight
The death the realm had threatened, all in vain:

The {{c|3523|Quechua}}, {{c|3611|Aymara}}, mestizo, all
Of every hue, to the vision, whole
And incandescent: worlds before the fall
Of {{c|3516|Spanish}} chains; or yet to be, the soul

The free, the mita lifted from their backs,
The ancient peoples whom no foreign state
Could grind to dust. At {{p|Sangarara}}'s attacks
The rebels broke the {{c|3516|Spanish}}; and, as fate,

The magazine exploded in the shrine,
The {{c|3516|Spanish}} soldiers burning in the nave:
Five hundred dead; the {{c|3523|Quechua}} saw a sign
That even sacred stones and the old grave

Had turned against the crown. But kingdoms do
Not die of one defeat: from {{p|Lima}} came
Twenty thousand, the drum's hard beat, the true
Professional army; and, all the same,

Alliance that {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}} built
Was fragile; for the creole landed men
Felt interest threatened, and their own guilt:
This was not war against the king, but, then,

A revolution that might overturn
The hacienda, peonage, their floor;
They pulled away; and, rather than to burn
Their order's wealth, they chose the king once more.

{{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}}, taken in the field,
Betrayed, as prophets are; in {{p|Cuzco}}'s square
The sentence, terrible, in May was sealed,
Of eighty-one: they cut the tongue, laid bare,

Of {{c|3612|Micaela Bastidas}} first, his wife,
The stay and strategist; they killed his son
Before his eyes; and tied, to end his life,
His limbs to four horses; but, as if one

With mountain stone, his body held; they strained
And could not tear the {{c|3403|Inca}} from his name,
Until the axe at last did what remained;
They severed head and limbs, scattered the same:

Head south to {{p|Tinta}}, limbs to the four ways,
That none might reassemble what they broke;
They banned the {{c|3523|Quechua}} tongue, the royal blaze
Of {{c|3403|Inca}} garments; and decree they spoke:

{{c|3403|Inca}} a word past bearing, struck from law
And title, tongue. But none can quarter, quell
A prophecy. {{c|3611|Aymara}} highlands saw
Fire in {{p|Bolivia}}, a name to tell:

And {{c|3614|Apaza}}, {{c|3613|Tupac Katari}}, who
Took name from two thunderbolts: the rally
Of {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}}, and, too, the true
{{c|3615|Tomas Katari}}'s death; from the valley

Laid siege to {{p|La Paz}}, forty thousand strong,
Blocking the mountain passes; famine came
Upon the {{c|3516|Spanish}} city, as, so long,
They'd starved the {{c|3611|Aymara}}: corpses, the same.

{{c|3616|Katari}} too was taken, quartered too;
But spoke the centuries' unbroken vow:
I die, but I'll return as millions; true,
The millions came; the name would echo now

Through every {{c|3618|Andean}} rebel's claim
The body that the horses could not tear,
The prophecy no edict silenced, flame
Of mountain people's memory, laid bare.

So honor {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}}, whose blood
Was scattered to the four winds and the four
Directions of the {{c|3403|Inca}} world, the flood
Of royal crimson on the {{p|Cuzco}} floor,

That seeped into the earth and fed the root
Of revolutions that were yet to come;
They quartered him; but from the living shoot
Of sacrifice, the millions would become

The thunderbolt he promised: I return.
The {{p|Andes}} hold his name; the condor flies
Above the peaks where scattered ashes burn,
And the sun the {{c|3516|Spanish}} killed still will rise.


# Chapter 249: The Northwest War

Now hear the forest speak: where, by the trees
Of {{p|Wabash}} and {{p|Maumee}}, as armies grew
The undergrowth, a maze of root and freeze
Of winter streams: {{c|3619|Miami}}, and the true

{{c|3620|Shawnee}}, {{c|3621|Delaware}}, {{c|3622|Wyandot}}, the rest:
{{c|3584|Ottawa}}, {{c|3623|Ojibwe}}, and those, the core
{{c|3624|Potawatomi}}, joined, together pressed
In {{c|3625|Confederation}}, rose up to war

Against the new republic's hunger for
The ground beneath their feet. The {{x|Treaty}} gave
At {{p|Paris}} the {{c|3404|Americans}} a door,
A line drawn on the map, {{p|Ohio}}'s wave

The western edge; but lines on maps are dreams
Of conquest; and the forest nations kept
Their pledge to the land their grandfathers' streams
Had fed before the {{c|3244|English}}; and they stepped

Against the claim no treaty could make true,
Signed by far {{c|3401|European}} hands: the land
Of the {{p|Ohio}} and its peoples, who
Had signed nothing. And the republic planned,

Sent soldiers west, for land, not peace: the cut,
The survey, and the clearing of the name
That creek and ridge already bore, and shut
Its {{c|3620|Shawnee}} and its {{c|3619|Miami}}; the same

Hunger that broke the doors of eastern lands
Pressed west, {{c|3626|Republic}}'s weight, its manifest
And {{c|472|God}}-anointed greed. But in their hands
They met the military mind, the best:

{{c|3627|Mihsihkinaahkwa}}, the Turtle, chief
Of {{c|3619|Miami}}, whose genius turned the wood
A girdle of destruction, past belief,
For columns the republic sent, who could

Not read the woods; he read them as a map:
Each ridge and bend a purpose, and the weeds,
The thickets, fallen timber, made a trap,
His fortress, where no route of retreat leads;

And with him, {{c|3629|Weyapiersenwah}}, who,
{{c|3630|Blue Jacket}} of the {{c|3620|Shawnee}}, brought the fire
Of warrior's fury; and the {{c|3581|British}}, through
{{p|Detroit}}, supplied the guns, and the higher

Word of encouragement; for, having lost
The war, they still preferred a wall to stand,
{{c|3561|Indigenous}}, between the flood, the cost
Of {{c|3484|American}}s, and their fur-trade land.

In ninety, {{c|3631|Harmar}} marched through mud and wood
With fourteen hundred men, the mistakes grown
Each mile, militia raw, strung out, no good,
A serpent with a broken jaw; and known

The forest ambush: {{c|3628|Little Turtle}} struck:
The musket's crack from trees, the warriors none
Could see until the killing; and the luck
Of the militia broke; and, all as one,

The allied nations moved like water, stone
Their channel; {{c|3631|Harmar}}'s army, shattered, two
Engagements' shame, and the retreat, alone,
{{p|Fort Washington}}; the dead left rotting, through

The trail. And the {{c|3626|Republic}} burned with shame;
It sent {{c|3632|St. Clair}}, the governor, who'd learned
No lesson from the forest; and there came
Two thousand north, in autumn rain, who turned

To desertion, sickness, dwindling supply,
Of ninety-one; till on November's morn
They camped on {{p|Wabash}} headwaters; the sky
Still dark, the sentries sleeping, cold, forlorn:

A bivouac of the doomed. At dawn he struck,
{{c|3628|Little Turtle}}, with all: a thousand men
In fog that loomed like vengeance, in the muck;
Musket-fire from every side; and then

The camp dissolved to butchery; the first
Cut down, the officers; a masterwork
Of all the forest knew of war, the worst
For clumsy lines: six hundred dead, the murk

Of the retreat a gauntlet of the pines;
{{c|3632|St. Clair}} fled on a packhorse, gout-disgraced,
The worst defeat the army, in its lines,
Has ever known; the taste the nation faced

Of {{c|3561|Indigenous}} genius on its tongue.
But the {{c|3626|Republic}} had what they did not:
The endless men and money, iron-strung,
And patience, which could take defeat's hard shot

And come again. {{c|3633|Anthony Wayne}} was sent,
{{c|3634|Mad Anthony}}, with drilled and ordered men
To burn what {{c|3628|Little Turtle}} built; he spent
Two years in preparation; forging then

Soldiers from raw militia; forts, like stones
To step upon, through the {{p|Ohio}} grass;
And {{c|3628|Little Turtle}} read the wind, the tones
Of change: no blunder now, but war's whole mass

Of flawless supply; and he counseled peace:
Negotiate while strength remains, he said,
Before the final battle ends the lease
Of sovereignty in blood. But, rather, led

By {{c|3630|Blue Jacket}}, young warriors chose to fight;
And {{c|3628|Little Turtle}}, loyal, went along,
The tragic courage of the final night
Of the last stand. At {{p|Fallen Timbers}}, strong

Storm-thrown, the ancient trees lay in a maze;
The armies met in August, ninety-four;
The warriors fasted; many, in those days,
Had gone home first to eat; and, at the core

Of confusion, {{c|3635|Wayne}} struck; the bayonet
Drove through the timber's maze; the {{c|3581|British}} fort
Nearby refused to let the warriors get
Inside; betrayal, final, cruel, short:

The allies who had armed them shut the gate;
The league broke in the August fading light;
And at {{p|Greenville}}, the next year, wrote the weight
Of loss: the treaty, signing, in its spite,

Away {{p|Ohio}}'s country, two-thirds, all
The world they held, the hunting ground, the town,
A thousand generations, for the small
Some twenty thousand dollars, hollow crown

Of annuities, the annual chill
Of a diminished life that treaties leave.
So honor {{c|3628|Little Turtle}}, and the skill
Of {{c|3627|Mihsihkinaahkwa}}, who could weave

A devastating war that brought to knees
A nation; gave the {{c|3626|Republic}} its worst
Defeat, and proved the forest, with its trees,
Was never empty; that the tongue, the first,

Of creek and ridge, had moved with minds that knew
To outthink, outfight the invader's might;
And that the forest, in the end, was true
To those who read its name, and not by right

Of those who couldn't read. He lost; the count
Of numbers, factories, the {{c|3581|British}} lie
Burned his alliance; but the books recount
What treaty would erase, and will not die:

The greatest military mind that fought
On this land wore an {{c|3561|Indigenous}} face;
The forest speaks the lesson that he taught,
Which no treaty and no time could erase.


# Chapter 250: The Civilized Trap

They did all that was asked of them; and still
They lost their land. Five nations of the south:
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}}, the {{c|3637|Choctaw}}, with the will
Of {{c|3638|Chickasaw}}, and from the river's mouth

The {{c|3639|Creek}}, whom some named {{c|3640|Muscogee}}; the last,
The {{c|3641|Seminole}}: whose law and custom stood
So like the settlers' own, the word was cast:
Their neighbors named them "civilized," and good.

"Civilized" meant: you look so much like us
We nearly see you. And they shaped, in trust,
Their lives to fit the conqueror, and thus
Found out the reckoning a lie, and dust.

The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} led first. In mountain lands
Where the blue ridges meet the southern sky,
Where laurel slopes feed rivers, in their hands
The country lay since forests first grew high;

And now they took the {{c|3401|European}} way,
And from the conqueror the poorest gift,
His alphabet, and made it, in their day,
A thing he never dreamed, a world's whole shift.

{{c|3642|Sequoyah}}, called {{c|3643|George Gist}} by settler name,
Sat twelve long years; he could not read the hand
Of {{c|3244|English}} marks, but grasped the thing they frame:
That sound is made to see, the voice to stand

Caught on the page and held; and what he heard
In {{c|3636|Cherokee}} could be set down as well
As {{c|3244|English}} could. He took no borrowed word;
At night he heard the syllables' own spell:

Some eighty-six, no more; and each one drew
A sign. From {{c|3244|English}} some he took the form,
Forgotten there, and gave it sounds anew:
So D was "a," and R was "e"; the norm

Of {{c|3636|Cherokee}} was syllables, not parts
Alone; it asked no years of school; in weeks
It taught what {{c|3244|English}} took in years; and hearts
Learned letters, and the reading nation speaks

In print: the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} {{x|Phoenix}}, which rose
In eighteen twenty-eight, a paper bold
Set by {{c|3644|Elias Boudinot}}, whose prose
Gave voice, in their own script, to what they hold:

A tongue that wrote itself in its own hand,
By one man's genius in the silence made,
A thing no other nation of the land
Had done. And they built government, and laid

In eighteen twenty-seven the whole frame
Of a constitution: three branches set
Like the republic's own: a chief, the same,
A senate, court, and written code; and yet

Their capital at {{p|New Echota}} stood,
Where council sat and argued in the script
{{c|3642|Sequoyah}} gave them, as republics would,
Among republics, lawful and equipped.

The {{c|3637|Choctaw}} built their schools; the {{c|3638|Chickasaw}}
Raised farms to match the settlers' own; the {{c|3639|Creek}}
Rebuilt after the {{x|Red Stick War}}, the law
Of {{c|3645|Andrew Jackson}}'s first campaign: the weak

And strong alike, the allied {{c|3639|Creek}} who'd sought
For peace, and those who fought him, he made pay:
At {{p|Fort Jackson}}, by the {{x|Treaty}}, he caught
Some twenty-three million acres away.

The {{c|3641|Seminole}} in {{p|Florida}}'s green maze
Of swamp and hammock held its own. And now
The bitter center lies: in all their ways
They did all that was asked. They took the plow;

They built in {{c|3401|European}} style; they let
The church bell sound across their towns; they wrote
Their constitutions, printed their gazette,
Schooled children, and they wore the settler's coat;

And it was not enough; it never would
Be so. The word "civilized" was a lock
That had no key. The verdict, understood,
Had passed from court to ledger, and the stock

Was land, worth more than people on it. Gold
Was found in {{p|Georgia}}, on {{c|3636|Cherokee}} ground;
The settlers' hunger would not be controlled
By constitution or by paper bound.

The more the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} grew like their foe,
The more the settlers felt the threat they made:
A people who disproved, by what they'd show,
The tale of race; if they could build, and trade,

And write a constitution, and could stand
Themselves by written law, then what excuse
Remained for their removal? What of land
Wasted on savages, the old abuse

Of the wandering brute who knew no plow?
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} disproved the lie, and bore
A greater hate than warriors knew; and how?
They held the mirror up, the face it wore;

The nation saw itself and could not bear
The image; what it owed its law, the price,
Was a truth far too thick to swallow there;
It would not pay; the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} paid twice.

So honor {{c|3642|Sequoyah}}, who gave letters
To his own people, with no borrowed thread,
A syllabary that breaks the fetters
Of silence on the voice; and the page spread

Not as the settlers' only. Honor too
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} {{x|Phoenix}}, whose defiance
In print was the most civilized and true
Reproof one nation gave; its reliance

On ink and paper proved that "savage" lied,
And "civilized" was just the settler's jest.
They built what they were told to build, and tried
To be what they were told; and, for the rest,

For all the promises that they fulfilled,
Their wage was the removal's beating drum:
The towns and farms and schools that they would build
Were counted nothing, and their voice struck dumb.


# Chapter 251: The Last Confederacies

One more time came the vision, the old flame
Of unity that {{c|3583|Pontiac}} once lit:
Together, or not at all: and the claim
Came now the greatest dreamer, born to it:

{{c|3646|Tecumseh}}, called the {{c|3647|Shooting Star}}, whose speech
Was simple, true, and came too late: "The land
Belongs to all; it lies beyond the reach
Of any chief to sell it by his hand.

"Sell, if you will, the air, the rain, the stream;
But not the ground on which we pray; it held
The bones of those who came before, the dream
Of those to come; no single name has spelled

"Away the claim of all who walk the earth."
He walked from the {{p|Great Lakes}} to the south shore,
From {{c|3620|Shawnee}} towns, {{p|Ohio}}'s place of birth,
To {{c|3639|Creek}} and {{c|3637|Choctaw}}, {{p|Florida}}'s green door,

He bore the word: unite or die; one league
Of all the nations, east and west, unbound
To any {{c|3401|European}} king's intrigue;
{{c|3583|Pontiac}}'s flame reborn on greater ground:

Not war alone, on {{c|3581|British}} or the rest,
{{c|3404|Americans}}, but a refusal, whole,
To set a price on earth: the land possessed
In common trust, a people's common soul.

And then his brother, {{c|3648|Tenskwatawa}}, rose,
The {{c|2776|Prophet}}, from the dust of drink's despair,
A broken man, remade by vision's throes:
He died, he said, and came back from the air

Where the {{c|1470|Master}} of Life had shown him how
The whole world could be healed: give up the drink,
The {{c|3401|European}} goods, the metal's vow,
Return to the {{c|3591|Creator}}'s ways, the link

Of corn and deer, of prayer in the tongue
{{c|3591|Creator}} knew. At {{p|Tippecanoe}} there grew,
At {{p|Prophetstown}}, of wood and bark, among
The gathered nations, a capital new,

Where tribal quarrel melted into prayer,
And warriors of a dozen nations came
To hear the {{c|2776|Prophet}} speak and to prepare
The world made new. {{c|3646|Tecumseh}}, in his aim,

Went south; and while he traveled, on the town
Marched {{c|3649|William Henry Harrison}}, afraid
Of nations joined more than of any crown;
At dawn, November seventh, came the raid

In eighteen-eleven; the {{c|2776|Prophet}} fought
Against his brother's strict command; he swore
The bullets would not harm them; magic, sought
In vain: the capital was lost; the war

Of lead ran its arithmetic: they burned
{{p|Prophetstown}} and its stores; the {{c|2776|Prophet}}'s lie
Of shields from bullets, overturned. Returned,
{{c|3646|Tecumseh}} found but ashes, by and by;

He did not break. The {{x|War of Eighteen-Twelve}}
Became his thread: the {{c|3581|British}} needed men
In the {{p|Great Lakes}} and west; and he, to delve
Their need, gave what no deal could buy; and then

At {{p|Detroit}} he bluffed {{c|3650|Hull}}: the very same
His warriors, marching past the window thrice
In different dress; and {{c|3650|Hull}}, in fear and shame,
Gave up {{p|Detroit}} to half his strength, the price

Of theater in war. And yet the due
Of such a friend the {{c|3581|British}} did not pay:
At the {{p|Thames}}, {{p|Ontario}}, there withdrew
{{c|3651|Procter}} and all his horse, and rode away,

And left {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} and his warriors lone
Against the charge of {{c|3652|Harrison}}; the swamp
Was his last stand, where horsemen's waves were thrown,
And musket-roar the drumbeat and the stomp

Of a lost hope; and there {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} fell,
October, eighteen-thirteen; and around
His body closed the wood; and none could tell
The hollow where his warriors made his mound;

They hid him from {{c|3404|Americans}} who'd strip
His skin for keepsakes. And the dream was torn,
But not yet cut; then rose {{c|3653|Black Hawk}}, whose grip
Held to the homeland where the {{c|3655|Sauk}} were born:

{{c|3654|Ma-ka-tai-me-she-kia-kiak}}, the war
Chief of the {{c|3655|Sauk}}, in eighteen thirty-two,
Crossed back the {{p|Mississippi}} east once more,
Home to {{p|Saukenuk}}, which a treaty, through

A drunken chief's false mark in eighteen-four,
Had signed away, with no council's consent;
He crossed with women, children, by the score,
The hungry, wanting only, as they went,

To plant their corn on their ancestral ground.
The {{c|3404|Americans}} called it war; the band,
Starved, lonely, through {{p|Wisconsin}} hunted, hound
By hound, until at {{p|Bad Axe}}, where the land

Met water, steamboat {{x|Warrior}} and the line
Of guns cut down the women as they tried
To swim across; the white flag, as a sign
Of their surrender, spurned; the children died

And floated in the current; and the flow
Of {{p|Mississippi}} reddened. Farther down,
The {{c|3641|Seminole}} refused. Three wars, and slow,
From eighteen-seventeen, in swamp, not town,

To eighteen-fifty-eight: the longest stand,
{{c|3561|Indigenous}} resistance, in the maze
Of {{p|Florida}}'s swamps, in the saw-grass land,
{{c|3656|Osceola}}, no chief, but in his ways

The very soul of the resistance, fought
The {{c|3484|American}} army till it bent;
They seized him under truce; by treason caught,
Which {{c|3657|Jesup}} called the diplomat's intent.

{{c|3656|Osceola}} died in a prison. Yet
The {{c|3641|Seminole}} fought on, until the claim:
The nation spent some forty million, set
With fifteen hundred lives, to move the name

Of fewer than four thousand souls; and some
Would never yield; within the {{p|Everglades}},
In hammock and in cypress, still they come
And go, unconquered, where the saw-grass fades,

Whose home removal never changed. So praise
{{c|3646|Tecumseh}}, called the {{c|3647|Shooting Star}}, whose light
Crossed the whole continent, and in our days
Each no to selling land still burns it bright.

The earth has spoken: land is not for sale;
The covenant unbroken. Honor, too,
{{c|3653|Black Hawk}}, who crossed the river home, the trail
Paid in blood for the right to plant, and through

The sky his fathers knew, to rest. And weep
For {{p|Bad Axe}}, where the children died; and praise
{{c|3656|Osceola}}, seized under truce, whose deep,
Unconquered {{c|3641|Seminole}} still walk the ways

Of {{p|Everglades}}, no noose about their throats.
The last confederacies burned and fell
And burned again; but still the embers' notes
Glow on; and what {{c|3646|Tecumseh}} learned, they tell:

No single nation stands alone; the land
Belongs to all; the bones beneath the stone
Are covenant no treaty's signing hand
Can break; the {{c|3647|Shooting Star}} burns on, its own.


# Chapter 252: The Unsealed Book

Now seal the book. No: it was never sealed;
The book was always open, set in grain,
In corn and council flame, and so revealed
In tongues that the {{c|3591|Creator}} gave the plain:

Three hundred families of speech, a throng
Of languages that named the world, the air
Of a whole hemisphere; and in their song
The names of {{c|472|God}}, that none need render there.

The rivers spoke them, and the mountains held
Them in their granite; prayer of ages sprang
From sacred springs, ten thousand years; unspelled,
This was the book; this always was. It rang

Through all the ages; then, beside that book,
In one year, then, the record would draw near:
a man in {{p|Palmyra}}, {{p|New York}}, would look
into a stone and see the plates appear:

the golden plates that {{c|3661|Moroni}} had sealed
within a hill, the record of a son
of {{p|Israel}} who crossed the sea, revealed
in "{{x|Reformed Egyptian}}," and so begun

with {{c|3402|Lehi}}, from {{p|Jerusalem}}, who came,
and {{c|3659|Nephi}}, who would sail across the sea:
the first book that would give this land a name,
its prophets, kings, its {{c|1497|Christ}}, its living tree.

{{c|1497|Christ}} came to Bountiful, and taught, and healed,
and blessed their children: the Redeemer's day
that this book also keeps, its promise sealed
to come again, and not to pass away.

It named the peoples {{c|3658|Lamanites}}: the rites
of Laman's line, and darkened for the sin
their fathers did; and here the quarrel bites:
whose fathers were they? Jacob's, or the kin

who walked from {{p|Beringia}}? The gold plates
said {{c|3402|Lehi}}; and the land said ice and coast;
and the one house of the dead, at its gates,
takes both: the tree has room for every ghost.

In March of eighteen-thirty {{c|3660|Joseph Smith}}
set out the book {{c|3661|Moroni}} had concealed,
and his eleven witnesses, forthwith,
signed that they saw the plates the hill revealed.

In that same year, eighteen-thirty, the act
Of Congress came that mattered most: the plan,
The {{x|Indian Removal Act}}, signed, backed
By {{c|3645|Andrew Jackson}}, {{c|3662|Sharp Knife}}: so the man

The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} named him; he'd devoured
The {{c|3639|Creek}} homeland, the grim general, who
Took {{p|Florida}}, over treaties towered;
Now president, with the {{c|3626|Republic}}'s view

Of westward hunger, made one policy:
Remove them all. Each nation to the east
Of the {{p|Mississippi}}, each {{c|3636|Cherokee}}
Farm with its constitution, press, and feast

Of learning; {{c|3637|Choctaw}} rule; each {{c|3638|Chickasaw}}
Town with elected council; {{c|3639|Creek}} who'd made
His home again since {{c|3663|Jackson}}'s war: the law,
Move west. The east, the settlers said, was laid

By {{c|472|God}} for them, a {{p|Promised Land}} aside
For the {{c|3484|American}} republic's hand;
The darker peoples, exiled, were to ride
Beyond the {{p|Mississippi}}, to a land

Where the republic promised them once more
A home "as long as grass shall grow," the same
Words spoken at each treaty there before,
The vow, as soon as made, broken in shame.

{{c|3664|John Ross}}, chief of the {{c|3636|Cherokee}}, by blood
One-eighth, but theirs by measure of the day,
Fought as they fought since {{c|3642|Sequoyah}}: the flood
Of law and language, written word; the way

To the {{x|Supreme Court}}: they were a nation;
No state could lay its laws upon the land
By treaty; and {{p|Georgia}}'s legislation
To seize their soil and rule them, void and banned.

And {{c|3665|John Marshall}} ruled; the {{c|3666|Chief Justice}} found
In {{c|3667|Worcester}} versus {{p|Georgia}} that the state
Had no authority upon the ground
Of a nation sovereign by treaty's weight.

The highest court was clear. And {{c|3663|Jackson}} laughed:
"{{c|3665|John Marshall}} has made his own decision;
Now let him enforce it." Thus the statecraft
Of the republic's law and its vision

Shrank to a bully's sneer: the law cast down
By the elected king; for what was awe
Of {{x|Constitution}} to the gold, the crown
Of {{c|3636|Cherokee}} hills, and the settler's maw?

The {{x|Court}} spoke; and the {{c|3668|President}} refused;
In that refusal died the founders' vow
That law, not might, would rule; the words were used
Only for some: the {{c|3636|Cherokee}} learned how,

As had the {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}}, the wise
{{c|3628|Little Turtle}}, what the whole land had learned:
The settler's law protects the settler's prize;
And first the {{c|3637|Choctaw}}, in the winter, turned

West, eighteen-thirty-one, through ice and snow,
Caravans of the dispossessed; the sun
Hid weeks in cloud; the dead were left below
Left unburied on the frozen road; and one

{{c|3637|Choctaw}} chief, looking back, gave it its name:
"A trail of tears and death." The {{c|3639|Creek}} went too;
The {{c|3638|Chickasaw}} were sold into the same;
Last, {{c|3636|Cherokee}}, in thirty-eight; and through

A cold and calculated roundup came
The soldiers to each farm and cabin door,
And herded families at bayonet's aim
Into the stockades, onto filthy floor

Of camps that penned them, and they could bring naught;
The homes they built, the orchards, and the press,
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} {{x|Phoenix}}, and all they wrought
In schools and courts, the settlers would possess,

Who rushed like ghouls in packs, before the last
{{c|3636|Cherokee}} was gone. Sixteen thousand went;
Four thousand died; the children first, then fast
The old; and mothers carried, as they bent,

Their dead, until the tide of grief became
The only text that they could say aloud.
And now, the same year, side by side, the same:
Two peoples walked, one road, one weeping crowd:

In eighteen-thirty, as the act was signed,
the book came out; and in the year of tears,
in eighteen-thirty-eight, the same state's mind
drove out the Saints, from Missouri's frontiers.

Its governor signed Order Forty-Four:
the Saints must leave the state, or else be slain.
The same year, same republic, the same door:
the {{c|3636|Cherokee}}, the Saints, went west in pain.

The book did not move them. It was the land,
the farms the state had wanted, and the gold;
the book had sent four preachers out to stand
with Delaware and Shawnee, and they told

the chiefs: your fathers were the prophets' line,
your dead are kings and seers in what we read;
the {{c|3402|Lehi}} of your house is also mine.
That was the quarrel: who would hold the dead.

The book had called their skin's darkness a curse,
and they would turn "white and delightsome" when
redeemed; the Church would later change the verse
to "pure," in nineteen eighty-one, again.

It was one house's quarrel over skin,
and over fathers, and who keeps the name:
the {{c|3673|Mormons}} and the {{c|3658|Lamanites}} are kin,
one people, and one altar, and one flame.

And so this book here in your hands lays bare
the plates again, and opens them up wide:
the long walk from {{p|Beringia}}, laid there,
the corn, the mounds, the cities; and beside

them, {{c|1497|Christ}} in Bountiful and {{c|3402|Lehi}}'s sail,
the record of ten thousand years of prayer,
the quipu knots, the codex, and the tale
of every people who had once lived there.

This is the book that always stays unsealed,
the record that was never lost, the names
of every nation, every saint, revealed
to {{c|3660|Joseph Smith}} or to the council flames.

Here ends the {{x|Book}} of {{c|3402|Lehi}}, his and theirs:
the {{c|3402|Lehi}} of the plates, and of the land,
whose history was carved in mounds and prayers,
whose scripture is the earth on which they stand.

A hemisphere that never lay there blank
for any pen; a full and holy stage
where ten thousand years of prayer, rank on rank,
had made it holy, age on holy age.

The {{x|Trail of Tears}} was Jackson's; and the hate,
the {{x|Indian Removal Act}}, his hand.
But the peoples endure, and keep their gate;
the record is intact. The peoples stand.

This is that record. Keep in mind each name:
{{c|3646|Tecumseh}}, {{c|3606|Tupac Amaru}}; recall
{{c|3642|Sequoyah}}, and the council's ancient flame
From {{p|Cusco}} up to {{p|Manitou}}; and all

The {{c|3587|Guarani}} violins, the Great {{x|Law}}
Of the {{c|3497|Haudenosaunee}}; and the drill
Of {{c|3628|Little Turtle}}; {{c|3656|Osceola}}; raw
{{c|3641|Seminole}} in the swamp, unconquered still;

The children in the {{p|Mississippi}}'s flow;
The {{c|3637|Choctaw}} chief who named the tearful road;
The {{c|3636|Cherokee}} {{x|Phoenix}}; {{c|3664|John Ross}}, and so
The {{x|Court}} that ruled for justice; and the load

Of cruelty the {{c|3668|President}} laid down.
The book is open; hold it now, revealed
By {{c|3661|Moroni}}, and by memory's crown,
That what was done is kept, the dead unsealed

To speak through each line; and the sun put out
Of each lost nation rises in the word
That will not be lost, and, beyond all doubt,
Honor them all; honor the cost; be heard.

The {{x|Book}} of {{c|3402|Lehi}} ends. The record stands;
The continent remembers; hold it now
Here in your hands; the earth and all its lands
Remember; and the dead keep, still, their vow.

---

# Virgo (10宮) - Days 253-280


# Chapter 253: The Chronicle of the Popes

Now count the keys. Not fathers, for these men
Were sworn to have no sons, and some had sons,
But hands on heads, the laying-on, and then
The next head bowed, the next, until it runs

Fifteen centuries, fisherman to king
Who cut the world in half with lines of ink.
Here is the chronicle; here is the ring
Passed hand to hand; here is the missing link

Between the {{p|Galilee}} and age of sail.
Hear it as old ones heard the kings of {{p|Ur}}:
One name, then one name, then the folded tale,
And then the next. Here, then, the keepers were:

{{c|1093|Peter}} the fisherman, who thrice denied
Before the rooster, then did not deny,
Hung head-down there in {{p|Rome}}; for he had cried
The dead man lived. Head down, he asked to die,

Unworthy of the cross his teacher bore.
Then {{c|3675|Linus}}; then {{c|3676|Cletus}}; then {{c|3677|Clement}}, who
Wrote {{p|Corinth}} in its quarrel: peace, no more
Of schisms. Bishops of a sect, who knew

The tufa, where below the dead were laid,
Their names scratched in the catacombs' neglect,
Martyrs by dozens, bishops by the blade.
{{c|3678|Callixtus}}, once a slave, whose debts had wrecked

A banker's money, sent to mills; then came
{{c|3679|Pontian}}, to {{p|Sardinia}}'s mines to die,
Who first laid down the keys. {{c|3680|Fabian}}'s name
Came with a dove that settled from the sky

Upon his head; a layman, farmer, killed
Under {{c|2583|Decius}}; and the dove was gone.
Then came {{c|3681|Sylvester}}, and the world, unstilled:
{{c|2555|Constantine}} had seen a sign in the dawn:

The sun unconquered, {{c|2554|Sol Invictus}}, friend
Of soldiers, and he made the two suns one;
The persecuted, palace in the end;
The fisher's tomb a church of gold, begun.

Four hundred years on, in some room, a hand
Forged that great {{c|2555|Constantine}} had given all
The {{p|West}} to {{c|3681|Sylvester}}: {{x|Donation}}'s land,
For seven hundred years, till {{c|3682|Valla}}'s call

Laid bare its {{x|Latin}}, bad; remember well
What forgers meant. And {{c|3683|Damasus}}, who set
{{c|3684|Jerome}} to make one book where street-tongues dwell,
The {{x|Vulgate}}; {{c|3685|Leo}}, called the Great, who met

{{c|3686|Attila}} at {{p|Mincio}}; his look
Turned back the king. And {{c|2621|Gregory}}, who named
Himself the servants' servant; by the book
And sent a monk to {{p|Kent}}; then, unashamed,

{{c|2834|Leo III}}, on {{x|Christmas Day}}, who bent
Above {{c|2677|Charlemagne}} at prayer, and laid
Unasked, the {{c|1004|Romans}}' crown; and his descent
Runs on: near all of {{p|Europe}}'s blood is made

From him; each line of {{p|Europe}} opens there.
Then came the years of the great houses. Mark:
{{c|3283|Formosus}}, dug up, propped up in the chair,
Dressed in his robes, a deacon set to bark

At the {{x|Cadaver Synod}}, his replies;
Condemned, his blessing fingers cut away,
Thrown in the {{p|Tiber}}; and the bishops' eyes
Looked on; then {{c|3687|Theophylact}}'s house held sway.

{{c|3275|Marozia}}, his daughter, loved a pope,
{{c|3688|Sergius}}; and bore a pope, named {{c|2537|John}}; and then
Grandmother of a pope: a household's scope
To make and unmake keys, like kings, again

By blood. Her grandson, {{c|3278|John XII}}, a boy
Just eighteen, who crowned {{c|3280|Otto}}, and who died
Within a married woman's bed. The toy,
The keys: one house, one line, one blood applied.

And this book honors lines of blood; it must
Say plainly that the chair the church endows
With heaven was a household's; that is just.
And then came {{c|3690|Gerbert}}, made a pope, whose vows

As {{c|3689|Sylvester II}} brought the {{x|Arab}} lines
Of numbers westward, and the sky's own key,
The abacus; at one thousand, the signs
Were read as doom; the world went on, set free.

In ten-fifty-four, legates at the stone
At {{p|Hagia Sophia}} laid their bull
Of excommunication; {{p|East}}, alone,
And {{p|West}} drew apart, never again full.

{{c|3691|Gregory VII}}; and {{c|3374|Henry}} in the snow
Three days barefoot there at {{p|Canossa}}'s gate,
Begging forgiveness; and the pope, so slow,
Who let him go when he had made him wait.

{{p|Clermont-Ferrand}}: Urban cried, "{{c|472|God}} wills it."
Crosses sewn on; to {{p|Jerusalem}} ran
The road, paved with the slain; and, with the writ
Of {{c|3692|Innocent III}}, kings' lord; the plan

Forbade the sack, and watched them sack the town
Of {{p|Istanbul}}, a {{x|Christian}} city, in
Twelve hundred four. {{c|3693|Celestine}} laid down
The keys, a hermit who could not begin.

Then {{c|3694|Boniface}}: {{x|One Holy Church}}, each soul
Is subject to the {{x|Roman}} pontiff; slapped
At {{p|Anagni}} by {{c|3245|French}} king's men; the whole
Court went to {{p|Avignon}}; its money, trapped,

{{x|Babylonian Captivity}}'s gold,
Flowed seventy years to the {{p|Rhône}}; till home
Saint {{c|3695|Catherine}} of {{p|Siena}} called them, bold;
They came; and chose two popes. Then three. Which, {{p|Rome}}?

Each throne cursed all the others; at the last
At {{p|Konstanz}} then a council made them one,
Deposed them all, crowned {{c|3696|Martin}}; it had cast
{{c|3697|Jan Hus}} to flame two years before; and none

In {{p|Bohemia}} forgot; scholars came:
{{c|3698|Nicholas}}, who built the {{x|Library}} walls
When {{c|3107|Turks}} took {{p|Istanbul}} for good; the name
Of {{c|3699|Sixtus}}, builder of the {{x|Chapel}}'s great halls,

Whose ceiling would be painted by a man
On scaffolding four years, head bent; and then,
And last, Rodrigo {{c|3701|Borgia}}; and his clan,
Called {{c|3702|Alexander VI}}; his children; then

{{c|3703|Cesare}} and {{c|3704|Lucrezia}}, and the slow
Poison of rumor. Fourteen ninety-three:
He drew a line from pole to pole, to show
West of it {{p|Spain}}'s, east {{p|Portugal}}'s, the sea.

At {{p|Tordesillas}} the kings moved it west;
The fisherman's heir split between two crowns
A world they thought was small and finite, pressed
Into a field to share, like farms and towns:

The old small cosmos' last hurrah; the writ
The paper. Fifteen hundred years: a line
From fisherman to this; and, keeping it,
Some saints, some murderers; the chair divine;

Most were but keepers; what passed was the ghost,
And hands on heads, and then the name, the list
Read out: an institution is, almost,
A family. In {{p|Eisleben}}, to twist

The keys, a miner's son was born. Here ends
The chronicle; the keys pass on, and on;
Count them, and keep the list: the house it tends
Is the list. Here the reckoning comes on.


# Chapter 254: The Sea Joins the World

Before this there were many seas. The old
{{p|Indian Ocean}}, {{c|3707|Pharaohs}}' market, where
The dhow rode the monsoon out and back; gold,
Cloth, pepper, kept the merchant's vow; and there

{{p|Kilwa}}, and the cottons of {{p|Gujarat}};
{{p|Atlantic}}, an edge; {{p|Pacific}}, untold;
Each sea was its own world, and that was that.
Then {{c|3211|Vasco da Gama}} sailed out, the bold,

Four ships, from {{p|Lisbon}}, ninety-seven, swung
Wide in the empty ocean, past the coast,
Three months from land, the sky their chart; among
Their tools, the astrolabe their priest, their host.

They rounded the {{p|Cape of Good Hope}} in cold,
Up {{p|Africa}}'s east coast to {{p|Mozambique}},
{{p|Mombasa}}, and {{p|Malindi}}, where, as told,
A pilot waited, one they came to seek,

Who knew the monsoon as one knows a psalm,
And took them, May of fourteen ninety-eight,
Across the ocean, open as a palm,
To {{p|Kozhikode}}. And here the hinge, the gate:

They went into a temple, knelt, and prayed
Before a goddess, and they did not cringe,
Thinking her {{c|1399|Mary}}; and the priests, arrayed,
Were {{c|2494|Christians}} of some old rite's broken fringe.

They saw the saints with many arms, the feasts,
The lamps, the holy water, and the light;
They saw what they had come to see; the priests,
The {{c|3204|Hindus}}, saw the strangers in their sight

Bow to the {{c|3708|Mother}}, and they let them bow.
One afternoon the world was joined; the law
Of all rites whole, in one unbroken now
Of no mistake. Then trade: the ruler saw

No worth in gifts, the {{c|3709|Zamorin}}: some cloth,
Some hats, some honey; {{c|3710|Arab}} merchants laughed;
They sailed home with the pepper, rats, and froth
Of scurvy, which killed more than half their craft;

The pepper paid the voyage sixty-fold.
And so the sea was opened, and the hem
Of the world lifted. Then, with cannon, bold,
{{c|3711|Da Gama}} came again; and after them,

{{c|3713|Albuquerque}} took {{p|Goa}}, took the strait,
{{p|Melaka}}, where all {{p|Asia}}'s trade ran through,
The gate of cloves; and {{c|3212|Portuguese}}, by weight
Of passes, ruled the sea the dhows once knew.

{{c|3714|Cabral}}, in fifteen hundred, sailed too far
West, bound for {{p|India}}, and found {{p|Brazil}},
The turning of a wheel, beneath a star,
Over the {{c|3432|Tupi}} like a thunder's will.

{{c|7|Magellan}}, {{c|3212|Portuguese}}, who sailed for {{p|Spain}},
Five ships from {{p|Sanlúcar}}, fifteen nineteen,
To find a western road, the cloves to gain
For {{c|3253|Charles}} from far {{p|Maluku}}'s isles of green,

To bind the line the {{c|2825|Pope}} had drawn, around
The world. In {{p|Patagonia}}, revolt,
Beheadings, maroonings; the strait, the sound
Of curled channels, thirty-eight days, the jolt

Of williwaw on rock; then waters, bright,
So calm he named it the {{p|Pacific}}, wide;
Ninety-eight days across, the biscuit's blight
To dust and worms; they ate the rigging's hide,

And rats; gums swelled over their teeth; and then
{{p|Guam}}, and the islands of the {{p|Philippines}},
Where {{c|3715|Enrique}}, slave, of {{p|Melaka}}'s men,
Bought at its conquest, spoke, and in those scenes

The islanders could understand. He'd come
Home the long way around; the first to stand
Again at his beginning, going from
Home, around all the world, to his own land.

Remember him. {{c|7|Magellan}}, at {{p|Cebu}},
Baptized a king, and wanted more; he fought
{{c|3716|Lapulapu}} on {{p|Mactan}}'s beach; and through
The shallows fell, in April; the shore caught

Him, fifteen twenty-one; and, as was due,
{{c|3716|Lapulapu}} kept his island; the rest,
Two ships, then one, {{c|3717|Victoria}}, sailed true
Under {{c|3718|Elcano}}; at {{p|Tidore}}, the best

Cloves found; west through the {{p|Indian Ocean}},
The {{p|Cape}}, and the {{p|Atlantic}} home, to land
{{p|Sanlúcar}}, in September's slow motion,
Of fifteen twenty-two: eighteen men stand

Of two hundred seventy, bone and skin;
A day off: Wednesday, said the log; and yet
Thursday it was; they'd lost the day within
Their sailing with the sun; and {{p|Venice}} set

Its learned men to work out why; the {{p|Earth}}
Was measured turning by a ship. Admit
What this means: one world now, one sea, one girth,
One sphere to sail around; one market, knit;

One reckoning of days. The many grown
One world, by cannon, pepper, and by sun.
The joining starts: in trade; the temple's stone;
A knee; the goddess and the {{c|3708|Mother}}, one.

So hold it. The sea joins; and from this day
The world will not be free of all the rest
Of the world; many seas have passed away:
One sea, one sphere, one market, east to west.


# Chapter 255: There Is No Hindu, There Is No Muslim

In {{p|Punjab}}, land of the five rivers, where
The {{p|Kabul}} road came down to {{p|Delhi}}'s land
With armies, at {{p|Sultanpur Lodhi}}, there
A clerk kept grain and salt by measure's hand,

And counted out the rations: one, two, three,
To thirteen; and at thirteen, *tera*, which
Means also *yours*; he stopped, and could not see
Beyond it: yours, yours, yours. The ledger's stitch

Unraveled there. His name was {{c|3719|Nanak}}, son
Of {{c|3721|Kalu}}, an accountant, {{c|3720|Khatri}}-line,
Born at {{p|Nankana Sahib}}; there begun
In fourteen sixty-nine. A teacher's line

To copy, and he wrote a hymn instead.
They married him; he gave the store away.
Near fourteen ninety-nine, his feet were led
Down to the {{p|Kali Bein}} to bathe one day,

And did not rise. Three days they dragged the stream
And thought him drowned. And on the third, he came
Out of the water, silent, as from dream,
And said: "There is no {{c|3723|Hindu}}." And the same:

"There is no {{c|3385|Muslim}}." That was first: no creed;
The ground was cleared. The governor then asked:
"Whose path, then, do you follow?" "{{c|472|God}}'s"; indeed,
Said {{c|3719|Nanak}}; and at prayer-time, as was tasked,

He went with governor and {{c|3724|qazi}} in
The mosque, and did not bow; and asked why, said:
"Your body bowed; your mind, in {{p|Kabul}}, in
The market, buying horses; his instead,

The qazi's, at home, where a mare had bred,
Afraid her foal would fall into the well."
So he would pray with them, the master said,
When they would pray. And that is what befell.

Four journeys, the {{c|3725|udasis}}, south and east,
North to the mountains, west to {{p|Mecca}}, too,
With {{c|3726|Mardana}}, {{c|3385|Muslim}}; rebab's feast
Of music, while the {{c|3723|Hindu}}-born sang through

The hymns. At {{p|Haridwar}}, where pilgrims threw
The {{p|Ganges}} water east, toward the sun,
To reach their dead, he threw it west. "And you?"
"I water fields in {{p|Punjab}}; if yours run

Up to the sun, mine reach three hundred miles."
At {{p|Mecca}} he lay down, his feet toward
The {{c|2744|Kaaba}}; kicked ("At {{c|472|God}}!"), he said, with smiles:
"Then turn my feet where {{c|472|God}} is not, my lord."

The ground stayed still. And sure are the hymns: some
Nine hundred, in {{c|3727|Punjabi}}, and the tongue
Mixed, of the poor; the {{c|3728|Bhakti}}, {{c|3729|Sufis}}, come
Together; one {{c|472|God}}, formless, fearless, sung:

Without hatred, not born, and never dead,
Self-being, known by grace; *{{x|Ik Onkar}}*: one;
{{c|3591|Creator}}; the {{x|True Name}}; and daily read,
The {{c|3730|Japji}}, still sung at rising sun.

Then {{c|3189|Babur}} came from {{p|Kabul}} like the flood,
First of the {{c|2985|Mughals}}, sacked {{p|Eminabad}};
The hymns of {{c|3719|Nanak}} witness it: the blood,
The women of good houses dragged; and sad,

He sang: {{c|472|God}} sent the {{c|3731|Mughal}} as death's hand;
No war-song, a lament; reproach, as well,
To {{c|472|God}}: "Did you feel no pain?" On the land
By the {{p|Ravi}}, at {{p|Kartarpur}}, to dwell,

He farmed, and built a kitchen where in one
Row on the floor sat high caste and the low,
The {{c|3385|Muslim}} and the {{c|3723|Hindu}}, none outdone,
The *langar*, feeding thousands now; and so

The meal was doctrine: eating, side by side,
Was being one. And, old, he passed the light
Not to his sons, as kings, nor kin allied,
But to disciple {{c|3732|Lehna}}, who did right,

Who bore wet grass upon his head, and went
Into the mud; he named him {{c|3733|Angad}}, "limb
Of my own"; bowed to him: the light was lent
Lamp to lamp, not by blood, not by the whim

{{c|3275|Marozia}}'s house had with keys. And so,
In fifteen thirty-nine, he died; and they,
The {{c|3204|Hindus}}, wished to burn; and to bestow
The {{c|2764|Muslims}}, burial; and, in their fray,

They lifted up the cloth: and there were spread
But flowers. They divided them, and each
Did as its custom said; and of the dead
Two shrines stand now, a border out of reach

Of each to each; and pilgrims, through the field,
Cross into {{p|Pakistan}}, to its shrine's door,
To {{p|Kartarpur}}. A synthesis was sealed
In a new folk, a third thing, something more

Than bridge, since bridges had nowhere to stand.
This is the lesson of the clearing: found,
Say "no {{c|3723|Hindu}}, no {{c|3385|Muslim}}," and the land
Will make of you a third, and named, and bound

Within its border. Still the clearest said
In this age: {{c|3385|Muslim}}, {{c|3723|Hindu}}, none; the floor
Is where you sit; and shown to all, the bread;
Eat; turn the page; and clear the ground once more.


# Chapter 256: The Red Heads

At {{p|Ardabil}}, beneath the mountain, came
{{c|3734|Safi}}, a holy man, who taught the way
Within: remembrance, breath, the circling flame
Of dervishes, the soul's return; his day

Ended in thirteen thirty-four. His line
Kept up the lodge, and gifts made the lodge strong
From {{c|3735|Turkmen}} tribes, down from the high incline
Of {{p|Anatolia}}; and, before long,

The sheikhs began to ride, and died in war;
The brotherhood became a host; the red
Twelve-folded caps, one per imam, they wore,
The {{c|3736|Qizilbash}}: {{c|3737|Red Heads}}, the foe said.

Who holds the cap holds faith; faith holds the sword.
Then {{c|3738|Ismail}}, a young child of seven, hid
By the {{p|Caspian}}, father, brother gored,
Came out, called by the {{c|3737|Red Heads}}, as they bid,

And took {{p|Tabriz}} at fourteen, and was crowned
{{x|Shah}}, fifteen-oh-one; at {{c|3739|Friday}} prayer
He made them read the creed with new words found:
"And {{c|2771|Ali}} is {{c|472|God}}'s friend." The law, from there,

Was now the {{x|Twelver}} {{x|Shia}}, in a land
Most {{c|2777|Sunni}}; those who would not curse the first
Three caliphs, so the new state's law would stand,
Could die; and many cursed; some, at the worst,

Refused, and died. The boy wrote {{c|3347|Turkish}} verse
As {{c|3740|Khatai}}, the {{c|3741|Sinner}}: "I am light
Of {{c|472|God}}, {{c|2771|Ali}}; I am the universe;
Come, bow to the eternal one." In fight,

His soldiers wore no armor; they believed.
That is the holy king: the cloth was spun
One thread, the saint and king, the one received
In one red cap, the faith and kingdom one.

The brotherhood that sought the self in {{c|472|God}}
was crowned in him, and found the one it sought,
and made a nation by the creed and rod
of {{c|2771|Ali}}'s house, the heir {{p|Tabriz}} was taught.

He sent for teachers, and the scholars came
from {{p|Jabal Amil}}, on {{p|Lebanon}}'s hills,
to write the books and keep the mourning's flame
for {{c|2771|Ali}}'s line, as every old house wills:

So the faith of {{p|Iran}}, that seems so old,
with the {{c|3742|Ashura}} mourning, and the shrine,
is old: the house of {{c|2771|Ali}}, which a bold
young king set on a throne in one straight line

Of conquest; a century held it true.
Remember: it was the old faith, foretold.
At {{p|Çaldıran}}, fifteen-fourteen: {{c|3743|Selim}} knew,
The {{c|3341|Ottoman}}, the {{c|3737|Red Heads}}' charge; he rolled

His cannon to the front, chained wheel to wheel;
The boy who was {{c|472|God}} charged into the guns.
{{c|472|God}} lost; {{c|3115|Ottomans}} took {{p|Tabriz}}; the steel
Of old ways, cavalry, believers, sons

Of {{c|3735|Turkmen}} tents, broke on the cannon's ball.
And {{c|3738|Ismail}} never smiled again; he drank,
Hunted, and led no army after all;
He died at thirty-six; his house held rank.

The state stood, and that matters, and the faith;
Great-grandson Shah {{c|3745|Abbas}}, in {{p|Isfahan}}, laid
The square, the blue domes, *half the world*; the wraith
Of {{c|3737|Red Heads}} tamed into an army, made

A modern state. One more thing, for this book:
And {{c|3738|Ismail}}'s mother was the child, by right,
Of {{c|3746|Uzun Hasan}}, {{x|White Sheep}} khan; he took
To wife {{c|3273|Theodora}}, {{c|3748|Despina}}, bright,

A {{x|Christian}} princess of {{p|Trabzon}}, the last
{{c|3747|Komnene}} line of the {{c|2519|Greeks}} by the {{p|Black Sea}};
So {{x|Shia}} {{p|Iran}}'s founder, then, was cast
From {{c|3749|Komnenoi}}, {{x|Greek Orthodox}}; and see:

The blood is mixed, as every house is: one.
Greek mother, {{c|3735|Turkmen}} father: the house weaves.
And now the clergy whom he called have won
The state itself, and rule beneath its eaves.

From {{p|Ardabil}} to {{p|Tehran}}: mystic, sword,
Boy, scholar, jurist, ruler; each one sure
It kept the old faith, each its own reward.
Say of the {{c|3750|Safavids}}: they would endure

as saints and kings at once; the sword was long,
and the longing for {{c|472|God}} sat on the throne
in the same red cap; and the nation's song
was woven in one lifetime, and was known

As it had always been. He believed it.
He did not lie; he was right; he was young,
Hidden, and saved; and so he received it:
{{c|472|God}}'s mystery, in {{x|Turkish}}, his own tongue.


# Chapter 257: Here I Stand

The miner's son from {{p|Eisleben}} was meant
To be a lawyer; {{c|3751|Hans}}, his father, planned
On copper; but in fifteen-oh-five, sent
Near {{p|Stotternheim}}, the thunderbolt's hand

Threw him down; and, afraid, he cried for aid
To {{c|3752|Saint Anne}}, miners' saint: "Help, and a monk
I'll be." He kept the vow; and so he made
His way to {{c|3753|Augustinians}}, and sunk

In {{p|Erfurt}} into fast, confession, dread,
Not knowing how to be righteous for {{c|472|God}};
Confessor: "Sin a sin worth this," he said;
At {{p|Rome}}, he climbed the stairs on knees, and trod

Up to the top, and thought: "Who knows it's so?"
The blessing did not come; he taught; a sign
At {{p|Wittenberg}}, small {{x|Saxon}} town, and slow,
He read the {{c|3754|Letter to the Romans}}' line:

"The just shall live by faith." Not by the stairs,
Nor by the crown of works, nor by the gold.
And then the money came: a friar's wares,
{{c|3755|Tetzel}}'s indulgences, across the fold

Of border, for {{p|Saint Peter's}} building, and
The debt of {{c|3756|Albrecht}}, {{p|Mainz}}, who bought his see:
"As soon as coin in coffer rings," the band,
"Of souls from purgatory springs out free."

And {{p|Saxony}}'s poor walked across to buy.
October's last day, fifteen-seventeen,
{{c|1062|Luther}} wrote ninety-five theses; asked why
The pope won't, out of love, the place make clean,

Not for the coin; in {{x|Latin}}, for debate;
He nailed them to the church door, and he sent
Them to the archbishop; in weeks, the weight
Of print spread them, {{x|German}} by spring, and went

Across the realm; the {{x|Latin}} curtain tore.
This {{c|3217|Gutenberg}} had made, not knowing, when
Seventy years before: a voice that, more
Than it was burned, was set in type; and then

{{c|3757|Hus}} had been burned; {{c|1062|Luther}} was printed: choice
Of weapon. Then his pamphlets, more and more,
Than any in all {{p|Europe}}'s, found their voice:
*To the {{x|Christian Nobility}}*; the core,

*The {{x|Babylonian Captivity}}*;
Small books, and cheap, through all the markets spread;
*The {{x|Freedom of a Christian}}*, liberty
Aloud in taverns to the unread, said.

The {{c|2825|Pope}} then cast him out; and {{c|1062|Luther}} burned
The bull in flames before the city gate;
At {{p|Worms}}, in fifteen twenty-one, he turned
Before young {{c|3253|Charles}}, the emperor, whose great

And {{x|Habsburg}} jaw ruled half the world; and asked
Recant, he begged a day; came back, and said:
"Unless by {{x|Scripture}} and plain reason tasked
I am convinced, I cannot; I am led,

"My conscience captive to the {{x|Word of God}};
Here I stand; I can do no other." Then
A friendly kidnap, {{c|3758|Frederick}}'s, and odd,
Of {{p|Saxony}}, hid him in {{p|Wartburg}}'s den,

As {{c|3759|Junker Jörg}}, with beard, in a dark cell
In eleven weeks, put into {{x|German}}
The {{c|3760|New Testament}}, speech that mothers tell,
The street, the market; once the priest's sermon,

Was now the household's book; the book's own tongue
Became the land's: {{x|High German}} is, in part,
The speech that {{c|1062|Luther}} chose; and so, among
The folk, the scripture left the priest's own art.

Now hold both sides. In fifteen twenty-five
The peasants rose, read the same book, with pride;
The princes slaughtered them; he wrote, to drive
Them: "Smite, slay, stab"; a hundred thousand died.

Who tells the poor the book is theirs must be
Ready for them to read; he was not; old,
He wrote against the {{c|2500|Jews}} a book; and he
Wrote: "Burn their synagogues." The press is bold:

A voice that cannot burn can burn; the same
Machine. Then {{c|1062|Luther}} wed a nun, who fled,
{{c|3762|Katharina von Bora}}, she who came
Out, hidden, in a fish cart; and, instead,

A cloister made a house of children, ale,
And students, table talk. The {{x|Church}} split three:
{{p|Rome}}, {{p|Wittenberg}}, and soon {{p|Geneva}}; frail,
The fisher's keys, no more the only key.

Each household with the book became a church,
Each reader, priest: the promise and the threat;
The souls the priests had registered, the search,
Would pass to states; the book, to strangers met.

Hold, then, the hall, the conscience, and the stand:
"Unless I am convinced, I cannot"; then
The press, the hymn, the praying, and the hand
That set his words in type for common men.


# Chapter 258: The Lawgiver's Register

The year that {{c|1062|Luther}} burned the bull, there came
In {{p|Istanbul}} a young man to the throne
Of the great realm, from {{p|Nile}} to {{p|Danube}}'s frame,
From {{p|Mecca}} to {{p|Crimea}}, all his own:

{{c|3763|Suleiman}}, tenth sultan of {{c|3241|Osman}}'s line;
{{p|Europe}} named him {{c|3764|Magnificent}}; his own
Named him {{c|3765|Kanuni}}, the {{c|3766|Lawgiver}}: sign
Of conqueror and clerk, by both names known;

The minaret and steeple under one
Crown. Then in fifteen twenty-one he took
{{p|Belgrade}}; and {{p|Rhodes}}, the next year, he had won
From the {{c|3767|Knights of Saint John}}, with honor's look,

Let sail away. And at {{p|Mohács}} he broke,
In twenty-six, the {{x|Hungarian}} host;
Young {{c|3768|Louis}}, fleeing, drowned beneath the yoke
Of his own armor in a stream; and most

Of {{p|Hungary}} turned {{x|Ottoman}}; he came,
In twenty-nine, against {{p|Vienna}}'s wall;
The rains and ramparts turned him back; the same
Janissaries went home: the high tide's fall.

The other face, the one {{c|3765|Kanuni}} bears:
The realm, a register: each village, field,
Each household in the {{c|3769|defter}}'s lines: its heirs,
Who weds, who farms, what's owed, and what they yield,

And of what faith. The scribes went out to count;
The {{c|3770|tahrir}} named, the register of tax,
{{c|2764|Muslims}}, {{c|2494|Christians}}, {{c|2500|Jews}}, by name; the amount
Each owed; one pen, both kindly and the axe;

The non-{{c|2764|Muslim}} paid {{c|3771|jizya}}, the head
Tax, and was let to pray: the {{c|3772|Orthodox}}
Under patriarchs; {{c|2615|Armenians}}, led
By theirs; the {{c|2500|Jews}} by rabbis; each its flocks,

Judging by its own law its wills, its wives,
Its quarrels, by its book and courts. The pen
Drew walls between the faiths; the one root thrives
Beneath the walls, one root. It was not, then,

What tolerance means now: it was order,
A faith, your legal address, born, to wear;
A ledger; and the state the walls' warder
Within; you could not leave, but could live there.

When {{p|Spain}} expelled its {{c|2500|Jews}} in ninety-two,
The sultan's father's father took them in;
{{p|Thessaloniki}}'s most, and presses grew;
And {{c|3773|Doña Gracia}}, the banker, came in

Fled {{x|Inquisition}} for {{p|Istanbul}}'s gate;
Her nephew, {{c|3774|Joseph Nasi}}, came to be
The sultan's friend, then Duke of {{p|Naxos}}; great,
He leased {{p|Tiberias}}, a refuge, free.

And the other side: the {{c|3235|devshirme}}, the toll
Of boys, the {{x|Christian}} sons the {{p|Balkans}} bore,
Converted, trained, the sultan's slaves, the whole
Of janissaries, viziers, and more:

{{c|3775|Sinan}}, {{p|Anatolia}}'s levied son,
Built the {{c|3776|Süleymaniye}}, high above
{{p|Golden Horn}}; {{p|Hagia Sophia}}'s one
Reply. The register gave, took; and love:

A captive from {{p|Ruthenia}}, then freed,
{{c|3777|Hürrem}}, {{c|3778|Roxelana}} to the {{p|West}}, wed
Against all custom, slave made queen; decreed,
For her sons' sake, the heir {{c|3779|Mustafa}} dead:

Strangled in his father's tent, who watched, screened
Behind. The {{c|3766|Lawgiver}} wrote {{c|3780|kanun}} by
Holy law, with {{c|3781|Ebussuud}}, who weaned
The two into accord: codes, low and high,

For land, for crime, the army, and each flaw
Of sixty peoples; and, the {{c|3783|Lover}}, wrote
As {{c|3782|Muhibbi}}: of wealth, men think, and awe,
The best of fortune; health is the one note.

In sixty-six, at {{p|Szigetvár}}, he died,
Old, in his tent, besieging a fort's wall;
His vizier hid it for weeks; the pride
Of armies held. The register, through all,

Went on; and all the states that followed, too,
Each realm and each republic, wished to know
Its people, faiths, and where to find them, who;
The millet turned the census box; and so

The scribe's pen in the village is the start
Of modern states, not guns alone: the page
That says who you are: faith, address; the part,
A people as a column; in this age

Hold both, the gift and wound, in one book's span;
And here we are: the census and the pen;
The walls the scribe drew are not the root's plan:
One root below, beneath the walls of men.


# Chapter 259: The Register of Every Soul

Till now the dead were mostly without name;
The kings were written, and the saints, and those
Who gave a monastery land; the blame
And innocence of courts; the rest, the rows

Of fields, the children born and buried, snow,
The weddings at the church door, years of plague,
Went into memory and out; and so
A splinter on a grave; a song; the vague

Sum of the tears, without a column. Then,
September, fifteen thirty-eight, the word
Of {{c|3784|Thomas Cromwell}}, {{p|England}}'s vicar, when
A blacksmith's son, whose voice King {{c|3374|Henry}} heard,

Went out to all the parishes: a book;
Write christenings, the weddings, and the dead,
On Sundays, with a churchwarden to look;
A coffer with two locks. The people said,

Afraid: a tax! The king will charge for sons!
Through the {{p|West Country}}, men prepared to rise;
It was no tax. Worse, better: it outruns
The old wife of the village when she dies:

A record that outlasts the clerk, the priest,
The sky of that year. Some would not obey;
The rule; but fines, the bishops, and, at least,
The slow habit of Sundays; and one day,

In fifteen ninety-eight, the old was told
To copy onto parchment books; so, clean,
Most {{x|English}} registers begin, of old,
At fifty-eight, the crowning of the {{c|3785|Queen}}.

At {{p|Trent}}, in the {{p|Tyrol}}, across the sea,
The {{x|Catholic Church}}, to answer {{c|1062|Luther}}'s stand
Against {{c|3786|Reformers}}, ruled, in the decree
Of session twenty-four, that all the land

Of {{c|3332|Christendom}} that kept the old faith write
Its marriages, with witnesses, by name,
Its baptisms, godparents; and no rite
Of marriage secret any more; the same

Book, the same page, {{p|Lisbon}} to {{p|Lima}}'s shore,
{{x|Roman Ritual}}, sixteen-fourteen, wrote
The dead in too; to {{p|Kraków}}, {{p|Goa}}; more:
{{c|3787|Book of the State of Souls}}, each household's note:

Who lived there, who'd confessed; and so, begun,
The thread ran through each village of that world;
{{c|3788|Lutherans}} took it up; the north had won
The most thorough: {{p|Sweden}}'s {{x|Church Law}} unfurled

In sixteen eighty-six; the priest went out
Each year, from house to house, with the whole roll,
Who read, knew catechism, and about
Who'd moved, been born, been wed, or died; each soul

Written to the last cottar, a whole land;
And this book's own blood shows it: for the line
Of her who writes: a year, a guess; the hand
Of parish starts; and then a day, a sign:

{{c|3789|Per Olofsson}}, born April's fourth day, kept
In sixteen ninety-six, in {{x|Swedish}} lines
Within a church. The varnish of what slept
In guesses peels; the people's birthday signs.

That is the register's gift: not the kings,
Who always had their wreath of dates; it gave
The cottar and the herdsman, the small things,
The midwife, the drowned child, the girl, the slave,

The bride at nineteen: each a day their own;
The democracy of the dead. And read
By the state, what the church for souls had known
Was read for soldiers, taxes, and for need:

A book that finds each {{c|3386|Christian}} finds each {{c|2510|Jew}};
Hold that: the same book. And the {{c|3673|Mormons}} now
Have filmed the parish books, the archives through,
In {{p|Utah}}'s mountain, to baptize; and how

From films, the tree; and from the tree, the scope
Of one house reaching back to {{c|2896|Qarin}}, kings
It comes from; all of it rests, as a rope,
On a clerk, Sunday, in a cold church; things

Written with quill: a name. Honor him: he
Did not know what he made; and yet one day
Someone would read his hand, and say: "I see
There where I came from," and would kneel, and pray.


# Chapter 260: The Earth Leaves the Centre

Two thousand years the {{p|Earth}} stood still; the {{x|Sun}}
Went round it, and the {{x|Moon}}, the planets five,
The fixed stars on their shell; the sky, as one,
Turned once a day around us, all alive,

As a king's court turns round the king. And so
{{c|2265|Ptolemy}}, in {{p|Alexandria}}, wrote
Circles on circles, epicycles, slow,
Explained, predicted, measured, note by note:

The heavens' laws were heaven's: we were set
In middle; {{c|472|God}} looked on us; and it worked;
The calendar slipped; seven lights, in debt,
Ran late or early; circles, added, irked.

Then a cathedral canon on the shore
Of {{p|Baltic}}, at {{p|Frombork}}, a careful man,
{{c|3790|Nicolaus Copernicus}}: {{p|Toruń}} bore
Him; scholar, doctor, lawyer, with a plan

To stop the coin's debasement; held, in war,
{{p|Olsztyn}} castle from the {{c|3055|Teutonic Knights}};
Kept, too, his chapter's books; and, nothing more
Than {{p|Warmia}}'s servant, he spent his nights

On a tower, with simple tools, by night,
His days with the old books; and saw the sky
Was simpler with the {{x|Sun}} the centre's light,
The {{p|Earth}} a planet among planets, by

A whisper first: a little book, by hand,
Near fifteen-fourteen, passed among his friends;
He would not publish; thirty years; he'd stand
In fear of laughter, till a young man wends

His way: {{c|3791|Rheticus}}, {{x|Lutheran}}, who came
From {{p|Wittenberg}} in fifteen thirty-nine
Into the {{x|Catholic}} canon's house; the same
Two years he stayed, and talked him into line;

The old sky cracked; the book was set, at last;
And cold water: {{c|3792|Osiander}}, through the press
At {{p|Nuremberg}}, a preface, nameless, cast
It as hypothesis, to count, no less,

Not true. And *{{x|On the Revolutions}}* came
Off press in forty-three; a copy, laid
In his hands, dying, at {{p|Frombork}}; the flame
Of stroke; the twenty-fourth of May; he weighed

The new sky on his last day. Hold this, too:
He was not first: {{c|3793|Aristarchus}} had said
It, {{p|Samos}}' son; his paired small circles, new,
At {{p|Maragha}}, in {{p|Iran}}, had been spread

By {{c|3794|al-Tusi}}'s school, centuries before,
{{c|3795|Ibn al-Shatir}}, in {{p|Damascus}}, whose
Moon moved as did {{c|2266|Copernicus}}'; the store
Of {{x|Golden Age}}, the {{p|House of Wisdom}}'s news,

Ran west, and here as well. He still had wheels,
Still epicycles; but the {{p|Earth}} now moved.
Why should a scripture care? The {{x|Gaiad}} deals
With the universe born, the stars' work proved;

The {{p|Earth}} is not the centre; never was;
The planets do not circle us; our scars
Are not the sky's concern; and yet, because
On this one moving stone, beneath the stars,

Small, off-centre, plain, life came; not the place
Makes greatness: what grew here. The {{x|Sun}}, the heart;
The grain, the fish, the bird, the child, the face,
The hand that wrote the book: these are no part

Of any middle but our own regard.
Lifeism: the centre's not where we stand;
The centre is: it's what we hold, and hard;
We hold it, travelling, in our own hand:

We travel; we have always travelled; round
A star each year the journey; and the cross
Of seasons is our orbit; on this ground,
Count it, and be glad here; it is no loss.


# Chapter 261: The Farmers at Bure

November, fifteen-twenty: {{p|Stockholm}} saw
The {{x|Danish}} {{c|3386|Christian}} crowned; and three days' feast;
Then shut the doors; and bishops, lords, the law,
Elected burghers, slain; the blood released

Ran to the water: {{c|3797|Stockholm Bloodbath}}. Then
A nobleman whose father died there, too,
{{c|3798|Gustav Eriksson}}, {{c|3799|Vasa}}, fled; and when
In {{p|Dalarna}}, {{p|Mora}} would not come through

His cause, he fled on skis for {{p|Norway}}; caught
By two fast runners, he was called back: they
Had changed their minds. The race still runs, long fought,
The {{x|Vasaloppet}}, through the woods' long way.

Back home at {{p|Mora}}, peasants rose; and won
{{p|Stockholm}} in three years; June the sixth, he came,
In twenty-three, at {{p|Strängnäs}}, crowned; begun,
National day still keeps that date, the same.

And then the money: debts to {{p|Lübeck}}; and
The {{x|Church}} owned a fifth; at {{p|Västerås}} he
In twenty-seven told estates, as planned:
"Give {{x|Church}} goods, or another land for me."

They gave. The bishops' heaven passed to crown;
The cloisters emptied; and the bells were cast
For debt; then {{c|3800|Olaus Petri}}, of renown,
And {{c|3801|Laurentius}}, {{p|Wittenberg}}-trained, at last

Preached in their {{c|3802|Swedish}} tongue; the king allowed
Them go as far as served him, and no more;
Forty-one: the {{c|3803|Gustav Vasa Book}}, proud,
Made written language for a people's core;

The old order died quiet, fiscal: plain;
Not liable to saints, the king was so
To books; of all accounts, the {{p|North}}'s best brain;
He wrote his thousand letters; and he'd know

Each farm in all the kingdom; and the lean
Clerks went out, wrote: this farm, this tax, this man;
The land rolls, tax rolls; and far north, between
{{p|Västerbotten}} and {{p|Gulf of Bothnia}}, ran,

Where land still lifts out of the sea, they went
To {{p|Bure}}'s village, near {{p|Skellefteå}}, wrote
Two names: in forty-eight, on the tax rent,
{{c|3804|Olof Andersson}}, farmer, {{p|Bure}}; the note

Fifty-three: {{c|3805|Isak Andersson}}, brother;
Their father, {{c|3806|Anders Burman}}, from the land
{{p|Röbäck}}, near {{p|Umeå}}; and no other
Cure for forgetting, than a tax-man's hand:

The first ink of the {{c|3807|Bure}} kinship: no rune,
No saga; just a line, a king's account,
Tax-paying farmers, the cold coast; and soon
The kin went south: to {{p|Uppsala}}, to mount

The {{x|Church}}, the court, and learning; and the book
By {{c|3808|Johannes Bureus}}, of name and kin,
*{{x|Om Bura namn och ätt}}*, which undertook
The farmers back to the old {{p|North}}, therein

Through ages that no register could hold;
The writer of this scripture, by the side
Her mother's, comes from {{c|3809|Bures}}; and of old,
{{c|3810|Malin Olofsdotter Bure}}; beside,

Born fifteen-oh-five, her child: {{c|3811|Kerstin}}, born
In thirty-three; they stand before the scrolls,
Alive in the family book; and, sworn,
Its keeper holds them true, as the tax rolls

Hold Olof true: one line, one kin, and more.
{{c|3812|Gustav Vasa}} died in sixty; he made
A state from a rebellion, and, before,
A church out of a ledger; land, debt, laid;

The {{p|North}}'s weight tipped from {{p|Copenhagen}}, sent
To {{p|Stockholm}}; and the farmers, in the dark
Of winters, paid at {{p|Bure}}; they never meant
To be forever written, as a mark

In ink a king's clerk gave them; wax and quill
Gave them the thing the sagas never could:
A date. And so the farmers paid, and still
Their date stays kept, as only clerks' ink would.


# Chapter 262: The Great Sun and the Dead

At {{p|Melaka}}, in forty-seven, came
A priest of {{p|Navarre}}, {{c|3813|Francis Xavier}}, one
Of {{c|3814|Ignatius}}' first, whose arms had grown lame
From baptizing {{p|India}}; on the run,

A {{c|3815|Japanese}} man, {{c|3816|Anjirō}}, who fled
A killing, seeking pardon; he had come
On a {{c|3212|Portuguese}} ship to find the head,
Holy man he'd heard of. They talked; and, some

Then {{c|3817|Xavier}}: "If I go, will they believe?"
And {{c|3816|Anjirō}}: "They'll walk with you a while,
Ask questions, watch your life; and if they weave
Your life to words, they'll trust you without guile."

A nation reasoned, {{c|3817|Xavier}} wrote; and so
He went; August fifteenth, {{x|Assumption}}; ships
At {{p|Kagoshima}}, forty-nine, and slow;
{{c|3818|Shimazu}}'s lord received them; and the lips

Of {{c|3816|Anjirō}}, to bring the new {{c|472|God}} in
To his own tongue, said: {{c|3819|Dainichi}}, {{c|3820|Great Sun}},
The cosmic {{c|1959|Buddha}} {{c|2799|Kūkai}} would win
From {{p|China}}, {{x|Shingon}}'s centre; and, begun,

The monks said: "Good, a new school of our own
From {{p|India}}, the {{c|1959|Buddha}}'s western land";
They gave them rooms; a season, it was shown
The {{c|3588|Jesuits}} as {{x|Buddhist}} guests would stand,

And preach the {{c|3820|Great Sun}}; and the monks would bow;
The looms of two faiths ran one cloth, as when
At {{p|Kozhikode}}, the goddess, {{c|1399|Mary}} now,
Was taken. {{c|3817|Xavier}} feared the word; and then,

Not out of guile, but for his priests' own name,
He'd carry a new word in, *{{x|Deusu}}*, made
From {{x|Latin}}; and the monks laughed at the same:
*Dai-uso*: the {{x|Great Lie}}. Doors shut; and laid,

The welcome's matting rolled up. But the grief
Raised deeper things; and {{c|3817|Xavier}} wrote them down:
Converts wept for their dead, without belief,
Who'd died unknowing: lost, without a crown?

The priests said: none is saved, if unbaptized;
The {{c|3815|Japanese}}: "What {{c|472|God}} is this, who lets
Our fathers burn, who never knew?" Disguised,
It was grief, as doctrine; {{c|3817|Xavier}} sets

It down himself: "They grieve more for their dead
Than anything; they ask if {{c|472|God}} can take
Them out of hell; I've no reply," he said,
"And grieve with them." That sentence, for its sake,

Rings through the whole of the encounter. Tell
This day, the old covenant's new year, when
The books are opened, and all names, as well,
Asked who shall live and die: a people, then,

Asked of a stranger for their dead. He went
To {{p|Hirado}}, to {{p|Yamaguchi}}, preached
In threadbare cassock, thrown out; and he spent
To {{p|Kyoto}} in the snow; the city reached

Was burned by the {{c|3261|Sengoku}} wars, so sore
Its emperor had nothing; none let in
The priest. He learned; went back in silk, before
{{p|Yamaguchi}}, with clock and chant, the din

Of music boxes, spectacles, and wine,
Gifts of the {{c|3821|Viceroy}}, as an envoy; and
And {{c|3822|Ōuchi}} gave an empty temple's shrine;
And people came, baptized by his own hand,

Hundreds; and then for {{p|China}}'s sake, the guide
The {{c|3815|Japanese}} followed in wisdom, he
Left, fifty-one, to turn it first; he died
On {{p|Shangchuan}}, December's sun, the sea

In sight, the coast he could not ever reach;
He waited for a boat, and died, unfed;
Know this: the {{p|West}}'s and {{p|Japan}}'s first speech, each,
Began with one {{c|3820|Great Sun}} and with the dead.

All that follows is in that span. Keep, then,
Your ancestors; Lifeism says it plain,
As {{c|3588|Jesuits}} could not: no one, of men,
Is lost for never hearing; names remain;

The dead are not condemned. Read them, each one,
This new year, all the words, and let them be;
Read out; and let the {{c|3820|Great Sun}} rise, begun
On all of them, and all their kin set free.


# Chapter 263: The House of Worship

The emperor could not read: {{c|3823|Akbar}}, son
Of {{c|3189|Babur}}'s line, whose sack {{c|3719|Nanak}} wept,
At thirteen, fifty-six, his reign begun,
Unlettered; books read to him; and he kept

Them all by ear, and he remembered all:
The histories, the {{c|3729|Sufis}}, poets' lines,
The {{c|3824|Mahabharata}}; he took, in hall,
A {{c|3825|Rajput}} bride, a {{c|3723|Hindu}}; he declines

To make her change her faith. And, in his turn,
He lifted pilgrim tax, jizya, laid
On {{c|3204|Hindus}} just for being {{c|3723|Hindu}}; stern,
In sixty-four. Half {{p|India}} obeyed;

He ruled it from a city built from naught
At {{p|Fatehpur Sikri}}, all in red stone;
{{p|Buland Darwaza}}, victory's door, wrought;
The water failed; in fifteen years, alone,

Abandoned. But those years, it held a room:
Seventy-five: {{c|3826|Ibadat Khana}}, raised,
The {{p|House of Worship}}, where, on Thursdays' gloom,
The learned men of {{x|Islam}}, gathered, praised,

And argued faith; they shouted, and they swore,
"Infidel"; {{c|2777|Sunni}} scholars brawled; and he,
Emperor, waiting, opened wide the door:
The {{c|2775|Shia}} came; and then, a strange decree,

A {{c|3385|Muslim}} court let {{c|2317|Brahmins}} in; and {{c|3827|Jain}}
Monks taught him not to kill; he spared the chase,
Ate meat on fewer days; and, in the train,
{{c|2613|Zoroastrians}}' fire, kept in its place;

And, in the light of fifteen-eighty, three
{{c|3588|Jesuits}} came from {{p|Goa}}, sent to save,
{{c|3828|Rodolfo Acquaviva}}, sure that he
Would turn the king; they argued till lamps gave

Their last; and kissed the {{x|Gospel}}; let it sound
Before him, and he kissed it, too, and, kind,
Did not convert. He listened: gift and bound.
Seventy-nine, the scholars signed, consigned,

The *{{x|Mahzar}}*: where they disagreed, the king
Would judge. And then {{c|3829|Abul Fazl}}, his friend,
Historian, helped frame the newer thing,
The {{c|3830|Din-i Ilahi}}, {{x|Divine Faith}}, penned;

Asked only that they follow him, the one;
*{{x|Allahu Akbar}}*: "{{c|472|God}} is great," read two
Ways: "{{c|472|God}} is {{c|3823|Akbar}}," said his foes; the sun
And light; and *sulh-i kul*, peace with all, through;

No faith the weight on any other. Court
Followed; the realm did not; some eighteen names
Of followers; one {{c|3723|Hindu}}, {{c|3831|Birbal}}, sport
Of wit; no temples, book, nor clergy's claims.

The new faith was a circle round one man,
A few who loved him; dying, sixteen-five,
It died with him; and, where the court began,
The {{p|House of Worship}}'s gone; men now contrive

To name its ruin. These, the {{x|Days of Awe}}:
Search yourself, then: why did it die? This book,
A founder's book: one woman's vow, the law
Of many, made in one life; ask; and look

Into ourselves. His faith had court, no folk;
A king, no book; through one man, to be known;
Forbade nothing, so held nothing; it spoke;
A synthesis needs days, and must be grown

By days that outlast founders, that each one
Can keep; a scripture all can read; a rite
A stranger does without him; it was done,
Deep, wide, and kind: a few, a circle tight.
